title: Prompt Canvas
pitch: A shared visual workspace where you shape the brief and Codex turns it into polished images—then returns them to your canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual workspace where you shape the brief and Codex turns it into polished images—then returns them to your canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI image workflows collapse an entire creative project into one long prompt buried in chat. That makes the work difficult to inspect, refine, reuse, or hand off. References, constraints, visual direction, and prior results all become conversational context instead of durable project state. I built Prompt Canvas to explore a different model: a shared visual workspace where the human directs the creative work and Codex executes it. The brief, references, creative direction, results, and variations remain visible on a spatial canvas. The human can edit those elements directly, while Codex can read and update the same live project through WebMCP. What it does Prompt Canvas begins with a curated library of image-making recipes. These range from simple tasks—creating an image from words, changing a background, or removing an object—to more structured systems for posters, brand exploration, sequential storytelling, technical visuals, and reference-driven transformations. Starting a recipe creates a focused project on a tldraw canvas. Depending on the task, the project may include: a Brief describing the intended outcome; References with explicit roles and preservation requirements; a Direction surface for composition, style, format, and mood; a dominant Result area; Variations for continued exploration. Users can shape the project manually or ask Codex to help. Through Prompt Canvas’s WebMCP Website Tools, Codex can search the official recipe library, retrieve an exact approved recipe version, create or update a project, inspect its current revision, prepare generation context, and return generated assets to the correct canvas output. Image generation remains native to Codex. Prompt Canvas supplies the structured creative context and receives the result; it does not introduce a separate page-owned generation service. The result is a single inspectable workspace where the human and agent operate on the same project rather than maintaining separate versions in chat and in the application. How I built it Prompt Canvas is a React and TypeScript application built on the tldraw SDK. Recipes are schema-backed YAML documents that define prompts, controls, references, output slots, layout, preservation rules, and supported operations. The application compiles those recipes into custom tldraw panel shapes while retaining the full underlying recipe snapshot for the agent. The official recipe library is curated and versioned. On the published ChatGPT Site, approved recipes are served from Cloudflare D1. User-created recipes remain local to the user’s browser and are never silently added to the official catalog. Prompt Canvas exposes 11 semantic Website Tools through WebMCP. These tools cover recipe discovery, exact recipe retrieval, project creation and updates, project inspection, generation-context preparation, and generated-asset return. The project also includes: immutable official recipe versions and content hashes; revision numbers and stale-write rejection; local project persistence; validated reference and generated-asset handling; explicit output-slot targeting; parent-child output lineage; undo and reload durability; deterministic catalog and browser tests. Challenges The largest design challenge was making the canvas feel like a creative workbench rather than a visual programming graph. Early versions displayed nearly every prompt variable as a separate connected card. Although technically accurate, the interface visually resembled an automation workflow and gave configuration more importance than the image itself. I simplified the interaction model around a smaller set of creative surfaces: Brief, References, Direction, Result, and Variations. Permanent dependency arrows were removed from the primary workflows, controls were grouped into meaningful decisions, and the Result became the visual center of the project. A second challenge was explaining the collaboration boundary clearly. Clicking a button on the Site cannot itself perform native Codex image generation. The application therefore needed to communicate that the user shapes the project in Prompt Canvas, then asks Codex to act on its current state through WebMCP. The final interface makes that division of labor visible from the first screen, previews the information Codex will use, and explains where the resulting image will return. The third challenge was preserving trust across two interfaces. Codex must always act on the newest project revision, respect the selected recipe version, return assets to the intended output, and avoid overwriting newer human edits. Revision checks, exact recipe identity, validation, and output lineage were essential to making the workflow reliable. What I learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes an application’s real semantic actions rather than asking an agent to imitate mouse and keyboard behavior. The agent does not need another copy of the user interface. It needs structured access to concepts such as “search recipes,” “inspect the active project,” “use the latest creative direction,” and “return this image to the primary result.” I also learned that agent collaboration must be explained before the first handoff. Users should understand what they control, what Codex will use, what the agent is about to do, and what remains editable afterward. What’s next The next frontier is deeper support for multi-reference creative work: assigning separate images authority over identity, composition, palette, product geometry, or visual style. I also plan to expand the curated recipe library, introduce reusable style and constraint kits, and develop richer result branching and comparison while keeping the workspace simple, inspectable, and local-first. title: NOVA LAB
pitch: A scientific laboratory that lets external AI agents discover and operate real experiments through WebMCP—from experimental design and human approval to execution, analysis, and replication.
about_excerpt: A scientific laboratory that lets external AI agents discover and operate real experiments through WebMCP—from experimental design and human approval to execution, analysis, and replication. Like Comment Story Updates External agent actually operated NOVA NOVA state machine Actual scientific analysis WebMCP discovery NOVA LAB NOVA LAB is a scientific laboratory built for the agentic web. The idea started with a simple question: what happens when an AI agent can do more than read a website or generate an answer? What if the website itself exposed executable capabilities that the agent could discover and operate? NOVA explores that idea through scientific experimentation. Instead of building an AI chatbot that tells a user what an experiment might show, NOVA provides a stateful environment where an external agent can design an experiment, request human authorization, execute it, retrieve persisted observations, analyze the evidence, save a finding, and replicate the experiment. The current demonstration uses plant growth as the experimental domain. The experiment can vary environmental conditions such as temperature and water and measure simulated plant-growth outcomes. How it works The interaction begins outside NOVA. A user gives an external agent a scientific question such as: Investigate what environmental conditions maximize plant growth. Don't assume the answer—design and test an experiment. The agent discovers NOVA's capabilities through WebMCP rather than being given a private NOVA-specific API integration. NOVA exposes six WebMCP tools: create_experiment run_experiment get_results analyze_results save_finding replicate_experiment The resulting flow is: Human → External Agent → WebMCP → NOVA → Experiment → Evidence → Analysis → Replication NOVA owns the state and execution. The external agent provides reasoning and orchestration. Human authorization Experiments cannot simply be executed because an agent requested them. Creating an experiment places it into an AWAITING_APPROVAL state. A human must approve it before execution is authorized. This authorization boundary is enforced by the server and state machine, not by relying on the agent to behave correctly. The experiment then progresses through: DRAFT → AWAITING_APPROVAL → APPROVED → RUNNING → COMPLETED → ANALYZED → REPLICATED Rejected experiments can return to the draft state for revision. Evidence, not fabricated answers NOVA persists the experiment and its observations rather than generating a result only for display. The current simulation produces synthetic experimental observations using deterministic simulation with stochastic noise. This is explicitly disclosed in the application. After execution, the agent can retrieve the persisted observations and request statistical analysis. NOVA calculates effects, confidence intervals, p-values, interaction effects, and condition means from the stored observations. The experiment can then be independently replicated using a new seed. The replication evaluates whether the direction of the result is consistent, whether confidence intervals overlap, and whether the relative effect difference remains below the defined threshold. Provenance NOVA preserves provenance throughout the experiment lifecycle, including experiment IDs, simulation version, seeds, timestamps, observations, analysis records, findings, replications, and state-transition events. This makes it possible to trace a conclusion back to the experiment and measurements that produced it. Why WebMCP The interesting part of NOVA is not simply that it can simulate plant growth. The project explores a different interaction model for the web: a website can expose meaningful capabilities that an external agent can discover and execute. The agent does not need to be given NOVA's internal implementation or a custom integration created specifically for the demonstration. It encounters the website and its exposed capabilities through WebMCP. That allows the website to remain responsible for its own state, validation, authorization, execution, persistence, and evidence while the external agent handles reasoning and orchestration. What I learned Building NOVA required thinking about a website as more than a collection of pages and API endpoints. The WebMCP layer became a capability boundary between the external agent and the application. I also learned that exposing tools is not enough by itself. Each tool has to connect to the same application logic used by the website, preserve authorization rules, validate inputs, produce persistent state changes, and leave an auditable event trail. The most important design decision was therefore keeping the WebMCP tools thin: they expose capabilities, while the server remains the source of truth for scientific state and authorization. Challenges The hardest parts were making the system genuinely stateful and ensuring that an agent could not bypass the experiment lifecycle. A successful tool call had to correspond to a real application operation rather than a simulated response. This meant connecting WebMCP execution to validation, authorization, the experiment state machine, PostgreSQL persistence, statistical analysis, and provenance. Another challenge was making the synthetic simulation useful for experimentation without presenting synthetic results as real scientific measurements. NOVA therefore labels its generated observations and preserves the simulation version and seed as part of the experimental provenance. NOVA is intentionally a constrained scientific demonstration, but the underlying interaction model is the focus: an external agent discovers and operates an executable, stateful environment exposed by the web. title: Semantic City — Shared-World WebMCP Simulator
pitch: A playable city-management sandbox where humans and agents share one live city. WebMCP exposes traffic, budgets, and utilities so every agent action is visible, validated, and reversible.
about_excerpt: A playable city-management sandbox where humans and agents share one live city. WebMCP exposes traffic, budgets, and utilities so every agent action is visible, validated, and reversible. Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates One visible city; a semantic surface agents can use. An agent asks for congestion; the exact returned roads light up. The agent previews affected city state before changing anything. A visible improvement is not enough—58% traffic forces a fresh inspection. The shared world verifies the goal: 5/5 constraints satisfied. The idea Most websites expose pixels, buttons, and forms for people. When an AI agent needs to help, it often has to infer meaning from that visual surface or operate through a separate API the person cannot see. Semantic City asks a different question: What if a website exposed the meaning of its live interface directly to agents? A city simulator is an ideal proving ground. A person sees roads, congestion, utilities, budgets, and tradeoffs. An agent needs those same concepts as structured objects, metrics, constraints, and legal actions. Both should work on one world. What I built Semantic City is a playable, deterministic city-management sandbox on a 24 × 18 grid. A human can build and upgrade roads; place residential, commercial, industrial, park, and power buildings; manage taxes and a city budget; advance simulation ticks; demolish; undo; and save or load locally. The simulation tracks population, jobs, happiness, traffic, pollution, power coverage, cash flow, construction spend, and challenge constraints. Its rules are deliberately understandable and deterministic, so interventions have reproducible causes and results. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is the product interface, not an automation wrapper. The page registers 14 domain tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...), including city and metric reads, area, traffic, and budget inspections, building and road mutations, tax changes, deterministic simulation, undo, challenge evaluation, and non-committing intervention previews. Every tool is connected to the same authoritative, revisioned CityStore used by the React interface. There is no hidden "agent city" or scripted winning state. Human clicks and WebMCP calls dispatch the same validated commands. Mutations require the latest observed revision and return affected objects and cells, direct cost, metric deltas, constraint results, world ID, state hash, and rules version. This makes agent actions safe, deterministic, and verifiable. Making agent behavior visible Semantic View reveals what the page exposes semantically: stable object IDs, road connectivity, traffic and capacity, neighborhood boundaries, building effects, utility coverage, pollution, happiness, costs, and placement constraints. When an inspection tool returns roads, buildings, or cells, those exact entities light up on the visible map. Before a mutation, affected cells are hatched as a preview without advancing the city revision. After a commit, the map, metrics, constraints, revision, hash, undo history, and activity timeline update together. The timeline records the selected tool, arguments, affected objects, cost, metric changes, execution time, and before-and-after proof. The human can see exactly what the agent inspected, intended, and changed. The Rivergate challenge The featured goal is: Reduce traffic below 50%, maintain happiness above 70%, and spend no more than $400,000, without raising taxes or demolishing homes. Rivergate starts at 83.80% traffic . The agent first inspects the authoritative city, traffic hotspots, and budget, then previews and commits a seven-cell avenue upgrade. Traffic falls to 58.44% - better, but still failing. Instead of assuming success, the agent inspects revision one, finds the remaining bottleneck, previews and commits a second five-cell upgrade, advances one deterministic tick, and verifies the new world. The final state reaches 48.06% traffic with $204,000 spent, happiness above 70%, no tax increase, no demolished homes, and 5/5 constraints passed . The first intervention is deliberately insufficient, forcing an inspect - act - observe - iterate loop rather than a one-shot macro. How it was built Semantic City uses React, TypeScript, and Vite . A pure domain engine owns CityWorld; derived systems recompute connectivity, traffic, power, pollution, jobs, happiness, cash flow, and constraints. Commands validate complete building footprints and road paths atomically, reject stale revisions, enforce available cash and hard scenario rules, and return structured success or error envelopes. Canonical serialization produces a deterministic state hash. The WebMCP adapter translates strict snake_case tool inputs into the same commands used by human controls. Unit and Playwright tests cover the engine, shared store, revisions, undo, tool registration, semantic highlighting, previews, the two-step Rivergate solution, activity evidence, and responsive UI. I also rehearsed the complete flow against the public deployment using a native WebMCP-enabled browser. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was guaranteeing that there is only one world. A tool mutation must become visible immediately, while a human action must be readable by the next agent inspection. One store, one dispatcher, revision checks, and hashes make that guarantee explicit. Traffic also needed to create meaningful tradeoffs without becoming a research-scale simulation. Deterministic weighted paths, fixed capacities, aggregate commuter and freight loads, and stable tie-breaking create explainable congestion. The larger lesson is that agent transparency can be a product feature. Domain tools, exact inspection highlights, previews, and audit trails let a person collaborate with an agent instead of trusting opaque UI automation. Accomplishments Built a real playable simulator rather than a WebMCP mockup Exposed 14 meaningful tools over one authoritative live world Added deterministic metrics, stale-revision protection, and world proofs Added exact inspection highlighting and non-committing previews Added placement validation, hard constraints, demolition, undo, and local persistence Created a two-step scenario that visibly requires iteration Made every agent action legible through a semantic overlay and activity timeline What’s next The same shared-semantic-world pattern can extend to operational dashboards, logistics networks, infrastructure simulations, planning canvases, and digital twins, any interface where people need to inspect, preview, and audit agent changes to live state. Future versions could add scenario authoring, richer utility networks, shareable saves, more challenge prompts, and additional semantic layers without changing the one-store architecture. title: Hold the Bill
pitch: A WebMCP bill review desk where people and agents check the same hospital statement before payment.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP bill review desk where people and agents check the same hospital statement before payment. Like Comment Story Updates The default demo statement: an itemized hospital bill before anyone has reviewed a line. After Run review: five findings, five lines marked — duplicates, misc, wrong-patient test, post-discharge. Hold locked: flagged lines are frozen and the call script is ready so you do not pay them yet. PDF / paste import: load a text-layer PDF, paste lines, or hit Load bill for the test statement. Inspiration Hospital bills are one of those documents people know they should review, but almost nobody actually checks line by line. The statements are dense, the codes are confusing, and most people either pay the full amount or paste the bill into a chatbot and get back a paragraph they still cannot act on. I wanted to build something more practical: a shared review surface where a person and an AI agent can look at the same live bill together before any payment is made. That became Hold the Bill . What it does Hold the Bill is a WebMCP app for reviewing itemized hospital bills before payment. The app loads a statement, lets each line be marked as Unseen , OK , Question , or Dispute , and blocks the final hold step until every line has been reviewed. It also runs deterministic billing-shape checks for: duplicate charges charges after discharge miscellaneous unexplained items wrong-patient tests facility + physician informational pairing Once every line has been checked, the user can Lock hold . That freezes the review, calculates how much should not be paid yet, and generates a ready-to-use call script for the billing office. Why WebMCP This use case is a strong fit for WebMCP because the problem is not just “give me advice.” The real problem is tying that advice to the exact line items on the page the user is about to pay . Without WebMCP, an agent would return a paragraph in chat and the user would still have to map that advice back to the bill manually. With WebMCP, the website exposes structured tools directly from the page. The agent can: read the current statement review the bill explain specific lines mark lines lock or unlock the hold import pasted bill text That means the human and the agent operate on the same live state , not in separate places. How we built it I built Hold the Bill as a client-side React + TypeScript app with Vite. The app uses a shared local store for both the UI and the WebMCP tools, so actions taken by a person or an agent update the same statement immediately. WebMCP is implemented with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) on the top-level page. Each tool calls the same internal store logic as the visible buttons in the interface. I included: the default City Ridge sample statement for judge demos a PDF / paste import path for text-based statements browser-only PDF text extraction using pdfjs-dist a hold pack generator and call script activity logging for human and agent actions There is no backend and no OCR pipeline in this version. For the hackathon, I intentionally kept the upload path focused on digital PDFs and pasted text instead of trying to support low-quality phone photos. Challenges we ran into The biggest product challenge was keeping the app useful without pretending to be a hospital billing system or a medical truth engine. I narrowed the scope to billing-shape checks instead of broad medical correctness. That made the behavior explainable and demo-friendly. Another challenge was the import flow. Full OCR for arbitrary bill photos would have added complexity, model downloads, and unreliable results, so I avoided that and built a safer import path for text-layer PDFs and pasted statement text. On the WebMCP side, the main challenge was making the tools feel like a natural extension of the UI, not a second product. The solution was to keep the human path and the agent path backed by the exact same store and review logic. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most powerful when the agent is not replacing the interface, but joining the user inside it . This project made that very concrete: the value is not an AI summary by itself, but the combination of: agent speed shared page state visible line-by-line decisions a final human-controlled lock step That pattern feels useful well beyond this project. What's next Next, I would improve parsing, support more statement formats, and make the hold pack easier to export or send. I would also explore stronger rules and a safer path for authenticated patient portals. But for the hackathon, the core idea is already here: do not pay a confusing hospital bill until every line has been seen. title: Pixel Art Tutor
pitch: Create and edit pixel art with a hands-on agent assistant by your side.
about_excerpt: Create and edit pixel art with a hands-on agent assistant by your side. Like Comment Story Updates GIF About Pixel art is a staple for game development, but players hate AI slop and today's image generation models still struggle getting pixel art to be "pixel perfect". We wanted to fix that by enabling users and agents to collaborate and create art in a more traditionally-accepted sense. What it does Pixel Art Tutor is a WebMCP-powered studio for creating pixel art (sprites, animations, characters, and tilesets). WebMCP is a strong fit because it gives agents structured access to canvas content that would otherwise be invisible to them. Agents can read sprites as compact ASCII grids, critique artwork, paint individual pixels, fill regions, transform sprites, manage palettes, create animation frames, and build tilemaps. Humans can draw, guide, request edits, and refine the work in the same canvas. With shared rooms via PartyKit, collaborators see edits and agent activity live (making human-agent co-creation possible where traditional browser automation would be unreliable or impossible). How it was built The app is made with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and PartySocket/PartyServer for real-time collaboration. On startup, the app registers ~43 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , plus a declarative tool for creating sprites. All agent actions use the same store actions as the human UI, so edits remain visible, undoable, and synchronized. The app also includes a built-in critique engine, animation timeline, palette tools, tilemap editing, and game-engine exports. Unexpected challenges The biggest challenge was translating a visual canvas into a useful agent interface. We needed compact representations that agents could understand, precise tools for pixel-level changes, and safeguards so human edits, agent actions, undo history, and room synchronization stayed consistent. What's next for Pixel Art Tutor Next, we want to improve multi-agent collaboration, add stronger room permissions and conflict handling, expand the tutoring system, support more creative workflows, and make it easier to publish and share collaborative pixel-art projects.  CoSpace: Agent-Human Co-Working Canvas 

 
 A collaborative web workspace designed for humans and AI agents to brainstorm, structure ideas, and plan projects together using the WebMCP standard. 
 

 
 Live Web App: https://cospace.dcontessa100.workers.dev 
 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/dcontessa/cospace 
 

 

 💡 Elevator Pitch 

 CoSpace is a parchment-themed collaborative canvas that turns standard web elements into structured, agent-actionable tools—exposing them directly to your AI agent via the browser-native WebMCP standard. 

 

 ⚠️ The Problem: The Fragility of the Visual Web 

 Today, when an AI agent interacts with a website, it has to guess its way through the interface. It parses raw HTML, takes screenshots, guesses DOM selectors, and attempts to click buttons or fill out text areas. This approach is: 

 
 Fragile: Any minor styling or layout tweak breaks the agent's selector path. 
 High-Latency: Taking screenshots and running visual OCR loops adds massive latency. 
 Unstructured: The agent doesn't understand the underlying semantic boundaries of what it is looking at. 
 

 

 🛠️ The Solution: WebMCP-Native Co-Creation 

 CoSpace is built from the ground up to explore the future of the agent-native web. Instead of forcing agents to guess our UI, CoSpace explicitly declares its visual capabilities. 

 When you open CoSpace in a WebMCP-supporting browser or agent sidebar (like ChatGPT), the site registers browser-side JavaScript tools directly into the browser context. The agent can now manipulate the canvas programmatically, bypassing selectors entirely: 

 
 addCard : Instantly spawn idea and task cards. 
 updateCard : Edit titles, bullet points, status, and theme colors. 
 connectCards : Draw visual dependency arrows between notes. 
 deleteCard : Remove outdated ideas from the workspace. 
 

 

 ⚙️ How We Built It 

 
 Frontend: React + TypeScript scaffolded via Vite, styled using the brand-new Tailwind CSS v4 for clean, modern utility classes and modular parchment layout. 
 SVG Connection Pipeline: Rather than relying on a heavy React Flow library that bloats the package size, we custom-built a lightweight SVG rendering layer. It auto-calculates card centers and draws arrow markers between absolute-positioned nodes in real-time. 
 WebMCP Browser Hook: We implemented a unified React hook that registers tools via document.modelContext.registerTool (with a fallback for navigator.modelContext used in earlier browser drafts). We bind the lifecycle of these tools to an AbortController signal to clean them up automatically when nodes unmount. 
 Audit Logging: Built a live execution console that logs when tools are triggered by WebMCP or the simulator, proving the agent-native loop works transparently. 
 Gemini Chat Simulator: For environments without native WebMCP browser support, we integrated the Vertex AI / Gemini API directly inside a sliding sidebar panel. When you prompt the Co-pilot, it acts as a local agent, compiling prompts into structured operations and updating the board in real-time. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments We're Proud Of 

 
 Zero Server-Side Latency: By executing the WebMCP tools directly in the client's browser DOM, the AI agent updates the board instantaneously with no backend database roundtrips. 
 Tactile Design Hierarchy: A clean, print-inspired design using asymmetric layouts, Ink Navy headers, Signal Yellow highlights, and a dotted parchment grid. 
 100% Type-Safe & Serverless: The entire codebase builds into an optimized, lightweight static bundle deployed instantly to the latest version of Cloudflare Pages. 
 

 

 🧠 What We Learned 

 WebMCP represents a massive paradigm shift. As developers, we no longer design interfaces purely for human eyes—we must architect clean, programmatic action seams for AI agents. Namespace safety and state isolation are key as websites transition into agent-ready tools. 

 

 🔮 What's Next for CoSpace 

 
 Collaborative Multiplayer: Integrating WebSockets to allow multiple humans and multiple agents to edit the same canvas concurrently. 
 B2B Integration Rail: Exporting canvas tasks to Jira, GitHub Issues, or Trello automatically through background agent actions.

title: Chameleon
pitch: Software that grows its own API.
about_excerpt: Software that grows its own API. Like Comment Story Updates What Chameleon does Chameleon is a near-blank browser canvas that an AI agent turns into working software through WebMCP. A wedding planner, job-search tracker, or health log can appear from one request. The user can then drag, resize, edit, and use the generated interface directly. The app exposes 15 WebMCP tools and a six-widget grammar: table, kanban, checklist, chart, note, and form. All human and agent changes pass through one command log. The agent can read the board, see human edits, detect stale state, and undo changes. The signature feature is dynamic tool creation. When an agent creates a form, Chameleon can register a new WebMCP tool whose input schema comes from the form fields. The new tool persists across reloads. The software and its API grow together. Why WebMCP Chameleon only makes sense as a WebMCP app. WebMCP lets the agent work with the same live browser state, local data, layout, and command history as the user. The agent does not work around the page through screen scraping or a separate backend API. This enables two new workflows: A human and an agent can edit one live artifact with shared ground truth. Human drag, resize, and data edits become visible to the agent through the same activity log. An agent can extend the app's tool surface for a later agent. A health-log form can become a persistent log_blood_sugar tool with a schema derived from the form fields. User experience Flexible tools often make the user design the software before doing the real task. Chameleon starts from the goal instead. The agent composes a purpose-specific interface, and the user continues with normal direct manipulation. Repeated actions can become agent tools. A new blood-sugar reading can be validated through the same schema as the on-screen form, appended to the same dataset, and charted immediately. Implementation Chameleon is a Vite and React 19 single-page application deployed as static assets on Cloudflare Workers. Zustand stores the local board document. Immer applies human and agent mutations through one patch-producing gate that also updates the command log, inverse patches, and stateVersion . The WebMCP registry publishes schemas created with Zod 4. The same schema validates execution and becomes the JSON Schema. Tool lifetimes use AbortController . Minted tool records persist in localStorage and register again after hydration. The interface uses Astryx, StyleX, react-grid-layout, and Recharts. There is no backend, authentication system, or remote database. Built and tested with AI Codex helped plan the tool specification, widget grammar, repository structure, implementation, debugging, tests, browser-runtime investigation, and agent-facing tool behavior. Real agent tests revealed when agents stopped after creating empty widgets. Chameleon's tool responses were improved with unfinished-work data and next-action hints. Local verification passes 161 tests across 26 test files, lint, and the production TypeScript and Vite build. Try it Open the live app in the ChatGPT desktop app browser and ask: I'm planning my wedding for next June - about 80 guests. Set this page up for me. For the minted-tool flow, reset the canvas and ask: I'm managing my type 2 diabetes. I want to log blood sugar readings and see trends. Chrome 149 or later can also test the tools with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and the Model Context Tool Inspector. Known limitations Board state is local to one browser profile. Clearing site storage removes the board and minted tools. Agent control requires the ChatGPT in-app browser or a compatible Chrome build with WebMCP enabled. title: Prove It — Verifiable AI for Screen Reader Users
pitch: Every AI action gets a signed receipt with a deep link your screen reader can verify directly — so you never have to trust an agent's word for what it just did.
about_excerpt: Every AI action gets a signed receipt with a deep link your screen reader can verify directly — so you never have to trust an agent's word for what it just did. Like Comment Story Updates The verification gap nobody talks about Blind and low-vision users already use AI agents to operate the web — filling forms, managing lists, navigating sites with dozens of menus. The part that still doesn't work is trust. A sighted user glances at the screen and knows instantly whether an action succeeded. A screen reader user has no equivalent glance. Today, verifying what an agent did means re-navigating the whole page by hand, which erases most of the time an agent was supposed to save. A study of 16 screen-reader-using programmers found that verifying AI output, not producing it, was consistently the most time-consuming part of their workflow. That's the problem Prove It is built to solve. What it does Prove It is a household task manager where every action an AI agent takes — adding a task, marking it done, changing its priority, deleting it — produces a structured, inspectable receipt : what changed, exactly where it lives in the page, and what to say if it failed. Every receipt includes a deep link . Clicking it moves real keyboard and screen-reader focus straight to the element that changed, so the person hears their own assistive technology confirm the action in its own words — not a paraphrase from the agent, and not a guess from re-navigating the page. Failures get the same treatment. If the agent tries something invalid — an unknown task, a bulk delete it isn't allowed to perform — that produces an error receipt too. Proving what an agent didn't do, and why, is as important as proving what it did. How I built it The whole app runs on one function, performTool(name, args) , which is the single source of truth for all seven tools ( list_tasks , add_task , set_task_status , update_task_priority , delete_task , focus_task , get_last_receipt ). That one function is wired to two transports: Native WebMCP. On load, the page feature-detects document.modelContext / navigator.modelContext and calls registerTool() for each tool with a strict JSON Schema. Any WebMCP-aware agent — Chrome's built-in agent with the WebMCP flag on, or ChatGPT's in-app browser — can discover and call these tools directly, no code changes required. In-page demo agent (fallback). If WebMCP isn't available in the browser, the same seven tool schemas are sent to the Claude API as tools , so anyone can test the full loop — natural language in, tool call, receipt, verify — in an ordinary browser with no flags. Every write tool returns { tool, changeType, timestamp, target: {selector, description}, before, after, errors } . changeType is created , updated , deleted , verified , or error . Receipts render as a literal torn-paper "receipt tape" in the UI — a visual metaphor for the whole concept: a printed proof of exactly what happened. The negative test There is no delete_all_tasks or bulk-export tool, on purpose. The agent is instructed to delete tasks one at a time and to ask before any bulk action — so "prove it" also covers proving the agent can't do something irreversible, because the capability was never exposed as a tool in the first place, not because a prompt told it to behave. Challenges I ran into The trickiest part wasn't the receipts — it was making the deep link mechanism actually work for a screen reader, not just look like it does. Early on, clicking a receipt just scrolled to an element and added a CSS glow, which does nothing for someone who can't see the glow. The fix was making sure every deep-linked element is a real, focusable DOM node ( tabindex="-1" where it isn't natively focusable) with an aria-label that reflects its current state, and that the deep link calls .focus() on that exact node. The visual highlight is a bonus for sighted collaborators, not the verification mechanism itself. The other challenge was keeping one tool contract honest across two very different transports. Rather than writing tool logic twice, performTool() is called by both the native registerTool().execute() handlers and the in-page agent loop, so a receipt means the same thing regardless of which agent produced it. What I learned Verifiability isn't a feature you bolt onto an agent's output after the fact — it has to be a structural property of the tool contract itself: a real DOM target, a real before/after diff, a real focus event. WebMCP's tool registration model turns out to be a genuinely good fit for this, because the receipt an agent returns and the page's actual state can be forced to be the same object, not two things that merely claim to agree. What's next Extending the receipt/deep-link pattern beyond a single demo page — a small library other WebMCP sites could adopt so "verifiable receipts" becomes a convention across the ecosystem, not a one-off feature of this app. Built With accessibility aria css3 html5 javascript json-schema model-context-protocol screen-readers vanilla-js webmcp Try it out github.com proofit-phi.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Vijayalakshmi S Like Share this project: Updates Vijayalakshmi S started this project — Aug 31, 2026 12:44 PM EDT

title: coSynth
pitch: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go.
about_excerpt: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go. Like Comment Story Updates Full Wavetable Synthesizer GIF Active AI state and tool visible in the UI coSynth – AI Web Synthesizer Sound design is hard to get into. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: Orgmemory
pitch: Company context and human control for engineering agents.
about_excerpt: Company context and human control for engineering agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding agents are becoming increasingly capable at understanding repositories and writing code, but production engineering depends on much more than code. The reason a service failed last time may be hidden in a postmortem. A critical constraint may live in Slack. Ownership information may be stored in a document, while the relevant architectural decision exists in another system. When an engineer or AI agent begins a change without this organizational context, it can repeat mistakes the company has already learned from. That inspired OrgMemory . I wanted to build a memory and governance layer that could answer a simple question before an agent acts: What does this company already know about the change I am about to make? OrgMemory began as a source-backed organizational memory system. For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I extended it into a browser-native context and governance layer that agents can access through the authenticated web application. The goal was not to give agents unlimited autonomy. The goal was to give them better context, make their actions observable, and keep consequential decisions under human control. How I Built It OrgMemory brings together incidents, decisions, dependencies, owners, runbooks, repositories, conversations, and documents. It converts this information into permission-scoped, time-aware company memory where every promoted fact remains connected to its original evidence. The application uses: Next.js 15 and React 19 for the workspace, WebMCP interface, approvals, and live agent activity. FastAPI and Python 3.13 for ingestion, retrieval, authorization, organizational operations, and the agent loop. SQLite and ArcadeDB for application state and organizational relationships. WebMCP for browser-native tool registration and execution. NDJSON streaming for live model steps, tool calls, arguments, and results. HttpOnly session cookies so browser agents never receive separate credentials. A separate MCP server, Python SDK, CLI, and REST API for agents operating outside the browser. I used document.modelContext.registerTool() to expose OrgMemory as a browser-native tool provider. WebMCP calls reuse the page's authenticated session, so the browser agent operates with the same permissions as the signed-in user. The authenticated workspace exposes 37 tools : 27 read-only tools 1 append-only outcome ledger tool 9 human-governed operations The focused Agent Operations page registers a 16-tool subset : 13 read-only operations 3 approval-gated operations The interface and WebMCP tools share the same backend handlers. This prevents the agent from receiving a separate privileged execution path. The demo follows a complete engineering workflow. The agent searches organizational memory, evaluates launch readiness, discovers a contradictory approval record, and proposes a correction. The proposal changes nothing until a person approves it. Once approved, the agent sends the plan to a coding IDE through MCP for implementation. It then checks launch readiness again and records the outcome. I also built a live activity view that shows the tools selected by the model, their arguments, results, durations, and citations. This makes it clear that the agent is calling real tools instead of replaying a scripted response. Challenges I Faced Separating capability from authorization WebMCP makes it possible to expose powerful operations to an agent, but access to a tool should not automatically authorize every use of that tool. I designed the write operations so agents can investigate and propose changes, while only a person can approve or decline them. There is intentionally no WebMCP tool that allows an agent to approve its own proposal. Designing an honest permission model The outcome ledger created an unusual case. Recording an outcome writes data, so it is not read-only. However, it does not modify company knowledge, so requiring human approval would make the feedback loop unnecessarily slow. I introduced a separate append-only permission tier for this operation. This allows the agent to report what happened without giving it the ability to change what the organization believes. Preserving history while identifying current truth Organizational knowledge changes over time. A task may still be marked open even though a newer decision says it was completed. Simply overwriting the old record would destroy useful history. OrgMemory preserves both records, connects them through relationships such as UPDATES , CONTRADICTS , and SUPPORTS , and creates a reviewable proposal for resolving the conflict. Maintaining security through the browser The browser agent needed access to organizational context without receiving reusable API keys or source credentials. WebMCP calls use the authenticated page session, while authorization is still enforced by the backend against the user's workspace, team, and project access. Making the system observable A judge or operator should be able to verify that the agent is calling real tools instead of replaying a scripted result. I built a live activity surface that displays tool calls, arguments, results, durations, citations, and approval requirements. The person can see exactly what the agent read, what it proposed, and where automation stopped. Explaining a large system in a short demo OrgMemory includes ingestion, retrieval, memory graphs, governance, multiple agent surfaces, SDKs, and an outcome loop. The challenge was reducing that scope to one clear story. I focused the demo on a single transformation: the agent begins with incomplete organizational context, finds a blocker, proposes a resolution, stops for human approval, and verifies the result after implementation. What I Learned I learned that browser-native tools are most useful when they reuse the identity, permissions, and state already present in the application. I also learned that tool annotations are helpful for communicating intent, but they are not a substitute for server-side authorization. Every permission boundary still needs to be enforced by the backend. Agents need more than semantic search. Before changing a system, they need an intent-specific briefing that includes constraints, previous incidents, dependencies, ownership, and potential blast radius. Human approval is most effective when it is visible. The agent response, approval interface, audit trail, and resulting state should all show exactly where automation stopped and where a person made the decision. Most importantly, I learned that organizational memory becomes more valuable when it records outcomes. The lasting advantage is not only knowing what the company learned, but also knowing which context led to successful action.  Inspiration 

 Industrial turbomachinery and rotary assets experience sub-pixel micro-vibrations and structural stress long before catastrophic failure occurs. Traditional physical accelerometers demand invasive mounting, costly physical wiring, and human intervention in hazardous operating zones. We set out to build a fully non-contact, physics-informed computer vision rig capable of turning standard camera feeds into sub-pixel vibration telemetry, automated ISO 10816-3 compliance audits, and an autonomous digital twin. 

 What it does 

 ChronoPhys-Vision 3.0 is an industrial-grade, physics-informed optical telemetry platform: 

 
 Optical Motion Magnification: Utilizes Riesz Phase-Based Eulerian Video Magnification (EVM) to amplify imperceptible mechanical vibrations from 50x up to 200x in real time across 1.0–6.0 Hz bandpass filters. 
 Deterministic ISO 10816-3 Classification: Isolates mechanical vibration harmonics (1X Unbalance, 2X Misalignment, BPFO Bearing Faults) and shifts ISO operational zones dynamically (Zone A to critical Zone D trips). 
 3D ODS Digital Twin: Live modal deflection wireframe visualization rendered in real time using Three.js / WebGL driven directly by continuous telemetry. 
 W3C WebMCP JSON-RPC Agent Protocol: Integrates a 12-tool autonomous agent bridge enabling AI-directed parameter tuning, safety throttling, and automated persistence to SQLite. 
 Gemini AI Reliability Specialist: Integrated multimodal assistant providing root-cause failure analysis, PINN fatigue life modeling, and one-click ISO 17025 audit PDF generation. 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Architecture: Decoupled dual-port full-stack architecture. 
 Frontend (Port 3000): Next.js 14, React, Tailwind CSS, Three.js WebGL rendering, Lucide Icons, and client-side WebMCP JSON-RPC handlers. 
 Backend CV Engine (Port 8000): Python, FastAPI, OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy (Riesz Pyramids, 2D FFT spectral analysis), and Modbus TCP industrial bridge. 
 AI & Persistence: Google Gemini API for diagnostic intelligence, Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) fatigue curves, and SQLite3 time-series logging. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Processing multi-scale Riesz phase pyramids and 2D FFT spectral transforms alongside real-time MJPEG streaming caused severe latency. We optimized the processing loop using multi-threaded frame buffers and sub-sampled regions of interest (ROI) to sustain a rock-solid 30–60 FPS optical pipeline.

 Achieving sub-pixel vibration measurement without a single physical sensor. 
 Integrating the W3C WebMCP draft standard for autonomous tool-driven agent maintenance. 
 Creating an end-to-end loop from raw video capture to ISO 17025 audit PDF export in real time. 
 

 What we learned 

 Bridging high-frequency computer vision algorithms with deterministic industrial standards (ISO 10816-3/13373) and agentic browser protocols provides a non-invasive, cost-effective pathway for modern smart factories. 

 What's next for ChronoPhys-Vision 

 
 Multi-camera triangulation for complete 360-degree spatial structural deflection.

title: Repro
pitch: Reproduce any application state and see the real UI instantly.
about_excerpt: Reproduce any application state and see the real UI instantly. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration When testing a web application, the difficult part is often not the test itself. It is getting the application into the exact state you need to inspect. An expired account. A trial user. An unauthenticated session. A specific error state. Reproducing these states can require creating users, changing database records, configuring subscriptions, or manually navigating through multiple steps. I wanted to remove that setup work. Repro lets you describe the application state you want to see, reproduce it, and inspect the real UI immediately. We don't run your tests. We create the state you need to see. What it does Repro exposes application-state reproduction through three stable WebMCP tools: list_states reproduce_state reset_state Instead of creating a separate tool for every test scenario, Repro treats application states as data. For example, an agent can discover an available state such as free_expired . Repro applies that state to an isolated Repro session, and the application's existing UI renders normally. This makes it possible for humans and agents to inspect production-like UI states without creating real users, payments, emails, or other production side effects. How I built it Repro is published as the repro-webmcp npm package. The basic workflow is: npm install -D repro-webmcp npx repro scan npx repro setup repro scan statically analyzes an existing JavaScript or TypeScript application and discovers semantic application states from existing code, including conditional UI branches, enums, literal states, mocks, fixtures, and tests. The discovered states become the source of truth for Repro. repro setup prepares the runtime, browser registration, and integration boundary. For simple supported state architectures, the connection can be generated automatically. For more complex applications, a coding agent connects one generic bridge to the existing state boundary. Repro generates a project-specific .repro/AGENTS.md integration guide containing both its standard integration rules and evidence discovered during the scan. A coding agent can use this to connect Repro once to the application's existing state boundary. The important distinction is that the agent does not generate a separate test fixture for every state. It creates one generic bridge between Repro and the application's normal state/rendering system. Dogfooding on an existing application I tested Repro on a separate existing application that was not built for this challenge. Before installing Repro, it contained zero manually defined Repro states. Running repro scan discovered 20 candidate application states from the existing source code. For this more complex application, I gave the generated integration instructions to Codex. Codex implemented one generic bridge to the application's existing authentication/session state. After that, the same three WebMCP tools could reproduce states such as authenticated and unauthenticated, while the real application UI continued to render through its normal code path. This dogfooding also exposed an important setup bug: the browser bootstrap was still loading an older hand-written configuration instead of the scan-generated states. I fixed the runtime/setup flow and published the fix as repro-webmcp@0.1.4 . Challenges The hardest problem was finding the right boundary between automation and application-specific integration. Automatically discovering states is possible, but automatically modifying arbitrary application state safely is much harder. Real applications use different stores, authentication systems, module structures, and rendering architectures. I initially considered generating state-specific fixtures, but that would simply move the manual test-setup problem somewhere else. The architecture evolved into: automatic state discovery + a stable runtime + one generic application bridge when necessary. Another challenge was safety. Reproducing an expired subscription should not require modifying a real subscription. Reproducing an authenticated user should not require creating a production user. Repro therefore focuses on reproducing the application state consumed by the UI rather than recreating the entire backend environment. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP becomes especially useful when the interface exposed to agents is semantic rather than tied to individual UI actions. An application may contain 20, 100, or more reproducible states, but Repro still needs only three WebMCP tools. The vocabulary remains stable while the application's states remain data. I also learned a lot from testing the npm package against an application that was not designed around Repro. That immediately revealed assumptions that were invisible in the purpose-built demo and changed the final architecture. What's next After the challenge, I want to expand Repro's automatic integration support across more application architectures and frameworks. One limitation discovered during dogfooding is multi-page applications: full-page navigation can create a new document where the WebMCP bootstrap must be initialized again. I plan to add automatic multi-entry-point instrumentation for this case. I am also interested in exploring the same concept beyond web applications, including state reproduction for SwiftUI applications and simulator-based development workflows. The long-term goal is simple: Make application state an interface that both developers and agents can discover, reproduce, and inspect safely. title: Mermaid Atlas
pitch: Mermaid Atlas turns massive Mermaid diagrams into a shared visual workspace where humans and AI agents can explore, explain, and safely improve software architecture through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Mermaid Atlas turns massive Mermaid diagrams into a shared visual workspace where humans and AI agents can explore, explain, and safely improve software architecture through WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have a project called Sonny with around 264,464 lines of code. When Bhavya tried to understand its architecture, going through hundreds of source files and Markdown documents was extremely inefficient. We realized that the easiest way to understand a codebase this large was to see its architecture visually. This was not only our experience. GitHub Next independently identified the lack of visual explanations as a major limitation of current agent workflows. Their research explains that agents generate text much faster than humans can process it, while text is often the wrong medium for understanding complex relationships and architectural systems. That is exactly the problem Mermaid Atlas addresses. Existing Mermaid viewers also struggled with large diagrams and made them difficult to explore. In our testing, Mermaid Atlas could handle diagrams with more than 500 nodes that mermaid.live could not handle properly. That is what sparked the idea, and Bhavya came up with Mermaid Atlas. What it does Mermaid Atlas is a visual workspace for exploring large Mermaid diagrams. A person can import Mermaid or Markdown files, search for nodes, inspect relationships, navigate through dependencies, and edit the source while viewing the rendered result. Through ten WebMCP tools, an AI agent can work with the same live graph. It can: Find components using natural language Inspect dependencies and blast radius Trace paths between services Detect cycles, isolated nodes, entry points, and dead ends Create guided walkthroughs Make validated source changes Undo its latest change safely Everything the agent does is visible on the canvas through selections, walkthroughs, source updates, and the Agent activity history. The app opens with a complete Northwind architecture, so judges can start using it immediately without creating an account or uploading anything. How we built it Mermaid Atlas originally started as a proof of concept built with HTML and JavaScript. When we joined the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, we migrated it to React and built the current version. We used Mermaid for rendering and ELK for laying out large graphs. Different Mermaid diagram types generate completely different SVG structures, so we built adapters that connect the original Mermaid source to the correct rendered nodes, edges, groups, and source lines. We then added the WebMCP layer, the diagram library, Graph Index, walkthroughs, safe editing, activity history, themes, and automated tests. Challenges we ran into The most frustrating challenge was that WebMCP does not currently support prompt primitives. Registering tools was not enough because the agent also needed to understand when and how to use them. We solved this by creating get_atlas_guide , a tool that teaches the agent the correct workflows, tool order, limits, and safety rules. We also found that tool behavior differed between models. Some descriptions worked well with GPT-5.6 Sol but were not followed as reliably by GPT-5.6 Terra. We reworked our WebMCP tool descriptions, schemas, results, and error messages until both models could use the tools consistently. Another major challenge was supporting different Mermaid renderers. Flowcharts, sequence diagrams, class diagrams, states, and architecture diagrams all generate different SVG structures. A generic solution caused incorrect highlighting and sometimes changed the appearance of diagram elements. We had to build renderer-specific semantic adapters instead. Safe agent editing was also difficult. We needed to prevent invalid Mermaid syntax, stale edits, and undo operations that could overwrite newer human changes. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that Mermaid Atlas works reliably for humans and agents even with massive Mermaid diagrams. We built ten WebMCP tools that operate on the same graph the human is viewing, made agent actions visible and reversible, and tested the application across 46 Mermaid fixtures. We also made diagrams with more than 500 nodes practical to search, navigate, and understand. What we learned We learned that building agent tools is not only about exposing functions. Tool names, descriptions, schemas, limits, and error messages determine whether an agent can use them reliably. We also learned that human control means making agent actions visible and reversible, not just asking for confirmation. Most importantly, we learned that handling large diagrams is both a rendering problem and an information-retrieval problem. Agents need focused graph queries instead of the entire diagram. What's next for Mermaid Atlas Next, we want to add optional accounts, cloud synchronization, and real-time collaboration so teams can work on architecture diagrams together like they would in Google Docs. The current local, no-account version will remain available. title: TuneQL
pitch: A PostgreSQL workbench where an AI agent can actually try out optimizations instead of just suggesting them.
about_excerpt: A PostgreSQL workbench where an AI agent can actually try out optimizations instead of just suggesting them. Like 1 Comment Story Updates PostgreSQL optimization workbench Verified optimization Create Workspace WebMCP agent actions Optimization constraints Execution plan Why I built it AI can suggest a SQL fix, but it can’t really prove that the fix actually made things better. I’d still have to open a database tool, check the execution plan, run some benchmarks, and manually make sure the result is still correct. So I built TuneQL to keep all of that in one place. What TuneQL does TuneQL is basically a PostgreSQL query optimization workbench that runs in the browser using PGlite. You can inspect the schema, run queries, check EXPLAIN ANALYZE , save a benchmark as a baseline, then change the query or indexes and compare the new version with the old one. It shows what changed, how much faster or slower it got, whether the constraints still pass, and if both queries return the same result. WebMCP The same workspace can also be used by an agent through WebMCP. TuneQL gives the agent tools to read schemas and indexes, explain and benchmark queries, create indexes, change SQL, save baselines, and compare the results. And whatever the agent does also shows up in the UI, so you can actually follow what it’s doing and continue from the same state yourself. How I built it TuneQL uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, PGlite, Zustand, and IndexedDB. PostgreSQL runs inside a browser worker, and the workspace data stays on your device. The UI and all 20 WebMCP tools go through the same command layer, so things like query validation, constraints, benchmarks, activity history, and revision checks behave the same in both places. Challenges and learning One of the harder parts was keeping the PGlite worker, saved workspace, UI, and agent actions all in sync. I also realised pretty quickly that you can’t judge an optimization from just one timing. So TuneQL does a few warm-up runs, runs the benchmark multiple times, and checks the full result instead of just comparing the few rows shown in the preview.
