title: ForgeTwin
pitch: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am both a mechanical engineer and a web developer , and this project came from combining these two parts of my experience. In mechanical engineering, having a good idea is only the beginning. The idea must become real geometry, materials, joints, forces, sensors, controls, and measurable results. In web development, I learned how a good interface and AI can make a complicated tool easier for more people to use. This made me ask one question: What if AI could do more than generate a picture or description of a machine? What if it could enter the same engineering workspace as the human, build the machine part by part, test it, see what failed, and improve it? This is why I built ForgeTwin. I wanted someone to describe a physical goal in normal language, without knowing every CAD command, and then watch an AI agent turn that goal into an editable, animated, and testable mechanical system. As an engineer, one principle was very important to me: A design should not be trusted only because it looks convincing. It should be tested with physics and evidence. Don’t generate it. Engineer it. What it does ForgeTwin is a browser-based AI engineering sandbox. The user describes a machine or mechanical goal, and ForgeTwin creates a versioned physical world from reusable parts. For example, a user can ask: “Build a conveyor that sorts red and blue boxes at 20 boxes per minute.” “Build an electric go-kart with four wheels, steering, accelerator and brake pedals.” “Build a brazing fixture that positions a heat exchanger and two copper pipes within 2 mm.” ForgeTwin then: Understands the requested machine, functions, and measurable requirements. Creates an engineering plan instead of returning only text. Breaks the design into assemblies and reusable low-level components. Gives every component dimensions, material, mass, position, and orientation. Adds physical connections, joints, motors, sensors, actuators, and control logic. Builds the machine in an interactive 3D workspace while the user watches. Runs a fixed-step 60 Hz Rapier simulation. Reads telemetry, collisions, movement, and requirement measurements. Finds the reason when a requirement fails. Changes the related geometry, physical property, actuator, motor, or controller and runs the test again. The app is not limited to conveyors. Its 39-part reusable vocabulary covers structures, power transmission, controls, road vehicles, motorcycles, aircraft, rotorcraft, tracked mobility, and articulated robots. It can compose cranes, lifts, bicycles, go-karts, motorcycles, cars, rovers, robotic arms, humanoid robots, gearboxes, suspension systems, airplanes, helicopters, solar trackers, bridges, warehouse systems, agriculture machines, recycling systems, HVAC fixtures, medical lifting mechanisms, and new systems made from smaller primitives. The current app includes 19 editable challenge briefs , but these are examples, not locked machine templates. The user can change the prompt, dimensions, load, speed, or target. If a special component is not already available, the planner can build it from lower-level parts such as beams, plates, tubes, shafts, wheels, pulleys, joints, sensors, and motors. The user can also: Use the built-in AI without entering credentials, or temporarily use their own OpenAI API key. Edit the existing design with natural-language chat instead of starting over. Select, move, resize, and rotate parts in X, Y, and Z. Orbit the full camera through 360 degrees with mouse or touch. Use a rotation gizmo, snapping, or numeric angle entry. Lock a manual change so the AI redesigns around it instead of moving it back. Animate the operating sequence of different machine families. Run physics and replay a failure in slow motion. Use X-Ray Mode to inspect joints, sensor paths, axes, collision boxes, actuator paths, and velocity information. Inspect requirement evidence and see what passed, failed, or was not evaluated. Undo changes, restore revisions, and compare a failed design with the improved design. Export the current world as PNG, JPG, PDF, STL exchange geometry, or complete ForgeTwin JSON data. How I built it ForgeTwin is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Rapier, and Zod . The main idea is that the machine is not saved as one opaque 3D model. It is stored as a shared engineering graph containing: Assemblies and individual bodies Dimensions, materials, mass, and rigid-body properties Position, rotation, and machine orientation Mechanical, power, and signal connections Fixed, revolute, prismatic, spherical, spring, rope, gear, and belt joints Motors, sensors, actuators, and control rules Simulation runs, telemetry, collisions, and failure evidence Human-owned edits and immutable revision history The 3D editor renders this graph procedurally. The same graph is used by the human interface, the built-in model agent, the physics simulator, the activity feed, exports, and an external WebMCP agent. The hosted AI uses GPT-5.6 Sol through the OpenAI Responses API . To keep generation faster and more reliable, the model creates a compact engineering intent: the object identity, architecture, motion, controls, primitive vocabulary, and requirements. ForgeTwin then expands that intent into the complete body-and-joint graph, validates it, repairs safe topology problems, and executes the design through guarded tools. The hosted key stays on the server, so judges can use the full AI experience without adding a key. A visitor can still connect their own key for the current browser tab. That key is kept only in memory and is not stored. If model access is unavailable, ForgeTwin also has a deterministic local engineering path for the main design, physics, optimization, and supported chat-edit operations. I also created one universal coordinate convention for every machine: +X is front, -X is rear, +Y is up, -Z is left, and +Z is right . This helped fix many problems with lights, wheels, propellers, steering, windshields, and joint axes. The design validator checks for missing supports, hubs, axles, joints, steering links, bad proportions, wrong orientations, floating components, incorrect joint axes, overlaps, blocked windshields, and unrequested systems. For example, a go-kart uses front wheel hubs, spindles, steering knuckles, separate kingpin axes, tie rods, a steering rack, column, and Ackermann-style steering instead of making the whole wheel rotate around one incorrect axis. Rapier runs the connected rigid-body world at a fixed 60 Hz and records replay frames and collision events. Some advanced engineering results, including aerodynamics, flexible cables, structural stress, detailed tire behavior, and some manufacturing processes, still use clearly labeled reduced-order checks. ForgeTwin is a concept-validation sandbox, not a replacement for certified CAD, FEA, CFD, medical approval, or safety analysis. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is what makes ForgeTwin an AI-operable engineering workspace instead of only a website with an AI button. ForgeTwin exposes 29 small, typed, state-aware WebMCP tools , including: inspect_workspace inspect_primitive_catalog set_design_goal create_assembly create_component set_dimensions , set_material , and set_mass move_component and rotate_component connect_components and create_joint add_motor , add_sensor , and add_actuator set_motor_speed , set_sensor_range , and set_actuator_timing set_control_logic and update_control_logic run_simulation inspect_telemetry , inspect_failure , and measure_constraint optimize_design remove_component and remove_joint compare_designs and restore_revision I did not create one giant generate_machine tool. The agent must inspect the current world, create parts, connect them, run the simulation, read the evidence, and make bounded changes. Every tool call is visible in the activity feed. This matters for human and AI collaboration. If I move a camera, sensor, or other component by hand, ForgeTwin creates a new revision and marks the transform as human-owned. The agent reads this new shared state and can redesign the rest of the machine without silently removing my decision. The built-in chat uses the same idea. It receives the current graph, selected component, latest measurements, human locks, and recent conversation. A request such as “move the right clamp 0.04 meters outward, preserve my camera position, and rerun the test” becomes a guarded change to the existing world, followed by a new simulation and revision. Without WebMCP, AI can give advice about the machine. With WebMCP, AI can work inside the engineering environment together with the human. title: Cherry
pitch: Cherry packages proven methods into verifiable, local AI tools. Teach once, run securely on your machine without API keys, and auto-verify completion with external checks.
about_excerpt:
Cherry packages proven methods into verifiable, local AI tools. Teach once, run securely on your machine without API keys, and auto-verify completion with external checks.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 1 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I follow a lot of builders on YouTube and LinkedIn. The useful part of what they teach never survives the watch. It stays in my head for a day, then it is gone, and my agents never learn any of it. Meanwhile every agent I use starts from zero on every task, no matter how much I have already figured out.
So I stopped trying to take better notes and built the thing that should exist instead. Content goes in, a skill comes out, and the skill lives where my agents actually work. 

 What it does 

 Cherry is a personal skill library that your agents can read.
Paste one link. A YouTube video, an article, a LinkedIn post. Cherry pulls the content, extracts the method inside it, and writes it back as a structured, reusable skill with prompts you can run.
Sources inbox. Everything you send lands in one lane and gets processed, so the library keeps growing without a ritual around each item.
The library is always available. Skills are versioned and editable, so a skill improves as you learn more rather than being frozen at the moment you saved it.
Connect it to your agents. Cherry runs as an MCP server, so ChatGPT, Codex, and Claude can list and pull your skills mid task. The site itself exposes WebMCP tools, so a browser agent sitting on the page can search the library and use a skill without any setup at all.
Bring your own reasoning. Connect your existing subscription or your own API key. Cherry does not resell tokens and is not trying to sit between you and your model.
The result is one library that follows you across every agent surface you use. 

 How I built it 

 Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel, React and Tailwind for the interface, Privy for auth with a guest first flow so you can try it before signing in anywhere.
The core is an extraction pipeline that takes a raw source, normalizes it into text, and runs a structured extraction pass that outputs a skill object rather than a summary. Summaries were the first version and they were useless to an agent. A skill needs steps, preconditions, and a prompt an agent can actually execute, so the schema is the product.
On top of that sit two access layers over the same library. An MCP server for desktop and CLI agents, and WebMCP tools exposed by the site itself for browser agents. Same skills, same source of truth, two doors in.
Everything is open source under MIT and designed to run at near zero cost, because a personal library you have to pay a subscription for is not a personal library. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Getting real content in. Ingestion that works on a demo link and ingestion that works on arbitrary real world URLs are different problems. I built a compliant runner based fetch path first and left the heavier scraping adapter for after the deadline rather than shipping something fragile.
Deciding what a skill is. This took the longest. Too loose and the agent ignores it. Too rigid and nothing real fits the shape. It took several rewrites of the schema before agents started using skills correctly instead of politely reading them.
Two agent protocols, one library. MCP and WebMCP have different assumptions about state and identity. Keeping one library honest across both without duplicating logic drove most of the architecture.
Scope. Building solo against a hard deadline, the temptation is to add surface. I cut features until the core loop of paste, skill, use was clean. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The core loop works end to end. One link in, a usable skill out, and that skill available inside a real agent session with no copy paste.
The site is a real MCP surface, not a landing page with a demo video. A browser agent can act on it directly.
It is fully open source and cheap to run, so anyone can fork it and own their own library instead of renting one.
I built it solo and it feels like a product rather than a hackathon prototype. 

 What I learned 

 Agents do not need more context, they need better shaped context. The same information as prose gets skipped and as a structured skill gets executed.
WebMCP changes what a website is for. Once the page exposes tools, the interface stops being the only way in, and you start designing for a human and an agent reading the same thing.
Also, cutting scope is the feature. Every thing I removed made the remaining loop more obvious. 

 What's next for Cherry 

 A browser bubble that sends the current tab into Cherry in one click, so capture happens where you already are.
Skill proposals from watch history, so Cherry suggests what to learn instead of waiting to be fed.
A deeper ingestion adapter for sources that resist a plain fetch.
A visual watcher that learns from what happens on screen in a video, not just the transcript.
Scheduled runs, so skills get refreshed and re run on a cadence without you touching them.

 Inspiration 

 The name, of course! What's more fun than a project with confusingly similar acronyms? 

 What it does 

 The MCP MPC makes the laborious process of trimming samples and making beats easy by allowing users to describe what they want in plain language. They can say "Gimme a lo-fi hip-hop beat but with electronic drums" or "Take this sample and pitch it down until it sounds like a sad ghost". The great thing about this is that by using WebMCP, musicians can actively collaborate in real-time with AI to make music - there's no automatically generated end result. 

 How we built it 

 With lots of Codex! I had the idea that the theme should follow the period in which the MPC became popular (90s) so I directed Codex to go with the 16-bit console theme. I also steered Sol to keep things fun and simple. I decided to deploy this to ChatGPT Sites as I had never done that before so wanted to learn more about it. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Codex and I have different tastes in music! Some of the synthetic sounds and sample choices were, eh, interesting. They mostly sounded quite harsh and abrasive. Not the laid-back defaults I was hoping for. I also had a small CORS issue on Sites which was easily fixed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I think it's a really fun collaborative tool to use! Users can invoke the WebMCP interface to try out new ideas or tweak something existing. This seems like a glimpse into the future of music-making. I like giving the model really esoteric descriptions of drum patterns and seeing what happens. 

 What we learned 

 I'm glad I learned how powerful WebMCP could be in that I used it not just for pushing buttons on screen, but for altering precise values of sample timing as well. I was also surprised at how it encourages you to not solely use either the chat or the web interface. I've been using both 50:50. 

 What's next for The MCP MPC 

 I'd like to build out a more "pro" version, giving it even more capabilities. The problem with a lot of musical equipment is that its power is usually locked behind a thousand menus and a massive manual. WebMCP feels like it could cut right through that.

title: Payment Recovery Agent
pitch: A WebMCP-native recovery workspace where browser agents help small businesses prioritize overdue invoices, draft guarded reminders, create payment handoffs, and audit recovery.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native recovery workspace where browser agents help small businesses prioritize overdue invoices, draft guarded reminders, create payment handoffs, and audit recovery.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Small businesses lose time and cash flow not because they do not know invoices are overdue, but because follow-up is messy. A freelancer, tutor, consultant, or agency owner has to decide who to chase first, what tone to use, whether a payment link exists, whether a client promised to pay, and when to stop sending reminders. 

 Most payment dashboards are built for humans clicking around tables. I wanted to explore what changes when the dashboard becomes agent-operable through WebMCP. 

 What It Does 

 Payment Recovery Agent turns overdue receivables into a structured recovery workflow. 

 A human business owner stays in control of sensitive customer communication, while a browser agent can use WebMCP tools to: 

 
 inspect the recovery snapshot 
 list at-risk payments 
 identify the highest-priority overdue invoice 
 create a guarded recovery plan 
 generate a payment handoff 
 draft a WhatsApp-ready reminder 
 mark promise-to-pay or recovered payments 
 simulate verified payment success 
 generate an audit trail 
 

 The result is not just a reminder tool. It is a human-supervised recovery workflow where overdue money becomes prioritized, actionable, and auditable. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP is a strong fit because payment recovery depends on page-local state and safe sequencing. 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to scrape visible tables, infer which invoice is selected, guess what buttons do, and risk taking the wrong action. With WebMCP, the site exposes explicit tools for each recovery step. 

 The agent gets structured access to the workflow, and the human gets a clear interface for supervision. 

 Human + Agent Experience 

 The human decides what kind of follow-up is appropriate and remains responsible for customer-sensitive actions. 

 The agent handles the repetitive work: 

 
 ranking the recovery queue 
 preparing next actions 
 drafting messages 
 attaching payment handoffs 
 updating recovery state 
 summarizing audit history 
 

 This division of labor matters because payment recovery is not one action. It is a sequence of decisions where mistakes are costly: chasing the wrong person, over-messaging, sending a reminder after payment, or forgetting a promise-to-pay. 

 How I Built It 

 The app is a static web app built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. 

 It registers 9 WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() , with fallback support for navigator.modelContext : 

 
 get_recovery_snapshot 
 list_at_risk_payments 
 draft_recovery_message 
 create_recovery_plan 
 mark_promise_to_pay 
 mark_payment_recovered 
 create_razorpay_link 
 simulate_razorpay_paid 
 generate_audit_trail 
 

 Tool schemas use JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false . Read-only tools are marked with annotations.readOnlyHint: true , and state-changing tools are marked as write actions. 

 The app uses synthetic demo data only and stores state in the browser for the demo. Every state-changing action writes to an audit trail. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing WebMCP tools that felt like a real agent workflow, not just buttons exposed to an agent. I had to decide which actions should be read-only, which actions change state, what guardrails belong in the outputs, and how to make the agent-human collaboration obvious in a short demo. 

 Another challenge was keeping the project public and demo-safe while still making it feel realistic. The app uses synthetic receivables and simulated payment handoffs rather than private production data or real payment credentials. 

 What I Learned 

 I learned that WebMCP is most powerful when the website exposes meaningful workflow steps, not generic UI actions. The best tools are not "click this button" wrappers. They are bounded capabilities with clear inputs, structured outputs, and human-readable audit trails. 

 What Is Next 

 A production version would connect payment handoffs to a secure backend, create payment links server-side, verify payment success through webhooks or signatures, and sync with the user's real invoice/payment system.

title: Volt
pitch: Plan EV road trips with an AI agent that compares routes, finds better chargers, and updates a shared itinerary while you inspect the map.
about_excerpt:
Plan EV road trips with an AI agent that compares routes, finds better chargers, and updates a shared itinerary while you inspect the map.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 EV route planning is a chain of tradeoffs: vehicle range, starting charge, arrival reserve, charging speed, detour time, price, and whether a stop has the amenities a driver needs. Traditional route planners make people manipulate those constraints one control at a time. Agents can help, but only if they can understand and safely update the same itinerary the driver is reviewing. 

 Volt explores a more collaborative model. The human stays grounded in a visual map, while an agent works through structured WebMCP tools that expose the route-planning decisions directly. 

 What it does 

 Volt is an interactive, charger-aware EV trip planner. Drivers can: 

 
 Select an EV profile and starting battery level. 
 Set a minimum arrival reserve. 
 Prefer charging stops near coffee, food, and restrooms. 
 Compare fastest, balanced, and comfort-focused route strategies. 
 Inspect charging power, estimated availability, price, amenities, and stop duration. 
 See every route or charging-stop change reflected immediately on the shared map. 
 

 The demo uses a Los Angeles to San Francisco corridor with realistic sample station data and four supported EV profiles. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Route planning is stateful and visual. The agent needs to know what the traveler currently sees and prefers, while the traveler needs to inspect every recommendation before relying on it. WebMCP lets Volt expose narrow, typed actions from the live page instead of forcing an agent to guess through UI controls. 

 The site registers seven JavaScript WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_trip_context reads the current vehicle, preferences, route, and stops. 
 list_vehicle_profiles lists supported EV profiles and range data. 
 find_chargers filters corridor chargers by power and amenity. 
 compare_route_options returns three complete route strategies. 
 create_trip_plan creates a route and updates the visible map. 
 set_trip_preferences changes the vehicle, reserve, or amenity preference. 
 replace_charging_stop replaces one stop in the visible itinerary. 
 

 Read tools return enough structured state to explain a recommendation. Write tools reuse the same React state and planning logic as the human interface, so agent actions and manual actions stay synchronized. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 A traveler can ask, “Keep me above 25% at every stop and find chargers with coffee.” The agent can inspect the current vehicle and route, search the charger set, update the reserve preference, compare alternatives, and apply the selected plan. The traveler immediately sees the resulting stops, duration, charging cost, and arrival battery on the map. 

 Without structured site tools, this would require brittle clicking, scraping labels, and reconstructing hidden application state. Volt gives the agent explicit operations while preserving a clear human review surface. 

 How it was built 

 
 React 19 and TypeScript for shared planner state and interactions. 
 Vinext and Vite for the application and Cloudflare-compatible build. 
 OpenAI Sites for public hosting. 
 Shadcn/Base UI components and Lucide icons for accessible controls. 
 WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool on the top-level page. 
 A fully client-side demo dataset, so judges need no credentials or API keys. 
 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing tool boundaries that were substantial without becoming overly broad. Route comparison and charger search are read operations, while applying a plan or replacing a stop changes the shared interface state. Each tool therefore has a narrow schema, a clear description, and a result that makes the action verifiable. 

 Another challenge was making agent actions visible. Volt includes a live activity card, charger detail cards, route-mode controls, and an itinerary summary so the human can always see what changed. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Seven working WebMCP tools with both read and write workflows. 
 One shared state model for manual interactions and agent actions. 
 Three coherent route strategies and six charger locations. 
 Responsive, accessible map and planner controls. 
 A complete public experience that requires no account or API key. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most useful when the interface is already good for people. The tools should not replace the product; they should expose its meaningful operations so the agent and human can collaborate on the same artifact. 

 We also learned that tool results should include verification data. Returning the applied route, selected stops, and updated preferences lets the agent explain the result and lets the interface confirm it visually. 

 What's next 

 
 Connect live charger availability and pricing providers. 
 Add nationwide routing and elevation-aware energy estimates. 
 Support saved vehicle profiles and road-trip collections. 
 Add weather, towing, and seasonal range adjustments. 
 Introduce opt-in live vehicle data adapters while keeping every external action reviewable.

title: AI Boardroom
pitch: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide.
about_excerpt: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide. Like Comment Story Updates One COO and 6 Ai Assistant Agents Inspiration Founders often need to make consequential decisions with incomplete evidence, changing constraints and too many disconnected conversations. AI Boardroom puts a founder and a browser assistant in one shared decision room where specialist perspectives, evidence and trade-offs remain visible. What it does AI Boardroom gives one browser AI six specialist perspectives: Product, Evidence, Commercial, Operations, Technology and Chair. WebMCP lets the assistant read the live brief, request named roles, post evidence-linked contributions, respond when constraints change, and retrieve the exact decision record. The central interaction is deliberately human-controlled. A fictional launch budget changes from R20,000 to R8,000; the previous recommendation becomes stale, the assistant reads the new revision, and a new recommendation can be prepared without rewriting the earlier record. The founder reviews alternatives and reservations, then approves, rejects or requests revision in the visible page form. This is stateful collaboration rather than a detached chatbot transcript. The app does not run six independent AI workers or call a model API. One browser assistant adopts the roles and the human retains the final decision. How we built it The app is built with the OpenAI Sites React and TypeScript scaffold, Vinext and D1. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes seven WebMCP tools: start_session, get_boardroom_context, update_agenda, request_perspective, add_contribution, prepare_recommendation and get_decision_record. UI actions and WebMCP tools share the same API and persistence logic. Mutation inputs use expectedRevision for optimistic concurrency and operationId for safe retries. Evidence is stored with the relevant contribution and rendered as untrusted text. The visible review channel is a workflow boundary, not proof of human identity. Challenges The design challenge was making an AI council useful without pretending that six hidden agents or automatic consensus exist. We made the roles explicit, preserved disagreement, invalidated recommendations when the brief changed, and kept approval out of the WebMCP tool surface. A second challenge was handling uncertain browser or network outcomes without duplicating or overwriting decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the agent can operate on the same visible, stateful interface as the human. Structured tools make the collaboration legible, while revision checks, evidence snapshots and a human review stop make the limits legible too. What's next Production use would require stronger identity and access controls, consent design, privacy and retention rules, abuse and rate-limit controls, independent security review, and integrations governed by explicit human approval. Disclosure All briefs, budgets, evidence and decisions in this project are fictional. The app does not make purchases, send messages, or change external systems. Browser-generated council text is created at runtime and is not preseeded consensus. title: THREAD
pitch: THREAD is a shared execution graph where humans and AI agents negotiate, simulate, and safely apply plans that can actually finish.
about_excerpt: THREAD is a shared execution graph where humans and AI agents negotiate, simulate, and safely apply plans that can actually finish. Like Comment Story Updates THREAD turns project planning into a negotiated contract: agents propose with evidence, and only humans approve. Agents can inspect, simulate, and recommend—but only a human can approve and atomically apply a plan. A live dependency graph keeps tasks, risks, constraints, critical paths, forecasts, and agent actions in one shared state. Compare Safest, Fastest, and Highest-impact proposals with exact graph changes, constraint checks, and seeded forecasts. Every approved change records its actor, reason, and evidence in the decision ledger, with full rollback available. 1. Forty-six WebMCP tools expose strict, debuggable state, backed by Cloudflare D1 persistence and browser-local recovery. Inspiration Most project-management tools tell you what needs to be done, but not whether the plan can actually succeed. A checklist might show 20 unfinished tasks while hiding the facts that only five determine the deadline, one uncertain task could delay everything, and the total plan has almost no chance of finishing with the available time and budget. AI assistants can suggest improvements, but those suggestions often remain trapped in a chat instead of becoming safe, visible changes to the real plan. I built THREAD to give humans and AI agents the same structured reality: one dependency graph, one planning engine, one simulation model, and one persistent workspace. What it does THREAD turns a goal into a living execution graph. Each task can contain: Dependencies Status and priority Minimum, expected, and maximum duration Confidence Cost Description and graph position A workspace also tracks deadlines, budgets, resources, hard constraints, risks, milestones, and available capacity. From this information, THREAD can: Calculate the critical path Identify slack, conflicts, and bottlenecks Show which tasks block the most downstream work Run reproducible Monte Carlo simulations Estimate finish probability, median completion time, P80, P95, and cost exposure Identify the risks and tasks driving schedule variance Compare immutable what-if scenarios Apply, replan, optimize, or roll back structured changes Record human, agent, system, and persistence activity The seeded demonstration models the work required to submit THREAD itself. It includes 14 tasks, 21 dependencies, three hard constraints, quantified risks, limited capacity, and a fixed budget. Its baseline simulation shows that a plan can appear reasonable while still having only about a 71% chance of finishing. Users can test alternatives such as cutting nonessential work, recruiting help, or adding more features. Every scenario runs through the same seeded engine, making comparisons reproducible rather than arbitrary. Human-agent collaboration THREAD is not a chatbot placed beside a task board. Through WebMCP, a compatible agent can directly understand and operate the project’s structured state. The live application currently exposes 38 native tools covering: Workspace, task, dependency, constraint, risk, resource, timeline, and activity retrieval Task, milestone, dependency, risk, resource, constraint, and scenario creation Task updates, completion, prioritization, movement, and risk resolution Critical-path analysis, conflict detection, bottleneck discovery, simulation, and feasibility calculation High-level plan application, optimization, replanning, scenario comparison, and rollback These tools use strict schemas and stable identifiers. Invalid relationships—including self-dependencies, duplicates, missing tasks, and dependency cycles—are rejected before they can corrupt the graph. Human actions and agent actions use the same domain services. When an agent changes a task, the human sees that change in the graph. When the human changes a constraint, the agent reads the updated value. The activity stream shows who performed each action, making agent participation visible and reversible. How I built it I designed THREAD around a shared application layer instead of implementing separate logic for the interface and WebMCP. The visual interface, planning engine, persistence system, and WebMCP tools all operate on the same workspace model. This prevents the agent-facing representation from drifting away from what the user sees. The planning engine performs deterministic critical-path calculations across the dependency graph. The simulation engine then evaluates task-duration ranges, confidence, costs, capacity, dependencies, and quantified risks across seeded iterations. Using a fixed seed means that the same plan produces the same result. That reproducibility is important when a human and agent are comparing alternatives: an improvement should come from the plan changing, not from random noise. Workspace state is persisted with Cloudflare D1, with browser-local recovery available when remote persistence cannot be reached. A dedicated WebMCP debugger displays the complete registered surface and can test read tools, mutation tools, malformed inputs, state synchronization, and reset behavior. The public demo requires no signup or API key, allowing judges to load a complete workspace immediately. Challenges The hardest challenge was keeping the human interface and agent interface synchronized. It would have been easier to create a collection of WebMCP wrappers that returned demonstration data. Instead, each tool needed to call the same validated services as the visible application and produce a real state change. Graph correctness was another challenge. Dependency editing must prevent cycles while continuously recalculating task timing, slack, and the critical path. Simulation also required care. A percentage is not useful if it cannot be explained or reproduced, so THREAD reports percentile estimates, cost ranges, failure sources, and variance drivers alongside the headline probability. Finally, I had to make a complex planning model understandable. The graph, inspector, risk panels, feasibility score, scenario cards, simulation results, and activity history all needed to reveal depth without overwhelming a first-time user. What I learned I learned that WebMCP becomes most valuable when it exposes capabilities that are difficult and unreliable to perform through visual clicking alone. An agent can retrieve an entire dependency graph, identify bottlenecks, simulate the plan, and apply a validated set of operations through structured tools. Meanwhile, the human retains the interface best suited to judgment: a visual graph, transparent comparisons, and an inspectable history. The strongest human-agent experiences do not hide the agent or replace the human. They give each participant the right interface while keeping both grounded in the same state. What I am proud of I am most proud that THREAD is more than a technical WebMCP demonstration. It is a functioning planning product with: A complete visual workspace Real dependency and risk modeling Reproducible simulation Persistent shared state A substantial native WebMCP surface Human and agent activity tracking Scenario isolation and rollback A dedicated verification console A judge-ready, no-signup demo What is next The next step is deeper plan negotiation: allowing agents to prepare several simulated proposals while humans lock non-negotiable constraints, compare visual graph differences, answer structured tradeoff questions, and approve the final plan. The long-term vision is for THREAD to become an execution environment where humans and agents do not merely discuss goals—they build, test, negotiate, and maintain a plan that has a measurable chance of succeeding. title: Roadway Design Compiler
pitch: Agent-native roadway design in the browser, powered by 39 WebMCP tools, a real geometry kernel, terrain-aware intelligence, and seamless vendor-neutral LandXML export.
about_excerpt: Agent-native roadway design in the browser, powered by 39 WebMCP tools, a real geometry kernel, terrain-aware intelligence, and seamless vendor-neutral LandXML export. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Roadway design has an unusually clear line of authority: a licensed Professional Engineer reviews, approves, and seals the work and carries personal legal responsibility for it. An agent can calculate geometry, generate alternatives, and prepare deliverables, but it cannot inherit that accountability. That made roadway engineering a strong test for WebMCP. The question was not simply “how much can the agent do?” It was: how can a website let an agent do real engineering work right up to, but never past, the point where a qualified human must decide? What it does Roadway Design Compiler is an agent-native conceptual roadway design studio with 39 WebMCP tools . From a supported agent, a user can ask the site to: read an existing design, alignment limits, curve and profile tables, cross sections, superelevation, terrain, and roadside quantities; author horizontal geometry, vertical profiles, cross-section templates, materials, template drops, coordinate systems, superelevation, and roadside items; import LandXML alignments, surfaces, site features, and as-designed reference sections; check configurable design criteria and propose multiple alternatives; create portable share links and prepare LandXML or construction-staking CSV deliverables. The key is the safety boundary. Every agent-applied change is stamped agent-proposed and enters a visible change ledger. While any proposal is unconfirmed, the site refuses both LandXML and staking exports. There is deliberately no WebMCP tool that can clear that gate. A person must review and confirm the change in the UI. This is conceptual design tooling, not construction software. The built-in criteria defaults are illustrative rather than an adopted agency standard, and every design still requires review and sealing by a licensed Professional Engineer. Why WebMCP is the right fit Traditional browser automation can manipulate fields, but it does not give an agent a trustworthy engineering contract. WebMCP lets the site expose typed, domain-specific actions and explicit refusal states. The agent chooses what to ask for; a deterministic engineering kernel decides what is geometrically and mathematically true; the human retains authority over adoption and export. That division creates a better experience for both sides: The agent can inspect the complete design instead of guessing from pixels or scraping a complex interface. It can preview a change, explain consequences, and request a commit through a typed tool. The user sees the exact proposal and its provenance in the same UI used for manual design. Safety does not depend on a prompt. The site itself enforces the confirmation and export rules. People and agents can now collaborate on a complete roadway concept—geometry, profile, corridor, criteria, terrain, alternatives, and interoperable deliverables—without pretending that the agent can take the engineer's legal role. How we built it Prior work and hackathon additions Roadway Design Compiler is an existing project that we meaningfully extended with WebMCP during the submission period (August 25–September 3, 2026). Before this period, it included a deterministic roadway geometry kernel, the RoadDesign schema and validation, a form-based Studio, LandXML export, and initial RoadBench benchmark tests. It had no agent interface. During the submission period, we built all 39 WebMCP tools and their registration bridge, preview-and-commit workflows, structured refusals, the agent activity log, and the agent-proposed change ledger with its human confirmation gate. We also added design alternatives, undo for unconfirmed changes, portable design documents, LandXML import, terrain and reference-section visualization, pavement and roadside authoring, coordinate-system support, and construction-staking CSV export. Only work added during the submission period is offered for evaluation. Our repository's prior-work breakdown and dated commit history document the distinction between the existing foundation and the hackathon additions. The application is TypeScript end to end. It registers 39 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool and validates their inputs and the cross-field design document with Zod. Tool execution returns typed results and typed refusals, while an agent activity log records calls from inside the WebMCP execute path so judges can distinguish real tool use from DOM automation. The authoritative geometry layer is a pure deterministic kernel for horizontal alignment, vertical curves, corridor sections, design criteria, superelevation, and terrain sampling. No model sits in that path. A Three.js view renders the authored corridor and imported ground; plan, profile, curve, and section views provide inspectable engineering outputs. The LandXML 1.1/1.2 importer handles alignments, TIN surfaces, site features, and reference sections. It computes geometry from coordinates instead of trusting inconsistent direction metadata, refuses unsupported spirals rather than approximating them, and pre-scans very large files before building a DOM. Before the hackathon, the exporter had been round-tripped into Bentley OpenRoads Designer as a native alignment and profile; Bentley's own annotation reproduced the curve table to 0.01 ft. The app runs on Vite and is deployed on Cloudflare. The repository includes 525 automated tests plus driver-owned browser harnesses for WebMCP registration, preview isolation, refusal→solve→commit workflows, superelevation, sealing gates, import, terrain, persistence, share links, and live deployment verification. Challenges we faced Drawing a boundary that code can actually enforce A warning in a system prompt was not enough. The difficult part was making preview, commit, provenance, confirmation, undo, and export operate as one coherent transaction model. The safest capability is sometimes an intentional omission: there is no agent tool for human confirmation. Handling real-world LandXML without fabricating data Public LandXML files vary widely. Some direction values are radians, others are degrees, and many do not say which. Some files contain hundreds of thousands of surface elements but no usable alignment. Spirals appear frequently, but this kernel does not model them yet. We chose explicit refusals over silent approximation, because a wrong road that looks plausible is more dangerous than a clear error. Keeping engineering truth deterministic The agent should decide what question to ask, not what the answer should be. Geometry, stopping-sight-distance relationships, K values, superelevation, runoff, cut/fill sign conventions, and export contents are computed by tested code with every coefficient disclosed as an input. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a tool description is not just an API hint but a declaration of responsibility. Typed refusals, preview-only execution, and site-enforced authority boundaries make agent behavior easier to understand and audit. We also learned that imported context must preserve provenance: existing survey features, terrain, and another designer's sections should remain clearly distinguishable from the active design. Accomplishments we are proud of A complete human/agent roadway workflow across 39 tools. A hard, demonstrable export gate that an agent cannot bypass. 525 automated tests and a live activity log proving WebMCP execution. Interoperable LandXML validated in production roadway-design software before the hackathon, providing the foundation for the new WebMCP export workflow. Fast indexed terrain sampling, portable no-account design links, and explicit refusals for unsupported or unsafe cases. What's next Next steps include clothoid spiral support, end-area earthwork volumes, agency-specific criteria packs supplied by the user, broader LandXML interoperability fixtures, collaborative review, and additional CAD round-trip validation. title: True GEO Engine
pitch: WebMCP enables True GEO Engine to discover where your website is invisible to AI, identify gaps, and guide improvements. helping make your site more discoverable, understandable, and actionable.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP enables True GEO Engine to discover where your website is invisible to AI, identify gaps, and guide improvements. helping make your site more discoverable, understandable, and actionable.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 TRUE GEO ENGINE 

 Inspiration 

 Search stopped being the only front door. People now ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude what to buy, who to trust, and which vendor to shortlist — and a brand either appears in that answer or it doesn't. Marketing teams have twenty years of tooling for the blue-links era and almost nothing for this one. 

 The tools that do exist have a credibility problem. Most GEO dashboards burn API budget hammering four models with the same prompt, then present whatever came back as if it were a measurement. Run it twice and the numbers move. That isn't visibility analytics — it's a screenshot of a coin flip. 

 We wanted the opposite: an evidence workspace where the same input always produces the same output , every synthetic value is labeled as synthetic, and no .env file, API key, or paid inference is needed to see exactly how the reasoning works. If a claim can't be traced to a rule and a row, it shouldn't appear on the screen. 

 What it does 

 TRUE GEO ENGINE is a brand- and industry-agnostic GEO/AEO workspace with two independent workflows that never share evidence. 

 AI Visibility takes one public page URL as a deterministic seed and generates a synthetic raw-HTML versus post-hydration comparison — without fetching the target page. The post-hydration state supplies one ordered master list of h1 – h6 , p , li , figcaption , blockquote , and td blocks. Both columns render that identical list in identical order, and each block is marked Fully extractable or Not visible to AI by signature membership: 

 status ( b ) = { Fully extractable if  σ ( b ) ∈ Σ raw   Not visible to AI otherwise 

 where $\sigma(b)$ is the normalized signature of block $b$ and $\Sigma_{\text{raw}}$ is the signature set of the synthetic raw HTML. Metadata, Schema.org JSON-LD types, and FAQ schema live in a separate machine-readable-signals section so structural signals never inflate the content score. Four deterministic crawler perspectives vary the evidence feeding answer-engine scores. Private-network URLs are rejected. 

 Run a Prompt replays a selected prompt from a bundled fictional benchmark — no LLM call, no API key, no page URL, no external request. The catalog holds eight scenarios across automotive, B2B technology, financial services, healthcare, travel, telecommunications, consumer products, and education. Each carries one high-intent prompt and measured brand, a benchmark answer, three competitors, four evidence sources, four answer-engine interpretations, and six sentiment topics. At runtime it expands to 

 8  prompts × 4  engines × 6  dimensions = 192  deterministic evidence rows 

 from which the pipeline computes visibility, coverage and citation rate, sentiment and recommendation quality, competitor leaders, ranked answer gaps, and next steps. 

 Both workflows populate the same five views — AI visibility, answer engine scores, content/answer gaps, next steps, and agent activity — while results stay isolated, so URL evidence is never relabeled as prompt evidence. 

 Eight WebMCP tools are registered imperatively in the browser, letting an agent drive the workspace directly: 

 
 
 Tool 
 Purpose 
 
 
 
 geo_ai_visibility_audit 
 Generate the synthetic URL-scoped page analysis 
 
 
 geo_analyze_prompt 
 Replay one exact prompt from the curated benchmark 
 
 
 geo_visibility_overview 
 Read the active score and evidence components 
 
 
 geo_list_tools 
 Export the browser WebMCP catalog 
 
 
 geo_content_gaps 
 Explain one ranked gap from active evidence 
 
 
 geo_generate_next_steps 
 Open page- or prompt-specific next steps 
 
 
 geo_download_package 
 Download the active evidence package 
 
 
 geo_export_action_plan 
 Export the active action plan 
 
 

 Each workflow exports a 16-file ZIP — disclosure, consolidated llms.txt , FAQs, JSON-LD and schema, preview HTML, the block audit or benchmark answers, scores, gaps, action plan, and WebMCP manifests. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js and TypeScript, with Drizzle for schema and a Vite-driven test setup. The whole app runs from npm run dev with no .env , no key, and no network dependency for either challenge workflow. 

 Determinism layer: 

 
 lib/synthetic-page-scan.ts — URL-derived raw and hydrated fixtures plus the four simulated crawler perspectives 
 lib/page-audit.ts — the ordered block classifier and structural-signal extractor 
 lib/visibility-scanner.ts — URL-scoped prompt and score analysis fed by those fixtures 
 

 Benchmark layer: 

 
 components/true-geo/demo-prompts.json — the curated benchmark, single source of truth 
 components/true-geo/demo-prompts.ts — deterministic expansion into the 192 evidence rows 
 

 Interface layer: 

 
 components/true-geo/TrueGeoApp.tsx — isolated workflow state and all tab wiring 
 components/true-geo/PageVisibilityAudit.tsx — the aligned Human vs AI block view 
 components/true-geo/PromptBar.tsx — mode pills, prompt selector, URL input 
 components/true-geo/page-audit.ts — the audit data model and client normalization 
 

 WebMCP layer: components/true-geo/webmcp.ts registers directly against the browser contract, and tool-manifest.ts keeps a portable catalog of the same eight tools so the manifest can travel with an export: 
 document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: entry.name,
 title: entry.title,
 description: entry.description,
 inputSchema: entry.inputSchema,
 execute: async (input) => JSON.stringify(await execute(entry.name, input)),
});
 
 API surface: POST /api/page-audit { url } , plus deterministic prompt and visibility endpoints. services/page-renderer/ holds an optional local Playwright reference for future live auditing — deliberately not wired into the public routes. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Keeping two workflows from bleeding into each other. Both feed the same five views, which makes cross-contamination easy and disastrous — a page-derived gap shown under a prompt run is a fabricated claim. We had to make workflow isolation a property of the state model itself rather than something the UI remembers to respect. 

 Making a schema that can't be misused. geo_analyze_prompt was an obvious injection point: give it a free-text field and an agent will pass an arbitrary prompt the benchmark has no data for, and the pipeline will happily score it. We constrained the field to the eight bundled catalog values and removed any URL or model parameter, so the tool cannot be talked into analyzing something that doesn't exist. 

 Honest columns are harder than pretty ones. The first Human vs AI view built each column from its own source, which meant the two lists drifted out of alignment and the comparison stopped meaning anything. Deriving both columns from one ordered master list and marking extractability per block was more constrained but is the only version where a row-by-row read is truthful. 

 Labeling everything without burying the product. Every synthetic value and every downloaded file needed a disclosure, and it would have been easy to end up with a workspace that reads like a legal notice. Getting "verify before publishing" to sit visibly on results and exports without drowning the analysis took more iteration than the scoring math. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Reproducible by construction — the same URL or prompt always yields the same evidence, so two people looking at one run see one set of numbers 
 Zero-key, zero-quota, zero-network for both challenge workflows; a reviewer clones, runs npm run dev , and sees the full product 
 192 evidence rows from a transparent expansion , not from an opaque model call 
 Eight WebMCP tools registered imperatively, plus a portable manifest that ships inside the exports 
 A schema that refuses out-of-catalog input rather than scoring it anyway 
 SSRF-conscious from the start — private-network URLs are rejected at the boundary 
 Synthetic labeled as synthetic , everywhere, including inside every one of the 32 exported files 
 

 What we learned 

 Determinism is a feature users can feel. We expected reviewers to treat the simulated benchmark as a limitation. In practice, being able to re-run a prompt and get the identical answer made the tool feel more trustworthy than a live-model version would have. 

 A tool schema is an access-control surface. Once an agent can call your functions, an unconstrained string field is an open door. Enumerating valid values isn't a UX nicety — it's what stops

title: 2D Room Planner
pitch: "Move the desk toward the window for the light, stay 80 cm from the bed, don't block the door." WebMCP lets the agent check that in centimetres, not pixels, then show you the floor plan.
about_excerpt: "Move the desk toward the window for the light, stay 80 cm from the bed, don't block the door." WebMCP lets the agent check that in centimetres, not pixels, then show you the floor plan. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most layout tools give the person and the assistant different information. The person sees a plan drawn to scale. The assistant sees a screenshot and guesses from it. That is how you get a wardrobe door that cannot open, a walkway 12 cm too narrow, or a desk that looks centred but sits a few centimetres to one side. I wanted the agent to work from the same measurements a designer would use, and I wanted the person to watch it work and step in whenever they want. WebMCP is how the agent gets the model the page draws from instead of a picture of it. What it does Room Planner is a 2D layout tool in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. You create a room by size or from a template, add furniture from presets or as custom rectangles, and arrange it by dragging, by typing exact coordinates, or with the keyboard. It puts doors and windows on any wall, flags collisions, out-of-bounds objects, and blocked door clearances, and lets you add rules such as "keep 80 cm between the bed and the wall" that turn green or red as you edit. Measurements are in centimetres and the plan persists to localStorage . How I built it Room Planner is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no build step and no dependencies. The floor plan is one JavaScript object that everything reads from. An SVG renderer draws it, and the WebMCP tools change it, both through the same update and validation code, so an agent edit and a hand edit are the same operation underneath. The geometry, including footprints, overlaps, distances, and clearances, is plain functions working in centimetres. The WebMCP layer registers on navigator.modelContext or document.modelContext when a host is present and falls back to a built-in shim otherwise, so the tools behave the same either way. I used several AI models and providers while building this, each on the parts it handled best, from writing code to checking the geometry to finding edge cases. Challenges I ran into Rotation math caused the most rework. xCm and yCm mark the top-left corner before rotation, but at 90 and 270 degrees width and depth swap for collision and distance checks. Getting that consistent across the renderer, the geometry module, and the tool schemas took several passes. Keeping the agent and the UI in sync was subtler. Any mutation that bypassed the shared update code could leave a layout that passed the validity badge while breaking a constraint. I routed every WebMCP tool through the same store mutations the UI uses. WebMCP itself is experimental. Neither the spec's document.modelContext nor the browser's navigator.modelContext is widely available, so I wrote a shim, a simulated host, and a console bridge that all call the same execute functions. Exporting a clean SVG took some care. It renders correctly outside the page only after every CSS class is inlined and every oklch() colour is converted to sRGB, with the capture clipped to the plan and no app chrome. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am a perfectionist, and I have lost whole evenings to a single floor plan. There is always a constraint you cannot see coming, or a sequence of moves that checks out at every step and then wrecks something you fixed earlier. Chatting with an agent that could actually reason about the geometry while I watched the plan take shape on screen was the best part of building this. What I learned Grounding did more for reliability than autonomy did. Once the agent had exact geometry, ordinary requests started working, and once every change animated on the canvas, people trusted the agent because they could see and undo what it did. Returning the validation result with every mutation removed most of the "did that work?" follow-up calls. Building against an unshipped spec is workable when the shim and the simulated host share code with the real path. What's next for the room planner? A 3D preview beside the 2D plan, from the same model. More constraint types: sight lines, traffic flow, natural-light scoring, accessibility clearances. Multi-room plans with shared walls and doorways. Agent-proposed layouts, such as "give me three arrangements that seat six people," with the person picking one to refine. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: ReliefMesh
pitch: A WebMCP-powered food-rescue workspace where AI agents create explainable meal-allocation plans and people approve every real-world commitment.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered food-rescue workspace where AI agents create explainable meal-allocation plans and people approve every real-world commitment.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 I was inspired by the amount of good food that can go to waste while community kitchens and shelters still need meals. I wanted to explore how an AI agent could help with this work without making decisions by itself. 

 ReliefMesh is a food-rescue coordination demo. It shows food offers, partner needs, meal quantities, dietary fit, and pickup windows. An agent can inspect this information and suggest a rescue plan. The plan is shown clearly in the app before approval. A person must review it and give the exact ``confirmation before the app records approval. 

 I build this app with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool to register five tools: inspecting rescue context, proposing a plan, staging an allocation, approving an allocation, and generating a pickup manifest. I deployed the project on ChatGPT sites and added the headers needed for WebMCP. 

 The main challenge was making the AI useful without giving it too much control. I separated planning from approval so that the agent can suggest and stage a plan but cannot make a commitment on its own. Another challenge was testing WebMCP in a supported browser. I also checked that document.modelContext was available and that all five tools were registered before recording the demo. 

 The project successfully registers five WebMCP tools in a supported browser. I am proud of the safety design: the plan is visible before approval, the confirmation must be explicit, and the demo never sends a real-world dispatch or notification. 

 I learned that a tool should say exactly what it can do and what information it uses. Also, that's how browser permissions, isolation headers, and structured tool inputs affect WebMCP. The biggest lesson was that human approval is not a limitation; it is an important part of a safe workflow. 

 

 
 Built With 

 chatgpt-sites css3 html5 javascript webmcp 
 

 
 Try it out 

 
 
 
 GitHub Repo 
 
 
 

 

 

 
 
 Submitted to

 I designed and built ReliefMesh as an individual project. I defined the food-rescue use case, designed the user interface and human-approval workflow, implemented the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application, and registered the five WebMCP tools. I tested WebMCP registration in Microsoft Edge, deployed the live app on ChatGPT Sites, created the GitHub repository and documentation, recorded the demo video, and prepared the Devpost submission materials.

title: PaperPup
pitch: A research library your AI can't wander out of — by design.
about_excerpt: A research library your AI can't wander out of — by design. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration PaperPup started as a personal itch, not a hackathon idea. It was needed to manage a real research library. There were real-world stakes in turning a recognized pattern of investigatory practices into a structured and AI-instrumented process. The frustration that actually drove the design: ask a general AI chatbot to help with research, and it happily answers from the whole internet, or from memory, or both — not from the specific papers you actually collected and have deemed useful. Drafts as well that needed controlled tests run against them against the literature that supported the research. Anyone who has followed a chatbot down a research rabbit hole and landed somewhere completely off-target knows the feeling. PaperPup was built to make that structurally impossible, not just less likely. WebMCP entered the picture partway through, and it fit almost too well. PaperPup already had a strict internal discipline — Library, Stack, and Room, each granting a narrower set of capabilities than the last with clear demarcation between them in the form of hand-off briefs. WebMCP was a way to expose any of that to an external agent with the demarcation points mapped to WebMCP site tools by context, and it was a natural fit. The hackathon became the deadline attached to work already in motion, not the reason the work started. What it does PaperPup is a personal, single-tenant research library. It is not a shared or social platform, and is organized around three deliberately narrowing contexts: Library — search, add, and organize the papers you've actually collected. Stack — pull a working set of papers together and investigate them with an AI, grounded only in that set. Room — promote a mature stack into a frozen, bounded investigation. The corpus locks at that point — nothing added, nothing removed, except through one specific human-approved channel. WebMCP added a twist to that because now the human had an AI agent on their side that, unlike the agents that PaperPup sandboxes and uses to pit literature against literature, this new agent was the user. Inside a Room is a bit more locked down for all because an investigating agent has constraints that make it genuinely useful. It can read the papers, follow a citation to a source that should be there but isn't yet, and propose adding it. What it can't do is add that source itself, or search outside the frozen set to find something else instead. There's no tool call that does either of those things registered in that context — not a rule the agent is trusting to follow, a door that structurally doesn't exist. WebMCP is what lets any AI agent someone already uses — ChatGPT, or any other WebMCP-capable client — work inside this system directly, live, in the same browser tab and session, rather than through a bespoke chat widget bolted onto the page. That enabled bring your own agent; PaperPup supplies the grounding. How we built it PaperPup is a Next.js app backed by PostgreSQL, with an adapter layer pulling papers from Zenodo, OpenAlex/Unpaywall, arXiv, bioRxiv, and CORE, plus citation resolution against PubMed and Crossref. The WebMCP layer lives entirely under one subfolder, src/webmcp/ : a declarative manifest.js listing every tool's name, schema, and which contexts register it; register.js , which walks that manifest and calls the real document.modelContext.registerTool() API, managing one AbortController per tool so the whole set can be cleanly unregistered and re-registered on every navigation; envelope.js , which maps the current context — library, stack, room, or nothing selected yet — to the tools that should be live; and one thin handler per tool. Every handler reaches application logic only over HTTPS, never a direct import of server-only code — a boundary now enforced by an automated test that walks the whole import graph and fails on any reach into the backend and database layer. Tools scoped to one specific stack or room don't take that stack or room id as a parameter - it is read directly from the page's own state since a tool visible only inside one specific room already proves which room that is. Asking the calling model to name it back would just be redundant. The user's agent translates both ways for the user to have flexibility in identifying resources in prompts and reading the responses after their agent has formatted the PaperPup response to present it however that agent knows their user likes to communicate. We tested against a real host end to end — ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled models — and, for fast local iteration before and alongside that, against @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , a real implementation of the same browser API with a dev-only testing shim for invoking tools directly with no AI client connected at all. Claude (architecture and design) and Claude Code (implementation and live verification) were genuine build partners throughout — a fitting way to build a project about grounding external-to-system AI agents in trustworthy work. Challenges we ran into A permission model that could actually be violated in code, even after we thought we'd designed it out. Early on, a Room-context tool for reading a paper's metadata took a global paper id. That meant there was nothing stopping an agent from simply naming a paper outside the room's frozen set and getting it back anyway. The interface didn't expose search, so it looked safe. The fix was structural, not a permission check: that tool now takes a position within the room's own paper list, not a global id. There's no way to even construct a request for something outside scope, because the parameter itself can't express it. This ended up being the single most important architectural decision in the whole submission — a stronger guarantee than any runtime check could offer. A crash that taught us to build a permanent test, not just fix the bug. One early handler reached for a server-only database module directly instead of going through an HTTP route, and it pulled pg straight into the browser bundle — crashing the app outright the moment that code path loaded. We fixed the immediate bug, then built an automated test that walks the entire import graph under the WebMCP layer and fails on any reach into server-only code, so the same mistake can't happen again silently. Getting genuine live verification, not just something that looked right in code. ChatGPT's WebMCP support turned out to depend on which underlying model was selected. One variant has it disabled entirely, which looks identical to a bug in your own tool descriptions if you don't know to check. The in-app browser also has no visible developer console by default, so confirming what was actually happening required either asking the model to report it back, or falling back to a real polyfill running locally for a tighter dev loop. Turns out, this was quite useful to see and gave us insights in how to structure the descriptions in our WebMCP site tool descriptions that allow the user's agent to learn the capabilities impressively well. Realizing a two-dimensional problem was actually a one-dimensional one. A room's frozen corpus can span multiple stacks, which made stack-plus-position addressing feel necessary at first. Checking it against an existing invariant — that a room's assigned stacks are frozen and can't change after assignment — showed a flat position across the room's whole corpus was just as safe and considerably simpler. The extra complexity wasn't buying anything. Accomplishments that we're proud of That the room-envelope guarantee is real, not asserted. An agent working inside a frozen investigation cannot search or read past its bounds. This can be confirmed by trying, not just by design intent, and it is immensely useful when running control tests whereby a standing agent must defend a corpus using only what is in that room. The only out is that the room's agent can propose a source, such as a citation reference that it wants the full text for, and the user must then intervene to approve whether that visibility will be allowed. Configurable of course, but that is a sizable document in itself to describe the capabilities envisioned and being built. That we built the discipline to actually verify claims rather than trust that code looked right: a manifest-invariants test that caught its own first-draft bug immediately; a boundary test proven with a deliberate red-then-green check rather than accepted on a single clean pass; a live investigation's output cross-checked word-by-word against the source papers to confirm it wasn't quietly blending in outside knowledge. That the two-way collaboration model — an agent can discover and propose, a human retains final authority, and neither side can silently override the other — came out of the architecture cleanly, rather than needing to be bolted on as an afterthought.
