title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Duet Studio
pitch: A step sequencer where a human and an agent edit the same song at the same time, with provenance, scoped selections and approval built into the tools.
about_excerpt: A step sequencer where a human and an agent edit the same song at the same time, with provenance, scoped selections and approval built into the tools. Like Comment Story Updates Amber is the human's, violet the agent's. The teal range is a live selection, handed over as edit_selection. Every tool call is logged. DevTools, Application > WebMCP: live tool calls with input and output, and the 18 tools including the selection-only edit_selection. Duet Studio is a step sequencer and piano roll that exposes the song itself to your browser agent — and then lets both of you work on it at once. You tap in a kick, the agent writes the hats, you drag a bass note, the agent adapts the chords — all in one grid, while the loop keeps playing. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Most agent integrations run one turn at a time: the agent produces something, then hands the interface back. A live instrument breaks that model. The loop is playing, the human is tapping in a kick while the agent is writing a hi-hat, and both are editing the same sixteen steps. Simultaneous editing raises questions a single-turn integration never has to answer. Who authored this note? How does the agent learn what the human changed since its last read? How does the human aim the agent at one region instead of the whole song? What happens when the agent proposes something destructive? Screenshots and clicks cannot carry any of that — and an agent cannot hear the loop it is editing. So the song has to be a structured, shared document, and the tool surface has to carry authorship, change awareness, scope and consent. get_song returns the arrangement as a compact text grid plus transport and selection state, so the agent "sees" what the human hears. It also stays inside Chrome's output guidance on a song of any size: it shortens long note lists until the overview fits and points the agent at get_song track="<id>" for one track in full. set_drum_pattern , set_notes , set_chords , humanize and set_tempo let it write musically rather than mechanically — at the level of groove, harmony and dynamics instead of simulating fifty clicks. The imperative API is what makes the surface honest: the tool set changes with the UI. Shift-drag a range of steps and an eighteenth tool, edit_selection , is registered and scoped to exactly that range; clear the selection and it is unregistered through its AbortSignal . The agent never sees a tool that does not match what is on screen. Prior art, and what is different here OpenAI's own WebMCP showcase includes Fieldwork // 12, a browser beat machine where Codex composes a beat, adjusts its groove and shapes sounds through site tools. It is the closest reference point to this project, and the overlap is real: both are browser sequencers driven by WebMCP. The thesis is different. Fieldwork // 12 shows that an agent can produce a track you then edit. Duet Studio asks what WebMCP needs to look like when both sides edit at once — and everything below follows from that question: Provenance in the grid. Every step and every note carries its author; agent cells are violet, human cells amber. Selection-scoped tools. edit_selection exists only while the human holds a selection. Dynamic registration and AbortSignal unregistration are used as a live collaboration primitive, not as a demo of the API. Change awareness. get_recent_changes gives the agent a diff of human activity since its own last read — with the exact step index each edit touched — so the two sides stay in sync without a full re-read. Approval as part of the tool contract. Destructive tools block on an in-app confirmation the agent cannot bypass, and the result tells it what the human decided. Shared history. One commit path, one undo stack and one session log across both actors. Harmony, not only rhythm. A piano roll with scales, chord voicing and key-aware helpers alongside the drum grid. Host resilience. The page runs against hosts that implement only document.modelContext.registerTool , proven by a dedicated smoke suite. How it creates a better user experience Nothing is hidden behind a chat window. The studio opens on a finished two-bar loop credited to the human, so there is something to react to on the first screen and the agent's first edit stands out against it. The human keeps the transport running, taps in a kick, drags a note, mutes a track — and the agent's edits land in the same grid, tinted violet, while the human's stay amber. Every cell and every note carries its provenance. A session log lists each tool call with a one-click revert, and a shared undo history covers both parties. Edits are heard on the next sixteenth note; playback never restarts. Destructive actions such as clear_song open an approve/decline dialog in the app, and the tool result tells the agent what the human decided. The grid scrolls inside its own panel and the controls wrap, so the studio is usable on a phone as well as on a desktop. No account, no sign-in. The studio, the audio and the whole song live in the browser. It feels like two people at one instrument rather than a form being filled in. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Point and delegate. Shift-drag four steps and say "make this a snare fill" — the agent acts on exactly that range, because the range is a tool. Compose against a moving target. Ask for a bassline in the song's key and watch it appear while the loop plays; then move a note by hand and let the agent read the change through get_recent_changes and adapt the chords to it. Delegate craft, keep taste. Let the agent tidy velocities across the whole kit in one call, then undo just that if you disagree. Borrow music theory. Scales, chord voicings and groove conventions come from the agent; direction and the final say stay with the human. None of this is reachable by screen-scraping a sequencer grid. How we implemented WebMCP Each tool is a plain object — name, title, description, JSON schema, execute — in src/lib/webmcp/tools.ts . A React effect registers each one with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , typed with the official webmcp-types , and aborts the signal to unregister on unmount: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "set_drum_pattern", title: "Write drum pattern", description: "Write a 16-step pattern onto a drum track", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }, { signal }); 18 tools: 17 always available, plus edit_selection , which exists only while the human holds a selection. Read tools are annotated readOnlyHint: true ; outputs are capped well under 1,500 characters so a tool result stays cheap to reason about. Every mutation goes through commit(actor, label, mutate) , which records provenance per cell and per note, feeds the undo history, and appends to the session log. Errors throw with actionable text — No track matches "nope". Available: Kick (id 9fIVdodL), Snare (id tO9qZ20b), Hats (id n-D3x3_B)… — and reach the agent as isError results. User-authored text is marked as untrusted content. Host compatibility is defensive. ChatGPT's in-app browser exposes a plain object with only registerTool — no getTools , executeTool or addEventListener . Everything past registerTool is feature-checked, and WebMCP-facing widgets sit inside error boundaries. A dedicated probe ( bun run smoke:hosts ) injects a minimal document.modelContext both at load and 2.5 s late to prove the page survives it. A headless Chromium test ( bun run smoke ) drives the real getTools() / executeTool() API to assert registration, titles and annotations, validation errors, the dynamic selection tool, playback, the confirmation flow, a share link that reopens the song in a fresh browser context, output sizes, and a clean console. The tools are also covered by an eval suite. evals/duet-studio.json holds fourteen cases of what a user would plausibly say plus the tool calls each should produce, in the format of Chrome's own webmcp-evals CLI; bun run evals executes all 21 steps against the live page, no model and no API key required. A fallback agent ships in the page: with a visitor's own OpenAI key it discovers the same tools through getTools() and calls them with executeTool() , so the WebMCP surface is exercisable in any Chrome with the flag, not only in an agent browser. Architecture Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4 and shadcn/ui. Tone.js drives live and offline audio (the sequencer re-reads the song every sixteenth note, which is why agent edits are heard immediately); Tonal handles music theory; Zustand + Zundo hold state and undo history; @tonejs/midi exports MIDI and Tone renders WAV offline. The studio is client-only — the sole server code is a share endpoint that swaps a song for a ten-character /?s=<id> link, size-caps the body and re-parses it before storing; with no blob store connected the browser falls back to a self-contained lz-string link. title: AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence
pitch: A WebMCP-native command center enabling people and AI agents to securely discover, compare, prioritize, and shortlist business opportunities using structured web tools.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native command center enabling people and AI agents to securely discover, compare, prioritize, and shortlist business opportunities using structured web tools.

 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence: WebMCP-powered decision support for people and AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live opportunity dashboard showing structured records, decision scores, deadlines, and the shared shortlist. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence: WebMCP-powered decision support for people and AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live opportunity dashboard showing structured records, decision scores, deadlines, and the shared shortlist. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence: WebMCP-powered decision support for people and AI agents. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Business owners and innovation teams face more opportunities than they can manually assess. Key information is often scattered across dashboards, websites, documents, and portals. Traditional browser agents must interpret visual interfaces and guess which controls to use, resulting in slow and unreliable performance. 

 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence introduces a new approach: a website designed for both people and AI agents. WebMCP enables the site to present clear, structured capabilities while maintaining the visual experience and user control. 

 What it does 

 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence serves as a WebMCP-enabled opportunity command center. Users can instruct an AI agent to: 

 
 List the opportunities available on the page 
 Compare two opportunities using their scores, strategic fit, deadlines, and other decision factors 
 Add a selected opportunity to the shortlist 
 

 The agent uses registered website tools rather than guessing through the interface. Because the page and agent share the same context, results appear directly in the user interface. 

 The prototype shows how WebMCP can support business research, innovation portfolios, grant discovery, accelerator applications, procurement opportunities, and other decision-intensive workflows. 

 How we built it 

 We developed a responsive web application with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, and deployed it on Vercel. The application registers structured WebMCP tools with defined names, descriptions, inputs, and outputs. 

 The core tools support three stages of the decision workflow: 

 
 Opportunity discovery 
 Side-by-side comparison 
 User-directed shortlisting 
 

 The interface displays structured opportunity records, and the WebMCP layer provides agents with reliable access to these capabilities. We tested the deployed application using ChatGPT’s in-app browser by issuing natural-language requests and confirming the correct tools were identified and executed. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our main challenge was designing tools that were useful to agents without being too broad or ambiguous. Tool descriptions, parameter schemas, opportunity identifiers, and results needed to be predictable. 

 We also needed to make agent interactions visible and understandable to users. Because shortlisting changes application state, the workflow required clear intent and observable feedback instead of hidden automation. 

 Testing an emerging browser standard required validating both the traditional user interface and the agent-driven experience. 

 Accomplishments that we’re proud of 

 
 Built and deployed a working WebMCP-enabled application 
 Registered multiple focused tools instead of one unrestricted tool 
 Demonstrated an end-to-end agent workflow 
 Enabled structured comparison between opportunities 
 Connected an agent action to visible shortlist state 
 Preserved a useful interface for people who interact with the site manually 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how websites communicate their capabilities. Visual design remains important for users, while structured tools give agents clearer instructions and more reliable actions. 

 We also learned that the most effective agent tools are focused, well-described, and based on visible application state. Human control and transparency become increasingly important as agent capabilities grow. 

 What’s next 

 Next, we plan to expand the prototype into a comprehensive AIZOYA portfolio command center with authenticated workspaces, live opportunity sources, evidence-backed scoring, deadlines, reminders, bilingual support, audit history, and approval controls for key actions. 

 Our long-term vision is a human-centered intelligence system that enables organizations and their AI agents to discover opportunities, evaluate them consistently, and act more quickly and with greater accountability.

title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. title: Agent SEO Studio
pitch: Point your AI agent at any site: it audits AI-search readiness, ranks you against competitors, and writes the fixes - 13 WebMCP tools it calls by name while you watch and steer.
about_excerpt: Point your AI agent at any site: it audits AI-search readiness, ranks you against competitors, and writes the fixes - 13 WebMCP tools it calls by name while you watch and steer. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration SEO asked one question for twenty years: 'can Google read my page?' Then GEO arrived - 'can an AI assistant cite my answer?' We think WebMCP opens the one that actually matters next: 'can the agent finish the job on my site?' The unlock clicked when we realized an AI agent literally cannot answer "is my website ready for AI search?" from a browser. It can't fetch other sites cross-origin — CORS blocks it. It can't read the HTML only a server sees. It can only guess from training data. Those are exactly the gaps WebMCP is built to close: the page hands the agent real, named tools that do the work the agent can't do alone. So we built a studio where a business owner and their agent audit, rank, and repair a site together — and, because it felt right, made the studio able to audit whether a site is itself WebMCP-ready. What we built Agent SEO Studio registers 13 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . An agent can audit a site's AI-search readiness, compare it against competitors, mystery-shop whether an agent could book/buy/contact on it, scan a whole market server-side, generate ready-to-paste JSON-LD fixes, and project the score climbing. Every tool call renders into a shared on-screen workspace the human watches and steers — and a live dashboard counts every agent call by tool and by AI engine, a metric no static SEO tool can show. How we built it Frontend + tools: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, deployed on Vercel. The WebMCP layer ( src/lib/register-tools.ts ) registers tools with the standard registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) shape and returns MCP { content: [{ type: "text", text }] } results. Tools reach the app through a thin StudioBridge seam, so the tool layer never touches React directly. Server route ( /api/audit ) does the cross-origin fetch + deterministic measurement, guarded by an SSRF check that blocks private/metadata IPs and re-validates every redirect hop. Market discovery uses OpenStreetMap's Overpass API (keyless). Fix generation is provider-agnostic — OpenAI or Anthropic — with a deterministic template fallback so the demo always produces valid output and never fabricates facts. State-dependent tools: verify_fix and export_report register the moment the first audit lands; analyze_gaps after a market scan — so an agent that re-reads the tool list finds actions that weren't there a step ago. Challenges we faced CORS is the whole point — and the whole problem. The reason this needs WebMCP (agents can't fetch cross-origin) is also what forced every measurement server-side. We leaned in: the server-side fetch is the product. Honest confidence for check_webmcp . A static server fetch can't run the JavaScript that registers a site's tools at runtime — so "is this site WebMCP-ready?" can't always be answered with certainty. Rather than fake it, the tool reports its confidence honestly (confirmed in served markup vs. likely from a linked bundle vs. none). Never guess. Our hardest self-imposed rule: every finding must trace to a fact observed in the page's HTML. A site that doesn't load scores 0 with a reason ; a JavaScript-rendered SPA is flagged as such, not falsely accused of having no content. Backed by 57 unit tests on the pure logic. Tools that don't stall the agent. A raw rejection is opaque to an agent and stops it cold, so every tool is wrapped to return a descriptive text miss instead of throwing — "loose schema, strict code." What we learned WebMCP is less about "add tools to a page" and more about designing a surface a human and an agent share. The tools that felt best weren't the ones that did the most — they were the ones whose results landed somewhere the human could see and redirect . And the honest-confidence work on check_webmcp taught us that the most trustworthy agent tool is one that knows, and says, what it can't be sure of. title: Pokefinder.app WebMCP
pitch: Pokémon cards scattered across stores and priced differently. We built the agent-driven marketplace that turns 30min of tab-switching into a 30sec conversation: search, compare, buy, all by asking.
about_excerpt: Pokémon cards scattered across stores and priced differently. We built the agent-driven marketplace that turns 30min of tab-switching into a 30sec conversation: search, compare, buy, all by asking. Like 4 Comment 2 Story Updates Adding card to a basket Getting card details Listing top 10 Pokemon sets Analyzing card image and identifying card by its image Inspiration PokéFinder started because my son wanted to track down a few rare Pokémon cards. We tried eBay first and quickly ran into the usual problems: noisy listings, inconsistent naming, and the same card priced differently across a dozen stores. So we built PokeFinder.App to make the search easier. It brings live listings from Shopify Catalog together in one structured place through UCP, then enriches them with set, rarity, and grading data from the Pokémon TCG API. When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, the idea immediately made sense to us. The hard part of buying Pokémon cards is not simply finding listings. It is knowing enough about the hobby to make sense of them: holo versus reverse holo, set codes, grading, and which cards were released last week. An LLM can close that knowledge gap, but only if it can do more than answer questions in a chat window. It needs to work with the page alongside the user. That is what made WebMCP so interesting to us: it turns “AI can help you shop” into “AI can shop with you.” Whether someone is a lifelong collector or a complete beginner, the experience can meet them where they are. What it does PokéFinder is a single-page marketplace where humans and AI agents shop the same catalog side-by-side. A user can browse trending cards or every connected store, search by card name, set, or rarity, snap a photo and let AI identify it, filter by country, currency, price, or grading, compare prices across stores, save cards to a wishlist, sign in with magic link or Google or Discord or Shopify, and check out. An AI agent can do all of the same things by driving the page directly. PokéFinder registers thirteen tools through WebMCP. They split into three categories: Data queries (also exposed via MCP for external agents): search_pokemon_cards —> search the live catalog across every connected store browse_card_database —> browse all cards with full pagination get_card_details —> fetch the full detail page for a specific card list_sets —> list every Pokémon card set currently in the catalog find_cards_in_set —> find all cards within a specific set get_filter_taxonomy —> return the filter fields with brief explanations for non-experts get_featured_cards —> return the curated featured / trending cards compare_prices —> compare prices for the same card across every connected store Image / AI (also exposed via MCP): analyze_card_image —> extract set, rarity, grading, and condition from a card photo identify_card_image —> identify the card from a photo, then return matching listings Page actions (WebMCP-unique, these are what the agent-driven web unlocks): highlight_card —> light up a specific card on the live page so the user sees exactly which one was selected apply_filter —> filter the visible grid by price, country, rarity, or grading add_to_basket —> add a chosen card to the cart The data and image tools give the agent everything it needs to reason about the catalog. The page-action tools give it the ability to drive what the user actually sees. How we built it We started with the PokéFinder backend we had already built: a Cloudflare Worker in front of the UCP catalog, plus a D1 mirror of the Pokémon TCG database for metadata enrichment. That foundation already gave us a strong search experience. The WebMCP layer was the new part. We registered the same tool set through WebMCP for in-browser agents and through MCP for external agents such as ChatGPT, Claude, and custom MCP clients. The tools keep the same names and arguments on both surfaces, and they share the same underlying backend logic. Through WebMCP, however, the browser-facing tools can also update the page the user is looking at. That distinction became central to the project. A catalog search can return the same listings through MCP or WebMCP. But with WebMCP, the agent can also highlight its recommendation, apply the requested filters in real time, and add the chosen card to the basket. MCP gives the agent data; WebMCP lets the agent use that data with the user on the live page. One part of the build that we particularly enjoyed was resurfacing capabilities we already had. The server already knew how to search the catalog. We exposed that same capability through WebMCP, then connected it to the result grid so the agent could work with actual items on the page instead of returning a block of text. We used the same approach for filtering and highlighting. We only added a page action where changing the page genuinely helped the user. Our stack is Cloudflare Workers, D1 for the Pokémon TCG mirror, KV for search caching, Workers AI with Llama 3.2 11B Vision for image identification, and the UCP catalog endpoint. The frontend is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was making the tools feel like a natural part of the page. WebMCP is not just a chatbot sitting beside a website; the agent needs to interact with the experience itself. The hardest design decision was deciding what should be a data query and what should be a page action. The rule we eventually settled on was simple: if the agent needs the result to reason, it is a data tool. If the action changes what the user sees or does on the page, it is a WebMCP page action. Turning backend results into page actions A search endpoint normally returns a JSON list. On the page, that list also needs to be rendered in a way the agent can work with. We built a thin layer that gives each result a stable ID. Follow-up actions such as highlighting a card or adding it to the basket can then target the exact item the user and agent are discussing. Making image identification reliable The vision model sometimes produced a confident but incorrect identification when the photo was low resolution. Instead of pretending that uncertainty did not exist, we added a confirmation step so the user can correct the result before the Worker searches for listings. What began as a reliability problem ended up becoming a useful part of the experience. Keeping the experience fast Browser-side tool calls introduce a network round trip. When an agent makes five calls in sequence, the delay adds up even if every individual call is reasonably fast. We cached aggressively and pre-rendered what we could so the experience would still feel responsive. Accomplishments that we're proud of Thirteen WebMCP tools now cover the full catalog journey, including search, comparison, image identification, filtering, highlighting, and adding to the basket. The same underlying capabilities are also available to external agents through MCP. A discovery-to-purchase journey that once meant opening ten browser tabs can now happen in one conversation in around 30 seconds rather than 30 minutes. We tested PokéFinder with people who knew very little about Pokémon TCG, including some very patient family members. They could find specific cards simply by describing what they wanted in plain English. The interaction becomes more useful as the agent learns what the person is actually trying to find. That makes the hobby much more approachable for beginners without getting in the way of experienced collectors. The image search works as a real shopping tool: take a photo of a card and get matching listings from every connected store. What we learned The page actions are what make WebMCP feel genuinely different. Highlighting, filtering, and adding to the basket turn an agent from something that gives advice into something that can work alongside the user. Resurfacing is a powerful pattern. Many useful agent actions do not require a completely new backend feature; they require an existing capability to be exposed with a stable, UI-addressable ID. Latency compounds quickly. Caching and pre-rendering matter just as much for a WebMCP experience as they do for any other real-time interface. When an LLM can work directly with the page, conversational clarity becomes part of the UX. Some of our best improvements came from simplifying the interface and letting the agent handle the complexity. Context makes the experience accessible. The agent can explain unfamiliar terms and narrow the catalog at the same time, which helps beginners shop with much more confidence. What's next for Pokefinder.app WebMCP More agent surfaces. Today, WebMCP connects to ChatGPT in the browser. We would love to see first-class integrations with tools such as Cursor, Claude, and Comet. Built-in chat. We want to add a “search with AI” experience directly to the site so people without a separate AI assistant can shop in the same way. Promoted placements through UCP. When the Shopify program

Threadwise turns body measurements into brand-specific apparel size recommendations, helping shoppers avoid poor fits with explainable, privacy-first WebMCP tools.

 Threadwise 

 Threadwise helps online shoppers find the right apparel size when every brand uses a different size chart. 

 The Problem 

 A shopper may wear a medium in one brand and a large in another. 

 Traditional size labels are too generic, and product pages often make it difficult to compare chest, waist, shoulder, and sleeve measurements. 

 This leads to uncertainty, poor fit, and unnecessary returns. 

 Our Solution 

 Threadwise lets shoppers enter their measurements and preferred fit, then compares them against each garment’s own size chart. 

 It returns: 

 
 A recommended size 
 A confidence score 
 Area-by-area fit details 
 Possible warnings 
 An alternative size 
 

 Threadwise also supports real product links. 

 A shopper can paste a product URL and the size-chart rows from that page, then receive a real-time recommendation without requiring marketplace scraping or retailer credentials. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP allows Threadwise to expose structured tools that AI agents can discover and use. 

 The available tools include: 
 list_garments
get_size_chart
recommend_garment_size
compare_product_fits
analyze_product_link
 
 Instead of guessing from labels such as “medium” or “large,” an agent can call the appropriate tool, provide structured measurements, and receive an explainable result. 

 The shopper remains in control of their measurements and decisions. 

 Privacy First 

 Measurements stay in the browser by default. 

 Threadwise does not require an account and does not send body measurements to retailers. 

 The app does not use body photographs, infer sensitive personal attributes, or claim guaranteed fit. 

 Recommendations are presented as transparent estimates, not certainty. 

 Built For 

 Threadwise is designed for online apparel shoppers who want more confidence before ordering. 

 The same approach can later help independent apparel stores reduce size-related returns and improve product size charts. 

 What We Built 

 The prototype includes: 

 
 A responsive apparel catalog 
 Store-specific body and garment size charts 
 Unit conversion between centimeters and inches 
 Slim, regular, and relaxed fit preferences 
 Explainable scoring and confidence levels 
 Real product-link analysis using user-supplied chart data 
 WebMCP tool registration 
 Browser-only measurement handling 
 Accessible and responsive UI 
 

 Future Improvements 

 Future versions could support authorized merchant feeds, official retailer APIs, better garment-category models, and feedback loops based on anonymized fit outcomes. 

 Threadwise’s goal is simple: make apparel sizing feel less like guessing and more like an informed decision.

title: StagedOps
pitch: An agent-native endpoint change lab where AI detects policy conflicts, simulates impact, and stages safe remediations - while humans authorize execution and rollback.
about_excerpt: An agent-native endpoint change lab where AI detects policy conflicts, simulates impact, and stages safe remediations - while humans authorize execution and rollback. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Managing endpoint policies is rarely difficult because of a missing button. It is difficult because administrators must understand overlapping assignments, affected devices, exceptions, and potential side effects before making a change. AI agents can help investigate this complexity, but giving an agent unrestricted write access creates a new risk. We built StagedOps to explore a safer model: the agent analyzes and prepares changes while the human remains responsible for authorization. WebMCP makes this collaboration possible inside the same live application instead of separating the user interface from the agent's context. What it does StagedOps is a human-guided endpoint change lab built around a realistic simulated device fleet. An agent can: Inspect fleet health and compliance Find affected devices Explain policy conflicts Simulate a proposed remediation Calculate the expected impact and blast radius Stage a change for review Apply an authorized change Inspect the audit trail Roll back the last change The administrator sees every agent action reflected immediately in the dashboard. Before execution, StagedOps presents a clear change plan containing the configuration diff, affected devices, expected compliance improvement, and remaining risks. A staged change cannot be applied until the human explicitly authorizes it in the interface. This creates a genuine handoff between agent reasoning and human accountability. How we built it StagedOps is a client-side web application built with React and TypeScript. It contains a deterministic fleet model with devices, groups, policies, assignments, conflicts, staged changes, and audit events. The user interface and WebMCP tools share the same state and domain logic. This means an action performed by the agent behaves exactly like an action performed through the regular interface. The WebMCP integration uses document.modelContext.registerTool() with narrow JSON Schemas, explicit tool descriptions, read-only annotations, structured results, and clear error responses. Read-only tools are always available. Write capabilities follow the application's workflow: the agent can prepare a change, but the execution capability is only made available after the user authorizes the staged plan. Tool availability therefore reflects the current application state. StagedOps does not require its own AI backend. The website provides safe, well-defined capabilities while the browser agent supplies the reasoning. Browsers without WebMCP can still use the complete human interface. How we use WebMCP WebMCP is not an extra chat box added to StagedOps. It is the primary collaboration layer between the application and the agent. It provides: Structured discovery of application capabilities Reliable inputs through JSON Schema Direct access to the current page state Visible state changes in the human interface Separate read and write operations Dynamic capability changes during authorization Verifiable results and audit events Safer execution than interpreting buttons and forms through DOM automation The central workflow—an agent staging a remediation, a human reviewing it, and the agent applying it after authorization—would be significantly less reliable without WebMCP. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was designing tools rather than merely wrapping interface buttons. Each tool needed a narrow purpose, useful structured output, and enough context for an agent to choose the correct next action. We also had to keep WebMCP actions and manual UI actions synchronized through one source of truth. The authorization workflow required special attention. We wanted human approval to be part of the actual application state, not just a sentence in a prompt. We therefore modeled staging, authorization, execution, and rollback as distinct states with corresponding audit events. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that StagedOps demonstrates a complete and understandable product workflow rather than an isolated tool-calling demo. The agent can investigate a problem, produce a measurable remediation plan, hand control to the administrator at the critical moment, execute the approved change, and verify the result. Every step remains visible and reversible. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools expose product intent rather than implementation details. A small set of carefully designed tools can give an agent a more accurate understanding of an application than a large collection of generic actions. Shared visual state also builds trust: users can see what the agent discovered, what it proposes, and what actually changed. Most importantly, human-in-the-loop design does not have to reduce agent usefulness. A well-designed approval boundary allows the agent to do more while keeping consequential decisions under human control. What's next for StagedOps Future versions could connect to real endpoint-management platforms, introduce role-based approvals, support signed change records, compare multiple remediation strategies, and run changes through deployment rings. The same staged-authorization pattern could also be applied to cloud infrastructure, identity management, security operations, and other environments where agents can help—but should not act invisibly. title: Bazaar — Agent-Native Store
pitch: Bazaar turns e-commerce into an agent-native experience where AI agents can discover products, manage carts, and complete purchases using real WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
Bazaar turns e-commerce into an agent-native experience where AI agents can discover products, manage carts, and complete purchases using real WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Traditional e-commerce websites are built mainly for humans. AI assistants can recommend products, but they usually cannot directly interact with a website to perform real shopping actions. 

 We wanted to explore a simple question: What if an AI agent could actually shop on the same website as a human? 

 That idea inspired Bazaar — Agent-Native Store. We built Bazaar to demonstrate how WebMCP can turn a traditional e-commerce website into an agent-native experience where AI agents can discover products, make decisions, manage carts, and complete purchases. 

 Our goal was not to build another AI chatbot, but to make the website itself usable by AI agents. 

 What it does 

 Bazaar is an agent-native e-commerce store powered by WebMCP. 

 It exposes 12 functional WebMCP tools that allow AI agents to: 

 • Search and filter products
• View product details
• Compare products
• Get recommendations
• Add products to the cart
• Update cart quantities
• Remove products
• View the cart
• Clear the cart
• Checkout
• View order history
• Browse product categories 

 For example, an agent can receive a request like: 

 "Find me running shoes under ₹2000 and add the cheapest one to my cart." 

 The agent can search the catalog, find the best matching product, and add it directly to the user's cart. 

 The most important part is that humans and AI agents share the same application state. When an agent adds a product, it immediately appears in the user's normal cart and is marked as "Added by agent." 

 Bazaar also includes a live Agent Activity feed so users can see what the agent is doing. 

 How we built it 

 We built Bazaar using Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Zustand, Prisma ORM, SQLite, and WebMCP. 

 The WebMCP integration uses: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool() 

 We created 12 tools with clear descriptions, input schemas, and execution functions. 

 A key architectural decision was to make WebMCP use the same application logic as the human interface. 

 The WebMCP tools call the same Zustand store actions used by the React UI. 

 This creates a shared architecture: 

 Human UI → Zustand Store ← WebMCP Tools ← AI Agent 

 Because both interfaces use the same store and business logic, humans and AI agents share the same product catalog, cart, application state, and order flow. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel and includes an Agent Activity system for transparent tool execution. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was understanding how WebMCP tools are exposed and executed in the browser. 

 Initially, we expected tools such as search_products() to behave like normal JavaScript functions. We learned that WebMCP tools are exposed through the browser's model context instead. 

 We also had to carefully design tool descriptions and input schemas so AI agents could understand what each tool does, which parameters it accepts, and what information it returns. 

 Another challenge was synchronizing agent actions with the human UI. 

 We did not want the AI agent to have a separate cart or application state. Instead, every agent action had to use the same business logic as the human interface. 

 Testing complete workflows such as product search → selection → add to cart → cart management → checkout also required careful integration between WebMCP and our application state. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Bazaar goes beyond simply registering WebMCP tools. We built a complete agent-native shopping workflow. 

 Our key accomplishments include: 

 • 12 functional WebMCP tools
• Shared human + AI shopping cart
• Agent actions visibly marked in the UI
• Live Agent Activity feed
• Natural-language product discovery
• Price filtering and product sorting
• Product comparison and recommendations
• Cart management and checkout
• Order history
• WebMCP connected directly to the same business logic used by the UI
• A fully deployed live web application 

 The biggest accomplishment is demonstrating that WebMCP can transform a traditional e-commerce website into an application that AI agents can actively operate, not just read. 

 What we learned 

 Building Bazaar taught us that creating an agent-native application is more than adding an AI chatbot. 

 The tools themselves become an important part of the application's interface. 

 We learned that WebMCP tools need clear descriptions, well-defined schemas, predictable outputs, and reliable execution. 

 We also learned the importance of shared application state. By connecting WebMCP directly to our existing business logic, agent actions behave consistently with actions performed through the human UI. 

 Most importantly, we learned that websites can be designed for two types of users: humans through visual interfaces and AI agents through structured tools. 

 WebMCP provides an exciting way to bridge these two experiences. 

 What's next for Bazaar — Agent-Native Store 

 Bazaar currently focuses on the core agent-native shopping experience. Our next goal is to make the platform more intelligent, autonomous, and user-controlled. 

 Future plans include: 

 • More intelligent personalized recommendations
• Conversational shopping experiences
• Multi-step autonomous shopping workflows
• Better agent activity and audit history
• Permission controls for sensitive actions
• More payment and checkout options
• Improved mobile experience
• Integration with external commerce services
• Multi-agent shopping workflows 

 Our long-term vision is to build an e-commerce platform where AI agents can safely discover, compare, purchase, and manage products on behalf of users while keeping the user in control.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Online shopping is overwhelming. You open a store, scroll through dozens of products, compare specs in separate tabs, hunt for coupon codes, and try to figure out which product actually has good reviews. What if an AI could do all of that for you, right on the store's website? 

 That question led to ShopLens. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge was the perfect opportunity to explore what happens when you give an AI agent real tools to interact with a website, not just read it, but actually take actions on it. 

 Shopping is something everyone does, and the pain points are universal. WebMCP makes it possible for an AI to become your personal shopper, searching, comparing, reading reviews, and managing your cart , all while you watch the UI update in real time. 

 What it does 

 ShopLens is a web-based shopping assistant that registers 10 structured tools using the WebMCP standard. When an AI agent like ChatGPT visits the site in its built-in browser, it discovers these tools and can use them to help the user shop. 

 The 10 tools: 

 
 search_products — search by keyword, category, price range, and minimum rating 
 get_product — view full product details including specs and stock status 
 compare_products — compare 2 to 4 products side by side in a table 
 get_reviews — read reviews with average sentiment analysis 
 find_similar — find products similar to one the user likes 
 add_to_cart — add a product to the shopping cart 
 remove_from_cart — remove a product from the cart 
 get_cart — view cart contents with subtotal, discounts, and total 
 check_deals — find available coupon codes and deals 
 apply_deal — apply a coupon code to get a discount 
 

 The app has a live Activity Log at the bottom of the screen that shows every tool call the AI makes, with timestamps and results. This makes the WebMCP integration transparent and verifiable, you can see exactly what the AI is doing and when. 

 The product catalog includes 40 products across 5 categories (Laptops, Headphones, Cameras, Smart Home, Accessories), over 100 user reviews, and 8 coupon codes. Everything runs client-side with no backend required. 

 How we built it 

 The app is built with Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript). The UI uses Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui for a clean, professional look. State management is handled by Zustand , which gives us a single store that both UI components and WebMCP tool handlers can access. 

 The WebMCP integration works through a WebMCPProvider component that wraps the app. On mount, it checks for document.modelContext , the WebMCP entry point. If present, it registers all 10 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool is a single object with a name , a natural-language description (so the AI knows when to use it), an inputSchema (JSON Schema defining accepted arguments), and an async execute function that manipulates app state and returns structured data to the AI. Unregistration is handled via AbortController signals for clean cleanup. 

 The key architectural decision was using Zustand's getState() in tool handlers. Since tool calls come from the AI agent (not from React event handlers), they run outside React's render cycle. getState() gives direct access to the store from anywhere, which made the WebMCP integration clean and straightforward. 

 The product data is bundled as TypeScript arrays, no database, no API, no loading states. The app deploys to any static hosting platform in seconds. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was getting the registerTool API format right. Chrome's WebMCP implementation expects a single ModelContextTool object with name , description , inputSchema , and an async execute function, not separate arguments. The early documentation was sparse, so we had to debug TypeError: The provided value is not of type 'ModelContextTool' by reading the Chrome source and experimenting. We also discovered that cleanup uses AbortController signals instead of an unregister() return value. 

 Another challenge was making tool handlers work correctly outside of React. WebMCP tool calls come from the AI agent, not from user clicks, so they execute in a different context than normal React event handlers. We solved this with Zustand's getState() pattern, which gives direct access to the store from anywhere. 

 Designing tool descriptions that an AI would understand and use correctly was harder than expected. The descriptions need to be specific enough that the AI picks the right tool, but general enough to work across different user requests. We iterated on the wording until the AI reliably chose the correct tool for each task. 

 Making the UI responsive to tool calls was also tricky. When the AI calls compare_products , the right panel needs to switch to the Compare tab and populate the table. When it calls add_to_cart , the cart badge in the header updates. Every tool call has UI side effects, and coordinating those through a single Zustand store required careful planning. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud of the Activity Log . It is the feature that makes the demo click. Without it, the tool calls are invisible, the UI just magically updates. With the Activity Log, every interaction is transparent. Judges and users can see exactly what tool was called, what arguments were passed, and what the result was, all with timestamps. It turns an abstract protocol into something you can watch happening in real time. 

 We are also proud of the tool design . The 10 tools cover a complete shopping workflow from discovery to purchase. They are not just CRUD operations, find_similar uses a scoring algorithm based on price proximity and shared tags, get_reviews includes sentiment analysis, and apply_deal validates coupon eligibility against the cart contents. Each tool is genuinely useful, not just a wrapper around a database query. 

 Finally, the fact that the entire app runs client-side with zero backend is something we are proud of. It deploys in seconds, works offline after first load, and has no infrastructure costs. The simplicity of the architecture is a feature. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how websites interact with AI. Instead of the AI scraping text from a page, the website offers structured tools that the AI can call with typed parameters and receive structured responses. The website becomes an active participant in the conversation, not a passive document. 

 We learned that tool descriptions are the most important part of the integration . The AI decides which tool to call based entirely on the description. A vague description means the AI won't use the tool. A description that's too narrow means the AI won't use it when it should. Getting this right is an art. 

 We also learned that transparency is everything when demoing AI integrations. The Activity Log was an afterthought at first, but it became the centerpiece of our demo. Being able to point at a log line and say "the AI just called search_products with these parameters and got these results" is worth more than any slide deck. 

 What's next for ShopLens 

 There are several directions ShopLens could go: 

 
 Real product data — Connect to a real e-commerce API (Shopify, WooCommerce) instead of bundled data, so the AI shops across real stores. 
 Multi-store support — Let the AI compare products across multiple WebMCP-enabled stores, finding the best price and reviews across the web. 
 Checkout integration — Add payment tools so the AI can complete a purchase on behalf of the user, with confirmation steps. 
 Personalization — Track user preferences over time so the AI gets better at recommending products the user will like. 
 Voice interface — Combine WebMCP with a voice assistant so users can shop hands-free: "Hey, find me a birthday gift for someone who likes photography, under $300." 
 

 The bigger vision is that WebMCP becomes a standard that every e-commerce site supports. When that happens, AI agents won't need site-specific integrations — they'll visit any store, discover its tools, and shop on your behalf. ShopLe

title: Even Split
pitch: A shared ledger where one sentence becomes three expenses with three different participant lists. The agent proposes, you approve, and every balance is shown, not asserted.
about_excerpt: A shared ledger where one sentence becomes three expenses with three different participant lists. The agent proposes, you approve, and every balance is shown, not asserted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Six people go to Lisbon for ten days. One shared apartment, and everyone pays for random things along the way. At the end somebody has to work out who owes who, and it falls to one person, takes an evening, and gets argued about for a week. Apps for this already exist and are widely installed. People still do not use them properly, and the reason is not the arithmetic. It is that logging one dinner means opening a form, typing an amount, choosing a payer, and ticking six checkboxes. Nobody does that on the last night of a holiday. So the ledger stays half empty and the group reconstructs it from memory. The bottleneck was never the maths. It was the typing. That is a data entry problem, and it is exactly the shape of problem WebMCP is good at. What it does Even Split is a shared ledger for splitting costs across a group. Every expense knows who paid and who shares it, so a dinner somebody missed stays off their tab. Splits can be even, by shares, or exact amounts per person. A balance rail puts everyone on one scale, owing to the left and owed to the right. Any person opens to a line by line breakdown of how their balance was reached. A settlement panel works out the shortest set of payments that clears the whole group. All of that works on its own, with no agent involved. The page also registers 14 WebMCP site tools, so an agent can work the same ledger at the same time. Verified in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser against the live deployment: "Log these: I paid 180 for the apartment split six ways, dinner Tuesday was 90 that Sam paid but Priya wasn't there, and the taxi was 40 for me, Sam, Dana and Jo." It called list_people to orient itself, then made three separate add_expense calls with three different participant lists. That sentence cannot go into a form, because a form takes one expense with one list of people. "Sam gave me 40 back in cash on Tuesday, and take Jo off the grocery run." record_payment and update_expense from one sentence. A four day old correction, and every downstream balance re-derived in view. "Alex says he shouldn't pay full share for the groceries since he doesn't drink. Sort that out." No tool named, no amount, no split method. It found the right expense, inferred a weight change, and left Sam's existing double share alone. "Why does Jo owe so much?" explain_balance returned the itemised trace and opened the same breakdown on the page. Nobody accepts a number from a chat message, so both sides read the same thing. "Settle everything up." It staged five payments and stopped, reporting that nothing was recorded until the person approves. How we built it React and Vite, no backend. The ledger lives in localStorage and never leaves the browser. The domain logic sits in one pure module: splits, balances, settlement, and explanation, with state in and values out, no React and no DOM. Every state change goes through a named action in a reducer. src/lib/webmcp.js holds the whole tool layer and contains no business logic of its own. Each tool translates JSON Schema input into one of those named actions, which is the same action the interface dispatches when somebody clicks a button. One code path, one set of validation rules, two ways in. person clicks "Add expense" ─┐ ├─► actions.addExpense ─► reducer ─► render agent calls add_expense ─┘ Registration uses document.modelContext.registerTool with an AbortController , so tools unregister cleanly and never double register. Because WebMCP only runs in origin-isolated documents, the dev server and both deploy configs send Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 . Three details do the reliability work. Names resolve instead of ids, since an agent says "Priya" and not "p5", with "me" mapping to the current user and ambiguous input returning the real options rather than a guess. State is read through a ref, so a tool called ten minutes after registration sees the live ledger. And errors are written for the caller: a short exact split replies with how far off it is, an unknown name lists who is actually on the trip. Money is integer cents throughout, with the largest remainder method for splits, so ten euros across three people comes out 3.34, 3.33, 3.33 and the shares always add back to the exact total. Challenges we ran into Making the agent's work visible. A change you cannot see is a change you cannot overrule, and that is the whole premise of co-presence. Five things now react on the page while an agent works: the beacon in the top bar names the running tool, an activity panel logs every call, the row that changed flashes, the balance panel is outlined when its figures are re-derived, and explain_balance opens the breakdown drawer so the agent can point at what it is discussing. Stale closures. Tools register once, but they get called minutes later. Reading state directly at registration meant a tool would happily operate on a ledger that no longer existed. State is now read through a ref at call time. Errors an agent can act on. The first version threw generic validation failures, and the agent would either give up or retry the same wrong thing. Rewriting every error message to name the actual problem and list the valid options let it correct itself without a round trip to the person. Testing without a browser. Registration is the only part that needs a browser, so a headless script drives all 14 tools against the real reducer, including bad input, through a full realistic session. That turned a slow debugging loop into a fast one. Deciding what not to give the agent. Every settlement is a money decision, so no tool can commit one. Accomplishments that we're proud of One sentence became three tool calls with three different participant lists. That was the central claim and it is demonstrated rather than asserted. The agent inferred a split change from "he doesn't drink." No tool named, no amount, no method. It found the right expense, adjusted the weights, and noticed Sam already had a double share and left it alone. Nothing in the tool surface can commit money. An agent stages a settlement and the payments appear in amber with nothing recorded. Approving is a button only the person can press, and the test suite fails if a tool matching commit or approve is ever added. When asked to settle up, the agent read that constraint out of the tool's return value and told the user to approve it on the page. It refused to create duplicates. Asked to log three expenses that were already present, it checked existing state first and declined rather than blindly appending. The maths is provably right. One suite asserts that every expense's shares sum to its total, that all balances sum to zero, and that applying a settlement brings every balance to zero. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product. More of the reliability came from rewriting descriptions than from writing code. The difference between an agent guessing and an agent orienting itself first was a sentence telling it to call list_people when it needs names. Return the result, not an acknowledgement. Once every write replied with the per person shares and everyone's new balance, the agent started verifying its own work instead of assuming it had landed. Errors are an interface. An error message is read by a model that can act on it, so it should name the problem and list the options. WebMCP is not MCP with a different transport. The thing that matters is that the tools run in the page the person is looking at. MCP servers wrapping a hosted expense API already exist. None of them let somebody watch a balance re-derive and drag it back. Being honest about prior art is stronger than claiming novelty. Newer split apps do parse a single spoken expense. Saying so, then drawing the real distinction, is more convincing than pretending the category is empty. What's next for Even Split Symmetry in the tool surface. There is add_person and no way to remove one, which an agent noticed by going looking for the button instead. The version worth building refuses with a reason: "Jo is on seven expenses and one payment, so I cannot remove them. Take Jo off those first?" Receipts parsed in the browser. Local OCR would keep the no-server property while removing the last bit of manual entry. Multiple currencies , which any real trip needs and which the integer cents model already accommodates. The same architecture where the money is bigger. The propose-then-approve boundary and the itemised explanation matter more when reconciliation is an obligation rather than a social nicety: shared utilities across tenants, freelance collectives splitting project revenue, small business expense matching. The chore is the same shape and the stakes make the visible reasoning worth paying for. Built With javascript model-context-protocol re

title: ImageLens
pitch: ImageLens — Agent-Native Image Forensics\nAn image forensics engine that gives AI agents structured evidence to investigate and explain through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
ImageLens — Agent-Native Image Forensics
An image forensics engine that gives AI agents structured evidence to investigate and explain through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Images are increasingly difficult to evaluate. 

 AI assistants can explain images, but they often don't have direct access to the forensic evidence behind an analysis. 

 I wanted to explore a different approach: what if an image forensics application could expose its own analysis directly to an AI agent? 

 This led to ImageLens — a forensic analysis tool designed to work with AI agents through WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 ImageLens analyzes images using its own statistical and forensic detection engine. 

 It examines multiple signals and produces structured results such as: 

 
 Detection scores 
 Forensic signals 
 Image metadata 
 Noise characteristics 
 Frequency-domain analysis 
 A combined forensic report 
 

 Through WebMCP, an AI agent can access these results directly from the application. 

 The agent can then investigate the evidence and explain the findings in natural language. 

 The important distinction is that the AI does not perform the underlying forensic analysis. ImageLens does. 

 How we built it 

 ImageLens is a web application with a client-side forensic analysis engine and a WebMCP integration. 

 The application's analysis engine produces structured results that are exposed through WebMCP tools. 

 The agent can query capabilities such as: 

 
 analyze_image 
 get_detection_score 
 get_forensic_signals 
 get_metadata 
 get_frequency_analysis 
 get_report 
 

 These tools provide the agent with the same information available inside the application, without requiring the user to manually copy and paste results into an AI assistant. 

 The application and its WebMCP tools share the same underlying analysis logic, keeping the agent's information synchronized with the actual application state. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was deciding where the responsibility between the application and the AI should stop. 

 We deliberately did not make the AI the detector. 

 The forensic engine is responsible for analyzing the image and producing evidence. The AI is responsible for querying that evidence, connecting the different signals, and explaining them. 

 Another challenge was turning complex forensic information into structured WebMCP tools that an agent can understand and use effectively. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that ImageLens is more than an image analyzer with an AI chatbot attached to it. 

 The WebMCP integration allows an agent to directly access the application's real forensic data. 

 An agent can independently retrieve different types of evidence, combine them, and produce an investigation-style explanation. 

 This creates a clear division of responsibilities: 

 ImageLens analyzes.
The agent investigates.
The human makes the final judgment. 

 We also designed the application to avoid making absolute claims about image authenticity. Forensic signals can indicate suspicious characteristics, but they cannot provide mathematical proof that an image was generated by AI. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP can be particularly powerful for specialized applications. 

 Instead of trying to make the AI reproduce the application's domain-specific logic, the application can expose its expertise through structured tools. 

 This allows an AI agent to become an interface to specialized software without replacing the software itself. 

 We also learned that good WebMCP tools should expose meaningful domain-level capabilities rather than simply reproduce UI interactions. 

 What's next for ImageLens 

 The next step would be to expand the forensic toolkit with additional analysis methods and comparison capabilities. 

 Possible future features include comparing multiple images, detecting inconsistencies between image regions, generating more detailed forensic reports, and allowing agents to conduct multi-step investigations across several images. 

 The long-term goal is to make ImageLens a specialized forensic engine that AI agents can use as part of larger investigation workflows. 

 ImageLens doesn't just detect. It gives agents evidence they can investigate and explain.

title: AgentDraw
pitch: A local-first whiteboard where people and AI agents inspect, draw, prototype, and undo together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A local-first whiteboard where people and AI agents inspect, draw, prototype, and undo together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent integrations live behind a chat box or a server API. I wanted a shared visual workspace where a person can sketch, select, move, and annotate freely while an AI agent can understand the same canvas and make precise, reversible changes. AgentDraw turns Excalidraw into that collaborative surface with WebMCP. What it does AgentDraw is a local-first whiteboard that exposes eight site tools to an agent: capabilities, structured canvas inspection, atomic patches, selective patch rollback, focus, visual capture, export, and scene import. The agent can create labelled shapes, bound arrows, frames, images, and live HTML prototypes. A person can draw freehand marks around a component; inspection reports nearby element IDs so the agent can understand references such as “this step.” Human and agent edits share Excalidraw’s undo history, while revision and epoch checks reject stale writes instead of overwriting recent human work. A particularly useful workflow is app prototyping: ask the agent to draw a flow, circle a step by hand and request a correction, then ask for an interactive form beside the diagram. The prototype runs as sandboxed HTML inside the canvas. The agent can later replace its source, export the result as SVG or an Excalidraw document, or revert only one of its own patches without removing the person’s work. Challenges The hardest parts were preserving Excalidraw semantics while allowing structured agent edits, coalescing noisy pointer events into useful revisions, keeping arrows and labels attached during moves and resizes, and preventing selective rollback from clobbering later human changes. Another challenge was giving the agent both structural understanding and visual grounding without dumping an enormous canvas into context. What I learned WebMCP is especially powerful when the browser page itself is the shared state. It removes a separate MCP server and lets the agent work in the same authenticated, visual session as the person. I also learned that good agent tools need explicit concurrency, compact read models, strong validation, and reversible writes—not just a large set of actions.
