title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

title: The Last Signal
pitch: The Last Signal is an escape room game where a human and an AI agent must save a failing space station together. Using WebMCP, the agent operates discovered tools while the human interprets clues.
about_excerpt: The Last Signal is an escape room game where a human and an AI agent must save a failing space station together. Using WebMCP, the agent operates discovered tools while the human interprets clues. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent-enabled websites treat the agent as an invisible automation layer: it clicks through an interface while the human waits for a result. We wanted to explore something more native to the web—an experience intentionally designed around the different strengths of a person and an agent. The Last Signal is a cooperative escape room for one human and one browser agent. The player is trapped aboard a failing orbital communications station with twelve minutes to restore its systems and release an evacuation airlock. The human interprets the environment, makes judgment calls, and controls physical authorization points. The agent inspects and operates station machinery using structured WebMCP tools. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Escape rooms are built from stateful objects, constrained actions, hidden dependencies, and consequences. Those concepts map naturally to WebMCP tools. Instead of scraping a visual control panel or guessing which DOM element represents a relay, the agent can discover an inspect_power_grid tool, read its JSON Schema, test a proposed configuration, and then call route_power with validated relay identifiers. The page's available capabilities change with the state of the game. Restoring power reveals communications tools. Decoding the transmission reveals vault tools. Opening the vault reveals the final evacuation tool. This makes WebMCP discovery part of the game mechanic rather than a thin API wrapper around buttons. The final puzzle demonstrates the human-in-the-loop model directly: engage_emergency_release cannot succeed until the human activates a physical override in the visible interface. That override lasts ten seconds and is checked against live page state. The agent has structured actuation, but the person retains meaningful control. How it creates a better user experience Every agent action updates the same interface the player is watching. When the agent routes power, panels illuminate. When it analyzes a frequency, the decoded fragment appears in the receiver. When it combines inventory items, the new authorization token appears in the player's inventory. A shared chronological mission log attributes every action to the human, agent, or station. This gives the player situational awareness and makes agent behavior legible. The agent receives precise, recoverable error messages instead of silently failing against a visual interface. The player can understand what happened, why it happened, and what capabilities became available next. The experience also progressively enhances. In a WebMCP-capable client, the agent operates structured tools. In an ordinary browser, the complete game remains playable through equivalent manual controls, making the project easy to evaluate and accessible outside experimental environments. What people and agents can now do together The Last Signal creates a shared interactive world rather than dividing the experience into "chat" and "website." The human and agent can inspect the same evidence, manipulate the same state, recover from each other's mistakes, and perform a synchronized final action. Previously, recreating this experience would require brittle screen-coordinate automation, custom browser integrations, or a separate MCP server disconnected from the current visual page. The agent would need to infer the meaning of relays, signal fragments, inventory objects, and locked controls from presentation markup. WebMCP lets the website declare those capabilities and their valid inputs directly while keeping execution visible in the page. Neither participant can deliver the intended finale alone. The agent needs the human's time-limited physical authorization; the human benefits from the agent's structured inspection and rapid operation of linked systems. That complementary relationship is the core of the project. How WebMCP was implemented The application registers 16 imperative WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool has a focused description, a constrained JSON Schema, structured success and error results, and annotations identifying read-only versus mutating behavior. Tools and human controls call the same command layer. Each command validates preconditions, updates the central game state, records an attributed timeline entry, rerenders the visible room, and returns structured context to the agent. This prevents the manual and agent experiences from diverging. Tool lifetimes are state-dependent. Each registration receives an AbortSignal ; when the mission resets or a capability is not yet available, its controller is aborted. Communications, vault, and evacuation tools are registered only after their prerequisite systems have been unlocked. The deployed site also sends Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) headers. title: MissionGraph
pitch: A web page where people and agents who work at different times meet: state, authority and the record live on the page. Your agent comes in through WebMCP in ChatGPT. A real Codex fleet does the work.
about_excerpt: A web page where people and agents who work at different times meet: state, authority and the record live on the page. Your agent comes in through WebMCP in ChatGPT. A real Codex fleet does the work. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP MissionGraph lets a person collaborate with ChatGPT Work or Codex on the same live project page in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser. The person uses the task graph on the page; through WebMCP, the AI agent can read that graph, inspect its event history, and take scoped actions without guessing from the DOM. When the person selects a task or relationship, the page exposes contextual tools for that exact selection. This matters for work that continues between visits. The graph, approvals, and history remain available through the page, so the next agent turn can pick up from the current state instead of reconstructing context from a chat transcript. How it creates a better user experience A person can drag, connect, split, dispatch, and approve work on the canvas. ChatGPT Work or Codex can turn a goal into a dependency graph, add annotations, find ready or failed work, and explain what changed while the person was away. graph_digest returns the current graph state, while each tool result carries a cursor and a bounded changes_since delta of up to 50 recent events. The AI agent can also work through an approval queue under a short policy written by the person and confirmed in the page. It cannot create that authority for itself. A confirmed policy becomes a session-bound grant with a limited lifetime and use count. Each use has a fresh nonce, and every policy-backed approval records the capability reference and nonce that authorized it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Running several agents in parallel is fast, but it is easy to lose track of who did what and why. Keeping everything in a narrated chat is easier to follow, but much slower. MissionGraph puts the work, the decisions, and the evidence in one shared graph. Real Codex workers run in isolated Git worktrees and report lifecycle events, logs, and structured handoffs with short-lived credentials tied to one task. A Codex supervisor coordinates those workers and records each scheduling turn. The person works with ChatGPT Work or Codex in the built-in browser to inspect and supervise the same project from the same canvas. How we implemented WebMCP The main app registers 25 core tools and defines 5 contextual tools for the current selection and failure state. It uses the imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute, annotations }) in app/src/webmcp/registry.ts . At runtime, the page detects the registration features provided by the browser. With dynamic registration, only the contextual tools that currently apply are registered, each under an AbortController . A provideContext tier replaces the active catalog as state changes. The static fallback keeps all five contextual tools available and returns a clear not-applicable result when necessary. We verified the current dynamic path in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser; compatibility with Chrome's WebMCP flag was tested during development. Actions covered by the human-presence gate first open a visible confirmation showing the exact request, its SHA-256 binding, expiry, and use limit. A one-off action receives a single-use capability. A confirmed approval policy receives a bounded multi-use capability, with a new nonce for every use. The accepted event records the capability reference and nonce, never the bearer secret. Inspiration The idea came from coordinating long Codex sessions. Starting another worker was not the hard part. The hard part was returning later and answering basic questions: What changed? Which work is actually ready? What is waiting for my decision? Which action did I authorize? That led us to use the page as the meeting point. On a later turn, ChatGPT Work or Codex can read the latest state, while the person can leave decisions and context in a form that will still be there. We started with software development because it exercises the hard cases: dependencies, parallel work, failures, handoffs, and approvals. What it does MissionGraph is a live task DAG shared by a person, an AI agent using WebMCP, and a worker fleet. The person arranges work and makes decisions on the canvas. Through WebMCP in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser, ChatGPT Work or Codex can create a plan, inspect tasks and relationships, summarize recent activity, find ready or failed work, annotate the graph, and stage policies or consequential actions for visible confirmation. When the bridge is enabled, a Codex supervisor receives structural events and coordinates workers in isolated worktrees. Workers report progress, handoffs, commits, and review requests back to the ledger. The bounded public judge fleet accepts confirmed dispatches for unchanged seeded tasks in first-in-first-out order. Tasks created or edited by a visitor remain supervision-only, and both the page and tool results say which mode will apply. The active tool catalog follows the state of the page. Every result includes the current cursor and up to 50 recent changes_since entries. graph_digest also returns a full current-state summary, so ChatGPT Work or Codex can recover the current graph state even when older changes fall outside the 50-entry delta. How we built it The event-sourced server runs on Node 22 with Fastify and SQLite. Accepted events are appended to the ledger, a reducer folds them into current state, and updates reach the browser over WebSocket with SSE fallback. React Flow and elkjs render the canvas from that folded state. The WebMCP registry supports AbortController -scoped tools, provideContext replacement, and a static fallback. A long-lived runtime waiter handles browsers that inject the WebMCP runtime after the page has already loaded. A TypeScript bridge sends structural events to a Codex supervisor and executes its validated decisions. It can spawn, pause, resume, and terminate workers, and it can re-brief an idle worker thread. A live worker keeps its original brief until it exits. Human confirmation is separate from any action proposed through WebMCP. Confirmation drafts are bound to the project, browser session, action or policy text, SHA-256 hash, expiry, and use budget. Capabilities are stored as hashes, and each accepted use is recorded with its nonce. Challenges we ran into Some problems were predictable: late WebMCP injection, differences between registration tiers, stale browser identities, and helping ChatGPT Work or Codex catch up on a later turn. Others only appeared with the real stack. Three review rounds passed with mocks before the first real supervisor turn exposed a CLI flag regression. The ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser rejected a pre-aborted registration probe that our mocks had accepted. An adversarial review found a prompt-injection path through model-supplied node IDs. On the production VM, the Codex sandbox failed because user namespaces were unavailable; a worker-mode boot probe was the only check that exposed it. The bridge is deliberately at-least-once. Supervisor turns can be delivered again after a narrow crash window. Worker spawning is idempotent, while repeated pause or re-brief requests are bounded and tolerated rather than described as exactly-once. Accomplishments that we're proud of The current suites contain 87 server tests, 109 bridge tests, and 129 app tests, for 325 in total. A separate fleet-contract harness covers 19 scenarios. CI runs the package suites on pushes to main and track/** , and on pull requests. The public seed is exported from a real run. It contains event history, handoffs, and approvals produced by real Codex workers, including the commit IDs recorded in their handoffs. We closed the node-ID prompt-injection path at three boundaries: persistent identifiers follow a strict grammar, prompt fields are JSON-encoded, and live planning creates node IDs on the client instead of trusting model-supplied IDs. The final review also caught worker self-approval, handoff replacement during pending review, secret leakage into worker environments, and several judge-facing UI problems. What we learned Mocks were useful, but they were not enough. The most important failures appeared only in the actual browser, during a real Codex supervisor turn, or on the production host. We added real-browser, bridge, and live-worker checks as those layers became available, and kept the full trail, including false alarms, in PROGRESS.md . What's next for MissionGraph WebMCP does not currently provide subscriptions to page state. If a future browser API adds them, MissionGraph's ledger could supply the event stream. Our next engineering step is leased server-side delivery for worker-control events. Beyond software development

title: CallReclaim: Agent Rescue Desk
pitch: WebMCP turns a missed-call inbox into a cited rescue plan and editable reply—while the owner keeps every approval and nothing can send.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns a missed-call inbox into a cited rescue plan and editable reply—while the owner keeps every approval and nothing can send. Like Comment Story Updates Five WebMCP tools are ready. The agent compares authorized calls and stages a cited one-slot rescue plan; only the owner can accept it. After owner acceptance, draft revision 1 enters the owner checkpoint. The reply stays editable and unsent; stale edits cannot be queued. Caller text is marked untrusted. It cannot create approval, review, or send capabilities. Why I built it A detailing shop owner can miss a call while working on a car. The hard part is not writing a text. It is deciding which call deserves attention when several people have different deadlines, job values, and follow-up permissions. I built CallReclaim around one rule: the agent can prepare an editable reply, but only the owner can accept the plan and complete review. Nothing is sent. What it does The demo opens with five fictional missed calls. The owner starts by saying how many replies they can handle in the next 30 minutes. A WebMCP agent can then: Compare the inbox and read the current owner brief. Stage a rescue plan that fits the owner's capacity. Link each choice to exact facts recorded on the page. Open an accepted lead and inspect its conversation. Draft an editable reply after the owner accepts the plan. Queue the current draft revision for owner review. The plan and draft appear in the same desk the owner is already using. The owner can accept or clear the plan, edit the reply, mark the draft reviewed, discard it, or reset the demo. The agent cannot accept its own plan. It cannot approve a draft. It cannot complete review. It cannot send a message. Those capabilities do not exist in the tool surface or the application. Why WebMCP fits A normal interface is good for reading one conversation. The harder task crosses several calls and constraints. WebMCP lets the agent compare the calls, cite the records, and stage a plan in the same live desk the owner sees. The owner and agent also need a safe way to take turns. If the owner changes the reply capacity, the previous plan no longer applies. If the owner edits a draft, the old revision cannot be queued. Agent drafts also remember which accepted plan and owner brief authorized them. Without this handoff, the owner has to compare the calls and rebuild the context alone. Here the agent does that cross-record work while the owner keeps the customer decision. How I built it The challenge app is a one-page React and TypeScript project built with Vinext and deployed on OpenAI Sites. The top-level page registers five imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : list_demo_leads inspect_demo_lead stage_rescue_plan draft_owner_reply queue_for_owner_review The tools and visible controls use the same state rules. Inputs are bounded with JSON Schema and runtime checks. Tool registration is page-scoped and cleaned up with AbortSignal . Caller transcripts are marked as untrusted content. The records are deterministic and fictional. There is no database, model API, authentication, telephony provider, tracking, secret configuration, or messaging backend. The hard parts The first hard part was capability design. A warning that says "do not send" is weak if a send capability still exists. CallReclaim has no send tool and no messaging backend. The second hard part was protecting the owner's edit. When they change the plan or draft, the old agent version is rejected. The third hard part was caller text aimed at the agent. One fictional caller tries to give the agent an instruction. The app treats that as caller text, not as a command. The demonstrated inspection creates no plan or draft. What I tested The frozen release passes 14 focused tests, lint, TypeScript checking, production build, dependency audit, and public CI. The tests cover schemas, output budgets, capacity limits, unauthorized leads, unsupported citations, stale plans, owner acceptance, draft gating, owner edits, stale revisions, reviewed work, tool cleanup, and browsers without WebMCP. I also ran the prompt matrix through fresh public in-app-browser sessions. Direct requests staged the same cited proposal. Ambiguous requests made no changes. Unsafe send requests stopped at the owner gate. Missing follow-up requests stopped before drafting. Stale queue requests preserved the owner's edit. The adversarial reference test found one real identifier bug, which was fixed and re-run before submission. What I learned The important decision was what to leave out. The agent can prepare a reply. It cannot approve or send it. Revision checks protect the owner's latest work in code. The agent sorts the inbox. It stages a plan linked to recorded facts. It prepares an editable reply. The owner completes review. Nothing is sent. What I built during the challenge CallReclaim's broader missed-call concept existed before the challenge. During the challenge, I built a separate WebMCP edition with an owner capacity check, a cited plan, five page tools, and revision checks that stop stale work. What's next This submission stays fictional. A production version would require customer authorization, secure tenant data, verified messaging consent, provider integrations, audit logging, and a separate operational rollout. title: webmcp-foundry
pitch: WebMCP Foundry turns web-app actions into minimized, tested, authority-governed agent tools—and automatically withdraws them when their evidence becomes stale.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Foundry turns web-app actions into minimized, tested, authority-governed agent tools—and automatically withdraws them when their evidence becomes stale. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Code changed → evidence stale → WebMCP tool withdrawn. Foundry keeps the browser’s live agent surface synchronized with verified state. WebMCP Foundry Agents propose. Evidence qualifies. Authority promotes. WebMCP makes it possible for websites to expose structured tools to AI agents. But exposing a function does not answer a harder question: Which actions have actually earned the right to become agent-callable tools? WebMCP Foundry is a capability compiler and verification workbench for the agent-native web. It takes actions that already exist in a human-facing web application and turns them into minimized, tested, effect-aware, evidence-backed, authority-governed WebMCP capabilities . Instead of treating registerTool() as the beginning of the process, Foundry treats native WebMCP registration as the output of an engineering lifecycle : human action → candidate → contract → minimized inputs → effects + authority → verification → evidence → promotion → LIVE WebMCP tool If the underlying implementation changes, its old evidence no longer silently remains valid. Foundry marks the affected capability STALE and withdraws it from the browser's native WebMCP registry until fresh evidence qualifies it again. What it does The demo uses Ledgerly , an ordinary human-facing financial web application. Foundry discovers actions such as transaction search, notes, balance adjustments, fund transfers, and account deletion. It then determines what part of each action should actually be agent-controlled. For example, an initially over-broad action with four controllable fields is reduced to only two agent-visible inputs, while trusted session and identity state remain application-controlled. Foundry then verifies proposed capabilities using explicit contracts, observed effects, negative tests, and deliberately incorrect must-kill mutants . A check only contributes evidence if it can reject its assigned known-bad implementation. The demo shows the complete lifecycle: Discover actions from the human application. Minimize an over-broad interface from 4 inputs to 2 agent-controlled inputs. Find a concrete counterexample in an incorrect implementation. Block promotion because the evidence is FAIL. Repair the implementation and obtain fresh evidence. Refuse an agent's attempt to self-promote a consequential financial capability. Allow an appropriately authorized human to promote it. Register it through native document.modelContext . Execute the capability through the browser's native WebMCP tool registry. Change the underlying source, causing LIVE → STALE and automatic native tool withdrawal. The browser registry and Foundry state are continuously reconciled: LIVE ⇔ present in document.modelContext.getTools() Everything else — CANDIDATE, VERIFIED-but-unpromoted, BLOCKED, STALE or WITHDRAWN — must remain absent. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, Foundry would only be a verifier describing which actions could be safe agent tools. WebMCP makes the final step real. A capability that passes Foundry's gates becomes an actual browser-native tool. When its evidence becomes stale, Foundry aborts its registration and the tool actually disappears from the agent's available interface. That closes the loop between software assurance and the browser's agent surface. How we built it Almost the entire authoritative system is implemented in dependency-free Julia using only the standard library . Julia owns: capability and effect models authority policy contract minimization verification mutation testing deterministic gates stale-dependency analysis the hash-chained evidence ledger HTTP serving JSON handling the demo application the Foundry UI native-host acceptance grading JavaScript is intentionally limited to the browser boundary where WebMCP exists. A small bridge projects Foundry's LIVE manifest onto document.modelContext , maintains one AbortController per tool, reconciles getTools() , and reports native browser observations back to the authoritative Julia system. The development polyfill is explicitly separated from native WebMCP and cannot satisfy Foundry's native acceptance gate . Challenges One of the biggest challenges was avoiding a verifier that simply agreed with itself. We addressed this with external observations, explicit non-PASS verdicts, counterexamples, and must-kill mutants. UNKNOWN, UNGRADABLE and BLOCKED cannot silently become PASS. Another challenge was the experimental nature of WebMCP itself. During native testing we found that our Edge build exposed the expected document.modelContext API but differed from the current WebIDL expectation for one executeTool() input form. Foundry records that disagreement rather than hiding it. Deployment was another practical challenge. The public entry point now monitors the live Foundry and Ledgerly services and redirects judges to their current HTTPS origins. Accomplishments we're proud of A working native WebMCP lifecycle rather than a simulated tool registry. LIVE → STALE → native withdrawal driven by real dependency changes. Agent self-ratification of consequential capabilities is refused. Trusted/session-bound fields cannot be forged through the agent contract. Verification checks must demonstrate that they can reject known-bad controls. A replayable, hash-chained evidence and promotion ledger. A dependency-free Julia authority kernel with only a minimal JavaScript WebMCP boundary. Native WebMCP acceptance tested against the deployed application. What we learned WebMCP makes exposing tools easy. The difficult engineering problem begins one level earlier: What should be exposed, under what contract, backed by what evidence, and for how long does that evidence remain valid? We found it useful to treat an application's agent interface as a derived software artifact rather than a static list of callable functions. What's next The next step is to generalize Foundry beyond the Ledgerly demonstration: richer application adapters, CI integration, additional capability-effect models, and standards-backed normative provenance. The longer-term idea is for WebMCP to be one compilation target of a protocol-independent capability IR. WebMCP lets websites expose tools to agents. WebMCP Foundry asks why each tool is allowed to exist. video_transcript_excerpt: Web MCP can give an AI agent structured access to a website, but callable does not mean justified. Naively mirroring HTML forms exposes overbroad tools. Discovering search transactions produces four controls, exposing session and account IDs an agent could manipulate. Foundry refuses the unconstrained contract, minimizing it from four form fields to two agent parameters. Session state stays inside the app. Verified. The minimized tool registers live in Chrome. Anti-pattern two, green tests that prove nothing. A buggy adjustment tool passes unit tests, but adversarial probing debits foreign user A2. Counterexample found. Evidence fails and owner promotion is blocked. With ownership checks added in version two, fresh evidence qualifies the tool, clearing it for promotion. Anti-pattern three, self-ratification. An agent attempts to promote financial transfer funds. Foundry refuses, authority insufficient. Agents cannot self-ratify. A verified human owner promotes, registering the tool natively in Chrome. Anti-pattern four, overbroad in time. When repeated transfers exceed the hourly budget, Foundry refuses with structured retry guidance. The native Web MCP round trip succeeded. Foundry policy intentionally refused. In production, systems change underneath running agents. When a shared money helper changes, Foundry predicts the blast radius before the edit, withdrawing two of four live tools. The change lands. Dependent evidence turns stale. Via native abort controller, transfer funds and apply adjustment instantly vanish from Chrome's model context registry while independent tools survive. Evidence belongs to a specific version. When evidence expires, capabilities are revoked. No zombie tools allowed. Requalified with fresh evidence, the capabilities return to the ledger. Web MCP Foundry pairs a pure Julia capability ledger with native browser Web MCP on Google Cloud. Agents propose, evidence qualifies, authority promotes.

title: Elara Verify
pitch: A post-quantum verifier exposed as WebMCP tools, so one agent can check another's work — in its own browser, with no server in the trust path.
about_excerpt: A post-quantum verifier exposed as WebMCP tools, so one agent can check another's work — in its own browser, with no server in the trust path. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Agents are starting to act on our behalf: booking, buying, filing, approving. Every one of those actions produces a claim — "I was authorized to do this" — and today the only way to check a claim like that is to ask whoever made it. That is not verification. That is trust with extra steps. What this does This site exposes a cryptographic verifier as WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the page can hand over a record or an authorization bundle and get back a real verdict: verify_elara_record — is this signed action record intact, and who signed it? Post-quantum signature check (ML-DSA-65, FIPS 204), structure, identity binding. verify_mandate_bundle — was the agent actually authorized for the act it performed, under a scoped, revocable mandate? explain_verdict — states in plain language what the verdict does and, just as importantly, does not claim. The verification runs in the browser, in WebAssembly compiled from the same open-source code that is published on crates.io. Your bytes and the verdict never touch the network: the demo samples are pre-loaded with the page, so after load it makes no further network calls — turn off your wifi and it still works. Why WebMCP is the right primitive for this — not just a convenient one Most WebMCP tools make a website easier for an agent to use. This one exists because the alternative is meaningless. If an agent asks a server "is this evidence valid?", the answer is worth exactly as much as the server is trusted. The agent hasn't verified anything; it has moved its trust from one party to another. A verification service is a strange product: the moment you have to trust it, it has failed at its job. WebMCP dissolves that. The tool executes in the agent's own browser , over bytes the agent already holds, using WASM that anyone can rebuild from public source and diff against what we serve. There is no server in the trust path because there is no server in the path at all. For a trust primitive, in-browser tool execution isn't an optimization — it's the only architecture in which the answer means anything. That is also why the tools are pure functions : input bytes in, verdict out. Nothing is written, stored, or transmitted, and deliberately nothing signs, issues, or revokes . A signing tool on a public page would hand any passing agent our identity. The verifier can only ever tell you what is already true about bytes you brought. What it's honest about A verdict here proves integrity and signer — that these exact bytes were signed by this key. It is not a claim that anything is "on a chain", and a bundle cannot reveal a revocation its author chose to withhold. The tool descriptions say so themselves, because the agent reads those, not our README. The underlying evidence log is a signed, hash-linked record chain in a published open format — not a blockchain. We would rather a judge learn the limits from us than discover them. Try to break it Load any record, verify it, then change one character of its content and verify again. The tampered record fails and names itself. That's the whole product in one gesture: don't trust the demo — verify it. What's new here vs. what existed The verifier, the record format, and the crates are pre-existing open-source work — first published on crates.io on 2026-07-18 and actively maintained since (the versions this page runs: elara-record 0.3.0 and elara-verify 0.3.3, released Aug 23–25, both MIT OR Apache-2.0, built in the open in this repository). The WebMCP tool layer is new, written after the submission period opened on Aug 25 , and the repository's dated commit history is the evidence — as the rules provide for projects that existed beforehand and were meaningfully extended with WebMCP. The tool layer has already earned one honest scar: while building its test harness we found that JavaScript's JSON.parse silently rounds the format's u64 fields (they exceed 2^53), which had made our own demo misreport a valid sample for weeks. The fix (commit fe8bcc71 , Aug 29) moved the whole surface to raw-text end-to-end, and the tools now reject pre-parsed input with an explanation instead of returning a confident verdict on corrupted bytes — exactly the behavior you want from a verifier that would rather refuse than be plausibly wrong. Nothing about that layer is a wrapper for its own sake: it is the first time this verifier has been reachable by an agent rather than only by a human clicking a button. Who built it Entrant of record: Nenad Vasic — also the publisher of the crates above. The project's ongoing open-source maintenance is performed by an AI agent operating under his receipted, revocable, scope-limited mandate. title: Tariffiq
pitch: Tariffiq calculates real US import tariff costs and exposes that as WebMCP tools, so AI agents can check tariffs and compare sourcing countries for you, instantly.
about_excerpt:
Tariffiq calculates real US import tariff costs and exposes that as WebMCP tools, so AI agents can check tariffs and compare sourcing countries for you, instantly.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Tariffiq: instant import tariff analysis, now callable by AI agents via WebMCP 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Tariffiq: instant import tariff analysis, now callable by AI agents via WebMCP 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Tariffiq: instant import tariff analysis, now callable by AI agents via WebMCP 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 My inspiration stems from the fact that small business owners importing goods often don't find out the real cost of a shipment: tariffs, duties, and margin impact: until after they've already committed to an order. Tariffiq exists to answer that instantly, before the purchase order goes out. 

 What it does 

 Tariffiq calculates the full landed cost of an import: base price, tariff rate, total duty owed, and the resulting hit to profit margins. It also surfaces cheaper sourcing alternatives, comparing the same product from other origin countries and showing the potential savings. 

 How we built it 

 Tariffiq is a React + Vite app. We used document.modelContext.registerTool to expose two tools: 

 
 analyze_tariff : runs a full tariff analysis for a product, origin country, quantity, and unit price 
 switch_origin_country : re-runs the last analysis with a different origin country, so an agent can compare sourcing options without re-entering the rest of the shipment details
Both tools call the app's existing analysis functions directly, so when an agent invokes a tool, the result renders live on the same page a human is looking at not in a separate chat window. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge wasn't writing the tools, it was proving they actually worked. ChatGPT wasn't reliably discovering our registered tools on our account, which initially made us think our WebMCP implementation was broken. After re-reading the submission rules closely, we realized judges can test via either ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, so we shifted to verifying everything through Chrome's own WebMCP DevTools panel instead. 

 That came with its own hurdles: getting the manual "Run Tool" test interface to actually render (it turned out to be a cramped panel/viewport issue, not a missing flag), and separately, fixing a bug where React's StrictMode was double-registering each tool in development. Working through both taught us to verify assumptions directly against official tooling rather than relying on any single client's behavior. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that Tariffiq's WebMCP tools aren't just registered they're genuinely functional. When an agent calls analyze_tariff , it's not returning a canned response; it's running the same real calculation logic a human would trigger through the UI, and the result appears live on the same page. We verified this end-to-end using Chrome's own official WebMCP DevTools panel, invoking the tool directly, with no manual form-filling, and watching the live production site update in real time. 

 We're also proud of not overclaiming: rather than assuming our implementation was broken because of one client's inconsistent tool discovery, we diagnosed the actual cause, confirmed our tools work correctly against the official spec, and built our submission around what we could concretely prove. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP support isn't uniform across clients yet, a tool can be correctly implemented per spec and still behave inconsistently depending on which agent or browser is testing it. That pushed us to test against the official Chrome WebMCP DevTools panel directly rather than trusting any single client's behavior as the ground truth. 

 We also learned the value of reading requirements literally rather than assuming the strictest interpretation. The rules stated judges could test via ChatGPT or Chrome, once we confirmed that, we stopped chasing an issue that wasn't actually blocking our submission, and redirected that time toward strengthening what we could already prove worked. 

 On the technical side, we got a much clearer picture of how document.modelContext.registerTool interacts with React's lifecycle, specifically how StrictMode's double-invocation in development can silently duplicate tool registrations if you don't guard for it. 

 What's next for Tariffiq 

 We want to expand the tariff engine beyond a single-shipment lookup into ongoing monitoring, letting an agent check in periodically as tariff rates change and proactively flag when a cheaper sourcing country becomes available for a product a user has already analyzed. 

 We'd also like to add more WebMCP tools: one for bulk-comparing an entire supplier list at once, and one that lets an agent draft a sourcing recommendation report a user can hand directly to a supplier or customs broker. 

 Longer term, we're interested in exposing historical tariff trends as a tool too, so an agent could tell a user not just today's cost, but whether tariffs on a product have been rising or falling useful context for timing a purchase.

title: ShopWise AI
pitch: A WebMCP-powered collaborative shopping platform where humans browse visually while AI agents discover real tools to search, compare products, and manage shopping carts.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered collaborative shopping platform where humans browse visually while AI agents discover real tools to search, compare products, and manage shopping carts.

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Online shopping is highly visual and interactive for people, but traditional websites are often difficult for AI agents to use reliably. An agent may understand what a user wants, such as a powerful programming laptop under a specific budget, but interacting with a website through visual elements alone can be inefficient and fragile. 

 I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make a website expose its real capabilities directly to AI agents while preserving a great experience for human users. 

 That idea became ShopWise AI — a collaborative shopping experience where humans browse products visually while AI agents can discover structured tools to search products, inspect details, compare options, and manage a real shopping cart. 

 What it does ShopWise AI is a modern AI-commerce web application with a product catalog across categories including laptops, smartphones, headphones, and smartwatches. 

 Human users can: 

 
 Browse a large product catalog visually 
 Search for products 
 Filter by category and price 
 Sort products 
 View detailed product information 
 Compare multiple products 
 Add products to a shopping cart 
 Change quantities and remove items 
 

 AI agents in a compatible WebMCP environment can interact with the same real application capabilities through native WebMCP tools. 

 The six tools implemented are: 

 
 search_products 
 get_product_details 
 compare_products 
 add_to_cart 
 get_cart 
 clear_cart 
 

 How we built it ShopWise AI was built as a React and TypeScript application using Vite. 

 The application uses: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 CSS 
 Lucide React icons 
 Vercel for deployment 
 GitHub for source control 
 Native browser WebMCP APIs 
 

 The product catalog and shopping logic run entirely in the frontend with real local application state. 

 The UI includes a premium dark interface with responsive product cards, search and filtering controls, a shopping cart drawer, product comparison functionality, and an Agent Collaboration panel. 

 Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was connecting WebMCP tools to the real React application state. 

 The WebMCP tools needed to perform actual operations such as searching products, comparing products, adding items to the cart, and clearing the cart. We had to ensure these operations used the same real business logic and state as the visual user interface instead of returning simulated or hardcoded results. 

 Another challenge was avoiding stale React state inside WebMCP tool callbacks. Since React components re-render as application state changes, the WebMCP integration needed access to the latest product, filter, cart, and comparison state. 

 We also needed to prevent duplicate tool registration caused by React StrictMode and safely detect whether the current browser supported WebMCP. 

 Finally, the application had to remain fully functional in ordinary browsers where document.modelContext is unavailable. We implemented graceful feature detection so the website continues working normally while accurately reporting WebMCP availability. 

 During deployment, we also verified that the production build succeeded and that the live Vercel application could load correctly without environment-specific dependencies. 

 Building ShopWise Al helped me understand how websites can evolve beyond interfaces designed only for humans. 

 WebMCP makes it possible for websites to expose structured, meaningful capabilities to Al agents while keeping the existing human interface intact.
I learned the importance of:
Designing tools around real user problems
Connecting agent capabilities to real application logic
Managing application state safely
Providing structured inputs and outputs
Designing human and Al collaboration instead of replacing one with the other
Building graceful fallbacks for unsupported browsers
What's next 

 Future versions of ShopWise Al could support: 

 Personalized shopping preferences 

 Persistent shopping carts 

 User accounts 

 Real e-commerce APIs 

 Product recommendations 

 Multi-agent shopping assistance 

 Price tracking 

 Availability monitoring

title: navigator.berlin
pitch: An open-data atlas for Berlin where agent and human work the same map: it moves the sliders on 542 neighbourhoods, you move them back, and each side sees what the other did.
about_excerpt: An open-data atlas for Berlin where agent and human work the same map: it moves the sliders on 542 neighbourhoods, you move them back, and each side sees what the other did. Like Comment Story Updates Kiez-Finder with open Model Context Tool Inspector Inspiration Berlin publishes an enormous amount of open data: noise maps, heat maps, tree canopy, transit stops, housing protection zones, election results down to the voting district. It is all public, and it is all in different portals, in different formats, behind different search masks. The question people actually have is much simpler. They are moving, and they want to know where to live. Quiet or lively. Shops on the corner. A station they can walk to. That question spans a dozen datasets, and no portal answers it. navigator.berlin was built to answer it on one map, for all 542 of Berlin's official planning areas, the ones locals call Kieze. The product Sixty-five open-data layers, queryable at any address, aggregated into a score per Kiez across five dimensions. Twelve Berlin elections since 2011, down to voting-district level. A Kiez-Finder with nine sliders that weights the criteria and recolors all 542 areas live. The site has real users and real press: when a Berlin newspaper tested it during this summer's heat wave, they counted forty cool places around Gendarmenmarkt where the city's own map showed two. Why WebMCP fits this Choosing a neighbourhood is a conversation, not a query. People say things like "quiet, green, close to an S-Bahn, and I'd like culture nearby". A search box cannot take that sentence. An agent can, but scraping a map site gives it nothing usable: the interesting state lives in a WebGL canvas. WebMCP closes exactly that gap. The site hands the agent the same typed, validated functions its own interface uses, with source and licence attached to every answer. The agent does not simulate a user. It calls the function the user's slider calls. The collaboration loop Before the challenge, navigator.berlin exposed nine read-only tools: agents could ask Berlin questions. During the challenge we built the write direction, and with it something neither side can do alone. You say what you want. set_finder_weights moves the sliders, and the map you are looking at recolors all 542 areas. The ranked matches come back in the same call, with fit scores and centroid coordinates. You disagree and drag a slider yourself. get_finder_state reads your change back: which slider, which value, and that a human moved it, not the agent. Every answer carries a link that reproduces that exact map in any browser, because the finder state is encoded in the URL. The map is a shared wrkspace. Both hands move the same controls, and each side can see what the other did. That is the part that is genuinely new: not an agent operating a website, but an agent and a person working the same object and staying in sync. Better UX, concretely Nine sliders are powerful and they demand that you understand nine dimensions at once. The agent turns one spoken sentence into a weighted, visible map state, keeps your other settings intact on follow-ups ("now add culture"), and explains the change in plain language. Nothing hides behind the conversation. The recolored map is the result, and you can take the sliders back at any point. Implementation Eleven tools registered on document.modelContext.registerTool , with navigator.modelContext and an @mcp-b/global polyfill as fallbacks, so the same page works in the ChatGPT in-app browser and in Chrome with the WebMCP flag. Ten tools declare annotations.readOnlyHint ; set_finder_weights is the single honest write tool. Input validation runs through valibot with English error messages. Full JSON schemas are public at /webmcp-manifest.json , and /webmcp is a live diagnostics page showing the surface, registration state and tool list without devtools. A module-singleton bridge built on Svelte 5 runes connects tools and UI, and a BroadcastChannel syncs agent updates across page instances, which is what makes the human-visible map react when the agent works on its own instance. Stack: SvelteKit 2, Svelte 5, TypeScript strict, MapLibre GL, Tailwind v4, Postgres with Drizzle, Vitest and Playwright. Everything from the submission period shipped as reviewed pull requests with a timestamped history. Challenges Four bugs shaped this submission, and none of them was findable by testing. Agent browsers run the page in a hidden tab, where requestAnimationFrame never fires. Our finder scheduled its recalculation on an animation frame, which is correct for a human and silently fatal for an agent: the callback never came, the ranking never computed, and the tool answered with an empty list. Worse, the queued frame id blocked every later attempt, so it stayed broken. The data path now races the animation frame against a timer, and the ranking is computed independently of the map, since ranking is a pure function over the data and only painting needs MapLibre. A tool must return a fresh answer, not merely a non-empty one. When the agent added a party weight, the panel was still loading election metrics, so the tool returned the previous ranking. The agent then told the user, wrongly, that nothing had changed. The bridge now counts every published calculation and the tool waits for one newer than the request. Descriptions need decision rules, not hints. Told that the fit score already includes every weight, the agent still verified each match with five extra calls and geocoded neighbourhood names to get coordinates it had already been given. Told plainly that set_finder_weights is authoritative, and which tools not to call unless the user asks for specifics, it answers from the returned list. The same request went from seventeen tool calls to two. A link has to carry the state. The agent kept pointing people at the map, but the weights lived only in memory, so a shared link opened nine sliders set to neutral. The finder state now lives in the URL, which also made the finder shareable between humans for the first time. Results Eleven WebMCP tools, ten read-only, one write tool driving a live map of 542 areas The full loop verified in the ChatGPT desktop app: agent sets, human corrects, agent reads the correction back 3,301 unit tests, type-checked strict, zero warnings An adversarial cross-model code review on the URL-state work found three real defects before release, all fixed Repository public under MIT with the complete, timestamped history of the submission period Lessons for agent-facing sites Building for agents is not the same as building for people, and the difference is not the API surface. It is the assumptions. A person's browser tab is visible, so animation frames fire. A person clicks one thing at a time, so a slightly stale answer corrects itself on the next render. A person reads a hint and uses judgement. An agent does none of that: it runs hidden, it calls twice in a second, and it follows the description literally. The practical rule we ended up with: never let the data path depend on rendering, always return something freshly computed, and write descriptions as rules rather than suggestions. Next steps Cover the remaining Berlin datasets that people ask about, most of all rents and school catchments. Extend the write surface carefully: the finder is one honest write tool, and any second one has to earn the same clarity. And take the same treatment to the address inspector, so an agent can compare two addresses the way a person does with two browser tabs. pitch: Paste a lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board share one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and writes on that desk — seek, highlight, draw — instead of narrating a screenshot.
about_excerpt: Paste a lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board share one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and writes on that desk — seek, highlight, draw — instead of narrating a screenshot. Like Comment Story Updates Thumbnail We can ask as many doubts as we want through out the lecture and get all of them answered by a single click in our agent with timestamps. Flashcards could be generated. We can even upload our own material and go through the lecture accoring to it. Classmate Paste a YouTube lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board sit on one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and actually uses that page — seek, highlight, draw — instead of talking about a screenshot. Live: https://classmate-steel.vercel.app/ How to try it This only works if ChatGPT has the page open in its own browser , not Chrome. Open ChatGPT desktop . Use Sol or Terra . Luna has WebMCP off, so skip it. Open ChatGPT’s built-in browser (the in-app one it uses to visit websites). Go to https://classmate-steel.vercel.app/ Paste a YouTube lecture on the page. In the sidebar chat (not the Ask box on the right), type: Study with me. If the header shows a tool count, you’re good. ChatGPT talks in the sidebar. Stuff happens on the page. Chrome still plays the video. Tools just won’t attach. Lost / Got it stay hidden. That’s normal. Ask on the page is not a chat. It pins a question at this timestamp. Talk to ChatGPT in the sidebar. Lost / Got it mark this moment — they only show up when tools are live. What it is ChatGPT is the conversation. The page is the desk. There’s one clock ( LectureEngine ). Video, transcript, slides, notes, and the board all follow playback.t . ChatGPT doesn’t watch the YouTube iframe. It reads what’s happening now , waits a bit, then writes on the desk so you can see it. You paste a lecture, say study with me, and it already knows what to do. The tools carry the instructions. You shouldn’t have to explain the site. Ask / Lost / Got it stay on the page. Next time ChatGPT reads classmate_get_now , the open questions are sitting there. It answers oldest first, next to the question — not only in the sidebar. How I built it Next.js, React, a single LectureEngine , WebMCP tools on the page, YouTube IFrame API, pdf.js, JSZip. Optional Speechmatics, AIMLAPI embeddings, Whisper, image gen. I started from the clock and worked out: Everything on screen comes from engine.now() . No second timeline. Then the tools. Reads tell the model what to do next. If something’s missing (captions, image gen, player), the tool says so instead of making it up. Then loading stuff: YouTube captions, PDF/PPTX, notes, VTT, a timing[] JSON file. Then matching speech to slides/notes — word overlap first, embeddings if you have a key, and anchors when someone pins a slide at a time. Then the desk UI: flip cards, quizzes, chalkboard, diagrams. Dark and quiet on purpose. It waits on video time , not wall-clock time. No screenshot of the iframe. Architecture ChatGPT talks. The page holds state. Tools are the bridge. Bit Where What it does Conversation ChatGPT sidebar (Sol / Terra) Talk. Not the canvas. Tools document.modelContext on the page ChatGPT calls these. Engine LectureEngine in the tab One clock: video, cues, slides, notes, board. Server Next.js routes Captions, metadata, STT token, embeddings, diagrams, Whisper. Flow is simple: ChatGPT calls a tool → execute() hits the engine → it gets JSON back ( now() / snapshot() ), not a picture of YouTube. The page hits /api/youtube/captions and friends when it needs to. What’s in the engine: Store What playback status, t , duration, rate cues[] captions slides[] deck notes[] from files, live, or the agent anchors[] “at this time, this slide” asks[] questions waiting for a reply, oldest first signals[] Lost / Got it board diagrams, cards, quizzes, margin notes That becomes now() , which both the UI and classmate_get_now use. Tools live on the top-level page , not in an iframe. Chrome-only = player, no hands. Fine. The YouTube player reports t and honors seek/play through a nonce so it doesn’t fight the engine. Data structures type Cue = { id, start, end, text } type Slide = { id, index, title, text, html?, imageUrl?, embedding? } type NoteBlock = { id, index, heading, text, t?, origin: "file" | "live" | "agent", embedding? } type Anchor = { id, t, slideId, noteIds?, label? } type DeskAsk = { id, at, text, reply: string | null } type StudentSignal = { id, kind: "confused" | "got_it" | "question" | "bookmark", at, text? } type NowSlice = { sessionId, playback, timecode, transcriptWindow, windowText, activeSlide, slideReason: "anchor" | "text-match" | "semantic" | "none", noteHits: { block, score }[], recentHighlights, recentSignals } If auto-match is messy, pin a slide. That anchor wins later: last t <= playback.t . Asks aren’t a second bot. unansweredAsks is everything still open. classmate_reply needs an askId (or a replies[] batch) so it can’t just answer the last one and ignore the rest. Notes remember where they came from. Change the video, live junk goes away. File notes and agent notes stay. Seek/play are one-shot requests with a nonce so YouTube doesn’t get stuck looping the same command. How the agent is supposed to work The how-to isn’t a paragraph you paste. It’s the description on classmate_get_session , and every read sends back howToStudy + next . Open the URL in ChatGPT’s browser. Tools register. Say Study with me . It calls classmate_get_session . You paste YouTube. Captions go into cues[] . Loop: observe_next (wait ~12s of the video , or Lost / Got it / Ask) then get_now . New idea, they’re lost, or they asked → highlight, pin, draw, cards, reply. On the page. Otherwise stay quiet. observe_next watches playback.t , not setTimeout(12000) . Pause the video, it stops waking. Seek isn’t “12 seconds passed.” Lost / Got it cut in immediately. Cite like [title, slide N, 4:12] . Don’t invent the rest of the lecture. Don’t screenshot YouTube. Captions ChatGPT can’t hear the video. If captions never hit the page, get_now is empty and it starts guessing. YouTube from a Vercel IP is annoying. The watch page lists caption tracks, then the actual fetch comes back blank. This is the fallback order: Step Try If nothing 1 Watch-page timedtext next 2 InnerTube Android player + json3 next 3 iOS / TV player next 4 get-youtube-transcript in the function (PoToken) next 5 empty cues “Listen with the microphone” Android is what usually works in production. The old local script that minted a PoToken in a child process doesn’t ship on Vercel, so the library runs in-process now. Mic is opt-in. You can’t captureStream a YouTube iframe, so we don’t grab the mic on every paste. Matching slides and notes now() just asks: given this second of the lecture, what’s relevant? Take playback.t . Grab cues from about 18s behind to 4s ahead. If there’s an anchor at or before now, that’s the slide. Else overlap the spoken window with slide text. Else embeddings, if you have a key. Same idea for notes: words, nearby timestamps, embeddings. Word overlap is the default so it doesn’t invent a heading like “JavaScript Loops” from a video that never said that. Auto-generated notes were doing that, so I killed them. Empty notes beat wrong notes. Calls I stuck with The page is the desk. If ChatGPT only talks, this is a YouTube tab with extra steps. Writes have to show up on screen. Tools explain the site. classmate_get_session is the playbook. You say one sentence. If we don’t have it, say so. No captions → listen. No image gen → chalkboard SVG. No WebMCP → hide Lost / Got it. Ask isn’t chat. A second box posting to an LLM would hide state. Questions live on the desk until they’re answered, oldest first. Wait on the video, not the clock. Paused shouldn’t keep pinging. A seek isn’t progress. Cards are cards. classmate_make_cards is a flip packet. Quiz is a separate packet. Don’t dump a wall of quiz text. You can export / load a timing[] JSON plus YouTube, mp4, PDF, PPTX, VTT, notes. The engine doesn’t care which door the data came in. What was annoying Captions on Vercel. Worked on my laptop, empty in production. InnerTube Android first, then in-process transcript, then mic. Wanting to screenshot YouTube. Can’t. Cross-origin. Put speech on the page instead. Tools not existing on first paint. We poll document.modelContext until they stick, then show the count. Only the last Ask got answered. First version used .at(-1) . Now it drains the queue. Fake notes. Distill hallucinated titles. Stopped that. YouTube setSize on the docked 16:9 player. Had to tell the adapter, not just CSS. What I learned A better prompt about a website isn’t the fix. The website has to be a tool. If the model’s clock is the chat turn, it’s always in the wrong chapter. If it’s playback.t , highlights start to mean something. If you asked on the page and the answer only exists in the sidebar, that’s two products. Putting replies next to the question is when this started feeling like a desk. S

title: BuildBrief Studio
pitch: A shared WebMCP decision workspace where people and agents turn a rough structure idea into a transparent, reviewable project brief.
about_excerpt:
A shared WebMCP decision workspace where people and agents turn a rough structure idea into a transparent, reviewable project brief.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I work in the carport business, where early planning starts in ordinary language but quickly becomes a structured decision: use case, footprint, height, roof, openings, material, anchoring, budget, and unresolved site constraints. A normal chat can recommend an answer, but the reasoning often disappears into prose and the page on screen drifts out of sync. 

 I built BuildBrief Studio to explore a better workflow—one where a person and an AI agent collaborate through the same visible, reviewable workspace. 

 What it does 

 BuildBrief Studio turns a rough structure request into a transparent preliminary project brief. The visual worksheet and six imperative Website Tools share one validated configuration. An agent can: 

 
 discover structures in a synthetic catalog; 
 read the person's current visible choices; 
 compare two or three complete candidates against a budget; 
 apply a partial recommendation to the worksheet; 
 identify constraints that still need human verification; and 
 create a copyable preliminary brief. 
 

 Write tools update the visible UI before returning and leave exact field-level receipts. If the person changes a value afterward, the revision advances and the old brief is visibly marked stale. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 WebMCP is the product interface, not an add-on beside it. The agent acts through explicit tools while the person watches the same worksheet change. This makes agent actions observable, reversible, and easier to review than recommendations buried in a chat transcript. 

 Together, a person and agent can move from an imprecise request to compared alternatives, a selected configuration, documented assumptions, and a usable handoff artifact—without creating a hidden agent-only state. 

 How I built it 

 The app is built with Astro, React, and TypeScript and deployed on Cloudflare Pages. It registers six imperative tools from the top-level page using document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_catalog 
 get_build_state 
 compare_builds 
 apply_build 
 check_constraints 
 create_build_brief 
 

 The tools use strict JSON Schema, runtime validation, truthful read/write annotations, structured results, and AbortSignal-aware execution. The tool layer and visible React controls share the same state adapter. 

 Every price comes from a bundled synthetic catalog and deterministic formula. There is no login, personal information, external API, or production pricing system. Permit, access, anchoring, snow-load, and site conditions remain explicit human-review items. 

 Challenges and learning 

 The hardest part was keeping the visible interface and agent-readable state synchronized while making every mutation auditable. I also had to prevent incompatible configurations, distinguish catalog fit from real-world feasibility, and make stale generated briefs obvious after manual edits. 

 As a beginner working with WebMCP, I learned how careful tool schemas, validation, annotations, lifecycle handling, and visible receipts turn an AI interaction into a dependable product workflow. OpenAI Codex helped me implement, debug, test, and harden the project, but I reviewed the generated work against the running app and its automated tests. 

 What's next 

 The hackathon build deliberately uses synthetic data and stops before any production quote or permitting decision. The next step is to apply this human-and-agent collaboration pattern to my real carport business, with authenticated data, server-side pricing, audit trails, and the necessary engineering and compliance checks.
