title: DONE / PROVEN
pitch: Agents can challenge the definition of done. Humans keep authority. Proof stays current when reality changes.
about_excerpt: Agents can challenge the definition of done. Humans keep authority. Proof stays current when reality changes. Like Comment Story Updates Done is a claim. Proof is a state. AI agents are getting very good at producing work and increasingly good at reporting that the work is finished. The remaining trust problem is deeper: did the agent prove the right definition of success, did it have authority to act on that definition, and is that proof still valid after the world changes? DONE / PROVEN is a proof-carrying work layer for humans and agents. A human owns the mission and the semantic authority to decide what success means. An agent can inspect the mission and acceptance contract through WebMCP and can attack that contract by submitting a concrete counterexample: an outcome that appears to satisfy the current definition of done but should still count as failure. The system evaluates that counterexample deterministically. If the unacceptable outcome would pass, DONE / PROVEN surfaces a false-green contract defect to the human. The agent cannot rewrite the contract, approve its own fix, or impersonate the human decision. After the human admits a corrected contract, execution evidence can earn PROVEN state. If a dependency later changes, DONE / PROVEN invalidates only the proof that depended on the change. Unrelated evidence remains valid, and the system produces a minimum re-proof plan. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns the page from a dashboard into a structured human-agent collaboration surface. The release exposes seven tools that let an agent read the mission, inspect authority, inspect the candidate contract, list known contract risks, inspect evidence state, request a bounded human decision, and submit an adversarial counterexample. The key tool is submit_counterexample . It lets the agent actively pressure-test the human-owned definition of done while keeping semantic authority with the human. Better human-agent UX The point is not to make people write longer specifications. The system concentrates human attention on the few decisions automation cannot safely settle, gives the agent a typed way to expose loopholes, and keeps deterministic code responsible for evaluation and proof state. A later dependency change reopens only evidence that actually depended on what changed rather than discarding all prior proof or trusting a stale green checkmark. What people and agents can do together The agent can inspect mission, authority, candidate acceptance criteria, contract risks, and proof state; request a bounded human decision; and submit a concrete adversarial counterexample. The human owns unresolved meaning and admission. Deterministic code owns evaluation, proof validity, dependency impact, and minimal re-proof. Demo The demo begins with an agent claiming a landing-page task is DONE. The initial acceptance contract is deliberately wrong in two directions: False green: it forgets to require the waitlist signup to actually persist. False red: it requires one exact headline even though the human said wording does not matter. The agent submits a broken-waitlist counterexample. The deterministic engine returns EXPOSES_FALSE_GREEN , records the visible challenge, and leaves the active contract unchanged. The human resolves the genuinely semantic admin-privacy question, the corrected contract is admitted, and five requirements earn evidence-backed PROVEN state. Then a dependency changes. Exactly two of five proof receipts become STALE while three remain PROVEN. Re-running only the affected checks restores 5/5. WebMCP implementation Seven imperative tools register through the current document.modelContext surface when available, with the older navigator path retained only as compatibility fallback. submit_counterexample uses a narrow JSON schema, additionalProperties: false , runtime size/type validation, and an untrusted-content hint. It is non-read-only only because it records a visible challenge. It has no capability to edit or admit the acceptance contract. Evidence boundary This project does not claim that AI can automatically infer arbitrary human intent, that acceptance contracts themselves are novel, or that every verification problem is solved. The demonstrated contribution is narrower: an agent can adversarially falsify the human-owned definition of done without becoming the authority, and proof can remain dependency-aware after reality changes. The final licensed release passes 38/38 deterministic tests , TypeScript typecheck, static build, responsive browser verification, seven-tool WebMCP current-API harness registration, adversarial counterexample execution, agent-content injection probes, deployment-header verification, and zero unauthorized contract mutation. Existing-project disclosure Existing project, meaningfully extended during the challenge. The underlying contract-adequacy and continuous-validity research began before August 25. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, the project was materially extended with the responsive human product surface, authority reconciliation, seven WebMCP tools, the agent-submitted counterexample mechanism, WebMCP trust boundaries and runtime validation, current-API harness verification, deployment-origin and permissions hardening, browser/mobile/injection verification, public-release packaging, and challenge-specific testing/documentation. Dated commit history and release evidence preserve that distinction. title: Auralis WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP-powered human-agent listening experience that illustrates how hearing loss and competing sounds can make family conversations harder to follow—while keeping the person in control.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered human-agent listening experience that illustrates how hearing loss and competing sounds can make family conversations harder to follow—while keeping the person in control. Like Comment Story Updates Auralis transforms into a shared agent-guided interface with three synthetic hearing profiles. The agent plays the source reference and illustrative result while the person retains control The agent proposes one bounded scene change based on what the person reported Inspiration I work as an audiology technician, and every day I encounter not only hearing loss itself, but also the communication gap that forms around it. An audiogram can show numbers and curves. What is much harder is helping a family understand why a conversation with the television on can be exhausting, why the speaker’s position matters, or why someone may hear that speech is present without understanding it clearly. The original Auralis was therefore created as an illustrative, non-clinical listening experience. It lets people compare the same family scene under different synthetic listening conditions. It is not intended to diagnose hearing or reproduce any individual person’s perception exactly. Its purpose is to create a shared and understandable starting point for conversation. WebMCP took that idea much further. What began as a human-controlled illustration became a shared live space where a person and an agent collaborate over the same scene, the same state, and the same safety boundaries. What it does Auralis begins as a normal human-first application. Simply opening, browsing, or clicking the page never activates agent mode. The first successful stage_demo_session call transforms the full presentation into Agent Reveal . This is not merely an agent clicking through the existing website. The page gains a new information hierarchy, session progress, controls, and a final summary designed specifically for a shared human-agent journey. The person and the agent are not operating two separate applications. Both work through the same revisioned ExperienceState . A typical session works like this: The agent explains the illustrative, non-diagnostic purpose. The person must confirm consent directly. The agent introduces three approved synthetic profiles and may recommend the one with the clearest demonstration contrast. The person can override the choice by clicking or by responding to the agent through text or voice, where the current host and phase support it. Auralis automatically prepares the fixed family scene. The person visibly confirms a safe and comfortable listening level. They may separately grant the agent permission to start audio. The agent prepares and starts the reference A and illustrative B listening comparison. The person describes what they noticed in ordinary language. The agent translates only that stated meaning into bounded, non-diagnostic fields. It can then change one approved variable at a time—for example, turning off the television, adding illustrative left-ear support, or changing the speaker’s position when explicitly requested. The session ends with a deterministic summary of what was compared and what the person actually reported. The person retains consequential authority throughout the experience. WebMCP cannot provide consent or acknowledge physical listening volume on their behalf. Agent-started playback requires a separate grant, and Stop remains immediately available. Interrupted audio never counts as heard. Two defining WebMCP features 1. Agent Reveal and a real transformation of the experience The first successful stage_demo_session call transforms the complete page presentation into Agent Reveal. Later WebMCP calls change only approved listening variables through the shared ExperienceState . The agent can therefore substantially change the flow and presentation of the experience without receiving arbitrary DOM control or bypassing the safety model. A direct human click is also a real event in the same session. The agent does not need to imitate that action through Computer Use. 2. A continuing session that can wait for the person One of the hardest problems was preventing the agent from treating every human step as the end of the session and waiting for an entirely new prompt. I built wait_for_session_change as a bounded, read-only call tied to the exact session and revision. Normal human or technical steps use a four-minute window, while the optional profile override deliberately uses a shorter 15-second window. A bounded wait_for_session_change call can keep the current agent run pending while the host keeps the tool call active. When the page revision changes, the call returns the new semantic state and the agent can continue with the next allowed step without model polling. Direct page actions and technical page progress resolve the wait. Typed or spoken responses are handled by the compatible host, which can then invoke the next allowed WebMCP tool. This is not a WebSocket, durable backend persistence, or a mechanism that can revive a turn the host has already ended. It is a practical way to keep an active human-agent interaction connected through ordinary WebMCP calls. How I built it Auralis uses: Next.js, React, and TypeScript; the Web Audio API for deterministic in-browser audio processing and playback; Zod for strict input and output contracts; WebMCP for the semantic connection between the page and a compatible agent; Vitest for domain and browser-adapter testing; Playwright for complete browser journeys. The WebMCP extension exposes exactly seven narrowly scoped tools: get_auralis_state stage_demo_session prepare_comparison play_listening_comparison record_user_observation get_session_evidence wait_for_session_change allowedNextTools is the sole authority for what may execute in the current phase. Every mutation is bound to an expected revision and protected against stale, repeated, or conflicting requests. Auralis does not expose raw audiogram thresholds or free-text observations through WebMCP. Session evidence contains only a bounded, ordered, and attributable record. Auralis’s server-side OpenAI explanation layer is optional and never controls the audio. Agent Reveal itself requires a compatible external WebMCP host and agent. The complete deterministic human journey remains available without the internal OpenAI explanation layer and when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges I ran into Keeping one truthful state for both direct human actions and agent tools. Allowing the agent to wait without polling or pretending that the page has durable backend persistence. Ensuring that the agent continues correctly after a human decision. Separating the full visual Agent Reveal from the agent’s deliberately bounded authority over listening variables. Keeping consent, physical listening volume, the playback grant, and Stop under human control. Preventing the agent from speaking over the audio. The page therefore inserts an eight-second quiet lead-in before agent-started playback, and the tool remains pending until completion, failure, or a human Stop. Translating ordinary human descriptions into structured observations without diagnosing or inventing meaning. Preserving a complete human fallback for browsers without WebMCP. There was also one technical challenge I did not manage to solve: the hackathon deadline has no Pause button. With a few more days, Auralis would probably already be explaining why I still have not slept. Accomplishments that I’m proud of WebMCP is not just a wrapper around clicking; it is a semantic part of the product. The agent can activate a completely different presentation and guide the person through the full experience. The person can intervene directly in the same session at any time. After explicit permission, the agent genuinely starts the listening comparison instead of telling the person to press Play. Audio, profiles, scene conditions, adaptations, observations, and the final summary remain consistent. The original human Auralis journey remains intact, with the WebMCP work preserved as a traceable extension above it. The repository includes domain, browser-adapter, and Playwright journey coverage; separate owner-observed sessions covered native typed and voice-guided use. What I learned The most important lesson was that a good agentic application needs more than a list of tools. It needs a clear continuation contract, explicit ownership of state, and an exact answer to who is allowed to perform the next action. I also learned that waiting is not merely a technical detail. In a human-agent product, it is part of the user experience. The agent must understand when to act, when to explain, when to remain silent, and when to genuinely wait for the person. WebMCP made it possible to keep the human as an active participant and owner of consequential decisions, rather than reducing them to a spectator of automation. What’s next for Auralis I want to develop Auralis into a broader e

title: pact
pitch: Gives agents only the exact authority needed for one approved transaction, with stale-state protection, verification, auditability, and receipts.
about_excerpt: Gives agents only the exact authority needed for one approved transaction, with stale-state protection, verification, auditability, and receipts. Like Comment Story Updates PACT PACT is a transaction and authority protocol for AI agents performing consequential actions inside web applications. Most agent systems give an AI broad access to application tools and rely on instructions such as “only change these resources” or “do not touch billing.” PACT treats that model as insufficient for high-impact operations. Instead, PACT turns every consequential task into an explicitly scoped transaction. The workflow is: Intent → semantic preview → exact-plan approval → scoped authority → commit → canonical verification → receipt. Before any mutation occurs, PACT determines the exact effects required by the task. The human sees precisely what will change and what will not change. Approval is bound to the specific plan, its hash, and the canonical state on which it was created. If the underlying state changes after approval, the plan becomes stale and commit authority disappears. The agent must re-plan and obtain approval for the new state instead of silently executing an outdated operation. PACT includes protections for stale state, duplicate commits, idempotency, version conflicts, approval expiry, negative invariants, post-condition verification, audit integrity, rollback conditions, and transaction recovery. Its key WebMCP contribution is that agent capability is not equivalent to permanent administrative access. Mutation capabilities can appear only after an exact transaction has been approved and disappear when the authorization is no longer valid. The reference implementation demonstrates this through operations such as contractor offboarding, ownership transfer, access revocation, and protected resources such as billing or deletion. The broader thesis is that agents should not receive permanent authority. They should receive narrowly scoped, temporary, verifiable authority for a specific approved transaction. title: PaperSpace
pitch: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI tools treat a research paper as a file to summarize or a block of text to retrieve from. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What becomes possible when a person and an agent share a paper's text and its spatial reading environment inside the browser? Reading a paper is rarely linear. A reader moves between related work, methods, equations, figures, experiments, and appendices while building a mental map of where each idea lives. Conventional PDF viewers collapse that map into one page at a time. Chat interfaces collapse it even further into excerpts detached from their visual source. PaperSpace preserves that spatial memory. Every page of every imported PDF is unfolded onto a borderless two-dimensional desk. Pages remain live, selectable PDF surfaces, but they can also be moved, grouped, searched, compared, and revisited as part of a persistent visual workspace. The browser is essential to this interaction. It owns the PDFs the person explicitly selected, the rendered pages, the local text index, the page geometry, the current camera, and the workspace the person is looking at. WebMCP gives an agent direct access to that authorized, browser-local state, keeping the person and the agent aligned on one live workspace. We built PaperSpace for the WebMCP Challenge as a focused, open-source, single-person tool centered on reading, understanding, and presenting research papers. PaperSpace is a shared spatial instrument where the person controls the source material and the agent helps organize attention inside the same visible world. What it does PaperSpace is a local-first spatial desk for research papers. When a person imports a PDF, PaperSpace unfolds every page from left to right and top to bottom using each page's real aspect ratio. Every page becomes an independently movable and resizable live sheet with selectable text. The complete paper stays visible as a spatial place with its reading order intact. PaperSpace extracts text and normalized page geometry locally with PDF.js. Each page becomes searchable as soon as its index is ready. A reusable inspect_workspace briefing reports exact coverage and compact sampled page excerpts, so an agent can prepare once and then read the broadest useful contiguous range in one call, including the whole paper when full context matters. Through WebMCP, the agent can search the available corpus, batch-read paper text, locate an exact passage, and guide the shared camera to that region. The camera first pulls back to establish spatial context, travels across the desk, and then lands with the source itself centered in a calm view with generous breathing room. The app exposes nine WebMCP tools: inspect_workspace returns reusable readiness, compact paper briefs, every page's world geometry, visual artifacts, sequences, and camera state. search_papers progressively searches indexed pages and returns page-level matches with normalized source regions plus exact coverage. read_paper_pages reads one contiguous range or a whole indexed paper in one call, with optional block geometry and an explicit caller-selected character cap. focus_region guides the camera to a search match or an explicit PDF region. arrange_papers reflows pages into reading-order grids and arranges complete paper groups. snapshot_paper_region places a source-linked raster crop from an exact PDF region. place_plot creates a safe declarative line plot from finite numeric data. place_image validates and places PNG, JPEG, and WebP visuals. present_sequence creates a captioned sequence of semantic paper regions and visual artifacts. PaperSpace also gives the agent an explicit delivery contract. When PaperSpace is available, substantive introductions, explanations, reviews, comparisons, and answers grounded across multiple paper regions are delivered through present_sequence . Chat provides concise supporting context, while a single grounded passage can use focus_region and simple localized Q&A remains lightweight. The sequence interaction is the heart of the product. Suppose one experiment is explained across related work, methods, and results on three distant pages. The agent can build a three-frame sequence with a caption for each view. When presentation begins, PaperSpace temporarily draws those original pages together beside their paper in first-appearance order. Quiet numbered source slots preserve the paper's topology throughout the presentation. The same original page can support several region frames through one staged page. Visual artifacts stay in their existing world positions. Exiting the sequence restores every moved page—including its position, size, and layer—and returns the camera to its exact entry state. Keeping a sequence saves its semantic frames; replaying it organizes pages again from their current positions and restores them again afterward. This enables requests such as: “Find where this experiment is motivated, defined, and evaluated, then organize those pages for me.” “Focus on the ablation equation and keep the surrounding paragraph in view.” “Read the method and results, plot the reported trend, and place it beside the source page.” “Present the three views in sequence and explain what changes between them.” Everything happens on the same desk the person can inspect and manipulate. Agent actions produce visible feedback, and temporary organization is transactionally isolated from the person's saved layout. Spatial mutation tools perform an atomic visual preflight inside the app. Standard calls place plots, images, source crops, and arrangements in clear areas. An agent can use force: true for an intentional dense layout, while media, schema, source-target, and security validation remain active. How we built it PaperSpace is a pure frontend SvelteKit and TypeScript application compiled as a static site for Cloudflare Pages. Browser storage and browser-authorized files provide the complete runtime state. The application is organized around four client-side layers: Svelte components render the infinite desk, unfolded PDF sheets, artifacts, search interface, frame editor, and presentation chrome. A single reactive workspace model owns paper metadata, per-page geometry, the camera, artifacts, semantic sequences, and all person- and agent-triggered state transitions. PDF.js renders pages and extracts text plus normalized block geometry in a same-origin Web Worker. IndexedDB stores validated workspace metadata, browser-authorized PDF copies, raster images, and saved semantic frames. The workspace schema stores a stable paper identity and page number for every PDF page, while position, size, and layer remain mutable world properties. PDF inspection records each page's true dimensions. A deterministic row-major layout uses a bounded column count to keep long papers spatially legible, and complete paper bounds are used to prevent different imports from overlapping. Every page has a DOM sheet so its identity remains stable in the world. PaperSpace activates detailed PDF canvas and text rendering near the viewport and above a useful zoom threshold, keeping long unfolded papers responsive. PDF rasterization uses a two-tier residency system. Every successfully rendered page retains a 288-pixel-wide aspect-preserving preview, while an LRU applies a 48-million-pixel budget to unpinned high-resolution page canvases. Pages in the strict viewport, the current focus target, and the active sequence frame are pinned and may temporarily exceed that budget. A compact preview preserves visual continuity as high-resolution canvases move through the working set. Raster canvases and selectable text layers have independent lifecycles, and a double-canvas pipeline swaps each completed bitmap into view atomically. Region targeting uses top-left normalized coordinates. The same semantic region can therefore be mapped through a page's current world geometry after the page has been moved or resized. Camera motion is handled by a cancellable controller with pull-back, travel, and landing keyframes, smooth center interpolation, logarithmic zoom interpolation, distance-aware timing, responsive caption-safe insets, and an immediate path for prefers-reduced-motion . Presentation staging is transactional. PaperSpace validates every frame before changing state, deduplicates source pages by first appearance, snapshots their exact geometry and the entry camera, stages the original pages, and exposes their source slots. Presentation mode pauses page manipulation, while persistence serializes the source geometry and entry camera to keep the durable desk unchanged. WebMCP is registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP adapter is intentionally thin: every tool calls the same workspace

video_transcript_excerpt: This is PaperSpace, a browser-native research workspace that exposes its live reading desk to AI agents through WebMCP. The paper is our test. Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: Fangorn.tv
pitch: Own your algorithm
about_excerpt: Own your algorithm Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration In 2020, NBC's Peacock officially launched and pulled the license for "The Office" from Netflix. I was bothered; another gatekeeper forcing yet another SaaS subscription to consume a single series could not be justified. Growing up with services like Limewire, this felt like a massive degradation in user experience. While the technology for distributing media has become more powerful, the consumer experience seems to be converging to the worst parts of cable TV again: fragmented catalogs behind increasingly costly paywalls, centralized recommendation systems, the reintroduction of advertisements, and increasingly little control over what you consume and how you discover it. This led to a multi-year journey into the depths of cryptography, storage, search, discovery, payment, privacy, and the many failed iterations of a sovereign, semantic web, in an effort to understand the economic and social factors that arise to bring us "Streaming services that are just TV again". Fangorn TV is an experiment of what it might look like if media curation, synthesis, and recommendation were designed for both humans and agents from the beginning. What it does Fangorn.TV is an agentic media platform that lives in the browser. It is a static site that exposes its own semantic dataset to agents through WebMCP. The key idea is that the site itself is the agent's data source, that the semantic index and media operations are exposed directly to an agent with WebMCP. Seeded from a slice of the Internet Archive, it holds ~20k titles to choose from. It has no ads, no login, and collects no user data whatsoever. For a human ( without an agent ), it lets you "own your algorithm": Maintain Client Privacy: privately search the archive by semantic meaning (e.g. "cats") entirely in the browser. Queries never get broadcast to a third party, your behavioral data remains yours. treat the internet archive as live TV channels that can be synced across viewers (i.e. watch with your friends), even building your own custom channels based on meaning Since all data in Fangorn.TV is a vector embedding, users can use ("train") a Markov kernel (over the embedding space) built on their actual behavior, providing newer ways to 'be your own discovery algorithm' Using WebMCP tools and an autonomous agent (like Claude Code): Agentic Media Curation: An agent can control playback based on your actual intent and preference, further amplifying the "own your own algorithm" capabilities. An LLM can be prompted to "Find that one episode of XYZ where THINGS happens", or "Create a new channel that only has shows and movies about dogs" and watch as it produces Dog TV in the browser. Byte-Level Range Requests: Agents can efficiently discover granularly labeled content and extract exact video slices directly using HTTP Range headers instead of downloading gigabytes of raw source files (e.g. efficient GIF extraction from media playing in the browser). Programmatic Media Synthesis: Allows an agent to efficiently synthesize disparate archival footage, builds seamless audio beds, applies dynamic text overlays, and executes frame-accurate FFmpeg cuts to produce polished short documentaries, GIFs, and audio clips. Zero DOM Scraping: Eliminates fragile HTML parsing, selector guessing, and simulated UI clicks. The agent interacts purely through typed, deterministic tool interfaces. Zero-Telemetry Local Discovery: Queries are resolved instantly against client-side vector bundles. The agent receives exact media segment URLs, transcript timestamps, and metadata in milliseconds—running search entirely on the client without exposing behavioral data to external backends. Beyond these immediate capabilities, Fangorn.TV does something less noticeable. It presents a reusable pattern for deploying static sites that simultaneously act as rich, agent-ready datasets with incredibly low overhead both in terms of storage, cost, and bandwidth. The same pattern can be applied to nearly any dataset. How we built it Fangorn.TV existed before we entered the hackathon, but without WebMCP integration. The majority of work during this hackathon involved both WebMCP integration and associated agentic tooling and testing. The application is built using the Fangorn SDK , a "git for knowledge graphs" protocol anchored to Arbitrum and backed by IPFS. We crawled the Internet Archive's Video and TV catalog, cross-referencing entries with wikidata and attempting to filter out content that either lewd/illicit/obscene, deemed low quality, or non-CC0/PD. We used the metadata to build a knowledge graph, organizing content hierarchically (e.g. title > series) and committing it onchain using Fangorn. Then, we run a multimodal feature extraction pipeline (developed during the hackathon in order to enhance the semantic richness of the embeddings), extracting timestamped subtitles using whisper and summarized video features using granite. This enriched data is then used to extend the KG that was committed to previously, adding new vertices and edges to map media to its extracted features. With the time available, we were able to execute this on roughly ~250 videos (using an RTX 3050/i9 - estimates indicate ~21 days for the entire catalog). The graph committed in Fangorn is then used to build vector embeddings (using Qdrant), where we leverage int8 scalar quantization to minimize the memory impact of the set of embeddings, make it small enough to efficiently live within a statically hosted Vite site. This site is deployed as a page on cloudflare, https://tv.fangorn.network , where WebMCP integration makes the bundled embeddings easily queryable by an agent. Challenges we ran into Restricting to Open/Public Domain Content: Navigating copyright boundaries requires strict filtering for CC0 and public domain assets. While we made a best effort to limit this, some content still made it through our filters. - Rich Semantic Embeddings Under Constraints: As mentioned above, our pipeline first extracts subtitles and video features, then builds a graph, and then on top of this embeddings. Due to computational and temporal constraints, we have only produced rich embeddings (i.e. including subtitles + features) on roughly 1.5% of the available catalog (so far). Accomplishments that we're proud of Autonomous Documentary: We used WebMCP to generate multiple 'documentaries' composed full of real archival footage. Zero telemetry RAG: Achieved fully private, semantic vector search running 100% inside the user's browser runtime through WebMCP. Massive bandwidth reduction: reduced data transfer by over 90% using HTTP range requests instead of pulling raw video files into an editor. What we learned Static sites can act as agentic backends : Instead of running a bespoke MCP server in order to make these embeddings available, we only need a static page deployed (e.g. on cloudflare), incurring virtually zero cost. By shipping quantized embeddings (built on top of a structured KG) and WebMCP, it becomes possible to turn a static webpage into a rich database that agents can natively query and leverage. The operational cost collapses to near zero. Efficient web tools can be used to optimize agentic compute : By using HTTP range requests and fine-grained timestamping (on the vids with enriched feature extraction), agents don't need local copies of massive datasets, instead benefiting from byte-level retrieval. A missing consumer class emerges : The Semantic Web of the early 2000s failed because there were no entities that needed to navigate RDF graphs. AI agents are the missing consumer that makes structured semantic data viable and necessary. What's next for Fangorn.tv While we used video streaming here, Fangorn TV is only a media-focused proof-of-concept for a broader architectural paradigm. The underlying pattern, where we leverage version controlled graphs, quantized vector embeddings, and client-side WebMCP interfaces, generalized to any dataset or web application. It fundamentally redefines how static web pages can host and serve data for both humans and agents. Generalizing Beyond Video By making the architecture reusable, we can allow developers to ship static, zero-latency, privacy preserving, agent-native applications across nearly any domain. For example: Private E-Commerce : Users and their agents can search and purchase items (using x402f - our x402-based private paymaster scheme using Semaphore) without sending query intent, browsing history, or shopping telemtry to centralized trackers. Documentation and Research : Static libraries, like docs, research catalogs, and corporate knowledge bases can instantly become queryable by LLMs. For example, we previously stood up experiments like the surgext manual to demonstrate search capabilities. The same approach could be useful for government laws, logs, and meeting notes, as evidenced by the official Piedmont, Alabama webpage , whose agenda and mi

pitch: Agents already work the web by scraping DOM and guessing at selectors.\nSignal Desk is a support workboard build with WebMCP so that agents inspect board, open case, create & propose a stage change.\n
about_excerpt:
Agents already work the web by scraping DOM and guessing at selectors.
Signal Desk is a support workboard build with WebMCP so that agents inspect board, open case, create & propose a stage change.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 This project began with a practical problem: important operational work often starts in WhatsApp. A customer message, an incident report, or a request for help arrives in a chat, then someone needs to understand it, assign it, follow up, and record the outcome. 

 We had already been exploring a local WhatsApp ingestion workboard. However, that system relies on private authentication and persisted chat/media data. It is intentionally local-only: publishing it would expose sensitive data and would not be a reliable fit for a serverless deployment. 

 That constraint became the inspiration for Signal Desk. 

 Instead of pretending that private WhatsApp data should be pushed to the public web, we built a safe, fictional, browser-only workboard that represents the workflow after a message becomes an operational case. It lets us demonstrate the meaningful question: how can people and AI agents work on the same case safely? 

 What it does 

 Signal Desk is a fictional support workboard where a person can create, review, edit, and move cases through New, Triage, Investigating, and Resolved. 

 The important difference is that the page also exposes focused WebMCP tools. An agent can list cases, open a case, create a new case, update its record, and propose a stage move using structured site capabilities rather than guessing from screenshots or clicking around blindly. 

 The human remains the decision-maker. When an agent wants to create, edit, or move a case, Signal Desk creates a visible pending action instead of silently changing the board. The person can approve or cancel it. After approval, the agent reads the actual board state back to verify the outcome. 

 This means the product supports both kinds of work: 

 
 Humans can use the normal visual interface. 
 Agents can use WebMCP to work through the same case model. 
 Important changes remain visible, reversible before approval, and verifiable afterward. 
 

 How we built it 

 We separated the original private WhatsApp concept from the deployable demonstration. 

 The original ingestion idea stays local, where private authentication and persisted conversations belong. Signal Desk is the public, safe companion: it uses fictional data that lives only in the browser and can be deployed to Vercel without exposing real messages, media, credentials, or customer information. 

 We built a case workboard with rich case details, notes, formatting, case creation, manual editing, stage movement, and a visible activity history. We then implemented WebMCP tools for the same operations. 

 For state-changing tools, we added an approval workflow: 

 
 The agent proposes an action. 
 The website returns an awaiting approval state and an approval ID. 
 A person can approve or cancel the specific action. 
 The agent confirms the approved action. 
 The agent reads back the resulting case or board state before claiming success. 
 

 Challenges we faced 

 The biggest challenge was not making an agent able to act. It was making agent action trustworthy. 

 A tool that can move a case directly is convenient, but it can also hide a consequential decision. We designed the approval state so that creating a case, changing its content, and moving it to Resolved are explicit, separate decisions. 

 We also learned that an approval alone is not enough. The agent must verify the result after the action completes. During testing, we improved the workflow so the agent does not merely report “done”; it checks the updated record or board state and reports evidence of the outcome. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is valuable because it gives an agent a clear contract with a webpage. The agent does not need private backend access, fragile screen automation, or permission to control everything. The website declares the useful actions, their inputs, and their safety boundaries. 

 Signal Desk shows how an ongoing, message-driven workboard project can become agent-interactive and deployment-ready without exposing the private WhatsApp layer behind it. 

 The goal is not to replace people with automation. It is to turn scattered reports into shared, structured work—where agents can help move work forward and people retain authority over the decisions that matter.

title: Signal - Self-Extending Tools (Task Board)
pitch: A task board where the agent can propose brand-new WebMCP tools and test its own code but nothing registers or runs until you approve it.
about_excerpt:
A task board where the agent can propose brand-new WebMCP tools and test its own code but nothing registers or runs until you approve it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most task boards treat an AI agent like a slightly faster mouse it clicks buttons, scrapes text, guesses what a status means. WebMCP flips that: the site tells the agent exactly what it can do. I wanted to push past "agent checks tasks off a list" and ask a harder question what happens when the agent isn't just using the tools I built, but proposing new ones? 

 What it does 

 Signal is a task board with three layers of WebMCP tools: 

 Task management get_overdue_tasks , search_tasks , add_task , and a heuristic tool, suggest_completions , that scans each task's activity log for real completion signals ("deployed," "merged and closed," "confirmed receipt") and tells the agent which overdue tasks are probably already done. The only tool that writes, bulk_update_status , is rejected outright by the server unless confirmed: true is set which only happens after a human clicks Approve in the UI. The safety isn't a prompt asking the agent to be careful. It's the API contract. 

 Tool Forge the part I'm most proud of. An agent can call propose_tool to define a new tool, composed only from a small whitelist of existing read primitives (chain a call, then filter the result). This does nothing on its own it renders an approval card in the UI. Only when a human clicks Approve does document.modelContext.registerTool() actually fire, live, in that session. No tool's execute() function ever calls registerTool() on another tool's behalf registration is a function of a real UI click, not one tool triggering another, which follows guidance from the WebMCP spec's own design discussion. 

 Project files + sandbox a small in-memory workspace the agent can write to ( write_project_file ), patch surgically without rewriting the whole file ( edit_project_file , which rejects the edit if the target text isn't uniquely identifiable), and execute ( run_code ) inside a hidden, network-disabled <iframe> sandbox with a 3-second timeout. Output streams back into the Agent panel. 

 How I built it 

 Plain Express backend, in-memory store, zero frontend build step the whole UI is vanilla JS calling document.modelContext.registerTool() . No React, no bundler, so it deploys to Render with no configuration. I wanted the WebMCP integration to be readable in a single file, not buried under abstraction. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 I built this solo under a 22-hour submission deadline. Most of the development started on my PC, but with no power for much of the deadline, I had to continue development and testing from my phone. Chrome's chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing flag and mobile DevTools were enough to verify that document.modelContext was registering tools correctly before I had desktop access again
The trickiest design decision was Tool Forge's safety model. My first instinct was to let the agent generate and run arbitrary code for new tools, then I realized that's exactly the kind of thing that looks impressive in a demo and terrible in a security review 

 So I deliberately constrained proposed tools to compositions of a fixed, whitelisted set of read primitives. A proposal can combine existing capabilities in a new way, but it cannot reach new data or perform writes. The same principle applies to the code sandbox: it is genuinely isolated with no network access and a hard timeout rather than simply being labeled safe.
The larger version I have designed goes further, including stronger isolation and actual test execution. For this submission, I focused on shipping a working, enforceable slice of that architecture rather than pretending arbitrary code execution was safe. 

 Accomplishments 

 Built Signal solo in roughly 22 hours, from deciding to enter the challenge on September 2 to a deployed, working WebMCP submission.
I implemented the WebMCP integration from scratch, including structured task tools, a server-enforced human approval gate for writes, and Tool Forge a constrained system where agents can propose new tools that only become registered after explicit human approval.
I also built the supporting project workspace and isolated browser sandbox, then deployed and tested the whole thing under a very limited development environment, continuing from my phone when I didn't have access to power for my PC.
The biggest accomplishment for me isn't the number of features it's that the core safety boundaries are actually enforced by the implementation rather than being claims made in the UI. 

 What's next 

 The sandbox here is JS-only. It's actually a small piece of a much larger AI agent I'm building separately, called Cipher, which has been in active development for a couple of months. This hackathon gave me a reason to ship one small, focused slice of it cleanly. If you're interested in what Cipher is building toward, I'm reachable at favourdev12@gmail.com or @favourdeve on Telegram. 

 Update 

 Devpost extended the challenge deadline after I'd already submitted. I used the extra time to add a real chat interface live tool-calling through the same tool contract described above, not a scripted walkthrough and used it to actually test every tool end-to-end, not just through the WebMCP browser path.

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Sightline
pitch: The human-approval layer between an agent and a live page. The agent finds what holds a page back, drafts the fix, and stops until you say yes — inside the page, through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The human-approval layer between an agent and a live page. The agent finds what holds a page back, drafts the fix, and stops until you say yes — inside the page, through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most "AI fixes your site" tools edit a copy of your page somewhere you cannot watch, then report "done". We wanted the agent on the live page, in front of you, through declared tools, with a hard stop before any change. WebMCP gives a page that control. The page declares the tools an agent may call, and apply_fix can keep a tool call open until you approve. What it does Sightline is an approval layer between a browser agent and a live page. The agent finds what holds the page back (accessibility, SEO, performance), drafts the fix, and waits for your click before the DOM changes. Nine imperative WebMCP tools cover three rule packs: accessibility (axe-core), SEO and performance. One engine, one gate. list_packs , then scan_page : 23 problems on the bundled fixture (14 accessibility, 5 SEO, 4 performance), overall score 54. highlight_issue : you and the agent look at the same live element. propose_fix refuses to invent human-facing content. For alt text, labels, roles, titles, descriptions and link text it returns needs_input plus page context, and the agent writes the text. The engine measures contrast, heading level and image dimensions from the live DOM. Each patch carries evidence[] and authoredBy . apply_fix stages the patch in a visible approval sheet and returns an unresolved promise until you click Approve or Skip. After approval it re-scans and returns the new score. revert_fix reverses approved changes. export_patch hands back approved work as a diff or a report. On the demo: 54 to 100 overall, 100 / 100 / 100 per pack, 23 approved changes, no planted answers. Why WebMCP fits Fixing a page is a loop: inspect the element, weigh the impact, propose a bounded change, apply it with judgment, verify. The loop is the same for a missing alt text, a generic title or an image without dimensions. A browser agent working from screenshots has to guess at that loop through unstable DOM controls. Sightline exposes each step as a WebMCP tool with typed inputs and safety annotations. The page registers the nine tools as state allows. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . Tools that return audited page content carry untrustedContentHint . Mutations wait until you confirm the before/after DOM in the approval sheet. You and the agent share one page, one focused element, one issue list and one score. How it improves the experience You stop hopping between scanner, chat, editor, browser and report. The agent prioritises and explains barriers by stable issue id. You see the highlighted element and keep the final say on each mutation. Sightline re-scans after each approved fix, lets you undo any one of them, and exports the approved set as a diff or report. The judging demo is deterministic: 23 real problems, per-pack and overall scores, and a visible path from 54 to 100. The agent authors nine of the fixes; the engine measures fourteen. The fixture contains problems and nothing else. What you and an agent can do together now Run one approval workflow across accessibility, SEO and performance instead of three tools with three reports. Point at the same live element without translating between report, chat, selector and source file. Turn audit output into reviewable DOM patches without running model-generated code. Pause an agent's tool call inside the page until you decide. Check each claim against the changed DOM instead of trusting "fixed". Export approved changes with rationale and a scope note. How we built it Sightline uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Each tool ships a JSON Schema, a plain-language description and annotations. Registration in Chrome uses AbortController cleanup and state-driven discovery, so tool-change events fire without re-registering active tools. One TypeScript engine drives the manual controls and the agent callbacks, so the two paths cannot drift. Scans run in an isolated 900 px audit frame, so results match on any viewport. propose_fix splits the work: the agent authors alt text, labels and ARIA roles (validated as plain text, length-bounded, roles allow-listed); the engine computes the passing colour from measured WCAG luminance and derives heading levels from the live outline. Patches carry evidence (measured ratios, current attributes) instead of a confidence number. apply_fix returns an unresolved promise while the approval sheet is open, then resolves with the new score. The bundled "Watch the agent work" demo is a WebMCP client that calls getTools() and executeTool() , the same path an external agent takes. Stack: React, TypeScript, Vite, axe-core, imperative WebMCP, Cloudflare Pages. No backend, no auth, no model API, no secrets. Challenges Holding a tool call open across a human decision. apply_fix resolves after approval and re-scan. Chrome 151's cancelInvocation does not fire the callback's AbortSignal , so the engine adds a 120 s timeout and a Skip path. Not cheating. Our first fixture carried planted answers in data-fix-* attributes. We deleted them and made the engine return needs_input , so the agent reads the page and writes. The fake confidence score became measured evidence . Viewport-independent audits. The 900 px audit frame gives an agent on a phone-sized viewport the same 23 issues a desktop judge sees. axe-core across realms. axe.run(HTMLElement) fails across the iframe boundary. We pass a selector string, and import axe.min.js?raw because production tree-shakes axe.source . Accomplishments We verified the full demo (23 to 0 across three packs) with an external agent through Chrome's native WebMCP surface (CDP WebMCP.* ). The launch video shows that run. The "Watch the agent work" button is a WebMCP client ( getTools() , executeTool() ). No side channel. A new rule pack is one file with { scan, fixers } plus its id in the PackId union and the engine's pack list. The tool surface, the gate, undo and export come with it. npm run smoke replays the verification: 15 invariants through Chrome's WebMCP DevTools domain. CI runs it against each build in headless Chrome; it also runs against the live URL. A Spec Kit constitution with six principles. The first: Approval Before Mutation. A source-level test checks that the DOM-mutating function has two call sites, approval and replay of approved history. Vitest covers the content validator, the WCAG contrast maths and the approval state machine, including a regression test for two agents overlapping the post-approval re-scan (a race we found in review). CI adds a bundle budget and a no-planted-answers check. What we learned A page can declare where the human sits in a workflow and make the agent wait there. readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint , staged registration and AbortSignal turn that from a convention into a contract. What's next Import any page (CSP and an import UI). Gate revert_fix behind the same approval. Add Playwright coverage of the native tool flow. More packs on the same engine: security headers, structured data, i18n hygiene. Scope Sightline demonstrates remediation with a human in the loop. It does not claim automatic WCAG compliance. Automated checks support manual and expert accessibility testing; they do not replace it. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Signal Timing Workbench
pitch: A San Francisco intersection that a human and an AI agent retime together. The simulation lives only in the tab, eight WebMCP tools let an agent search hundreds of signal timings while you supervise.
about_excerpt: A San Francisco intersection that a human and an AI agent retime together. The simulation lives only in the tab, eight WebMCP tools let an agent search hundreds of signal timings while you supervise. Like Comment Story Updates Interface What it is A four-arm signalised junction that a human and an agent operate together. The traffic simulation runs entirely in the tab — no backend, no API, nothing meaningful to scrape off a canvas. The state exists only in the page. That is the point. A conventional browser agent could screenshot this and learn nothing: it cannot read mean_wait_s out of pixels, and evaluating a candidate timing would cost it a slider drag, a button click and a screenshot round trip. It would manage perhaps five experiments while an agent with site tools runs two hundred. Not faster — categorically different. The junction exposes seven WebMCP tools. An agent arrives cold, reads the model specification, searches the timing space off the main thread while the traffic keeps flowing on screen, and hands back a scrubbable explanation of what it found. The operator watches, locks parameters mid-search, and decides. The design argument The interesting part is not the simulation. It is the shape of the tool surface, and three decisions in particular. run_batch reports physics. apply_config enforces policy. run_batch evaluates any timing, including ones that are illegal to deploy, and reports honestly what would happen. It checks nothing. apply_config is the only tool that can commit a timing to the junction, and the only one that enforces the constraints. Keeping those separate means the agent can discover that the fastest timing is inadmissible rather than being silently steered away from it. Under school-run demand the best-scoring timing is a permissive-left plan at 27.4 s mean wait; it is prohibited, because opposing volume × left-turn volume exceeds the phasing threshold. The best legal timing costs 45.8 s. An agent that only ever saw filtered results would never understand what admissibility cost. The refusal says so explicitly: a refusal is a fact about what may be deployed, not a scoring signal — a refused timing may well be the fastest one. Constraints ship with their derivations, and it changed agent behaviour describe_model publishes every constraint with the arithmetic behind it. Yellow and all-red are not tuning parameters; they are safety intervals derived from the ITE change-interval formulae: approach speed v = 15 m/s (54 km/h) yellow y = t + v/(2a) → 3.50 s → floor 4 s all-red r = (W + L)/v → 1.33 s → floor 2 s Two measured effects on a real agent run: Unprompted, it used 5 seeds and 60-minute runs. run_batch's description warns about ±2 s of simulation noise and recommends averaging at least 3 seeds; the agent went further on its own. It never hit the phasing refusal. Its 50-config refine batch was entirely left_protected: true — it read the cross-product rule, worked out that school-run demand mandates protected phasing, and pre-filtered its search space. Publishing constraints in full meant a careful agent self-checked instead of learning by rejection. Locks are a permission boundary with no unlock tool The operator can pin any parameter. read_state reports which are locked; apply_config refuses to change one and says so. There is deliberately no tool that unlocks a parameter. The agent can read the lock, reason about it, and re-optimise around it — only a human clicking the button releases it. A permission model expressed through the shape of the surface rather than a confirmation dialog. Tools Tool Kind Purpose describe_model read Parameters, metrics, constraints with derivations, scenarios read_state read Committed timing, phase, per-arm queues, locks, live metrics run_batch read Evaluate ≤50 timings in a Web Worker apply_config write Commit; enforces constraints and locks set_scenario write Switch demand profile; re-checks the committed plan pin_result write Surface a candidate to the operator with a rationale play_sequence write Narrated, scrubbable explanation Other choices worth naming: Tool results are budgeted. run_batch returns full per-arm detail for the top 3 rows and summary metrics for the rest, and does not duplicate the payload into structuredContent. Measured on a 36-config batch: 53,558 → 11,284 characters, a 79% reduction. Context bloat is what degrades an agent over a long session. run_batch runs in a Web Worker. A 50-config batch is ~500 ms; on the main thread that freezes the junction every time the agent thinks, and the premise is that the human watches a live workspace while the agent works. apply_config restarts the live run and says so, along with the ~4 simulated minutes before metrics settle. Otherwise the agent commits, re-reads two seconds later, and reasons about a transient. set_scenario re-checks the committed timing. Switching demand can make the deployed plan illegal. It reports that and leaves the plan committed — the agent asked to change the demand, not to redeploy the signal plan. pin_result re-measures over 3 seeds regardless of what produced the original figure, so two pins are always comparable. The agent's search is drawn in the domain's own notation. Evaluated candidates appear as miniature ring-and-barrier phase diagrams — the diagram a traffic engineer actually reads — with bar width encoding cycle length. A scatter plot would show convergence more precisely and say nothing about what was tried. Verification npm run agentsim mocks document.modelContext, registers the real tool surface, and drives the exact sequence a competent agent follows: cold discovery, coarse sweep, the constraint refusal, recovery inside the legal region, a lock refusal, malformed input, two pins, a scenario round-trip, a narrated replay, and AbortSignal cleanup. It runs in about four seconds and caught several schema bugs before any browser was involved. The simulation itself was validated before any UI existed: metric spread of 162 s against 1.6 s of seed noise, an interior optimum in cycle length that moves with demand (57 s under morning rush, 87 s under event egress), and four scenarios with four distinct optima. Notes on the model A stochastic cellular automaton (Nagel–Schreckenberg). Arrival rates are representative of a mid-size German town, not measured. Two modelling details matter for the decisions the agent faces: Opposing traffic is platooned. Gap acceptance uses the opposing flow concentrated into its green window, not the hourly average — the platoon is released by the same green in which a permissive left-turner is trying to cross. Without this, permissive lefts are far too easy and left_protected becomes a parameter with one always-correct answer. The left-turn bay is 60 m. When it fills, left-turners spill back and block the through lane behind them. That is why protected phasing is ever worth its cycle time, and why sizing the protected phase wrong is worse than not having one: at school-run demand, protected at 8 s scores 214 s against permissive's 74 s, while protected at 16 s is the best timing available. Running it bash npm install npm run agentsim # headless tool-surface harness npm run dev # then open in a WebMCP-capable browser Node 22+. WebMCP is secure-context only; localhost qualifies. Try: "Optimise this junction for mean wait under the school run scenario, then pin the two options you think I should choose between."
