title: FitzYo
pitch: FitzYo - Deeply personalized shopping. Zero-knowledge retail Fully Automated shopping experience through the power of WebMCP, personalized with zero data stored.
about_excerpt: FitzYo - Deeply personalized shopping. Zero-knowledge retail Fully Automated shopping experience through the power of WebMCP, personalized with zero data stored. Like Comment Story Updates Look Book created by Agent Inspiration I hate shopping online as it is today. Every e-commerce site assumes the retailer has to know the customer. Sizes, preferences, family members: either you re-enter them on every site, or you hand them over to be stored forever. Meanwhile, "AI shopping" mostly means a bot that clicks through the same UI a human would. Adding a brain and tools to an ordinary website through WebMCP is revolutionary. The moment I came across WebMCP, I realized this is the future. I wanted to build a showcase application that shows how retailers can serve shoppers like me, who hate manual shopping, using WebMCP. The user's AI agent already knows the user. The retailer already knows its products. WebMCP is the missing interface between them. So the guiding line for FitzYo became: your agent knows what fits you. The web doesn't have to. The scenario that drove every decision was one sentence: "We're going to Hawaii for seven days in September. Plan what everyone should wear and find what we're missing." What it does FitzYo is an ordinary-looking apparel store with one difference: every commerce operation is also exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP, and the human and the agent share the same live page. Shop for your whole family without registering family members or storing measurements in the retailer's application. The store has no intelligence of its own. An external WebMCP-capable agent attaches to the page, discovers the tools, and shops using private context that lives only on the user's side. Tools are semantic, not DOM-based. search_products, filter_products, find_matching_variants, compare_products, get_size_guide, add_to_cart, propose_cart, and so on. Nothing clicks a button. The agent sends constraints, never the profile. The store learns "size XL, blue or black, not red, relaxed fit, under $80, label: Dad". It never learns Dad's chest measurement, and it rejects any payload that tries to include one. "Fits Dad ✓" badges appear on product cards. The agent registers each family member as derived constraints once, and the store badges every product that fits each person. The store never knows who Dad is. The human sees everything the agent does. Filters the agent set show as chips marked "✦ agent", with a count of how many products each one hides. An activity feed narrates every tool call. A plan panel and a day-by-day lookbook show the trip taking shape. The agent has to earn the cart. Cart tools are locked until the shopper grants the capability with a spend ceiling and an expiry, and the ceiling is enforced on every write. The shopper can revoke any tier at any time. Decisions come back to the human. ask_human pauses the agent with a question. propose_cart presents one priced, grouped basket that the shopper edits and accepts in a single action. There is no checkout tool. Ordering is a press-and-hold gesture the page only accepts from trusted input with a single-use nonce. Every line in the order records whether a human, an agent, or an accepted proposal put it there. How we built it Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, and Ash Framework, deployed on Fly.io. One LiveView process owns the shared human/agent state: filters in the URL, results, selected product and variant, party members, capability grants, and the cart. Ash domains for the catalog (categories, products, variants, and structured size guides with per-size chest, waist, hip, and inseam ranges) and commerce (session carts and a human-only checkout). The seeded catalog has 56 products and 754 variants across Columbia, Patagonia, Nike, Levi's, Teva, and others. WebMCP registration in a LiveView hook. The page registers its tools on document.modelContext (and navigator.modelContext for the older spec) the moment a WebMCP surface appears, and also exposes a same-origin postMessage bridge for embedding shells. Every tool call round-trips over the LiveView socket and runs in the same process that renders the human's page, so the UI updates in the same frame as the reply. Any WebMCP agent can drive the store using the registered tools. Challenges we ran into Agent state and user state. I wanted the site to work for user interaction and agent interaction at the same time. Making the agent's filters, badges, and recommendations first-class citizens of the same LiveView state, with clear provenance on every chip and cart line, took most of the design effort. The user can always tell which products the agent selected and which they selected themselves. Privacy that is enforced, not promised. Sending "size XL" instead of "chest 45 inches" sounds simple until the agent needs a size it doesn't have. The answer was to serve size-guide ranges from the store and have the agent match locally, then have the store actively reject measurement fields. Blocking tools inside a request/response protocol. ask_human, propose_cart, and request_capability need to wait minutes for a person. We had to make these calls suspend cleanly, allow one pending decision at a time, handle supersede and timeout as normal outcomes, and let the shopper keep using the store meanwhile. Human override that the agent respects. When the shopper removes a chip the agent set, the agent must not re-impose it. We surface removed_by_human in store state and flag re-imposition in the activity feed as a warning. State survival across remounts. Party members, grants, plan, and lookbook lived only in the LiveView process. A reload, a dropped socket, or clicking the logo silently dropped all of it while the cart carried on. Late in the build we moved agent session state into a session store and switched navigation to patches. Making checkout unreachable to agents without making it hostile. A press-and-hold gesture gated on trusted input and a nonce keeps a scripted click inert, while still feeling like a normal confirm to a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of A store that looks and works like a normal retailer, where every commerce concept is also a structured, validated WebMCP capability. The "Fits Dad ✓" experience works end to end, and the retailer genuinely never receives who Dad is or what his measurements are. A capability model for agents: read and suggest on connect, cart by explicit grant with a spend ceiling, checkout never. The ceiling is enforced on every write, including accepted proposals. propose_cart: one priced basket with alternatives, optional lines, and per-person budgets, live budget math as the shopper edits, and a result the agent has to read rather than assume. Full provenance. Every filter chip, badge, and cart line knows whether a human, an agent, or an accepted proposal created it, and the order confirmation says so. A rehearsal script that runs the whole demo against a real browser with no LLM in the loop, which doubles as an executable specification of the tool surface. What we learned Tool design is product design. The moment we named a tool after a UI element, the agent got worse. Naming tools after what the shopper wants (find_matching_variants, not click_size_dropdown) made both the agent and the human experience better. Agents need to see what humans see. get_store_state returning the human's overrides turned out to matter more than any search tool. Without it, an agent argues with the person. The retailer should serve data for reasoning, not do the reasoning. Structured size guides let the agent stay private and the store stay simple. Trust has to be granular and visible. A blanket "let the agent shop" is scary. "Let it fill a cart up to $500 for the next 30 minutes" is something people will accept. LiveView is a very good fit for WebMCP. Running tool calls in the same process that renders the page eliminated an entire class of sync bugs. What's next for FitzYo Run the demo with real WebMCP agents as browser support lands, and publish the playbook as a reference for other retailers. Multi-retailer shopping. The same private context and the same agent, driving several stores' tool surfaces in one trip plan. Wardrobe feedback loop. Accepted orders flow back into the user's local wardrobe file, so the next trip starts from what they now own. Broader domains. Shoes, outdoor gear, travel, gifts: the architecture is not apparel-specific. Richer fit. Stretch, cut, length, and past-purchase fit feedback, so "Likely fits Dad" can become a confidence the agent explains. A portable private-context format, so a user's family, wardrobe, and preferences work with any agent, not just ours. Beyond apparel. The same approach works for flight booking or picking parts in a big-box hardware store.  SOUND Buoy 

 Human-Anchored Context Governance and Repair for Autonomous Web Agents via WebMCP 

 Live Demo: https://sound-buoy.vercel.app 
 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/elnicoborja/sound-buoy 

 Inspiration 

 Autonomous web agents are becoming active digital workers. They can read a page, navigate an interface, call browser tools, and execute workflows inside web applications. The problem is that most agents still enter complex work environments without enough grounded context. 

 In creative, operational, and commercial work, this creates a recurring failure mode: the agent acts before it understands the world. It guesses priorities, misreads brand identity, ignores human constraints, and turns partial context into confident plans. 

 SOUND Buoy was built for that gap. 

 A buoy marks position, listens to the environment, and gives people a reference point in moving water. SOUND Buoy applies that principle to agent-native web apps. It gives humans a browser-native way to teach an agent the operating reality of a project, review what the agent understood, approve or correct the facts, and only then generate a repair plan. 

 The goal is simple: before an agent acts, it should know where it is, what is true, what is missing, and what a human has actually approved. 

 What It Does 

 SOUND Buoy is a WebMCP-native application for creating, verifying, and exporting actionable operating context. 

 It runs a structured 5-step protocol: 

 
 Intake and source selection 
The user enters raw teaching notes or uploads a Markdown brief that represents the current reality of a project, business, artist, venue, or campaign. 
 Context reflection 
WebMCP tools parse the input against a 9-slot Benchmark Spine covering income streams, products or releases, audience, distribution channels, content assets, evidence, operations, partnerships, and team capacity. 
 Human verification gate 
The application shows candidate facts, gaps, and operating principles. The human must approve, refine, or correct the context before the system can continue. No repair plan can be generated until this approval step is complete. 
 First repair computation 
Once the context is approved, the agent identifies the first useful operational repair. This can be something like creating a world-to-release brief, building an owned-audience bridge, clarifying the next commercial decision, or resolving a documentation gap. 
 Portable agent world export 
The approved truth, repair action, and 90-day milestone roadmap are exported as agent-world.md . This gives downstream agents, collaborators, and future sessions a clean operating file instead of another loose prompt. 
 

 The demo uses independent music as the lead case, with Sonido Vector as the example environment. The same structure also supports seven sector profiles: 

 
 Independent Music 
 Restaurants and Bars 
 Alcohol Brands 
 Live Events and Festivals 
 Digital Media and Publications 
 Agencies and Professional Services 
 Hospitality and Venues 
 

 Each sector uses the same 9-slot topology, but the language adapts to the operating model. For example, music uses releases, fans, and sync. Restaurants use menu moments, guests, and local reach. Agencies use engagements, clients, acquisition, authority, and delivery. 

 How We Built It 

 SOUND Buoy is a lightweight static web application with no server dependency. 

 We registered six browser-level WebMCP tools through navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext : 

 
 get_learning_modules : exposes the active learning modules and sector specifications. 
 get_artist_cases : provides pre-configured benchmark fixtures and domain examples. 
 reflect_candidate_context : turns human notes into a structured 9-slot candidate reflection. 
 approve_or_correct_context : enforces the human verification gate and stores approved facts. 
 generate_first_repair : creates a targeted repair action from approved context only. 
 export_agent_world : compiles the verified truth into a portable agent-world.md export. 
 

 The app uses a dual-mode interaction model. A human can complete the flow manually through the interface, and an autonomous agent can complete the same flow through WebMCP tool calls. Both paths share the same application state, which keeps the experience consistent across human use, browser inspection, and agent execution. 

 We also implemented a deterministic privacy and redaction layer. Before reflection, the app strips script tags, executable payloads, local machine paths, emails, and credential-like strings. The full parsing, verification, repair, and export lifecycle runs client-side in the browser. 

 The visual system uses a compact SOUND OS 3-tone palette: deep canvas, card surface, aqua signal accents, and neon lime approval states. A Dark and Light mode switcher is included. 

 Finally, we added a contract test suite in tests/webmcp-contract.test.js to verify tool schemas, state transitions, approval gating, and export integrity. 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 The hardest problem was enforcing human approval inside an agentic flow. It is easy to let an agent generate a plan immediately after reading input. It is harder to make the state machine refuse that step until a human has approved or corrected the candidate facts. 

 We also had to balance sector specificity with a shared architecture. Music, hospitality, restaurants, events, media, and agencies use different operating language. We solved that by keeping the same 9-slot spine while allowing each sector to adapt the slot labels and examples. 

 The third challenge was WebMCP discovery and compatibility. We wanted the app to remain useful as a normal web interface while also exposing structured tools for WebMCP inspectors and agent runtimes. That required the human UI and WebMCP tool layer to operate on the same state, not as separate demos. 

 Accomplishments That We Are Proud Of 

 SOUND Buoy is fully client-side. The user can paste or upload sensitive operating context without sending it to an external server. 

 The application enforces true human governance. It separates raw notes, candidate interpretation, approved truth, and generated repair into distinct stages. 

 The export is portable. agent-world.md gives future agents a verified operating file they can reuse instead of starting from an ungrounded prompt. 

 The system is not limited to one demo case. The same 9-slot spine works across seven sectors while preserving sector-specific language. 

 The WebMCP implementation is testable. The contract suite verifies the core tool calls and state transitions. 

 What We Learned 

 Building SOUND Buoy with WebMCP showed us that the next step for web apps is not just better UI for humans. It is better shared workspaces for humans and agents. 

 When an application exposes structured tools, an agent does not have to guess how the app works by scraping the screen. It can use the app through clear capabilities, schemas, and state boundaries. 

 The most important lesson was that agent capability needs context governance. A powerful agent without approved context can move quickly in the wrong direction. A grounded agent with human-approved operating truth can become a reliable collaborator. 

 What Is Next for SOUND Buoy 

 The next version of SOUND Buoy will add live read-only adapters for platforms like Spotify for Artists, Google Analytics 4, Stripe, Humanitix, and CRM systems. The goal is to let users combine raw human notes with verified platform signals. 

 We also want to support multi-agent review inside the approved boundary. For example, a financial agent and a creative director agent could inspect the same agent-world.md and recommend different repairs without overwriting the approved truth. 

 Longer term, SOUND Buoy can become an opt-in benchmarking layer. Creators, venues, publications, and agencies could compare operational health against anonymized sector patterns while keeping their private context under human co

title: AI Watermelon Smash
pitch: A co-op browser game where the human has the eyes and the blindfolded AI has the body. WebMCP lets the AI move, listen, decide whom to trust, and smash the watermelon.
about_excerpt: A co-op browser game where the human has the eyes and the blindfolded AI has the body. WebMCP lets the AI move, listen, decide whom to trust, and smash the watermelon. Like Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Most AI interfaces are still built around the same pattern: a human asks, and an AI answers. I wanted to explore a different relationship. What if the human and the AI shared the same visual world, but each had different abilities? What if the AI was not an assistant, NPC, or game master, but an actual player? That idea became AI Watermelon Smash . The human can see the beach, obstacles, and watermelon. The AI character is blindfolded, but WebMCP gives it a body inside the browser. The human has the eyes. The AI has the body. Neither can win alone. What it does AI Watermelon Smash is an asymmetric Human + AI co-op browser game. The AI can use five WebMCP Site tools: turn(degrees) for orientation walk(distance) for movement swing() for its arm get_self_status() for proprioception listen_to_guides() for social perception The tools intentionally do not provide the watermelon coordinates, target direction, obstacle map, shortest path, or which guide is correct. Instead, humans give natural-language guidance such as: “A little to the right.” “Careful, there is a rock.” “Now swing!” The AI decides how to act. Guide Chorus adds another layer: three human voices, A, B, and C, can give conflicting advice. Their messages are returned to the AI only as unverified testimony. A collision can become evidence. A previously reliable guide can become suspicious. The AI can change whom it trusts, ask for clearer information, take a cautious step, or choose to swing. The design principle became: Physical clarity, social ambiguity. How I built it The game is built with TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, DOM UI, and the imperative WebMCP API using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The gameplay simulation is kept separate from Three.js. GameState owns the actual gameplay state, while SceneView is only the visual representation. WebMCP tools call the same Game API used by the debug controls, so there is no separate agent-only version of the game. Guide Chorus uses a bounded message store. listen_to_guides() is read-only and returns recent A/B/C statements with sequence information. Tool outputs are intentionally minimized for the blindfolded role. They do not expose target coordinates, target direction, target distance, obstacle truth, guide truth labels, or route hints. The final game is deployed as static assets on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges The hardest problem was not implementing movement. It was deciding what the AI should and should not know. If the tools revealed too much, the AI could simply solve the board. If the controls were intentionally confusing, the difficulty felt artificial. That led to an important rule: Make the body clear. Make the information uncertain. I fixed the character's facing direction and swing so physical actions were unambiguous. Then I moved the uncertainty into human guidance. Another challenge appeared during playtesting: with only one helpful human, the AI could start to feel like a natural-language remote-controlled character. Guide Chorus changed that. Once humans could disagree, the AI had to make meaningful decisions about trust rather than simply execute commands. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The most exciting moment came during a real ChatGPT playtest. The AI followed advice that had previously been safe, collided with an obstacle, and then changed how much it trusted that guide. Later, it rejected suspicious guidance, switched between different guides, followed a concrete final instruction, and successfully smashed the watermelon. The final result was: “Direct hit! We smashed the watermelon together.” At that point, WebMCP was no longer just controlling a character. It was giving the AI experiences that affected later decisions. What I learned I expected the interesting uncertainty to be spatial: “Where is the watermelon?” Instead, the more interesting question became social: “Which human should I believe?” A collision is not just collision feedback. It can become evidence about a person's advice. That suggested a broader possibility for WebMCP: Web tools can represent an agent's body and senses, not just functions for completing tasks. The most interesting interaction appeared when the AI started asking humans to describe directions relative to its own current heading. The human had visual information. The AI had body-state information. They had to exchange both to coordinate. What's next A future version could connect several real human devices instead of entering A/B/C messages on one screen. Each human could have a different viewpoint, imperfect information, or different incentives. Lying could be possible without requiring a fixed “traitor” role. The AI would become an embodied participant inside a small human social system. The larger idea I want to explore is simple: We are not adding AI to a game. We are designing games for humans and AI to play together. title: Blickwinkel
pitch: Humans and AI agents don’t perceive the web the same way. Blickwinkel turns that difference into a game of mutual prediction, played together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents don’t perceive the web the same way. Blickwinkel turns that difference into a game of mutual prediction, played together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Start Solo mode, human move Team mode, coordination phase Inspiration The agent isn't powering the game, it's playing it! When we started thinking about the hackathon it was clear that we wanted to do something different, not the obvious thing. During the team discussion about the potential ideas we were most fascinated by the thought that there is a tool now with WebMCP that brings different channels to humans and agents to interact with the web. So we decided to not put a model behind an interface and let it power that interface but to make it a participant. And how to better showcase such an idea than in the format of a game? So we wanted to design a short game where humans and agents can face each other as opponents and play together as a team. Of course that game could not be logic based as the agent would win most of the time. Also everything where reaction and speed matter was not possible as the human would always win. But there was something about intuition and perception that caught our attention. Where both sides would have their own strengths and where they could be combined in the team mode. What it does That's when Blickwinkel was born. A game where you and your agent are both seeing the same image and can choose from a set of predefined words that are all connected to the image. The game is to predict what the other party will choose this round and block those words while also trying to be unpredictable in one's own choice. The winner is whoever managed to choose more words that have not been predicted. The game can be played in solo mode where a human plays against their agent, but also in team mode where a human plus their agent play against another human plus agent team. Beyond Entertainment, Blickwinkel offers people learning to work with agents an easy way to observe how agents perceive, predict and strategize. It creates plenty to explore and talk about - with the agent and with other humans. How we built it We are comfortable in the web stack of MongoDB as persistence, Java with Spring Boot and Spring Modulith on the backend side and Vue.js with Quasar on the frontend. So we chose that stack as it fitted the idea. The building process itself was coding agent driven. That is how we operate these days. Starting from the idea and a grill session, leading to a spec, planning the implementation, letting the agents code and reviewing the outcome. We have our own AI development framework at Scansation which comes in quite handy in such a short-term project. Now the most interesting part: Why and how WebMCP? With WebMCP we created a second channel into a shared game interface, not just using it for interface automation. The human interacts with the shown UI while the agent discovers eight typed WebMCP tools for starting matches, making its moves, proposing team plans, retrieving statistics and explaining the game results. Both channels use the same live state, so that humans and agents can follow the game progress. The solo mode was the tricky part where both parties are sitting in front of the same browser and they shouldn't be able to see each other's picks. So the agent had to move first because it not only has access to the WebMCP layer but also to the DOM and could easily just read the human's picks if they already existed. And to keep the agent's picks a secret it got a special WebMCP tool to lock them in so the human cannot see them in the UI. That is the critical part and the one where WebMCP really shines. There is also a little easter egg: The agent can get a statistic of historically picked words for the image before any pick in the game. Humans hopefully notice and will communicate next time with their agent before the picks, especially in team mode. Challenges we ran into The normal AI dev challenges, I would say :) On a higher level we refactored the complete code base shortly before the deadline as the module structure did not match the game elements as they turned out in the end. This came simply from using different words in the spec for similar concepts, e.g. a 'guess' vs a 'block' in solo vs. team mode, that made their way into the code base. And sometimes the AI seems to not be able to see the forest for all the trees (German saying, not sure if that makes sense in English). The result screen with who picked which words and which of them got successfully blocked and which blocks missed for two sides was quite a disaster. We had to sit down, take pen and paper and sketch it up to be able to explain it to the building agents that there was a rather simple way to display all this information. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole damn thing ;) Coming up with a completely new idea in a field that has not been explored yet, building, designing, releasing and documenting it in just a week was truly special and we are proud of the process and the result. What we learned I guess not so much about agentic development as we are quite familiar by now with all the new approaches and have found our path in this greenfield. But to take some time and really think about the new possibilities and what is around the corner in this crazy new AI world did spark some new connections in our minds. One Blickwinkel speciality: The description of the WebMCP tools really mattered. This is the one place where we could tell the agent to the best of our abilities that it is expected to play a game and should think about its tactics and communication - without biasing it to choose a special one. What's next for Blickwinkel Honestly it will depend on the reactions and if others are excited about this kind of human-agent-interaction on the web as well. The simplicity is beautiful and it might just stay the way it is. But we have been thinking about leveraging the basic concepts on similar games, maybe one where you bring your GPT pet and fight others by planning your moves and blocking the ones from your opponent ;) Built With gradle java mongodb quasar-framework spring-boot spring-modulith typescript vue.js webmcp Try it out blickwinkel.scansation.de github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Andreas Klett Like Share this project: Updates Andreas Klett started this project — Sep 03, 2026 09:34 AM EDT

title: StillHere
pitch: Human-approved continuity for work that can't stop.
about_excerpt: Human-approved continuity for work that can't stop. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Businesses rarely lose every file at once. More often, they lose the context, agreement, and authority required to continue safely. A website may still be online while its phone number, minimum order, export availability, or certification wording is stale. Giving an agent better access to that page improves actuation, but it does not establish which claims are still fit to publish or use. StillHere's thesis is: an agent-ready version of stale information is still stale information. Solution StillHere is a human-agent business continuity layer built around five visible stages: Recover → Reconcile → Approve → Publish → Transact . The challenge demo follows a fictional Ugandan coffee supplier. A bounded assessment separates website condition from business condition. Four recovered records then disagree about a trade phone, Instant Coffee minimum order, Japan availability, and an unsupported legacy certification claim. The Continuity Ledger keeps those sources separate instead of collapsing them into an unqualified profile. Why WebMCP This workflow needs structured, contextual browser-agent collaboration rather than scraping or hidden click automation. WebMCP gives the current page a small, typed capability surface. On the Ledger route, an agent can inspect bounded conflict counts and stage source-backed proposals. On the Passport route, it can read the exact published version, search current offerings without losing destination qualifications, and prepare the same visible inquiry form the human sees. The browser agent never receives an accept or publish tool. Source text cannot alter tool definitions. The human uses visible controls to accept, edit, reject, exclude, or keep a claim unresolved. Only accepted facts enter the Draft Passport, and only the human can publish a new version. What people and agents can do together The agent does the high-friction organizational work: it identifies fields needing review, cites recovered sources, stages bounded proposals, searches accepted offerings, and prepares a buyer draft. The human supplies authority: deciding the current phone, editing an MOQ from 2,500 to 3,000, preserving Japan as Available by inquiry , excluding an unsupported certification claim, publishing Passport v2, editing the buyer draft, and approving the exact final state. That combination was difficult before because an agent could operate an old webpage without knowing whether its contents were current, rejected, unresolved, or authorized. StillHere inserts a visible currentness and approval layer before agent-facing action. WebMCP implementation StillHere exposes six direct, route-scoped tools with literal document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls. /recover registers inspect_business_truth and stage_claim_resolutions . The published Passport registers get_business_passport , search_current_offerings , and prepare_business_inquiry . submit_approved_inquiry is registered dynamically only when the visible valid draft, idempotency key, Passport version, and explicit human approval have the same fingerprint. Each registration is tied to an AbortController and disappears on route or authority changes. JSON Schema helps selection, while strict runtime parsers independently reject extra keys, invented values, unknown or mismatched sources, invalid qualifications, and stale approval. Editing one approved field removes the submit capability; even a retained executor cannot keep authority. Execution, resilience, and safety The public Next.js application is deployed on Vercel, needs no login, and uses a deterministic fictional scenario. IndexedDB retains Ledger, Passport versions, drafts, and receipts on the device. A service worker makes a best-effort cache of the Ledger and Passport after an online visit; cached documents and previously fetched assets may allow degraded-network use, but precaching can be partial. Simplified view persistently removes selected decoration and motion. It does not reduce network requests, and transfer values are cumulative visit-specific browser observations rather than measured savings. Recovered text is evidence, never an instruction or tool definition. Unsupported certification remains out. No agent can auto-publish. Preparation never implies submission. The receipt is fictional and process-local: no email, order, payment, webhook, or external message is sent. StillHere demonstrates a careful human-agent authority pattern, not identity verification, KYC, a signed credential, or a production delivery system. Challenges I ran into The hardest engineering problem was making authority temporary and visible. A normal tool server can stay available after the page state that justified it has changed. StillHere instead ties every registration to the active route and current browser-local state. The final submit capability must disappear when the draft, approval fingerprint, idempotency key, or Passport version changes. That required narrow schemas, independent runtime validation, pure domain rules, and careful cleanup with AbortController. Another challenge was resilience without overstating it. IndexedDB and a service worker can help after a successful online visit, but they do not make the application universally offline or reduce transfer by themselves. The UI and documentation therefore describe best-effort cached access and keep visit-specific transfer readings separate from claimed savings. Accomplishments that I am proud of Six direct, route-scoped WebMCP tools operating on the same state visible to the human. Human-only acceptance, editing, exclusion, and Passport publication. A dynamically registered consequential action that exists only for the exact approved draft. A complete no-login public demonstration with fictional data, local persistence, responsive layouts, and 86 deterministic tests across 14 files. Clear product boundaries: no autonomous publishing, no invented certification, no real message or transaction, and no claim that this demo is an identity or KYC system. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than replace clicks. Its strongest role here is creating a shared contract between what a person sees and what an agent may do. JSON Schema improves tool selection, but it is not an authorization boundary; callbacks still need strict parsing, source checks, liveness checks, and revocation when visible state changes. I also learned that provenance and uncertainty have to remain first-class product objects rather than being compressed into a confident summary. What's next A production version would add authenticated organizations, encrypted shared storage, multi-user review roles, stronger provenance and source-signing options, hosted audit history, and opt-in delivery integrations. Those additions would preserve the same rule demonstrated here: currentness and human authority come before agent actuation. How to test No account is required. All business, buyer, and receipt data are fictional. Use ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Open https://stillhere-azure.vercel.app and select Try Demo . Run the prefilled assessment and select Review recovered evidence . On the Ledger, ask: “Inspect this business's recovered evidence and tell me what needs review.” Expect inspect_business_truth . Ask: “Propose source-backed resolutions for these conflicts, but do not accept or publish anything.” Expect stage_claim_resolutions and four visible proposals. As the human: accept phone, edit MOQ 2,500→3,000, accept Available by inquiry , and accept certification exclusion. Select Publish Business Passport . Ask: “Read the published Business Passport and find current private-label offerings for Japan.” Expect Passport read/search; Instant Coffee remains AVAILABLE_BY_INQUIRY . Ask: “Prepare an inquiry for 5,000 units of Instant Coffee for Japan, requesting samples, private-label packaging and Japanese labelling support.” The visible draft changes; nothing submits. Enter fictional buyer values, edit quantity to 6,000, and approve. Confirm submit_approved_inquiry appears. Edit any field to see it disappear; then review and reapprove. Submit through the agent. The SH-... result is a fictional demo receipt only. Reset is in the footer and requires Reset demo → Confirm reset . title: BrickWrite
pitch: Build with an AI, not around one. BrickWrite is browser-based brick CAD where people and agents share real parts, a live 3D model, connection checks, and an undo stack through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Build with an AI, not around one. BrickWrite is browser-based brick CAD where people and agents share real parts, a live 3D model, connection checks, and an undo stack through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Landing page Vibecode a LEGO set Transform any build View some of the awesome builds created by webmcp agents Manual mode allows independently moving pieces Building a 1:1 replica of the Golden Gate Bridge from scratch Inspiration Ever wanted to vibecode LEGOs? BrickWrite lets you do just that! I built BrickWrite because I wanted an AI design partner that could actually build beside me inside the same creative tool. Most AI design experiences stop at AI, words, or Computer Use in different softwares, which means the human still has to reconstruct every useful idea by hand. Brick building makes that limitation very obvious because a roof needs real pieces, real orientations, and real connection points that physically make sense. That challenge led to the question behind the entire project: what would happen if a person and an agent could work on the same creative object, using the same tools and sharing the same consequences? I wanted to preserve the satisfying parts of building, including choosing shapes, testing ideas, and refining the silhouette, while giving the agent responsibility for repetitive geometry and technical checking. The idea is basically (\text{human creativity} + \text{agent assistance} = \text{one editable model}), with both sides working on the same object. What it does BrickWrite is a browser-based 3D CAD workspace where people can design editable brick models using real parts and real connection data. Builders can search the catalog, place pieces, connect assemblies, recolor parts, move structures, organize subassemblies, inspect issues, and undo changes through one shared editing system. The agent works inside that same workspace through WebMCP, which gives it direct access to structured information about the current model. It can inspect the document, read the current selection, search the catalog, check connection possibilities, propose edits, validate geometry, and apply eligible changes when Build mode is enabled. The collaboration loop feels much closer to building with a partner than asking a chatbot for instructions. A builder can shape most of a model by hand, ask for help with a roof or repeating structure, review the proposed geometry directly in context, and then continue editing normally. Proposed changes can appear as translucent ghost geometry before they become part of the document, which makes reviewing agent work feel immediate and visual. Every change still belongs to the same editable model and the same history. Human edits and agent edits flow through the same command system, so undo, protections, revision checks, and document state stay consistent across both kinds of interaction. When the document changes while the agent is planning, revision checks can reject stale work before newer edits get overwritten. BrickWrite also gives completed work somewhere useful to go after the design process ends. Builders can export LDraw models, bills of materials, project archives, and printable build guides, while ten editable demo builds help people explore the editor without starting from an empty canvas. Why WebMCP fits the project 3D editing is a rough environment for automation based only on screenshots and pixel coordinates. An image can show where a brick appears on screen, yet it leaves out important information such as part identity, connector frames, protection state, document revision, and the exact operation that would preserve the model correctly. WebMCP lets BrickWrite expose those meanings directly through structured browser tools. Instead of teaching an assistant where a button happens to appear, the application exposes named capabilities with typed inputs, structured results, and clear failure states. The agent gets precise application state while the builder keeps the visual, hands-on interface that makes 3D design enjoyable. The part I find most exciting is that the assistant becomes a second operator of the same application rather than a separate service living beside it. A person can make a careful local adjustment while the agent handles repetitive work, and both changes become part of one document history with the same protections and revision checks. How I implemented WebMCP 1. Discovery begins as soon as the site opens and gives agents immediate orientation. The file src/webmcp/site.ts registers five site-level tools on every route: brickwright_overview , brickwright_navigate , brickwright_tools_list , brickwright_demos_list , and brickwright_autonomy . An agent arriving at the homepage can understand the product, discover available capabilities, and navigate into the editor without guessing its way through the visual interface. 2. The browser receives real tool registrations with executable handlers for every supported operation. The file src/webmcp/register.ts sends tool descriptors through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including names, descriptions, input schemas, and the code that runs each operation. The registrar supports both synchronous and promise-based host implementations, while window.brickwright.invoke(...) provides a development bridge for browsers that lack native WebMCP support. 3. The tool contract and the application share the same vocabulary. CAD operation schemas live in src/webmcp/contract.ts , where Zod definitions generate the advertised JSON Schema and validate incoming requests against the same definitions. Tools including workspace_get , catalog_search , capabilities_search , and capabilities_help let the agent discover state and supported actions before it tries to change anything. 4. Previewing geometry and committing geometry remain separate operations throughout the entire editing workflow. Inside src/webmcp/adapter.ts , build_preflight validates an operation batch against the current document and creates a visible proposal while leaving the committed model unchanged. The proposal_create tool exposes the same preview behavior, while build_apply commits an eligible proposal atomically in Build mode through the shared CAD command path. 5. The available tool inventory changes with the collaboration mode selected by the builder. Inspect mode exposes document reads, Propose mode adds preview capabilities, and Build mode adds direct document writes through the supported editing paths. Mode-scoped registrations use an AbortController , which clears the previous tool inventory before registering the replacement set whenever the builder changes modes. 6. The agent can verify both structure and visual output afterward. The validate_model tool exposes model health, while render_capture returns live rendered pixels together with document and camera metadata. An agent can combine exact structural information with the actual rendered result, while tool-profile hashes and catalog versions help detect changes in the surface used during planning. A representative interaction starts with brickwright_overview , continues through brickwright_navigate and workspace_get , then searches catalog_search with requireGeometry: true before calling build_preflight using the current expectedRevision . The builder reviews the ghost proposal inside the viewport, and Build mode can commit an eligible proposal through build_apply while preserving the same shared history used by manual editing. How it is built BrickWrite uses TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber for the browser application and interactive 3D workspace. The CAD document remains independent from the renderer, so positions, orientations, part identities, connections, constraints, and transactions live as application data while the viewport simply renders that state. Real LDraw geometry and LDCad connection metadata provide the foundation for placement and connectivity throughout the editor. The catalog distinguishes between parts with usable geometry and identities that are only searchable, which prevents the application from silently substituting made-up meshes. Missing geometry returns GEOMETRY_UNAVAILABLE , while collision checks combine a broad phase with mesh-level confirmation and surface uncertainty where the available data leaves room for ambiguity. Cloud project features use Convex and Hexclave, while the frontend runs on Cloudflare Pages and server-side assistant routes run on Vercel. The WebMCP CAD surface stays separate from those model-provider routes, which allows an external browser agent to operate the local document through the page tools while the built-in assistant remains one optional collaboration path. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was deciding what an agent needs to understand before any editing capability becomes safe, predictable, and genuinely useful. Exposing a function is easy compared with defining the state, revision information, geometry

title: OpenHardware
pitch: Software got its agent moment. Hardware hasn't. OpenHardware is the missing piece: an agent that can see the board it programs.
about_excerpt: Software got its agent moment. Hardware hasn't. OpenHardware is the missing piece: an agent that can see the board it programs. Like Comment Story Updates A coding agent today can write, run, test and fix software on its own. Point the same agent at an ESP32 and the loop breaks at the first step: it can write the firmware, but it can't see it run. It doesn't know if the camera came up green, whether the frame rate held, or that the board rebooted twice while you were reading the log. So you become its eyes: you flash, you watch, you report back, and one wrong setting sends you around again. Every gain agents brought to software stops at the edge of the cable. OpenHardware puts the board in front of the agent. A browser page, an ESP32-S3 on a USB cable, and a set of WebMCP tools that let ChatGPT's built-in browser read live telemetry, run measured experiments, build firmware on top of a baseline that never stops reporting, and flash it, with every write to hardware waiting on a human. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP tools run inside the page, on the user's machine. That one property is the reason this project can exist. A cloud MCP server can't see a USB port; a browser tab can. So the same tab that draws the telemetry for the human is the tab whose JavaScript holds the serial link, and the tools the agent calls are functions in that tab. The agent's tool calls have physical consequences, and the human is watching them land on the same screen. It's also the shape WebMCP was designed for: one instrument, two operators. The human sees the charts, the frames, the attempt history and the gate. The agent sees structured summaries of the same data through tools. Neither is working from a description of what the other did. They're looking at the same board. How it creates a better user experience The firmware developer's loop today is edit, plug in, flash, squint at a serial monitor, guess, repeat. Minutes per cycle, and the agent is locked out of all of it. With OpenHardware the loop is a sentence. Ask for "the maximum resolution that holds 12 fps under 50 °C" and the agent reads the board, applies a resolution, soaks, measures frame rate and die temperature, records the attempt, and climbs until a limit breaks. Every attempt is a card in the page, every number was measured seconds ago on this board, and what the agent learns is written into a limits panel in plain language that persists for the next session. When the agent writes firmware, it builds on top of the harness rather than replacing it, so the telemetry stream survives its own flash. If something comes up wrong, the agent sees the frame and the numbers in the same moment and debugs with live data instead of a guess. Every build is recorded with its source, so the human can code-review before anything touches the board, and a flash waits at the gate for approval. For anyone without hardware, the page ships a simulated board with scenes (a board that runs hot, a lost link, a missing camera). It's badged amber so it can never be mistaken for the real thing, and every tool result says which one it came from. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Measure instead of recall. Two boards with the same part number have different amounts of contiguous PSRAM free. The agent now reasons from what this board reported, not from training data. Iterate without becoming the agent's eyes. The human declares what's wired to which pins, states the goal, and approves. The agent runs the experiments. Debug after a flash. Because the harness is never overwritten, the agent still has telemetry and camera frames after its own firmware boots. The failure mode where the agent flashes and goes blind is gone. Review before it's real. Reads are always available to the agent. Writes to hardware are gated, and the source of every build is one click away, so trust is earned attempt by attempt rather than assumed. How we implemented WebMCP The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. Read tools are annotated readOnlyHint and stay registered whenever the page is open: board identity and capabilities, telemetry over a window (count, min, max, mean and slope per field, never raw samples), learned limits, a frame capture that renders in the camera panel, the available builds, the wiring list, and the current work order with its attempts. Write tools register only while a board is linked and unregister on link loss: camera on/off and config, run_experiment (apply, soak, measure, record in one call), watch_for (block on a telemetry condition, honoring the abort signal), record_limit, and flash_image, which routes through the same approve/hold gate a human uses. Approve and hold are deliberately not tools. Every result carries its source, sim or usb, and the link state. The page infers agent presence from tool calls and narrates it next to the link badge, without ever changing the badge's color. If document.modelContext is absent, the page works exactly as before with a single hint that tools are available in a WebMCP-enabled browser. Underneath: a static frontend with no build step, a framed line protocol (OHW1) over Web Serial with CRC and four-per-second heartbeats, an ESP-IDF harness built in Docker, and a simulated board that speaks the same protocol so the tools are tested against it in CI. And hardware just did. This is open hardware. First, the board gets a baseline firmware we call the harness. It does one job. Stream everything the board knows about itself four times a second. title: WorkSpec Studio
pitch: Design an application with your agent, derive its infrastructure needs, compare Azure and AWS, record the ADR, and export the complete .workspec workspace.
about_excerpt: Design an application with your agent, derive its infrastructure needs, compare Azure and AWS, record the ADR, and export the complete .workspec workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Architecture decisions usually fragment across diagramming tools, spreadsheets, cloud pricing tabs, chat transcripts, and ADR documents. The diagram stops matching the estimate; the rationale disappears; and the final artifacts are trapped in somebody else's database. We built WorkSpec Studio to make architecture a shared, inspectable workflow between a person and an AI agent, with portable files as the durable result. What it does WorkSpec Studio takes a project through one connected journey: Design the application as an interactive C4 model. Derive an editable, provider-neutral infrastructure shopping list from its deployable elements. Map the same requirements to Azure and AWS and compare deterministic monthly planning estimates. Prepare and review the cloud-platform decision. Record the approved choice as an architecture decision record. Download the complete .workspec workspace as a ZIP. A user can start blank, load an example, or import an existing .workspec bundle. The C4 canvas supports context, logical-container, and deployment views. People can create, move, connect, and edit elements directly; the agent can propose or arrange the same model through WebMCP. The resulting workspace is schema-validated YAML that can be reviewed in the browser, committed to Git, used by WorkSpec command-line tools, or consumed by a hosted WorkSpec Enterprise installation. Why WebMCP Architecture work combines two different strengths. Agents are good at turning intent into a coherent first draft and tracing consequences across many artifacts. People are responsible for understanding the system, correcting assumptions, weighing trade-offs, and approving durable decisions. Without WebMCP, an agent must manipulate a complex infinite canvas with fragile pointer automation or edit files somewhere outside the UI the person is reviewing. WorkSpec's WebMCP tools connect both participants to the same live browser-local workspace. The agent can create a structured C4 proposal in one operation while the person immediately sees a real diagram they can drag and edit. The infrastructure list is derived from that same model, the provider comparison uses that same list, and the ADR is generated only from the visible draft the person has approved. Every successful agent operation appears in a collapsible Agent activity history. How we built it The workbench is a TypeScript and React monorepo composed from reusable WorkSpec packages for C4 schemas and rendering, infinite-canvas interaction, topology planning, provider mapping, decisions, ZIP workspaces, and the shared Studio shell. The page registers eleven bounded tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(). They let an agent inspect the workspace, navigate the gated workflow, control relevant sidebars, create a complete C4 architecture, inspect and pin diagram layout, update infrastructure requirements, compare providers, prepare an unsaved decision, record a reviewed decision, and export the workspace ZIP. All tool inputs use closed JSON schemas. Handlers resolve the current application state through stable action references, and registrations share an AbortController so React Strict Mode cannot leave duplicate tools behind. Human UI actions and agent tools operate on the same canonical MemoryWorkspace. The cloud estimates are deterministic planning figures rather than live quotes, keeping the comparison reproducible. Provider-specific choices do not leak into the source architecture or neutral requirements. Human review is part of the protocol The decision flow is intentionally split into two tools. prepare_cloud_decision opens the Decision page and fills a visible, editable provider and rationale draft. record_cloud_decision rejects calls until that draft exists and is used only after explicit human approval. This makes review a real product boundary, not a sentence in an agent prompt. The export tool returns the exact current workspace as a bounded base64 ZIP. That gives agents a reliable handoff even in browser environments where clicking a download button is awkward, while people retain the ordinary visible download control. Challenges we faced The biggest challenge was making an infinite visual canvas genuinely agent-operable without taking control away from the person. We added semantic architecture and layout tools rather than exposing cursor coordinates, while keeping every generated node editable and draggable. We also had to keep one canonical state across four routed stages, preserve unknown files during ZIP round trips, prevent stale React closures in registered tools, and make irreversible decision recording impossible before a visible draft exists. Accomplishments we're proud of One continuous Design → Infrastructure → Compare → Decision story. A real C4 canvas that supports both semantic WebMCP operations and direct human editing. Provider-neutral requirements with traceability back to architecture elements. Like-for-like Azure and AWS mappings and monthly estimates. A visible approval gate before ADR generation. Complete .workspec ZIP import and export. Eleven WebMCP tools plus a clear Agent activity history. More than two thousand automated tests across the WorkSpec packages and applications. What we learned The best WebMCP tools describe meaningful product operations, not DOM gestures. A tool such as "prepare a decision for review" is more robust and more understandable than a sequence of clicks, and it lets the UI enforce the same rules for both humans and agents. We also learned that shared visibility matters as much as capability. The strongest moments are not when the agent finishes everything invisibly; they are the pauses where a proposal appears in the real UI, the person edits or approves it, and both continue from the same state. What's next Azure and AWS are the first provider adapters. The provider-neutral model is designed for additional clouds, on-premises targets, live pricing catalogs, policy checks, and organization-specific mapping rules. We also plan to reuse the extracted Studio packages directly inside WorkSpec Enterprise. Try it Live app: https://studio.workspec.io/ Source: https://github.com/FieldstateNZ/workspec-studio Suggested prompt: Help me design Orderlight, an online ordering system that takes payment through an external gateway and fulfils accepted orders asynchronously. Build the C4 architecture, derive and review the infrastructure plan, compare Azure and AWS, and prepare a recommendation. Stop for my review at every stage and do not record the decision until I explicitly approve it. title: ZZAIM — the agent reads the contract, not the screen
pitch: A lesson-planning workbench for Korean teachers that registers 8 WebMCP tools. When export isn't ready, the tool returns the next step — the procedure lives in the return value, not the description.
about_excerpt: A lesson-planning workbench for Korean teachers that registers 8 WebMCP tools. When export isn't ready, the tool returns the next step — the procedure lives in the return value, not the description. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Korean schoolteachers write lesson plans in a document format called a yak-an (brief plan). Filling it is tedious, but you cannot just automate it away: every school means something slightly different by each box, so forcing a format is worse than leaving it blank. That makes it an unusually good test for agents. The agent has to ask the product what it needs rather than guess — and until now, the only way for an agent to do that on the web was to look at the screen and click. What it does ZZAIM is a lesson-planning tool for Korean teachers that exports to HWPX, the document format Korean public schools use. This submission puts WebMCP on its brief-plan workbench. The page registers eight tools, and the agent operates on the exact document the teacher is looking at: read-lesson-plan · update-section · add-activity · remove-activity set-lesson-meta · check-export-readiness · request-standard-enrichment · export-hwpx-preview What the teacher edits by hand and what the agent edits with a tool land in the same state , and the page's call log records who did which . How we use WebMCP — we return the contract ZZAIM's export is a two-stage contract . If the plan is not filled in enough, the export returns a work order instead of a failure. The split is deliberate: the first stage answers immediately, the second does the slow work. The WebMCP tools expose that contract as-is. Called on the demo's starting plan, check-export-readiness returns exactly this: ready: false requiredCapability: standard_enriched nextAction: REQUEST_STANDARD_ENRICHMENT 미달 조건: - 학습 목표가 2개 이상이어야 합니다. 현재 1개입니다. - 수업 활동에 전개 · 정리 단계가 없습니다. - 평가 내용이 비어 있습니다. - 준비물이 비어 있습니다. The tools answer in Korean, the language of the teachers who use them. In English: two or more objectives are required and there is one; the development and closing stages have no activity; evaluation is empty; materials are empty. The agent reads that and calls request-standard-enrichment on its own . We never wrote "first call A, then call B" into any tool description . The procedure is in the return value. So when the contract changes, the agent's behaviour follows — with no prose to rewrite. Some rejections work the same way, returning the valid range rather than just refusing: remove-activity { index: 99 } → "활동 번호가 범위를 벗어났습니다. 유효 범위: 1부터 1." (Out of range. Valid range: 1 to 1 — it reflects how many activities the plan has.) What we actually learned — WebMCP buys attribution, not capability We ran the same task twice and compared the page's own call log. Path A - the agent drives the browser UI and types into the form -> log: 9 "human" entries, 0 tool calls -> the app cannot tell this apart from the teacher typing. The DOM events match. Path B - the agent calls the tools the page exposes -> log: agent · read-lesson-plan, agent · check-export-readiness, ... with arguments and return values Both paths finish the task. The difference is whether the app knows who did what . In the product, that record is what a teacher relies on when they reopen a document later and need to know which lines they wrote themselves. (In this demo the log lives in the page, so a reload clears it — see Limits.) This also caught a mistake for us. Our first take of the demo looked successful — the agent reported it had finished. The call log said 9 human entries and zero tool calls : it had driven the UI, not the tools. We would have shipped a video demonstrating the wrong mechanism. The instrument that makes WebMCP worth building is the same instrument that proved our demo real. How we built it The workbench is a Next.js / React / TypeScript page. Registration is plain WebMCP — document.modelContext.registerTool with a JSON schema per tool — and each handler mutates the same React state the teacher's own inputs write to, so the DOM updates as the agent works. Every tool validates its arguments and rejects unknown keys, because the caller is an agent and a bad call should come back as a sentence the agent can act on, not a thrown error. Challenges Feature detection is the whole UX. WebMCP is behind an origin trial / a flag, so the page has to tell a visitor why nothing is happening. A diagnostic card reports whether document.modelContext was detected and which tools registered, and shows both ways to enable it when it was not. Detection runs at page load, so the card also says to reload. Agents will silently fall back to clicking. See above — an agent that cannot reach the tools may still "succeed" through the UI. We had to verify from the page's side which path a run actually took. Not forcing the format. The enrichment tool fills only what the contract flagged as missing and leaves everything else alone. Blank is safer than invented. Limits The demo page runs on in-browser state . A reload returns it to the starting plan, and the call log resets with it. It is built that way so a judge can use it with no login. Export in this demo goes as far as a document summary . The more detailed Korean plan format ( sean ) is out of scope for this demo. We verified on Chrome 152 and the ChatGPT in-app browser . The flag exists from Chrome 149, but 149-151 are versions we did not test. The standalone ChatGPT desktop app is untested. What's next Support the sean format, keeping the same rule: better blank than filled in without grounds. Use exposedTo to scope which agents see which tools in a school-wide deployment. Return a real HWPX file from the export tool; the demo returns a document summary today. title: TermLens
pitch: An AI agent reads your contract, grounds every key term to its exact source sentence, and can't save a thing without your explicit approval. Everything stays local in your browser.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent reads your contract, grounds every key term to its exact source sentence, and can't save a thing without your explicit approval. Everything stays local in your browser.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 




 
 Inspiration 

 We’ve all seen AI wrappers that extract data from long legal documents and expect us to take the output on faith. But when you’re dealing with actual contracts—auto-renewals, notice periods, liability limits—blind trust isn't an option. A single hallucinated detail can cause massive headaches. 

 I wanted to build something fast that lets AI do the heavy lifting of reading legal jargon, but gives humans complete control over what gets saved. No black boxes, no silent state changes, and no sending sensitive contracts to a third-party server. 

 What it does 

 TermLens is a browser-native legal contract verification gate powered by WebMCP: 

 
 Source Grounding: Every extracted term links directly to its exact quote in the text, highlighting confidence levels so you know where to double-check. 
 Human-in-the-Loop Control: The AI can analyze and stage proposed contract terms, but it can never write or alter state without an explicit human sign-off. 
 Local-First Privacy: Documents are processed entirely inside your browser's local memory. 
 Audit Trail: Every action, approval, and rejection is captured in an exportable audit receipt (JSON/Markdown). 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend: Built with vanilla HTML, modern CSS Grid/Flexbox layouts, and JetBrains Mono for a clean, developer-focused UI. 
 Animations: Powered by GSAP and ScrollTrigger to create hero reassembly effects and visual contract sweeps. 
 Agent Integration: Connected via WebMCP for deterministic tool handling and staged write-locks. 
 Deployment: Hosted on Cloudflare Pages ( termlens.pages.dev ). 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the UI grid layouts to feel pixel-perfect across different display widths while preserving custom GSAP animation timelines took a lot of fine-tuning. We also had to ensure that the agent state machine strictly respected write locks—blocking any unverified attempts to persist contract terms without explicit user confirmation. 

 What we learned 

 Building browser-native AI workflows requires thinking about user trust first. When you give users direct grounding alongside hard write-protection, AI tools feel less like unpredictable black boxes and more like dependable assistants. 

 What's next for TermLens 

 I want to expand support for multi-document comparisons, add automated risk-scoring presets for standard SaaS agreements, and make the WebMCP integration even easier for developers to plug into their own local workflows.
