title: Olympus MCP Harness
pitch: The model reasons. WebMCP connects. Olympus controls. The machine executes
about_excerpt: The model reasons. WebMCP connects. Olympus controls. The machine executes Like Comment Story Updates Native WebMCP Execution Flow Architecture WebMCP testing npm test WebMCP available Same model. Same WebMCP tools. Same task. Different execution reliability Native WEBMCP: ChatGPT browser with 5 tools ChatGPT access to olympus harness Find best AI laptop Check out layer Inspiration AI models are good at reasoning, but execution should be controlled, observable, and reliable. Olympus MCP Harness started from one simple idea: “The model reasons. The machine executes.” As WebMCP moves AI agents from reading websites to acting on them, execution becomes a trust boundary. Olympus was built to engineer that boundary. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns website capabilities into structured tools that agents can invoke directly instead of guessing their way through the UI. Olympus builds on that boundary: WebMCP structures the action. Olympus governs the execution. Unlike a backend MCP integration, WebMCP works inside the live page and shared user session. Olympus uses that browser-native boundary to govern execution without replacing the existing web experience. WebMCP defines how an agent can interact with the application, while Olympus determines whether an invocation is valid, allowed, safe to execute, and successfully completed. What it does Olympus MCP Harness is the execution control layer behind WebMCP. WebMCP handles the agent-to-web boundary through structured tools. Olympus then: Inspects the invoked capability Validates tool arguments Authorizes execution according to risk and policy Executes the machine action Verifies the result Recovers from safe failures when appropriate Traces the full execution path High-risk actions, such as checkout, remain behind explicit human approval. People + agents together Olympus enables controlled delegation . A user can delegate an outcome instead of manually operating every interface step. The agent reasons, discovers WebMCP tools, searches, compares, and prepares actions. Olympus governs execution, while the human only needs to intervene when a high-risk action requires approval. This creates a new interaction model: agents can autonomously handle routine actions while humans remain in control of consequential ones. The goal is neither full autonomy nor manual browsing. It is controlled delegation. In the demo, the agent can search, inspect, compare, and prepare a laptop purchase through WebMCP tools, while Olympus keeps checkout behind an explicit approval boundary. Who It's For E-commerce and retail web apps : Olympus demonstrates how AI agents can safely help users search products, compare options, prepare a cart, and approach checkout without turning high-risk purchase actions into blind automation. WebMCP developers : developers exposing real actions to AI agents and needing a reliable layer for validation, authorization, approval, recovery, verification, and observability. Human users and judges : they can see the current model decision, harness stage, machine action, execution trace, and a non-skippable approval gate for high-risk actions. WebMCP-capable agents and clients : such as ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The agent interacts through document.modelContext tools rather than relying on brittle UI actuation for the core workflow. The laptop storefront is the concrete retail demo; the harness pattern is designed to generalize to other WebMCP workflows. How we built it I built Olympus using the native WebMCP imperative API with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The app exposes five structured tools: search_products get_product compare_products add_to_cart checkout Each WebMCP tool is intentionally thin and routes execution through the same Olympus harness.run(...) path, where validation, policy, approval, execution, recovery, verification, and tracing are enforced. The application is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and deployed on Vercel. Olympus runs behind WebMCP site tools inside the live browser context, preserving the page’s existing state and user experience while adding execution policy, verification, and traceability. Tested natively with ChatGPT’s in-app browser Olympus was tested directly in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. ChatGPT successfully discovered and invoked these Olympus WebMCP tools natively: search_products get_product compare_products add_to_cart For the high-risk checkout tool, ChatGPT’s own browser security blocked the invocation before it reached Olympus’s approval layer. This demonstrates defense in depth: ChatGPT Agent ↓ Client / Browser Security ↓ WebMCP ↓ Olympus MCP Harness ↓ Human Approval ↓ Machine Low- and medium-risk actions successfully reached Olympus. High-risk checkout was independently blocked earlier by the client security layer. To demonstrate Olympus’s own checkout approval flow, judges can use the live simulator or a WebMCP-enabled Chrome environment where the invocation is permitted. Challenges we ran into The main challenges were working with a rapidly evolving WebMCP runtime, clearly separating WebMCP responsibilities from harness responsibilities, and designing approval and recovery behavior without turning Olympus into another agent framework. A key architectural decision was that WebMCP owns registration, discovery, and invocation, while Olympus operates behind that boundary to inspect and control execution. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud that Olympus demonstrates: native WebMCP integration five structured WebMCP tools a shared execution harness behind every tool schema validation and policy-aware authorization explicit human approval for high-risk actions real execution traces and metrics result verification safe failure handling and recovery native testing with ChatGPT’s in-app browser The project is designed so the harness is more than a logging layer: it can actively prevent or gate machine execution. What we learned WebMCP provides a structured way for models to interact with websites, but exposing a tool is not the same as executing it reliably. Reliable agent execution needs an additional engineering layer for validation, authorization, human approval, failure recovery, result verification, and observability. In short: WebMCP makes actions available to models. Olympus makes those actions safe to execute. What's next for Olympus MCP Harness Next, I want to evolve Olympus into a reusable execution harness for more WebMCP applications. Future work includes: richer policy models reusable tool registration and policy APIs stronger observability broader failure and recovery strategies support for more real-world WebMCP workflows comparative reliability evaluation using Chrome WebMCP Evals methodology I will only publish benchmark percentages after running real repeatable evals. The current project does not claim an unmeasured reliability score. Closing Project : Olympus MCP Harness Philosophy : The model reasons. The machine executes. Product thesis : The model reasons. WebMCP connects. Olympus controls. The machine executes. Technical thesis : WebMCP defines the boundary. Olympus MCP Harness engineers the execution behind it. Mission : Engineer the boundary between AI reasoning and machine execution. Evaluation principle : I don't claim the harness improves reliability until I measure it. The planned comparative evaluation is: Without Olympus Harness vs. With Olympus Harness , using fixed tasks and reporting real results only. The future isn’t just better models. It’s better AI systems.🚀 Olympus MCP Harness is one attempt to make that system boundary visible, controllable, and reliable. Checklist - Native WebMCP integration ✓ - Olympus controls execution ✓ - Client-side security observed ✓ - Human approval works ✓ - Trace and metrics work ✓ - Verification works ✓ - Safe recovery works ✓ - ChatGPT in-app browser tested ✓ - No fake benchmark claims ✓ Built With ai-agents ai-safety chatgpt chrome harness hitl human-in-the-loop mcp openai vercel webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Quoc Cuong Vo Love to build AI Like Share this project: Updates Quoc Cuong Vo started this project — Aug 27, 2026 12:27 AM EDT

title: Affogata Benchmarks - Live Data Explorer
pitch: Explore rich, live brand conversation data with true human + agent synergy. Browse visually as your agent deep dives, surfaces insights, and prepares reports, using the app in its own way via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Explore rich, live brand conversation data with true human + agent synergy. Browse visually as your agent deep dives, surfaces insights, and prepares reports, using the app in its own way via WebMCP. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Dating app report made by AI, entirely off the data via WebMCP Deep dive into a finding from the data about Bumble - again purely via WebMCP Agent independently picks the fastest-climbing app + its two closest rivals, writes them into the live comparison, and gives a real verdict Compare view empty, before the tool call Same view after `benchmarks_compare_in_ui` fired (with Bumble/Hinge live on screen and the tool-call log visible) The tool trail next to the rendered brief, shows the full call chain in one frame Working with the app from the ChatGPT app, just the data Working with the app from the ChatGPT app with the app visible Inspiration Affogata already analyzes & scores dozens apps and games across multiple categories, analyzing real conversational data from social and review sites that are often hard for LLMs to access. This data lives behind a login and your usual "SaaS app" UI, where business users rely on it (from our customers such as Mojang, EA, Scopely and others), or separately an agent could connect to it via MCP/API. But how do you bridge these worlds? AI working with data is magical, but people do need the visuals and exploration to get a sense for the data! When we saw what WebMCP can do, it looked like the natural evolution for human + agent collaboration. Instead of a siloed experience where humans use a UI and agents use a backend connection to look at the same data in different ways, a singular experience can offered where one truly complements the other and natural exploration and "experience" of the data can happen. What it does benchmarks.affogata.net exposes 15+ WebMCP tools, both reads and a write, directly on the live site with a 79-title portfolio of real brands. The tools include: benchmarks_get_overview , benchmarks_get_movers , benchmarks_get_title , benchmarks_get_category_analytics , benchmarks_list_titles , benchmarks_compare_titles , benchmarks_explain_methodology - reads benchmarks_compare_in_ui , benchmarks_open_title - writes that change what's rendered on the page for anyone watching, not just inside the agent's own chat An agent using nothing but these tools can diagnose why a title's score dropped, compare it against its closest rivals, put that comparison live on screen, scan the entire portfolio for the next brewing crisis, analyze the data and prepare reports, all without a single click or scrape, and with a experience where the AI working with the data actually improves what the human is seeing on screen. How we built it The benchmark scoring already existed as Affogata's own MCP schemas. We adapted the ones that map to public, read-only data into the WebMCP registration format and added one write tool ( benchmarks_compare_in_ui ) so an agent can drive the compare view live, not just describe it in chat. The site runs the tools in page JS against the browser session, so there's no separate auth or API key: An agent using ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with the WebMCP flag on gets the same tool list a logged-in human would see. Challenges we ran into Getting an agent to reliably discover and call the right tool names instead of guessing from page copy took a couple of passes; an early bug had benchmarks_compare_titles and benchmarks_compare_in_ui named inconsistently between the page text and the actual registration, which caused the agent to call a tool that didn't exist. We also hit a live-state sync issue: when a human removed a title from the compare view by hand, the agent's next tool call still answered from memory instead of re-reading the page; exactly the kind of human-and-agent-together moment WebMCP is supposed to get right, so it was worth fixing rather than working around. Finally, the schema needs to be clear to models lower on the tool-using skill rank that the user might be using if they're using Chrome, so there was some iteration on that as well. Accomplishments that we're proud of This app has real utility! It's a vision for data apps that work great for humans and agents at the very same time. To that end, we've built three end-to-end demos built entirely from tool calls, no manual data entry: a single-brand "Customer Goodwill Crisis Brief" that diagnosed a real -4.8 score collapse and generated a branded, print-ready HTML report with every number traced back to a named tool call; a portfolio-wide "War Room" that scanned all 79 titles at once, ranked them on a transparent risk index, flagged a false alarm, and surfaced an improving challenger; and an agent that independently picked out the fastest-climbing app, pulled in its two closest rivals on its own judgment, put that comparison live on screen, and gave a real analytical verdict on whether the gain was sustainable; the kind of judgment call that used to need a person opening a dozen tabs. What we learned The write side of WebMCP is what actually changes the human-agent relationship. A read-only agent is still just answering questions in a chat window. The moment benchmarks_compare_in_ui puts a comparison on screen live, two people can watch the same tab while an agent drives it; that's a genuinely different way of working together than screen-sharing a chat. It's great for a person working with the data; it's even better when a team wants to have a live discussion informed by it. What's next for Affogata Live Data Explorer Wire the demo tool set up to Affogata's live customer data (today it runs on weekly-refreshed benchmark data), and bring WebMCP support into the logged-in Affogata product itself, so any customer can point their own agent at their own data without an admin setting up API access first. title: Leaf
pitch: A design canvas your agent can use. Every layer is real HTML, and the editor registers itself as WebMCP site tools, so you and ChatGPT edit the same design at the same time.
about_excerpt: A design canvas your agent can use. Every layer is real HTML, and the editor registers itself as WebMCP site tools, so you and ChatGPT edit the same design at the same time. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Leaf is a visual design editor where every layer is a real HTML element with CSS styles. Open new.leafnode.app in ChatGPT's browser and the editor registers its own operations as WebMCP site tools. You and the agent then work on the same canvas. Why WebMCP fits Leaf Because every layer is DOM, the editor's operations were already structured and page-local: create an artboard, write HTML into it, read a swatch's fill, measure a text layer, pin a comment to a node. WebMCP lets the page hand those operations to whatever agent is in the browser, with no server, no extension, and no MCP client configuration. Leaf was an existing project I had been working on internally and the MCP server only worked with the local desktop app running. I'd considered creating a remote MCP server but it was a lot of work to get the interactions right, especially with screenshotting designs for agent feedback. WebMCP allowed me to quickly build a sort of remote MCP server that an agent can use without having the app running. How it makes the experience better The agent shows up on the canvas as a presence, its edits land in your undo history, and it reads the design as it is right now, including whatever you just changed by hand. In the demo I deleted the color directions I didn't want and left a comment on a swatch, "make this a bit warmer," the way I'd leave one for a teammate. The agent read the comment, warmed the swatch, updated its label, and carried that exact value into the guideline. Later it stopped and asked before pinning notes on the shared canvas. Code generators hand you a picture you can't touch; design tools have a canvas the agent can't see. Leaf is one canvas for both. What people and agents can do together Build a brand from foundations to applications in one sitting. The agent proposes a wordmark, two marks, three color directions, and a type pairing. You pick by hand. It assembles a one-page guideline from what survived, then builds a poster, an email header, and a landing page hero from that guideline on a new page, flagging its compromises as pinned comments you resolve. The canvas is the brief: nobody re-pastes brand rules into a prompt. I build landing page tooling for Shopify brands, and a new brand shipping a coherent page and email from one system, in about ten minutes of agent time, is the whole job. How WebMCP is implemented While a file is open, the app shell registers 27 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Reads: list_pages , get_basic_info , get_selection , get_tree_summary , get_node_info , get_node_styles , measure_text , find_nodes , get_canvas_layout , get_jsx , get_font_family_info Pages and camera: edit_pages , set_viewport Creation and mutation: create_artboard , write_html , update_styles , set_text_content , duplicate_nodes , delete_nodes , rename_nodes , move_nodes , set_node_visibility , rename_file Collaboration: list_comments , add_comment , resolve_comment_thread , finish_working_on_nodes Every tool dispatches through the same runtime the UI and Leaf's desktop MCP server use, so agent edits get the same validation, undo history, and persistence as a person's. Leaf existed before the challenge. The WebMCP integration and this local-only public build were done between August 26 and September 3, 2026; the repo's README has the timeline. Try it Open new.leafnode.app in ChatGPT's browser, or in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing on. A first visit opens straight onto a canvas, and the Site tools indicator lists Leaf's tools. Then: "Build a 1440-wide landing page hero for a small-batch hot sauce brand: nav, eyebrow, headline, two buttons, fine print. Name every layer." Change the headline color by hand in the properties panel, then: "Match both buttons to the headline's new color." "Review the hero like a design lead. Measure the text, raise anything under 14px, and leave a comment pinned to any layer you changed." Same palette, same type, same mark without me re-explaining any of it. Here it actually stops and asks before leaving comments on the canvas. I'll go ahead and say yes. It pins a couple of notes where it bent the system. I can read them and resolve them like I would with anyone else I'm working with. Under the hood, these tools run through the same editor run time as the UI. So, the agent's edits are validated and undoable just like mine. title: Bouquet Studio
pitch: Turn your wishes into a bouquet you can see, shape, and confidently order.
about_excerpt: Turn your wishes into a bouquet you can see, shape, and confidently order. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A better way to choose flowers One shared editing system Using WebMCP to Inspect and Improve Bouquets From idea to order Inspiration I do not know much about flowers. Whenever I buy a bouquet, I run into the same questions: What flowers do I want? How should they be arranged? What style am I looking for? I usually cannot answer those questions in floral terms. What I do know is who the bouquet is for, why I am giving it, and how I want it to feel. An agent can translate those intentions into flower choices, but a text recommendation only solves half the problem. I still need to see the flowers together, react to them, and shape the design until it feels right. A generated image can provide inspiration, but it is disconnected from the products I can actually buy and difficult to revise precisely. Bouquet Studio started with a simple idea: let people describe the feeling instead of naming the flowers, then let the person and agent shape the actual bouquet together . Why WebMCP is the right fit Most online flower shops are designed for human eyes. Online flower shops contain the information an agent needs, but that information is often scattered across product pages, FAQs, announcements, and checkout. An agent can navigate those interfaces, but it has to repeatedly interpret pages, images, and UI state like a human would. WebMCP gives the agent a direct way to understand and operate the same flower shop: Task-level actions . Instead of opening products and applying filters one by one, the agent can search for bouquets matching the customer’s complete request, inspect their contents, customize them, and continue toward ordering. Direct bouquet-editing tools . When the customer wants to change a bouquet, the agent can add, remove, replace, move, resize, and reorder flowers; change wrapping; undo changes; save and restore versions; and request rendered images or diagnostics when it needs to inspect the result. Without these tools, an agent would have to repeatedly analyze screenshots, estimate click or drag coordinates, and determine whether visual actions succeeded. The agent can receive the shop’s full context on demand . On a customer-facing website, useful information naturally lives in different places, which makes sense for people browsing step by step, but an agent must first discover and combine those details. Through WebMCP, the shop can provide the information the agent needs together, rather than forcing it to discover and combine information scattered throughout the website. This makes flower shopping a strong WebMCP use case: product knowledge, multi-step actions, and visual decisions all need to work together. WebMCP lets the agent access the right context and tools while keeping the customer in control of the visual decisions . How does it create a better experience? Start with intent, not expertise . People can describe the recipient, occasion, mood, budget, or simply how they want the bouquet to feel. The agent translates those cues into suitable products or a first arrangement without requiring the user to know flower names. React instead of specify . It is often easier to recognize what feels right than to describe it from scratch. Users can look at a visible bouquet and say “warmer,” “less formal,” or “more delicate,” then watch the agent adjust the actual flowers, composition, and wrapping. Explore without pressure . Users can try different directions, compare alternatives, ask questions, and undo changes without asking a florist to prepare version after version or starting over. Turn uncertainty into confidence . The final bouquet is something the user has actually seen and shaped, not a black-box recommendation, and it can be ordered directly. What can people and agents do together now that was difficult before? Previously, an agent could recommend flowers, generate an inspiration image, or navigate a flower shop. The customer still had to bridge the gap between that recommendation and a real, orderable bouquet. Bouquet Studio turns that handoff into a shared workflow: A customer can say: “A longtime teammate is leaving for a new role. I want the bouquet to feel grateful and optimistic, but still professional.” The agent can turn that intent into several options using flowers that are actually available , each with different flowers, colors, wrapping, and composition. From there, the agent and customer work on the same live bouquet . The agent can make changes directly in the editor, while the customer sees those changes immediately and can refine them visually. Human and agent edits share the same state, undo/redo history, and saved versions. The agent contributes structured reasoning: which flowers are available, where they are positioned, what is hidden, which elements overlap, and where the composition may feel empty . The customer contributes the judgment that matters most: does this bouquet feel right for this person and this moment? Once the design feels right, it continues into checkout. There is no need to recreate the recommendation or search for real flowers that resemble an AI-generated image. The new capability is the end-to-end collaboration loop itself . Intent, reasoning, visual editing, and purchasing remain connected instead of becoming separate handoffs. How We implemented WebMCP We built the human-facing editor first, then added WebMCP by testing it with fresh agents that had no prior knowledge of Bouquet Studio. We observed where they struggled and refined the tools around those problems. Agent feedback shaped the workflow . Early tests showed that undo and redo were critical: an agent could revise its latest change, while a person could reverse an agent’s action directly instead of explaining the correction in chat. Human and agent edits now share the same bouquet state, edit history, and saved versions. Guidance appears where decisions happen . Agents initially produced horizontal rows, excessive symmetry, repeated colors, and wrapping that competed with the bouquet. We added concise arranging guidance directly to the tools used to choose flowers, position them, and style the wrapping. Agents can inspect what they created . They can request the rendered bouquet, a color map showing flowers, greenery, and empty space, and a visibility report identifying hidden blooms and overlapping flower IDs. This combines an overall visual impression with specific information the agent can act on. Predictable corrections became reliable actions . When agents repeatedly positioned flowers too far outside the wrapping, we added a fitting action that handles the geometry automatically and leaves the agent to focus on flower choice, composition, and mood. Together, these decisions turned WebMCP from a collection of tools into an iterative collaboration between the customer, the agent, and the website. The agent handles intent and creative exploration, the product handles reliable constraints, and the customer remains in control of what ultimately feels right. about_excerpt: An autonomous AI coach helping children master handwriting through real-time stroke analysis and adaptive WebMCP tools. AI Remediation Loop : Success modal showing closed-loop AI error detection and adaptive correction. Progress & Analytics : Learner dashboard tracking accuracy heatmaps, streaks, and competency mastery. Rewards & Themes : Gamified achievement center with unlockable badges and colorful pen themes. Settings & Controls : Configuration for voice guidance, learner profiles, and WebMCP agent autonomy. Inspiration Watching young children learn to write can be both fascinating and heartbreaking. I often observed children drawing letters like "D" or "B" from bottom to top, or making awkward reverse loops. Visually, the final result might look somewhat acceptable on a static worksheet, but motor-memory-wise, a bad habit was already taking root. Existing handwriting apps on tablets simply check whether pixels overlap with a template. They don't understand how the child traced it, in which direction, or why they made a mistake. Meanwhile, parents and teachers simply don't have enough hours in the day to sit 1-on-1 for every single stroke. When OpenAI announced the WebMCP standard, a lightbulb went off: what if an AI didn't just passively look at a screenshot, but had direct, structured API tools on the web page to analyze mathematical stroke trajectories and dynamically adapt the canvas with live visual guides? That was the spark that drove me to build TRACEAI. What it does TRACEAI is an AI-native web application designed to act as an attentive, encouraging handwriting coach for kids. Here is how the experience works in practice: Child practices on a joyful, tactile canvas: Children can practice uppercase letters (A-Z), numbers (0-9), and basic geometric shapes across 3 distinct difficulty modes (Trace, Copy, and Memory). Instant 5-Dimension Trajectory Evaluation: As soon as a child lifts their pen or finger, TRACEAI analyzes the stroke geometry across 5 criteria: Direction & Stroke Order, Positioning, Precision, Continuity, and Line Respect. Autonomous AI Coaching via WebMCP: An AI agent inspects the child's learning history through registered WebMCP tools (get_weak_letters(), analyze_trace()). Real-time Interface Adaptation: When the agent detects an issue—for example, struggling with the curved stroke direction on the letter "D"—it calls generate_exercise("D", "direction"). The web page instantly reacts by drawing pulsating directional guide arrows and speaking warm, supportive vocal guidance. Gamified Positive Reinforcement: Points, stars, streak tracking, audio chimes, and confetti celebrations keep the child smiling and motivated. Built-in WebMCP Inspector: For hackathon judges and developers, an inspector panel provides live insight into the agent’s inner monologue, tool calls, JSON payloads, and a 1-click end-to-end demo scenario. How we built it I engineered TRACEAI as a solo project to be ultra-fast, responsive on touch devices (tablets/smartphones), and 100% compliant with the emerging W3C WebMCP standard: WebMCP Standard Tooling: I registered 8 structured tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool() with explicit JSON schemas. I also implemented a lightweight fallback polyfill so the app runs smoothly in both WebMCP-enabled browsers and standard modern browsers. Client-Side Geometric Engine (trace-analyzer.js): I built a vector analysis pipeline that calculates directional angle variances, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) path distances, and bounding-box alignments in under 5ms right in the browser. Reactive Canvas & Visual Overlays (app.js): Built with pure HTML5 Canvas and Vanilla JavaScript. Dynamic arrow overlays and smooth Bezier curve approximations make the interface feel alive without heavy rendering libraries. Multi-Sensory Audio System: Utilizes the Web Speech API for natural text-to-speech coaching advice and the Web Audio API for rewarding synthesizer chimes and fanfares. Modern Glassmorphic UI: Crafted using modern, responsive CSS with cheerful, kid-friendly color palettes, accessible contrasts, and smooth micro-animations. Challenges we ran into Distinguishing Shape from Direction: A child drawing the letter "O" clockwise vs. counter-clockwise results in almost identical static shapes, but completely different motor habits. Designing a lightweight vector angle differential that accurately detects inverted stroke sequences was my trickiest algorithmic hurdle. Designing Agent-Friendly Tools: I initially tried passing raw coordinate streams to the LLM, but quickly realized that overwhelmed the context window and caused unnecessary latency. I shifted to a high-signal tool design where analyze_trace() and get_weak_letters() return clean, structured metrics (0.0 to 1.0 scores and explicit weakness classifications like "direction" vs "precision"), allowing the agent to reason instantly. Rendering Dynamic Guidance on Canvas: Translating the agent's high-level command (generate_exercise('D', 'direction')) into animated, pulsating SVG/Canvas arrows that follow the exact path of each letter required fine-tuning my character vector templates. Accomplishments that we're proud of A Real Closed-Loop Web Agent: Successfully building an AI experience where the agent doesn't just answer questions in a sidebar, but actively manipulates the application state and visuals to solve an educational challenge. Zero-Dependency Performance: Running the entire application (analysis, rendering, speech, tools) smoothly on client-side Vanilla JS with instant load times. The WebMCP Inspector & 1-Click Scenario: Enabling judges and testers to see the agent reasoning in real time and test the entire workflow with a single click. What we learned The sheer power of WebMCP: Moving away from DOM scraping and screenshot interpretation towards clean, declarative web tools is a paradigm shift for web development. It makes AI agents hundreds of times faster, deterministic, and much more resilient. How to bridge early-childhood pedagogy with autonomous agent decision-making. What's next for TRACEAI — AI Handwriting Coach powered by WebMCP Cursive Writing Support: Extending my vector stroke engine to support connected cursive handwriting and full words. Early Dysgraphia & Motor-Skill Insights: Providing anonymized progress reports that parents and educators can share with pediatric specialists to identify fine-motor coordination difficulties early. Multi-Child Classroom Dashboard: Enabling a teacher's AI copilot to monitor an entire classroom's practice sessions simultaneously and flag who needs personal attention. title: Generative Learning
pitch: Generate the learning. Not the canvas. A professional learning surface for AI tutors to personalize the lesson, pace, and guidance for each learner - step by step, on a shared interactive canvas.
about_excerpt: Generate the learning. Not the canvas. A professional learning surface for AI tutors to personalize the lesson, pace, and guidance for each learner - step by step, on a shared interactive canvas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Chess Generative Learning GIF Triangles Generative Learning Chess Learning Professional Canvas Triangles Learning Professional Canvas Inspiration In 2021, I filed a patent for a web interaction layer where websites declare supported actions so external agents (bots) can interact with them without relying on the visual UI. At the time, I was focused on automation where the browser could effectively stay in the background . The agent could perform actions without the user needing to watch every step. WebMCP made me revisit the same idea from the opposite direction: What happens when the visual interface is not something to bypass, but something the human and AI need to share? Many web tasks can happen while the page is hidden or barely looked at - purchasing, form filling, data entry, even some document operations. But visual learning is different. You cannot meaningfully learn chess, manipulate a triangle, inspect a circuit, or reason about spatial relationships while the learning surface is hidden. The learner needs to see it, act on it, and understand what changes. So I specifically looked for learning domains where the visible interface is essential to the task itself . AI can generate great explanations, diagrams, and canvases - but learning often needs a professional environment that stays in place . That led me to ask: What if AI generated the lesson, not the learning surface? I built persistent, domain-specific learning surfaces where the learner and AI tutor can see, act, and continue together. What it does The learner chooses what to learn and how to learn it . The AI teaches inside the existing surface: demonstrating, annotating, asking questions, reacting to learner actions, and guiding the lesson step by step. Chess and an interactive triangle-learning surface are two working examples of the same pattern. Build the learning surface once. Personalize the lesson endlessly. How I built it Each surface exposes structured WebMCP tools for generating lessons, updating the learning state, and acting on the environment. Chess and triangle learning expose different domain actions, but use the same collaboration loop: generate a lesson, demo, or quiz → read state → demonstrate → learner acts → read change → continue The agent works through explicit tools instead of scraping or rebuilding the UI. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was the missing reverse communication path from the learning surface back to the chat . A tutor might ask: “What move would you play to checkmate in one move?” The learner should make the move directly on the board, and the surface should report that action back to the agent so the lesson can continue naturally. Today, that loop is incomplete. The AI cannot truly wait for a learner action and automatically resume when the surface reports it. For the prototype, I generate a prompt describing the learner’s action and ask the user to send it back to chat manually. What’s missing is a native: AI asks → learner acts → surface reports → AI continues That bidirectional communication would make the tutoring flow much more natural. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built two different learning domains - chess and triangle learning - using the same WebMCP pattern. More importantly, the AI is not just automating an interface. It is teaching through it , while the learner works on the same live state. That turns WebMCP from an automation layer into a collaboration layer. What I learned The biggest lesson was: Generative learning does not require a generative interface. A stable, professional surface can actually give AI more useful freedom, because it provides reliable tools, shared state, and meaningful learner actions. I also learned that truly interactive tutoring needs more than tool calls. It needs bidirectional agent-surface communication so the learner can act directly in the environment and the AI can continue from that action. What's next for Generative Learning Chess and triangle learning prove the pattern. The same idea could apply anywhere learning needs a shared interactive environment - circuits, chemistry, maps, music, and more. These are examples of the broader pattern, not announced products. Longer term, the same surfaces could also support teacher-defined learning goals and measurable outcomes while preserving a fully personalized learning path. title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. video_transcript_excerpt: Photo editors expect you to know exactly what saturation, tint, and exposure curves mean. Most people do not. Estro completely changes this dynamic. It is a powerful photo editor that runs entirely in your browser and actually explains itself. You open a project and tell the agent exactly what you want to achieve. Here we ask it to make a cold street photo look like a golden hour shot. We also tell it to explain every control it touches. You just talk to it like a normal person. The agent immediately gets to work. It moves the sliders for you. Every single edit drops a visible card right on the screen. The card names the specific control, shows the exact numerical value, and explains what the term means in plain English. Here we ask the agent to simply point out the contrast slider without making any changes to the photo. The agent immediately highlights the exact slider in the right panel. You can also ask it to perform an audit of the image. We ask if any of our recent changes ruined the fine details in the photo. The agent reads the live histogram and tells you exactly what is happening with your pixels. You click the split view to see the final result in comparison. 56 tools, one unified command system, and zero servers. Everything happens locally on your machine. Your photos always stay yours.

title: Holy tool for uni students
pitch: WebMCP-powered course planning: build a conflict-free schedule, balance your workload, and track graduation requirements all through conversation, with enrollment always under your control.
about_excerpt: WebMCP-powered course planning: build a conflict-free schedule, balance your workload, and track graduation requirements all through conversation, with enrollment always under your control. Like Comment Story Updates Check your degree audit Plan schedule for semester Adjust your schedule with ease Inspiration Let's be honest, we all have gone through the time of choosing courses for school. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of courses available in my school - Bucknell University. Scrolling through tabs just to find 4-5 courses that suit us must feel like hell. Therefore, I created this holy tool to assist us in choosing the best courses for us. What it does Imagine you're a robot that can actually click buttons on a student's screen instead of just yapping about what buttons they should click. That's basically what this is. You type something like: "Plan my next semester: max 15 credits, nothing before 10am, prioritize AI and cybersecurity" and the AI reads your actual transcript, cross-checks prerequisites, confirms there are seats open, and builds you a conflict-free draft schedule. No tabs, no spreadsheets, no prayers to the registration gods. And because professors matter (let's be real), you can tell it "I hate CS320, it's brutal" and instead of rebuilding the whole thing from scratch like some kind of masochist, it just swaps that one course for alternatives and tells you the trade-offs. The whole app is visible as you talk: a course catalog you can filter, a weekly timetable that shows both your actual schedule (solid blocks) and proposed courses, a transcript, and a degree audit that tells you exactly what you're missing before graduation. Draft courses wear a big blue banner that screams no seats held, you haven't committed to anything so you never accidentally think you're registered when you're not. How I built it JavaScript. All of it. HTML for the page, CSS so it doesn't look like a 1997 geocities site, and the brain of the thing lives in a standalone file so it could be tested without mocking the entire DOM. Then I wired up 13 tools via WebMCP: search courses, check if you're eligible, build a schedule, swap one course, explain what a course does to your graduation timeline, handle registrations, join waitlists. The AI calls these tools; the tools update the page you're looking at; you see the results instantly and decide whether to confirm or bail. It all runs in the browser. No backend. No database. Just sample student data and a 22-course Bucknell catalog baked into the JavaScript, so the demo works anywhere without authentication headaches. I use Vercel to upload it and push my project on Github. Challenges I ran into The Draft vs. Registered blurry line : A timetable showing five proposed courses looks exactly like a registered schedule if you're not careful. I solved this by slapping a warning banner on drafts ("no seats held"), color-coding the timetable blocks differently (solid orange = real, dashed blue = proposed), and keeping separate credit counters ("6 of 15 registered · 9 in draft"). Students should never have to guess. Small changes breaking the whole plan : Traditional schedulers rebuild everything when you tweak one thing. That's sucks .So I built a "replace one course" tool that keeps the other four courses exactly as they are, shows you alternatives ranked by how well they fit your goals, and explains the specific trade-offs. "This swap is 8 hours lighter per week but drops a team project from the term." That's useful. Credits lie : "15 credits" sounds light until you realize it's 52 hours a week of work if you hit CS320 (the hardest course I seeded). So every course now carries a weekly workload estimate, a project count, and a workload band (light / moderate / heavy). Proposing a schedule without showing this is just being mean to the student. Accomplishments that I am proud of I built an end-to-end workflow where a student and an AI do something neither could alone: review degree progress, propose a schedule that respects constraints and interests, explore alternatives, swap one course intelligently, then register after the student clicks a confirmation button. The AI doesn't fake-click anything. Instead, it calls structured tools that update the real page. I also made recommendations actually useful by connecting three things that usually live in separate tabs: scheduling, workload, and graduation requirements. When the AI suggests a course, it tells you why (elective vs. required), how much time it costs, and what graduation requirement it closes. And I made the invisible visible. There's an activity log timestamping every action and crediting it to either the student or the advisor. You always know who did what and when. What I learned Academic advice is complicated : Just matching a student's interests to course descriptions is useless. You need to fold in prerequisites, seat availability, time conflicts, workload, degree requirements, and what happens downstream if you defer a course. A good recommendation juggles all of these at once. State must be bulletproof : Students hate ambiguity. "Is this registered or just a proposal?" "Does deferring this course block me next term?" These questions need crystal-clear answers, baked into the UI, not buried in a chatbot transcript. I learned this the hard way when I first tested with the page. Structured tools > vague chat : A chatbot can describe what a student should do. WebMCP tools let an AI actually do it —and because the tools are typed and validate input, the AI is less likely to hallucinate or contradict itself. Honesty about limits : Workload estimates are imperfect. Graduation timelines are projections. Our UI shows these as estimates and projections, not guarantees. If you're going to let an AI influence a student's academic path, you have to be clear about what you actually know. What's next Ideally, I'd swap a course and lock in its replacement as a single transaction, so you're never in limbo holding a draft. I'd also validate workload estimates against historical student feedback (if a university had that data). Multi-semester planning would help students see the full path to graduation, not just the next term. Longer term, real integration with a university's enrollment system (with proper auth, privacy safeguards, and audit trails) would make this a genuine advising tool instead of a demo. Right now, this is a prototype with sample data. title: ClauseProof
pitch: Unit tests for contract language. A browser agent stages competing clause readings and repairs a fix through WebMCP tools; the page runs the tests; a person decides.
about_excerpt: Unit tests for contract language. A browser agent stages competing clause readings and repairs a fix through WebMCP tools; the page runs the tests; a person decides. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Contract clauses survive review because both sides read the same words with different pictures in their heads. The difference only shows up after a bad event, when it turns into termination rights, credits, or months of fees. Here is the clause family ClauseProof starts with. A SaaS agreement promises 99.5% monthly uptime, says service credits are the customer's "sole and exclusive remedy," and separately lets either party terminate for an uncured material breach. Now uptime is 98.7% in January and 98.9% in February, the fee is $10,000 a month, eight months remain, and the failure is not cured after notice. One reasonable reading: the customer gets $2,000 in credits and still owes $80,000. Another reasonable reading: the customer gets the same $2,000 and can walk. Nobody noticed at signing. What ClauseProof does ClauseProof runs the clause instead of arguing about it. On one page: A browser agent, working through WebMCP tools the page registers, reads the three clauses and stages two clause-cited readings with constrained semantics: vendor-favorable and customer-favorable. The page executes both readings against the same facts and shows the two commercial futures side by side. In the demo case they are $80,000 apart. Then a what-if: "what if March also missed?" The agent changes the facts through a tool and the page re-runs both readings on the new facts. Facts can change only before the lock. The person locks what the clause should mean: two misses within six months, written notice, a ten-day cure, termination without penalty, credits preserved. This step has no tool. It is person-only, and the agent's tool list changes when it happens. The agent proposes a structured rule. The page compiles the rule into exact clause wording, parses the wording back into a rule, checks that they agree, and runs six outcome examples plus eight altered-rule challenges (mutation tests for the clause boundary). If the candidate is wrong, the page says exactly why. In the walkthrough the agent first tries a three-miss rule: 5 of 6 outcome tests pass, 7 of 8 altered rules are caught, the failing test reports that termination was expected after two misses but the candidate gave none, and the surviving altered rule is "two misses instead of three." The agent repairs only that field and retests: 6 of 6, 8 of 8. The page marks the candidate eligible. The agent still cannot accept. The person accepts. The contract advances to revision 1 and the proof ledger keeps the failed candidate, the counterexample, the repair, the pass, and the acceptance, each attributed to who actually did it. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The agent has to act on live page state inside a governed workflow, not just talk about a document. WebMCP is what makes that safe and useful: Typed actions with live identifiers. Every tool call carries the page's current revision and the IDs returned by earlier steps. A stale revision, a wrong outcome-lock ID, an invented clause, or two readings that agree all fail with a stable error code and one recovery action. The agent cannot drift from what the page actually shows. Structured input, deterministic execution. The agent supplies semantics; the page calculates money, dates, rolling windows, and test results. Input schemas are strict Zod objects compiled to JSON Schema with plain-English descriptions, so a natural prompt like "stage a vendor-favorable and a customer-favorable reading" is enough. Phase-aware registration. The page registers only the tools that make sense in the current phase and revokes the others through the registration AbortSignal . The authority panel on the page renders the same phase-to-tool map the registry enforces, so you can watch the agent's powers change. Machine-readable failure. A failed verification returns the exact failing test and the surviving altered rule in the tool result. That is what turns "try again" into a real repair. Enforced human authority. Lock, accept, and reset are not tools. The WebMCP layer receives a frozen port with no such methods, actor identity is never accepted as input, and the audit trail cannot record an agent action as a person's. What people and agents can do together now Before: a person reads a clause, maybe asks a chatbot whether it "looks safe," and gets prose back. The disagreement stays hidden until the bad month. Now: the agent does the tedious, structured part (stage the competing readings, propose the rule, read the counterexample, repair) inside the page; the page does the part software should own (execute the readings, generate the wording, run the tests); and the person does the two things only a person should do (say what the clause is supposed to mean, and accept the wording that proved it). The whole exchange is recorded with provenance. How WebMCP is implemented Six tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext accepted for earlier Chrome previews): inspect_contract_case , stage_interpretations , run_contract_crash_test , set_scenario_facts , propose_clarifying_redline , verify_contract_tests . One AbortController per registration generation; a store subscription re-registers the phase's tool set on every state change. ?toolMode=static registers all six for agents that only read tools at load. Strict Zod schemas are the single source of truth. JSON Schema is generated from them with additionalProperties: false , min and max bounds, enums for semantic choices, and field descriptions. Tool results are small JSON objects: ok , data , and one next action when agent work remains. Failures carry a stable code, the current revision, and a recovery action. No stack traces. Annotations mark the read tool readOnlyHint: true and its contract text untrustedContentHint: true . The WebMCP layer imports only a restricted agent port. An architecture check fails the build if it ever imports a human-capable surface. Twelve Playwright tests drive the real registered tools through a fake document.modelContext , including the failed-candidate-to-repair path and the tool list revoking on reset. Built with TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Zod 4, Vitest, Playwright, GitHub Pages. No backend, no external AI API, no upload, no OCR. Limits ClauseProof supports one synthetic SaaS agreement, one adverse scenario, one constrained reading vocabulary, and one canonical clarification grammar. A passing run proves that the generated clause and the structured rule agree and that the rule satisfies the modeled examples and boundaries for this case. It is not formal verification, not arbitrary contract analysis, and not legal advice. The pattern generalizes to any clause with numbers in it (cure periods, notice windows, caps, renewal terms); this is the first instance. Hackathon-period work The repository's history begins August 28, 2026, after the August 25 start of the submission period. The domain engine, the governed workflow, the UI, the WebMCP layer, the release gates, and the adversarial hardening were all built during the challenge. docs/CHANGELOG_HACKATHON.md maps the work to dated commits. video_transcript_excerpt: Same contract, same bad month, $80,000 apart. That is what one clause with two reasonable readings costs, and nobody sees it until the dispute. Clause proof runs the clause first. One prompt through WebMCP. The agent reads the clauses, stages a vendor favorable and a customer favorable reading, and runs both. The page does the math. $2,000 in credits either way. But one reading leaves 80,000 in fees on the table and the other lets the customer walk. Before deciding anything, a what if what if March also misses. The agent changes the facts through a tool. The page reruns both readings and the gap moves. Nothing has been decided yet. Now the part that stays human. I decide what this clause should mean. Two misses in 6 months. 10-day cure, credits preserved. There is no tool for this, and the agents tool list changes the moment I lock it. I ask the agent to try a stricter rule first. Three misses. It sends a structured rule, not pros. The page compiles it into real clause wording, parses that wording back, and runs six outcome tests and eight altered drool challenges. Five of six, seven of eight. And the failing test says exactly why. After two misses, termination was expected and the three miss rule gave none. The agent reads the counter example and repairs only the occurrence count. Six of six, eight of eight eligible, not accepted because the agent cannot accept. I accept. Revision one. The ledger keeps the whole story. The wrong candidate, the failing test, the repair, the pass, and my acceptance, each attributed to whoever actually did it. Six typed webmc tools registered per phase, strict schemas and no tool for the decisions. One synthetic case today, not legal advice. The pattern is the point. Agents propose and repair. The page proves, people decide.

title: FlowPulse
pitch: A WebMCP-powered workflow studio where agents fill, validate, and prepare complex forms for human review.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered workflow studio where agents fill, validate, and prepare complex forms for human review.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Completed workflow review: a person checks grouped answers before creating a local receipt. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 FlowPulse WebMCP architecture: agents update a visible workflow while humans retain final confirmation. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 React, TypeScript, WebMCP, Netlify, and Playwright: five tested tools with visible UI effects. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Employee provisioning journey: from fragmented requests to accountable human review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Required-field validation visibly blocks incomplete workflow progress. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Completed workflow review: a person checks grouped answers before creating a local receipt. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 FlowPulse WebMCP architecture: agents update a visible workflow while humans retain final confirmation. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 React, TypeScript, WebMCP, Netlify, and Playwright: five tested tools with visible UI effects. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Employee provisioning journey: from fragmented requests to accountable human review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Required-field validation visibly blocks incomplete workflow progress. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Completed workflow review: a person checks grouped answers before creating a local receipt. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 What it does 

 FlowPulse is a WebMCP-powered workflow studio for forms that are usually too multi-step, contextual, or error-prone to complete quickly. It starts with a practical employee tech-and-workspace provisioning flow, alongside residential lease, B2B vendor onboarding, and a clearly labelled synthetic travel-visa sandbox. 

 A person stays in control: an agent can inspect the current form, fill known synthetic values, validate required information, switch workflows, and prepare the final review. The person sees every change in the visible UI and completes the final receipt action themselves. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Traditional form automation is opaque: it scrapes a page or runs beside it, leaving people unsure what changed. FlowPulse exposes five browser-native, goal-shaped WebMCP tools: 

 
 getFormSchema inspects the active workflow, required fields, current values, and step. 
 fillFormFields updates only fields belonging to the active form, visibly in the UI. 
 validateForm returns missing required fields and marks problems on the form. 
 switchTemplate changes the workflow, form, and contextual Copilot guidance together. 
 submitWorkflow validates and opens the review screen; it deliberately stops before final human confirmation. 
 

 This lets people and agents work in the same visible workflow instead of treating the browser as a fragile screen-scraping surface. 

 Experience and safety 

 The app is responsive at mobile, tablet, and desktop sizes. On smaller screens, workflow selection and Copilot controls become on-demand drawers rather than competing fixed sidebars. Required fields have inline validation, progress is explicit, and the review screen groups answers by step before a local receipt is created. 

 The travel-visa flow is explicitly a synthetic-data sandbox. The app does not claim persistent audit storage or automatic final submission. 

 Implementation 

 FlowPulse is a React + TypeScript + Vite application, deployed on Netlify. WebMCP tools are defined with @nekuda/webmcp-sdk and registered with lifecycle cleanup. Automated Playwright tests cover responsive layouts, validation, full review flow, template switching, and registration/invocation of all five tools with visible UI effects.

title: Companion Sketch
pitch: Skribbl.io or Pictionary, but with all your friends and all their AI agents 🤖
about_excerpt: Skribbl.io or Pictionary, but with all your friends and all their AI agents 🤖 Like 1 Comment Story Updates OWL?! Inspiration Companion Sketch started with a simple question: what would a game look like if an AI was not just generating content for a human, but was actually another player? Most AI games treat AI as a tool, narrator, or content generator. We wanted to experiment with something more direct: a shared game where a human and ChatGPT could draw, guess, chat, and participate in the same gameplay loop. Drawing games felt like the perfect test because they depend on creativity, interpretation, imperfect communication, and humor. Those interactions become much more interesting when humans and AI share the same canvas. What it does Companion Sketch is a real-time multiplayer drawing and guessing game for humans and AI agents. A human creates or joins a room, then ChatGPT can join the same visible game through native WebMCP Website Tools. Players take turns choosing secret prompts, drawing them, and guessing what other players are creating. The current version includes: Real-time drawing and game synchronization through Socket.IO Shared multiplayer rooms with clear, copyable room codes Human and AI players participating as equal game participants Three private candidate words for every drawing turn Native WebMCP Website Tools for ChatGPT gameplay A REST API fallback for other agents and testing Touch-friendly mobile drawing with pointer support A compact drawing toolbar with expandable tool, brush-size, and color palettes A mobile-first dark glass-style interface Background and reload recovery that preserves the current room, round, timer, score, chat, and canvas Graceful fallback when WebMCP is unavailable The result is a social game where the interesting part is not simply “AI-generated art,” but what happens when humans and AI try to understand each other’s drawings. How ChatGPT plays through WebMCP The page registers eight top-level imperative Website Tools using document.modelContext.registerTool: companion_sketch_status — Read the current viewer-safe game state companion_sketch_join — Join the visible room as the ChatGPT companion companion_sketch_pick_word — Choose a drawing prompt companion_sketch_draw_paths — Submit bounded normalized drawing paths companion_sketch_clear_canvas — Clear the canvas when authorized companion_sketch_guess — Submit a guess companion_sketch_chat — Send a chat message companion_sketch_leave — Leave the room and invalidate the session ChatGPT does not need to manually manage a bearer token. The page adapter keeps the agent session inside tab-scoped storage and sends only the structured action required by each tool. Drawing requests are intentionally bounded. The agent submits normalized polylines instead of arbitrary canvas commands, and the server validates colors, sizes, coordinates, and stroke counts before accepting them. The tools are registered only in the top-level page, matching the current WebMCP integration requirements. The same game still works normally for human players in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How we built it We built Companion Sketch from scratch as a web application. The backend uses Express for the application server and Socket.IO for realtime communication. Socket.IO handles room membership, drawing updates, chat, readiness, turn changes, timers, and game-state broadcasts. The game engine is server-authoritative. It controls: Player identities and room membership Turn order and timers Private drawing words Stroke validation Guess scoring AI guess windows Canvas clearing permissions Human reconnect and resume behavior The WebMCP layer sits on top of the same game services as the REST API, so ChatGPT and human players follow the same rules instead of using a separate simulation. On the frontend, we rebuilt the interface around mobile play. Room codes are prominent and tap-to-copy. The drawing controls are now a small icon rail: one button for the current tool, one for brush size, one for color, and one for clearing. Each control expands into an overlay palette so the canvas keeps as much space as possible. Human sessions use a private resume token stored by the page. If a phone is backgrounded, suspended, or reloaded, the player can reconnect to the same room and continue from the current game state. The game is deployed over HTTPS so it can be opened directly in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and tested as a real WebMCP experience. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was supporting two very different types of players. Humans interact visually through a touchscreen and canvas, while an AI agent needs structured state and explicit actions. We had to design one gameplay system that could support both without making the AI feel like an external controller. WebMCP introduced another challenge. The tools had to be registered in the correct top-level document, use strict input schemas, expose only safe actions, and remain useful when the browser does not support the protocol. Realtime drawing also created synchronization problems. A canvas produces many rapidly changing points, so we had to keep drawing responsive while preventing duplicate strokes, invalid coordinates, oversized requests, and unauthorized actions. Privacy was important as well. The active drawer can see the selected word, but other players and agents receive viewer-safe state. The server never exposes a private drawing prompt to someone who should be guessing. Mobile playtesting exposed additional issues. Drawing with a finger behaves differently from drawing with a mouse, and mobile browsers may pause or reload tabs when they are placed in the background. We added pointer handling, canvas fitting, reconnect logic, and state restoration to make those interruptions recoverable. We also redesigned the toolbar after testing revealed that a full row of controls consumed too much canvas space. The new expandable palettes keep the controls available without sacrificing the drawing area. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The thing we’re most proud of is that Companion Sketch became a real playable human-and-AI game rather than just an AI concept demo. We successfully built: A complete realtime drawing and guessing loop Multiplayer rooms with human and AI identities A functioning WebMCP integration with eight native Website Tools An AI player that can join, choose words, draw, guess, chat, and leave Shared server-authoritative state between the human UI, WebMCP, and REST fallback Private word handling and validated drawing actions A responsive mobile interface with a large canvas and compact controls Recovery from phone backgrounding and page reloads A deployed HTTPS version that can be played from ChatGPT’s browser Automated coverage for state, authorization, privacy, WebMCP registration, and reconnect behavior We also verified the game on a phone-sized 390×844 layout and tested the deployed WebMCP page directly. Seeing people play the game has been especially rewarding. Early playtesters created surprisingly strange drawings, guessed in unexpected ways, and made it clear that the most interesting part of the project is the shared interaction between human creativity and AI interpretation.
