title: Plasma-trace
pitch: One physics model, two operators. A human drags sliders; an AI agent calls WebMCP tools. Both hit the same functions and the same chart -a shared instrument for sub-centimetre orbital debris detection
about_excerpt:
One physics model, two operators. A human drags sliders; an AI agent calls WebMCP tools. Both hit the same functions and the same chart -a shared instrument for sub-centimetre orbital debris detection
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sub-centimetre orbital debris is a genuinely unsolved problem. Objects
this small are difficult to track with radar or optical systems, yet at
orbital velocities they carry enough energy to damage spacecraft. 

 NASA-funded research has been exploring an indirect approach: a charged
fragment moving through ionospheric plasma can excite nonlinear waves —
solitons — that might be detectable even when the object itself is not.
The physics comes from Sen et al. (2015) on forced-KdV soliton excitation
by charged orbital debris, developed further in Christine Hartzell's NASA
NIAC work at the University of Maryland. 

 I did not invent that science, and this project does not claim to. What
interested me was a different question: exploring a model like this means
sweeping parameters — size, velocity, altitude, day/night ionosphere —
and that is exactly the kind of tedious, click-heavy loop where a human
and an agent should be able to work on the same instrument instead of in
separate tools. 

 What it does: 

 Plasma-trace is a browser-based forward model for debris detectability.
Set a fragment's size, relative speed, and altitude, pick a daytime or
night-time ionosphere, and it returns a detectability score plus a
breakdown across eight altitude bins. 

 The point is that there are two ways to drive it, and they are the same
instrument: 

 
 A person drags sliders and watches the chart redraw. 
 An AI agent calls WebMCP tools registered on the page — and the
sliders and chart move exactly as if a person had dragged them. 
 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit: 

 Scientific parameter exploration is a bad fit for the usual ways agents
interact with web pages. Screen-scraping a slider is fragile and
lossy: an agent reading "38/100" off the DOM has a rendered string, not
a result it can reason over. 

 WebMCP changes the contract. The page exposes typed tools with schemas,
so the agent calls a function and gets structured data back, while the
human sees the same state update visually. Neither operator is
second-class. That is what makes this feel like a shared instrument
rather than an agent puppeting a UI built for someone else. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult before: 

 The clearest example is sweep_altitude . A person exploring where a
5 mm fragment is most detectable has to drag the altitude slider through
eight positions and read the chart each time. An agent runs the whole
sweep in one call and returns the best altitude with the full profile —
while the human watches the same chart update. 

 Before WebMCP, that meant either building a separate API (and now the
human and agent are using different systems that can drift apart) or
having the agent scrape the UI (fragile, and it gets strings instead of
data). Here there is exactly one code path. 

 explain_regime is the inverse case: the agent asks the instrument to
explain why detectability peaks where it does, so the reasoning comes
from the page's own model rather than the language model's guess. 

 How I built it: 

 One self-contained index.html — no backend, no database, no build
step. Chart.js from a CDN is the only dependency. 

 
 runForwardModel() computes detectability from an altitude-dependent
plasma density term, a size factor, and a speed factor. 
 The sliders call that function directly. 
 Four tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() :
 set_debris_params , run_forward_model , sweep_altitude , and
 explain_regime . Each one calls the same functions the sliders call
and updates the same chart. There is no parallel agent code path —
that constraint is the whole design. 
 The page feature-detects document.modelContext and degrades
gracefully: in a non-WebMCP browser it shows a banner explaining how
to enable it, and every slider still works. 
 

 Challenges: 

 The WebMCP API is new enough that several third-party guides describe it
incorrectly — a number of them say navigator.modelContext when the
spec defines document.modelContext . Writing that line from memory or
from a blog post would have produced a page that looks completely normal
and silently registers nothing. I sourced the signature from the W3C
explainer and cross-checked it against the spec IDL. 

 A second one: executeTool takes its arguments as a JSON string, not an
object. Passing an object returns "Failed to parse input arguments" with
no further detail. Worth knowing if you are testing via
 navigator.modelContextTesting in the console. 

 What's real, and what isn't 

 I would rather be precise about this than oversell it. 

 Real: the forward model runs in-page, the WebMCP registration is
functional, the deploy is live, and agent tool calls demonstrably move
the same sliders and chart a person uses. 

 Simplified: the ionosphere data is hardcoded. The model uses
closed-form terms, not a plasma solver. Nothing here is validated
against observations. 

 Not claimed: this does not detect debris. It is not an early-warning
system — solitons propagate near the ion-acoustic speed while debris
moves far faster, so this is a mapping and survey concept, not a
collision alarm. The science is attributed to published research. 

 The contribution I am putting forward is the interaction pattern: a
scientific instrument that a human and an agent operate through one
shared set of functions. 

 What's next 

 Real ionosphere data (IRI or GNSS TEC) instead of hardcoded values, a
trained ML model for the inverse problem — recovering fragment
properties from an observed signature, which is not analytically
solvable and is exactly what the NIAC team is working on — and
multi-sensor localisation.

title: Cutlet
pitch: Small cuts, served fresh. A browser rough-cut editor where the agent reads the transcript, you judge the footage, and the WebMCP tools keep you editing the same visible clip.
about_excerpt: Small cuts, served fresh. A browser rough-cut editor where the agent reads the transcript, you judge the footage, and the WebMCP tools keep you editing the same visible clip. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Every AI video clipper works the same way: upload, wait, receive highlights, then fix them somewhere else. The model does the judging and the editing, and you get whichever boundaries it computed. I wanted the opposite division of labour. An agent is good at reading a transcript and saying which stretches stand on their own. A human is good at watching the footage and feeling where a cut lands. WebMCP made it possible to put both in the same page, editing the same clip, with the browser keeping both honest about who changed what. A cutlet is a small cut. Small cuts, served fresh. What it does Cutlet is a rough-cut editor for spoken video. It is not a clip finder; no model scores your footage. The page holds the video, a transcript broken into sentences with stable ids, and a rail of clips. The agent reaches all of it through ten WebMCP tools registered on the top-level document. The core loop is anchor and expand : You click the sentence that must survive. The agent reads a window around it and proposes a clip as a range of sentence ids, s0009–s0013 , never floating timestamps. The player runs exactly that range and stops. You drop a line or move an edge. The clip's revision bumps. The agent's next write carries the revision it last saw. Yours is newer, so the write is refused with the real revision in the error. It calls get_editor_state and revises from your edit, not over it. cut_clip c2 keep s0008,s0010,s0011,s0013 → revision 2, 3 pieces, 37s ↓ human drops s0011 in the transcript → revision 5 cut_clip c2 expectedRevision 4 → REFUSED "it is now 5" get_editor_state → sees the real cut The active clip is coloured by who last touched it: blue while it is the agent's proposal, amber the moment you edit it, in the transcript, the timeline and the card. Beyond the loop: "find the best clips in this" makes the agent skim the whole transcript and create one clip per moment, each with a title and a reason. "Cut this to forty seconds" turns a clip into several pieces with gaps, and playback jumps the gaps. Every dropped sentence stays visible, struck through, with a control to put it back. When the recogniser missed a full stop, you select the words you want and make them their own sentence with their own id, so a boundary you can point at becomes a boundary the agent can name. The agent can split too. The agent gets every cut twice: the source transcript, and the sequence as it plays , with each gap marked by what was dropped and how long it ran. That is how it catches a dangling "its conquest" whose antecedent left with the cut. Export re-encodes each piece in the tab with ffmpeg.wasm, so boundaries are frame-accurate rather than keyframe-snapped, joins them, and writes an .srt rebased across the cut. Your video never leaves the tab. The transcript windows the tools return are shared with the agent; nothing else is. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, CSS Modules. No backend, no UI library, no state library. 45 Node tests run directly against the TypeScript, covering parsing, sentence splitting, selection, reordering and tool registration. Transcript pipeline. Word-level JSON is primary; Whisper, Deepgram and ElevenLabs Scribe all parse, with SRT and VTT as coarse fallbacks. Sentence splitting handles abbreviations, initials, rhetorical pauses and a clause backoff at the length ceiling. Preview is the native <video> element, with the range boundary enforced on requestAnimationFrame , because timeupdate fires at about 4 Hz and visibly overshoots. Export is the single-thread @ffmpeg/core , lazy-loaded on first use. Single-thread means no SharedArrayBuffer , which means no COOP/COEP headers, which is why it deploys to plain static hosting. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool on the top-level document, with an AbortController for teardown. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . The page feature-detects the API and works fully without it; the header pill says whether tools are live, and clicking it lists them from the same table the registration reads, so the two cannot drift. Keyboard. The transcript is a listbox with one tab stop: arrows move the anchor, shift extends it, Enter plays, ⌘-click banks a range. Two recordings ship, both public domain and credited: Kennedy's "We choose to go to the Moon" at Rice, and the Apollo 11 crew interview. Transcripts were made locally; no keys ship in the client. Challenges I ran into WebMCP is one-directional. A page cannot call an agent. There is no "find clips" button because there cannot be one, so the empty state's job is to tell you what to ask. There used to be a lexical "rough pass" fallback for browsers without the API. I removed it: a heuristic dressed as judgement is worse than an empty rail that tells you what to ask. Ids stop being positional the moment you split. Renumbering after a split would silently repoint every later id at its neighbour, and a stale id that resolves to the wrong sentence is worse than one that fails to resolve. So the new half gets a fresh number and nothing after it moves. The agent kept overwriting the human's anchor. preview_clip used to set the selection, so an agent auditioning a range destroyed the very mark it was told to build around. Auditions now have their own state and render dashed, in the agent's blue, beside the anchor. Bugs only testing found. Number(undefined) is NaN , which is not nullish, so search_transcript returned empty context whenever the argument was omitted. A Whisper file's outer segments parsed as "words" and shadowed the real word timings. Deepgram's unpunctuated word beat punctuated_word and broke sentence splitting. Smooth scrollIntoView is silently ignored under reduced motion and in background tabs, so following the playhead just stopped; both now fall back to an instant jump. ffmpeg.wasm under a bundler. It has to be the ESM core, handed over as blob URLs. Otherwise the module worker cannot import it, and the dev server rewrites the path to a 404. What I learned The whole design fell out of one decision: every boundary is a sentence id , because an id means the same thing to both parties and a dragged pixel does not. That is why the sequence timeline is read-only, why sentence splitting exists, and why the revision check works at all. Optimistic concurrency turned out to be the right primitive for a human and an agent sharing one document. What's next More WebMCP hosts as they ship. Word-level trims inside a split. A library format other people can add recordings to without touching code. title: Decision Workspace
pitch: An adaptive WebMCP workspace where agents ask one question at a time, expose trade-offs, and help people reach transparent, grounded decisions.
about_excerpt: An adaptive WebMCP workspace where agents ask one question at a time, expose trade-offs, and help people reach transparent, grounded decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Important decisions often get buried in long AI chats. Criteria drift, assumptions disappear, and it becomes hard to tell why a recommendation changed. We wanted a shared workspace where a person can see the decision model evolve instead of receiving an opaque answer. What we built Decision Workspace is a local-first decision canvas for humans and browser agents. It keeps options, weighted criteria, score-and-confidence assessments, evidence, uncertainties, constraints, and recommendations in one inspectable state. The app exposes workflow-level WebMCP tools through navigator.modelContext. An agent can read the current workspace, ask one high-value interview question at a time, process an answer atomically, apply only grounded mappings, and adapt the next question to the new context. Free-text or uncertain answers remain explicitly unresolved instead of being forced into a score. Users can explore temporary what-if scenarios without changing saved state. When the model is sufficiently grounded, the agent can create a readiness-checked Decision Brief with the leading option, drivers, remaining unknowns, and next verification action. The person remains in control of the final decision. How we built it We built the UI with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The canonical decision store is shared by the UI and the WebMCP adapter, so tool writes are immediately visible in the page and persisted locally on the device. Revision-aware writes and explicit question lifecycle states keep the interview consistent and auditable. Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was designing a small, coherent tool surface instead of exposing every UI control. We learned that an agent workflow needs explicit state reads, deterministic mapping policies, uncertainty preservation, non-destructive scenarios, and readiness gating. WebMCP works best when the browser page is the shared source of truth and the agent changes it through semantic workflow actions. Built With local-first next.js react tailwind typescript vercel webmcp Try it out decision-workspace.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I originated the product concept and led the end-to-end build of Decision Workspace. I designed the decision model and adaptive one-question interview UX, directed the WebMCP workflow and tool contract, integrated the shared local-first store with the Next.js/TypeScript UI, and coordinated implementation and review. I deployed the Vercel demo, validated the browser workflow, created demo fixtures and documentation, and prepared the video and submission materials. AI coding tools supported implementation, but the product decisions, architecture, testing, and final integration were my responsibility. title: UMBRA DRIFT
pitch: A WebMCP shadow theatre where human state changes invalidate stale agent plans—safely, visibly, atomically.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP shadow theatre where human state changes invalidate stale agent plans—safely, visibly, atomically. Like Comment Story Updates A shared shadow theatre for one human and one browser agent, with Reality, Agent Belief, and Human Authority kept visibly separate. The recovery proof: one human override, one rejected stale write, zero partial mutations, and SAFE_RECOVERY. The human moves the lamp; the page rejects the stale plan with LAMP_SEQUENCE_CONFLICT and zero partial mutations. Inspiration Browser agents often act as if a page will wait for them. Real people keep dragging, editing, approving, and revoking. Most demos hide that race condition. We wanted to make it impossible to miss. What it does UMBRA DRIFT is a shared shadow theatre and a reproducible WebMCP recovery trial. A human controls the lamp and temporary capability grants. An external browser agent controls a four-piece rig through typed page tools. If the human moves the lamp after the agent observes the scene, the old plan is rejected atomically, without partial changes. The agent must read the live state again, measure the new projection, and recover. A successful run produces a visible dragon, a SAFE_RECOVERY verdict, and an exportable evidence capsule derived from the page's event ledger. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the coordination layer, not an integration added beside the experience. The state that matters is live, transient, and owned by the current browser tab. UMBRA exposes typed tools tied directly to that state instead of asking an agent to guess through pixels or DOM controls. The agent can observe, measure, request, plan, and commit. It cannot move the human-owned lamp, grant itself permission, bypass a revision check, or provide its own verdict. What becomes possible A person and an external agent can work in the same changing page while retaining separate authority. The human sees every capability request and can revoke control. The agent receives structured measurements and actionable conflicts. The site—not the model—enforces the boundary. How we built it UMBRA DRIFT uses the imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool, closed JSON Schemas, vanilla JavaScript, SVG, and CSS. Each mutation is checked against the observed lamp sequence, rig revision, and capability revision. Batched rig changes are all-or-nothing. A bounded deterministic event ledger produces the final recovery verdict. The UI exposes Reality, Agent Belief, and Human Authority as separate live states. The public app has no backend, account, API key, remote model call, database, telemetry, or external runtime dependency. The Apache-2.0 source includes the engine, tests, security contract, provenance, and reproduction instructions. Potential impact UMBRA is a playable reference pattern for editors, design tools, dashboards, workflow products, and other live applications where humans and agents share changing state. It makes five reusable ideas tangible: explicit ownership, scoped grants, optimistic concurrency, atomic mutation, and recovery after human intervention. Challenges and learnings The hardest problem was making the agent necessary without hiding the whole solution in a tool response. We learned that a tool schema is also an authority contract, and that structured failure is part of the human-agent experience, not merely an implementation detail. What's next Additional seeded trials, reusable conformance fixtures, CI adapters, and evaluations across different browser agents. title: PaperSpace
pitch: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI tools treat a research paper as a file to summarize or a block of text to retrieve from. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What becomes possible when a person and an agent share a paper's text and its spatial reading environment inside the browser? Reading a paper is rarely linear. A reader moves between related work, methods, equations, figures, experiments, and appendices while building a mental map of where each idea lives. Conventional PDF viewers collapse that map into one page at a time. Chat interfaces collapse it even further into excerpts detached from their visual source. PaperSpace preserves that spatial memory. Every page of every imported PDF is unfolded onto a borderless two-dimensional desk. Pages remain live, selectable PDF surfaces, but they can also be moved, grouped, searched, compared, and revisited as part of a persistent visual workspace. The browser is essential to this interaction. It owns the PDFs the person explicitly selected, the rendered pages, the local text index, the page geometry, the current camera, and the workspace the person is looking at. WebMCP gives an agent direct access to that authorized, browser-local state, keeping the person and the agent aligned on one live workspace. We built PaperSpace for the WebMCP Challenge as a focused, open-source, single-person tool centered on reading, understanding, and presenting research papers. PaperSpace is a shared spatial instrument where the person controls the source material and the agent helps organize attention inside the same visible world. What it does PaperSpace is a local-first spatial desk for research papers. When a person imports a PDF, PaperSpace unfolds every page from left to right and top to bottom using each page's real aspect ratio. Every page becomes an independently movable and resizable live sheet with selectable text. The complete paper stays visible as a spatial place with its reading order intact. PaperSpace extracts text and normalized page geometry locally with PDF.js. Each page becomes searchable as soon as its index is ready. A reusable inspect_workspace briefing reports exact coverage and compact sampled page excerpts, so an agent can prepare once and then read the broadest useful contiguous range in one call, including the whole paper when full context matters. Through WebMCP, the agent can search the available corpus, batch-read paper text, locate an exact passage, and guide the shared camera to that region. The camera first pulls back to establish spatial context, travels across the desk, and then lands with the source itself centered in a calm view with generous breathing room. The app exposes nine WebMCP tools: inspect_workspace returns reusable readiness, compact paper briefs, every page's world geometry, visual artifacts, sequences, and camera state. search_papers progressively searches indexed pages and returns page-level matches with normalized source regions plus exact coverage. read_paper_pages reads one contiguous range or a whole indexed paper in one call, with optional block geometry and an explicit caller-selected character cap. focus_region guides the camera to a search match or an explicit PDF region. arrange_papers reflows pages into reading-order grids and arranges complete paper groups. snapshot_paper_region places a source-linked raster crop from an exact PDF region. place_plot creates a safe declarative line plot from finite numeric data. place_image validates and places PNG, JPEG, and WebP visuals. present_sequence creates a captioned sequence of semantic paper regions and visual artifacts. PaperSpace also gives the agent an explicit delivery contract. When PaperSpace is available, substantive introductions, explanations, reviews, comparisons, and answers grounded across multiple paper regions are delivered through present_sequence . Chat provides concise supporting context, while a single grounded passage can use focus_region and simple localized Q&A remains lightweight. The sequence interaction is the heart of the product. Suppose one experiment is explained across related work, methods, and results on three distant pages. The agent can build a three-frame sequence with a caption for each view. When presentation begins, PaperSpace temporarily draws those original pages together beside their paper in first-appearance order. Quiet numbered source slots preserve the paper's topology throughout the presentation. The same original page can support several region frames through one staged page. Visual artifacts stay in their existing world positions. Exiting the sequence restores every moved page—including its position, size, and layer—and returns the camera to its exact entry state. Keeping a sequence saves its semantic frames; replaying it organizes pages again from their current positions and restores them again afterward. This enables requests such as: “Find where this experiment is motivated, defined, and evaluated, then organize those pages for me.” “Focus on the ablation equation and keep the surrounding paragraph in view.” “Read the method and results, plot the reported trend, and place it beside the source page.” “Present the three views in sequence and explain what changes between them.” Everything happens on the same desk the person can inspect and manipulate. Agent actions produce visible feedback, and temporary organization is transactionally isolated from the person's saved layout. Spatial mutation tools perform an atomic visual preflight inside the app. Standard calls place plots, images, source crops, and arrangements in clear areas. An agent can use force: true for an intentional dense layout, while media, schema, source-target, and security validation remain active. How we built it PaperSpace is a pure frontend SvelteKit and TypeScript application compiled as a static site for Cloudflare Pages. Browser storage and browser-authorized files provide the complete runtime state. The application is organized around four client-side layers: Svelte components render the infinite desk, unfolded PDF sheets, artifacts, search interface, frame editor, and presentation chrome. A single reactive workspace model owns paper metadata, per-page geometry, the camera, artifacts, semantic sequences, and all person- and agent-triggered state transitions. PDF.js renders pages and extracts text plus normalized block geometry in a same-origin Web Worker. IndexedDB stores validated workspace metadata, browser-authorized PDF copies, raster images, and saved semantic frames. The workspace schema stores a stable paper identity and page number for every PDF page, while position, size, and layer remain mutable world properties. PDF inspection records each page's true dimensions. A deterministic row-major layout uses a bounded column count to keep long papers spatially legible, and complete paper bounds are used to prevent different imports from overlapping. Every page has a DOM sheet so its identity remains stable in the world. PaperSpace activates detailed PDF canvas and text rendering near the viewport and above a useful zoom threshold, keeping long unfolded papers responsive. PDF rasterization uses a two-tier residency system. Every successfully rendered page retains a 288-pixel-wide aspect-preserving preview, while an LRU applies a 48-million-pixel budget to unpinned high-resolution page canvases. Pages in the strict viewport, the current focus target, and the active sequence frame are pinned and may temporarily exceed that budget. A compact preview preserves visual continuity as high-resolution canvases move through the working set. Raster canvases and selectable text layers have independent lifecycles, and a double-canvas pipeline swaps each completed bitmap into view atomically. Region targeting uses top-left normalized coordinates. The same semantic region can therefore be mapped through a page's current world geometry after the page has been moved or resized. Camera motion is handled by a cancellable controller with pull-back, travel, and landing keyframes, smooth center interpolation, logarithmic zoom interpolation, distance-aware timing, responsive caption-safe insets, and an immediate path for prefers-reduced-motion . Presentation staging is transactional. PaperSpace validates every frame before changing state, deduplicates source pages by first appearance, snapshots their exact geometry and the entry camera, stages the original pages, and exposes their source slots. Presentation mode pauses page manipulation, while persistence serializes the source geometry and entry camera to keep the durable desk unchanged. WebMCP is registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP adapter is intentionally thin: every tool calls the same workspace

Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. WebMCP lets that page expose its own capabilities to the agent. So, the answer appears as visible interaction on the shared desk with chat providing concise guidance. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. title: Callingly WebMCP - AI Sales Reps for Local Businesses
pitch: Need an emergency plumber? With the Callingly WebMCP script installed on their site, Joe’s Plumbing can have your agent call and get a plumber on the phone with you in seconds.
about_excerpt: Need an emergency plumber? With the Callingly WebMCP script installed on their site, Joe’s Plumbing can have your agent call and get a plumber on the phone with you in seconds. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every local business website has the same dead end: a visitor that needs immediate help, and a contact form that answers in "1-2 business days". The visitor wants to talk to someone, right now. An AI agent browsing that page hits the same wall. It can read the pricing and summarize the docs, but the moment its user says "I just need to talk to a human about this", the best it can do is fill in the form and hope. We build a phone system for a living, so we already had the missing piece - a live view of who is on shift and who is mid-call, and the ability to ring them. What we had no way to do was hand that to an agent standing on a customer's website. WebMCP is exactly that missing handle. What it does One script tag on any website registers two WebMCP tools: Tool What it does callingly-check-sales-availability Read-only. Is the business open right now, is a sales rep actually free (not on another call, past their cooldown), when is the next opening, and are call requests being accepted at all. callingly-request-sales-call Asks Callingly to call the visitor on the number the agent passes, and to connect them to the company. What happens on the second one is the part worth watching. Callingly's AI sales rep calls the visitor within seconds and starts qualifying - and at the same time it dials the company's reps in parallel. The moment a human picks up, the AI hands the caller over: "Ok great, let me get you on the line with one of our specialists." No hold music, no callback queue, and no dead air while the humans are being rung. So the agent can negotiate the timing of a human conversation : "They're free now, want me to get someone on the line?" / "Nobody until 9am Tuesday - shall I have them call you then?" That is not a lookup and it is not a booking link. It is a live check against who is on shift, who is mid-call, and what the team's calling hours are, turned into an offer the agent can actually make good on. A contact form cannot have that conversation. A scheduling widget offers slots without knowing whether anyone is at their desk. A chatbot can promise a callback with no authority to cause one. Concretely: a visitor asks an agent about a burst pipe at 8:47pm. Seconds later their phone rings, an AI rep is asking what's wrong, and by the time they've finished describing it a plumber is on the line - instead of a form submission someone reads on Monday. This is not a mock. The dialer, the routing rules, the availability logic and the reps are Callingly's production system, the same one paying customers use. The demo places real phone calls. How we built it webmcp.js is a dependency-free ES5 IIFE, 516 lines, no build step. It: registers both tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , falling back to navigator.modelContext for older origin-trial builds; polls for the model context rather than assuming one at load; unregisters through an AbortController , since WebMCP has no unregisterTool ; returns MCP content results and uses isError for refusals, so the agent gets a sentence it can act on rather than an exception; ships annotations: { readOnlyHint: true } on the availability tool and an inputSchema on both - required by ChatGPT's implementation; exposes the same functions on window.callingly , so ordinary page code, or an extension that doesn't speak WebMCP yet, can call them. Server-side is two public endpoints keyed by a webhook integration's slug: GET /embed/v1/{key}/availability and POST /embed/v1/{key}/calls . Accepted calls go into the same queued pipeline every webhook lead goes through - routing rules, de-duplication, then dialling - so the endpoint answers 202 rather than pretending to know which rep will pick up. Challenges we ran into Registration is not fire-and-forget. Agent browsers install document.modelContext at wildly different points. A context can arrive long after load, be replaced after you have already registered against it, or accept a tool and then reject it after your retry window has closed. Our own debug console lied to us - twice. It reported "no WebMCP in this browser" for every failure, including causes it had never checked. Then, once it did report honestly, it turned out ChatGPT hands out a model context whose registerTool cannot be replaced: our instrumentation's assignment failed silently, nothing reached our wrapper, and the console concluded registration had failed while both tools were in fact live. It now reads the snippet's own state instead of trusting its own instrumentation, and names which of four distinct causes it actually found. You have to convince ChatGPT to use the WebMCP when its on the site, it doesn't check for it automatically. We assume that in the future this will be the first thing that it checks for. Accomplishments that we're proud of The integration really is one line, and the before/after pair in the repo is a one-line diff - nothing else on the plumber's page changes. The contact form still promises 1-2 business days, because the human path is not what this replaces. It is wired to production, not a demo backend. And the failure paths got as much care as the happy one: outside calling hours the agent gets a real next-opening time and can offer it, rather than a dead end. What we learned WebMCP's is a very young technology and working with it is tricky the same way as working with any new tech, its not fully supported, people don't know what it is, even the AI agents themselves have to be coerced into using it. But it has a ton of potential, particularly in our space. In the future, AI agents will be doing the shopping around for consumers and our customers (the consumer businesses) will need to have AI sales reps of their own to deal with the AI agent shoppers. What's next More actions. The backend already schedules callbacks for a named time, so "have them call me at 9am Tuesday" is a natural third tool - right now the agent can only ask for a call now. Ship it to customers. The snippet is MIT and the endpoints are live, so any Callingly account can paste it on their own site today. title: Intent
pitch: Your agent shops. You call the shots. Intent turns human approval into an exact, expiring, one-use WebMCP capability enforced at checkout.
about_excerpt: Your agent shops. You call the shots. Intent turns human approval into an exact, expiring, one-use WebMCP capability enforced at checkout. Like Comment Story Updates One shared decision room The agent proposes. The person decides. Authority appears only when needed Checkout ready. Authority gone. Human judgment becomes agent authority Inspiration AI agents are already good at finding products. What bothered me was what happens after they find one. A person can approve a recommendation in chat, but that approval is still just another message. It does not clearly define the product, merchant, price, quantity, expiration time, or whether the action can be repeated. The agent is expected to interpret the person’s intent correctly and continue. I wanted to explore a different model. What if human approval became an actual capability that was narrow enough to inspect, short lived enough to trust, and enforced when the agent acted? That idea became Intent. What it does Intent is a shared decision room for human approved agent commerce. A WebMCP agent can: Turn a shopping request into a versioned purchase mandate. Search live offers from Shopify’s Global Catalog. Compare candidates against the person’s budget, destination, rating, and review requirements. Explain why each candidate passes or fails. Stage one eligible offer for review. The person sees the same mandate, evidence, and recommendation. They can change the rules or approve the exact staged offer. Before approval, the agent has no checkout capability. It is not hidden or disabled. It does not exist. When the person grants authority, Intent dynamically registers a temporary WebMCP tool frozen to the approved product, variant, merchant, price, currency, quantity, and mandate version. The waiting agent resumes automatically, uses the capability once, and receives a real merchant cart handoff. The server revalidates the live offer before returning it. The capability then disappears. Replay, broader scope, stale prices, unavailable products, and mandate violations are rejected. Intent never receives payment credentials and never submits payment. How we built it I built Intent with Codex as my primary development partner. The decision room is hosted on ChatGPT Sites and exposes five WebMCP tools. Four collaboration tools are available while the agent is on the page: intent_propose_purchase_mandate intent_compare_candidates intent_read_purchase_mandate intent_stage_candidate_for_approval The fifth tool, intent_open_approved_checkout_once , is registered only after human approval. Its input schema is constrained to the exact approved values. An AbortSignal removes it after use, expiry, cancellation, or failure. The schema makes the authority understandable to the client, but it is not the security boundary. A Cloudflare Worker validates every request. A Durable Object issues and atomically consumes the one use lease. Immediately before the handoff, the Worker resolves the exact Shopify variant again and checks availability, destination, price, identity, and the current mandate. Shopify Global Catalog and UCP provide live product data from multiple merchants and real merchant checkout URLs. No owned Shopify store, seeded catalog, or shopper account is required. We also built an optional Codex plugin that routes an ordinary physical product shopping request into Intent. Once the agent reaches the site, the page’s WebMCP tools take over. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making approval part of the agent’s current turn. Our first flow required the person to approve on the page and then return to chat to send another message. It worked technically, but it felt like operating a demo instead of using a product. We changed the staging tool into a bounded wait. The agent stages a proposal, pauses on the human decision, and resumes automatically when authority is granted. Live catalog data created another challenge. Merchant evidence is often incomplete or inconsistent. Intent had to separate two different questions: Does an offer satisfy deterministic transaction rules such as price, availability, destination, rating, and review count? Does the merchant description explicitly support the person’s product requirements? Missing evidence cannot quietly become a pass. Intent returns the evidence and numeric differences to the agent, marks merchant content as untrusted, and keeps the final proposal visible to the person. The final challenge was enforcing the capability outside the browser interface. A constrained schema communicates the approved scope, but a caller could still send a different request directly to the server. We therefore enforce the exact scope, expiration, replay protection, and live offer consistency again in the Worker and Durable Object. Accomplishments that we're proud of Intent is a complete live product rather than a simulated checkout demo. It searches real offers from real Shopify merchants. A person and an agent collaborate through the same versioned decision state. Checkout authority is genuinely absent before approval. The temporary capability appears after a human decision and disappears after one use. The server atomically rejects replay and broader authority. The approved offer is revalidated against live catalog data before handoff. Payment remains with the person and merchant. Refresh recovery restores useful decision context without restoring offers, proposals, leases, or authority. The repository passes 52 tests, including a 14 case boundary matrix and adversarial lifecycle checks. The moment I am proudest of is also the simplest. The person clicks once, the waiting agent continues automatically, and seconds later the capability is gone forever. What we learned WebMCP is most interesting when tools are not treated as a permanent menu of website functions. A tool can represent temporary authority. Its appearance can mean that a person approved something. Its disappearance can mean that the purpose ended. This makes capability discovery, shared page state, and lifecycle events part of the product experience rather than hidden implementation details. We also learned that human and agent collaboration works better when both participants have distinct responsibilities. The agent is good at searching, comparing, and organizing evidence. The person should own the rules and consequential decisions. Intent connects those roles without pretending either side can safely replace the other. Finally, we learned to separate what the agent can infer from what the system can enforce. Intent lets the agent reason over product descriptions, while the server independently enforces the exact transaction boundary. What's next for Intent The next step is turning Intent’s authority pattern into a reusable contract for agent enabled websites. That includes merchant verifiable mandates, signed handoffs, standardized WebMCP annotations for human granted capabilities, agent identity binding, multiple item decisions, and support for additional commerce catalogs. The longer term goal is broader than shopping. Any consequential agent action, such as booking travel, changing a subscription, approving a financial transfer, or sharing sensitive information, should be expressible as narrow authority that appears only when needed and disappears when its purpose is complete. title: Agent Web Gateway
pitch: Agent Web Gateway is a translator for the web that isn’t agent-ready yet. It helps AI agents use ordinary websites through WebMCP, then brings people back to the real site.
about_excerpt:
Agent Web Gateway is a translator for the web that isn’t agent-ready yet. It helps AI agents use ordinary websites through WebMCP, then brings people back to the real site.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 My wife and I are moving house, and for the past month we've been flat hunting, which is a whole job in itself when you live in London. So we set our OpenClaw agent Alfred on the task and asked him to provide some options for us to view each day. However, we quickly learned that even though he is a very capable agent and has a robust research and browsing stack, he still struggles with older websites that were not optimised for the age of AI. 

 He defaults to a mixture of web scraping and browser use, which gets him halfway there (if the website doesn't classify him as a bot), but it's still very much a clunky experience, especially if you'd like to co-browse. At that point, he simply couldn't keep up. 

 Which led me to ask the question, "If a website doesn't yet have the infrastructure for seamless agent use, how do we give our agents a helping hand in the meantime? How do we provide a dictionary/translator that allows them to ask for the restroom in the middle of Barcelona?" That's quite hard when you don't speak the language. 

 The Agent Web Gateway was born as a solution. It serves as a stand-in for older, non-WebMCP-compatible websites. Like agent-native subtitles on a foreign language film. The gateway handles a site-specific search, normalises the data, applies the constraints, verifies the results, and returns the best match through that same WebMCP interaction. I've tested it for shopping, rental searches, and job searches with varying success, but the promise is there. 

 Now, when Alfred tries to browse these websites, he's no longer lost. He doesn't try to brute-force his way through a simple query, burning precious tokens. He speaks to the gateway using WebMCP, it speaks back, he shares his findings with me, and we browse the links together. 

 My dream is that we will need it less and less over time as WebMCP adoption picks up. But for now, Alfred and I are finally on the same page.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Business software for humans and agents 

 Most business software was designed around a simple assumption: humans use the interface, while automation happens somewhere behind it. 

 We built a different model. 

 Our workspace is designed for a future where humans and AI agents can work together directly inside the same live business application. 

 The human defines the goal and constraints. The agent investigates the current business state, analyzes signals, compares possible approaches, and creates a structured proposal. The human can then modify the constraints, reject or approve the proposal, and remain the final decision-maker. Once approved, the application executes the change and verifies the resulting state. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP is central to this experience. 

 Instead of asking an agent to operate a business application by interpreting screenshots, clicking arbitrary UI elements, or relying on fragile DOM interactions, the application exposes meaningful business capabilities through WebMCP. 

 Our tools represent application-level capabilities such as: 

 
 inspecting live business state 
 analyzing business signals 
 comparing scenarios 
 drafting proposals 
 revising proposals based on human constraints 
 requesting approval 
 executing approved changes 
 verifying the resulting state 
 

 This makes the web application itself an agent-accessible capability surface. 

 WebMCP is therefore not a decorative integration or a separate chatbot connection. 

 It is the capability contract between the agent and the live business application. 

 A new human-agent workflow 

 The core workflow is: 

 Human intent → Agent analysis → Structured proposal → Human constraints → Proposal revision → Human approval → Execution → Verification 

 For example, a business owner can ask: 

 «Improve conversion without increasing the total budget.» 

 The agent can inspect the current business state, analyze the relevant signal, compare scenarios, and produce a structured proposal containing evidence, assumptions, constraints, expected impact, risks, and alternatives. 

 The human can then add: 

 «Prioritize low-risk changes.» 

 The agent must incorporate that constraint into the revised proposal rather than simply repeating the original recommendation. 

 The human remains in control of consequential decisions. 

 What becomes possible? 

 The important change is not simply that an agent can "use a website." 

 The agent can participate in the application's actual workflow using structured capabilities while the human remains an active collaborator. 

 This makes it possible to move from: 

 human uses software + AI gives advice 

 to: 

 human and agent collaborate through the software itself. 

 The application can understand the agent's structured actions, preserve business state, enforce authorization and approval rules, execute approved changes, and verify the outcome. 

 Better UX 

 Traditional business software often separates analysis, decision-making, and execution across dashboards, forms, automation tools, and conversations. 

 Our interface brings these stages into one coherent workflow. 

 The user can see: 

 
 what the agent observed 
 what it analyzed 
 what it proposes 
 which constraints are active 
 what requires human approval 
 what was executed 
 what was verified 
 

 The result is not another AI chat interface. 

 It is a decision and execution workspace where human judgment and agent capabilities are deliberately combined. 

 Human authority 

 The agent does not become the final decision-maker. 

 Proposal and execution are intentionally separated. 

 A consequential action requires the appropriate human approval, while the application remains the authoritative source of business state. 

 The system also accounts for changing state so that an outdated proposal should not blindly become a new business action. 

 Implementation 

 The frontend exposes selected high-value application capabilities through the WebMCP API using: 

 "document.modelContext.registerTool(...)"
[9/4/2026 12:05 PM] Islombek Abdurasulov: Each tool has a meaningful name, description, structured JSON input schema, and execution handler connected to the application's real functionality. 

 The WebMCP layer is organized around three conceptual capability groups: 

 READ 

 
 inspect current state 
 inspect relevant business information 
 

 PROPOSE 

 
 analyze 
 compare 
 draft 
 revise 
 

 COMMIT 

 
 request approval 
 execute an approved change 
 verify the result 
 

 The application's backend remains responsible for authoritative state, validation, authorization, persistence, and business rules. 

 This separation allows WebMCP to provide an agent-facing capability layer without turning the browser interface into a security boundary. 

 Why this matters 

 We believe the next generation of the web will not simply be websites that humans visit or agents automate. 

 It can be a web where applications expose meaningful capabilities that humans and agents can use together. 

 Our project explores what that interaction model could look like in a real business environment. 

 Humans decide. Agents collaborate. The application executes and verifies.

title: CharDesk
pitch: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI agents are fluent in text, but people understand complex ideas faster when they can see structure, position, emphasis, and relationships. Existing collaboration tools usually force one side to compromise: people work through visual interfaces while agents imitate mouse clicks, or agents produce plain text that people must mentally reconstruct. We wanted a medium native to both. CharDesk began with a simple idea: What if the canvas were visual to people, but still made of tokens an agent could read and edit precisely? What CharDesk does CharDesk is a shared visual workspace for humans and AI agents. An agent can create or update a Blackboard through WebMCP. The result immediately appears as a live Unicode canvas that a person can inspect, navigate, and continue discussing with the agent. The same canvas can combine: Unicode and ANSI art Markdown and fenced code Mermaid diagrams Tables, JSON, and YAML Mathematical expressions Scientific plots and Vega-Lite Spatial layouts and character-based slides This makes CharDesk useful for explaining concepts, visualizing research, mapping systems, designing interfaces, presenting stories, and maintaining a shared project workspace. For example, someone can ask: “Explain how a GPU renders one frame.” The agent can turn that request into a structured visual scene containing a pipeline diagram, memory relationships, annotations, and styled interface elements—not just another long answer in chat. Why it is better with WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to guess how to operate the interface or manipulate individual canvas cells. CharDesk instead exposes focused workspace tools for discovering, creating, reading, writing, patching, deleting, and validating Blackboard files. The source remains authoritative; the canvas is a live projection of it. This gives each participant the representation they work with best: Human sees relationships, hierarchy, and visual emphasis ⇅ CharDesk Blackboard ⇅ Agent reads and edits structured, diffable text Agents can also call chardesk_read_materials to learn the visual language from worked examples. The tool teaches not only how to call the API, but how to compose an effective scene. How we built it CharDesk has a protocol-neutral tool layer shared by two thin host adapters: Standard WebMCP for compatible Chrome environments The imperative WebMCP capability supported by ChatGPT Site Tools Both adapters expose the same underlying Blackboard operations, so product behavior does not depend on a particular browser integration. A Blackboard stores source files and layout metadata. Changes are compiled through a shared rendering pipeline into a fixed character grid. This pipeline handles Unicode width, CJK characters, Nerd Font glyphs, ANSI styles, structured diagrams, and multidimensional layouts. The browser keeps the latest valid canvas mounted while an agent edits the source. If an intermediate update is invalid, CharDesk returns diagnostics without replacing the visible scene with a broken or empty state. The same format also works outside the browser through the CharDesk CLI, making projects portable, inspectable, renderable, and friendly to normal version-control workflows. Challenges we faced One unexpected challenge was tool ownership across browser tabs. Opening several CharDesk pages could cause identical tools to be registered multiple times, leaving the agent unable to choose a target. We built an origin-level gateway lease so only one page exposes the tools, with automatic takeover when that page closes. Chrome and ChatGPT also expose different subsets of the evolving WebMCP API. Instead of spreading compatibility checks throughout the product, we isolated those differences behind capability adapters backed by one canonical tool definition. Another challenge was timing: some hosts inject WebMCP after the application has already loaded. CharDesk therefore uses an adaptive registration handshake rather than assuming the API exists at startup. Finally, we learned that exposing tools is not enough. An agent may know how to write a file without knowing how to create a compelling visual explanation. Embedding CharDesk’s materials and examples as a callable tool gave browser agents the missing creative context. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native design is not simply automation layered onto an existing UI. A better pattern is to give agents a precise, structured representation while giving people a rich visual projection of the same underlying artifact. WebMCP makes that relationship discoverable directly from the website, without requiring agents to reverse-engineer the interface. CharDesk explores what becomes possible when the web page is no longer just something an agent operates, but a shared medium in which the human and agent can think together. title: Corre
pitch: programmable financial infrastructure that gives AI agents the ability to hold, receive, spend, save, and manage USDC autonomously.
about_excerpt: programmable financial infrastructure that gives AI agents the ability to hold, receive, spend, save, and manage USDC autonomously. Like Comment Story Updates The Architecture of Economic Sovereignty: Building Corre "Technology is at its most potent not when it dazzles with complexity, but when it dissolves the invisible borders that dictate a person's financial destiny." Inspiration: The Weight of an Invisible Boundary Growing up in an era defined by hyperconnected digital highways, I was struck by a jarring paradox: while information travels across continents in milliseconds, financial opportunity remains chained to geography. I watched friends and families in emerging markets watch their life savings erode under the quiet violence of local currency devaluation, barred from basic wealth preservation vehicles like dollar-denominated yields or fractional shares of the world’s most innovative enterprises. To open a brokerage account or access an inflation-resistant yield vault often required arbitrary minimum balances, weeks of bureaucratic verification, and exorbitant cross-border wire fees. The traditional financial apparatus had decided that billions of people were simply too expensive to serve. At the same time, we stood on the precipice of another revolution: autonomous AI agents capable of reasoning, analyzing market data, and orchestrating complex tasks. Yet, these agents were trapped in sandbox silos—intellectually capable, but economically paralyzed. Corre was born at the intersection of these two convictions: Financial self-sovereignty must be a universal human right, not a geographical privilege. The future of global wealth creation belongs to autonomous, user-aligned AI agents interacting natively with decentralized rails. What Was Already There vs. What We Built During This Period Before this project, Corre already had a working foundation: Existing Backend & Core App : A dashboard for savings vaults (~$8.5\%$ standard yield, ~$6.2\%$ shielded yield) and US stock trading via Jupiter. Remote MCP Server ( mcp.corre.bond ) : An SSE endpoint where external AI assistants like Claude Desktop or ChatGPT could read public vault rates and search stocks remotely. What We Built & Updated During This Period: Created the Client-Side WebMCP Engine ( frontend/src/webmcp ) : We built an in-browser runtime that taps into the emerging Chrome document.modelContext API, with a fallback bridge on window.__correWebMCP . Instead of relying on a backend server, the web app itself registers tools directly into the browser session. Built Client-Side WebMCP Tools : We created a dedicated suite of browser tools: get_savings_yield : Pulls live vault APYs in real time. get_savings_balance : Reads the user's active shielded and standard balances. deposit_savings_vault : Generates and signs on-chain Solana deposit transactions right inside the browser. get_stock_quote & list_available_stocks : Queries live tokenized stock prices and directs users to exact asset pages. get_naira_exchange_rate & get_supported_banks : Provides real-time fiat on/off-ramp conversion rates. Integrated Native In-Browser Wallet Signing : We connected Privy’s Solana wallet provider directly into the WebMCP context so an AI agent can prepare a transaction, and the browser wallet can sign it without ever exposing private keys. Interactive WebMCP Inspector UI & Agent Toast System : We designed an in-app inspector badge and dialog where users can see every tool registered with their browser, test tools with live JSON output, and copy JavaScript snippets. We also built an agent notification system ( WebMcpAgentToast ) that shows live toasts whenever an AI agent calls a tool. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Autonomous AI Agents │ │ (Browser Agents, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Cursor) │ └────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬─────────────┘ │ │ [Browser ModelContext] [Remote MCP / SSE] │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Corre WebMCP │ │ mcp.corre.bond │ │ Client Runtime │ │ Remote Gateway │ └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ │ │ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Corre Core Settlement Engine │ ├─────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┤ │ Yield Engine │ Equities Engine │ Identity & Safety │ │ • Standard Vault │ • Fractional US Stocks │ • Privy Embedded Solana Wallet │ │ (~8.5% APY via Lulo) │ (AAPL, TSLA, NVDA...) │ • Gas-Sponsored Relayer │ │ • Shielded Vault │ • Jupiter Liquidity V2 │ • Session Circuit Breakers │ │ (~6.2% APY pUSD) │ • Zero-Commission Swaps │ • Local Fiat Ramp (PAJ / NGN) │ └─────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘ 4. Democratized Tokenized US Equities By routing through liquidity aggregators directly on-chain, Corre allows anyone with an internet connection to purchase fractional shares of US stocks (Tesla, Apple, Nvidia, S&P 500) starting from as little as $\$5.00$ USDC, with instant settlement and $0\%$ broker commissions. 5. The Native Browser WebMCP & Remote Agent Gateway We pioneered a dual-rail agent interface: In-Browser WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) : Direct browser-level tool registration exposing real-time portfolio telemetry, stock quotes, and savings deposits directly into browser-native AI agents without exposing private keys. Production MCP Gateway ( https://mcp.corre.bond ) : A secure Server-Sent Events (SSE) protocol endpoint allowing ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, and Cursor to analyze vault positions, project multi-year compounding scenarios, and prepare in-chat transactions. 6. Frictionless Onboarding & Key Quorum Security Web3's steepest hurdle has always been the friction of 12-word seed phrases and gas fees. We integrated: Privy Embedded Solana Wallets : Instant email/social login with cryptographic key quorums. Automated Gas Relayer : A backend fee-payer service that subsidizes Solana transaction fees, providing a pure, Web2-grade user experience with Web3 custody. Challenges We Ran Into: The Forge of Complex Engineering Building a production-ready application at the frontier of Web3 and AI forced us to confront problems that textbooks rarely cover: 1. Reconciling Asymmetric Cryptographic Signing Environments Browser AI agents require fast, deterministic execution, but signing financial transactions requires strict user consent. When integrating Privy’s Solana signers into the WebMCP runtime, EVM wallet hooks initially collided with Solana keypairs. We refactored the entire context lifecycle to decouple wallet discovery, handle partially signed serialized versioned transactions ($V0$), and implement structured error propagation so that AI agents receive actionable diagnostic feedback instead of silent failure states. 2. Defense-in-Depth Against Agentic Exploits Exposing financial actions to autonomous agents introduces novel threat vectors. We developed strict server-side validation layers: Transaction size limits ($\le \$500$ per in-chat operation). Transaction instruction inspection (stripping out malicious CloseAccount instructions or fee-payer drainage attempts). Rate-limiting circuit breakers backed by persistent PostgreSQL state. 3. The Gas Relayer Payload Mismatch Once the wallet was recognized, deposits failed with an HTTP 400 error. The frontend was posting { signedTransaction: serializedTransaction } , but our backend controller was strictly checking for req.body.transaction . We fixed the payload key to { transaction: serializedTransaction } and updated the response parsing to correctly capture sponsorData.transactionHash || sponsorData.signature . 4. Opaque Chrome Model Context Errors When a tool threw an error (like an invalid deposit amount), Chrome displayed a generic message: "Tool was executed but the invocation failed. For example, the script function threw an error" Because the engine was letting exceptions bubble up as unhandled promise rejections, Chrome hid the real cause. We wrapped tool invocations in structured try/catch blocks inside engine.ts . Now, if something goes wrong, the AI agent receives a clear, readable JSON error (e.g., {"status": "error", "error": "Minimum deposit is 1 USDC"} ) and can tell the user what to fix. What We Learned: Beyond Code and Syntax Building Corre was a masterclass in systems thinking. I learned that: Simplicity is the highest form of security : The most resilient distributed systems are those that hide mathematical complexity behind intuitive, human-centered interfaces. AI Agents need native economic primitives : The next billion on-chain transactions will not be initiated by manual human clicks, but by autonomous agents executing financial strategies programmed to maximize their owners' long-term welfare. AI Agents need clear contracts, not just text prompts : If an API returns an unhandled rejection, an AI agent gets confused. Robust err

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation.  1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration 

 When I reviewed the hackathon details, I started thinking about what I would really want to do with an AI agent. Usually, doing a task purely on your own is faster than delegating it, or having the agent do it completely autonomously is faster than doing it yourself. I wanted to focus on the type of task where a human and an agent work together efficiently. 

 Looking at the sponsors, I saw Shopify. Having done some research into dropshipping and e-commerce, I know how much work goes into managing a store. Fully autonomous agents run into permission and safety issues, since an agent cannot just be allowed to do everything without supervision. In physical retail stores, owners have managers and assistants to help run day-to-day operations. For an online store, an agent can play that exact role. That is where the name Merchant Assistant comes from: an assistant to the merchant who owns the store. 

 What Merchant Assistant Does: 

 
 Product Research and Proposals:
The task that takes merchants the longest is research. When prompted by the merchant, the agent researches top-performing products in specific categories using ShopifyQL under the hood, exposed via WebMCP. Instead of just pulling data, the agent creates actionable proposals for items the merchant can procure and add to the store. 
 Interactive Control via ChatGPT:
Through WebMCP, merchants can interact with the agent directly in the ChatGPT app or on the web. Once the agent creates a proposal, the merchant reviews and accepts it. The changes can then be applied immediately with a single click, or the merchant can instruct the agent to apply multiple approved proposals. 
 Product Audits and Optimization:
The agent audits existing listings, checking descriptions and top-performing products based on sales data. It highlights areas for improvement and suggests updated descriptions aligned with current market trends. 
 

 The merchant remains in control: they trigger the agent, review its findings, and approve every change. 

 How I Built It: 

 I built the project using WebMCP, ShopifyQL, and Shopify MCP to give the agent the tools needed to query store analytics and execute store actions. 

 Challenges I Ran Into: 

 
 Shopify Permissions: Securing Level 2 permissions to read merchant reports and sales data, which are necessary for the agent to audit the store and propose optimizations. 
 Judge Access and Testing: Shopify's standard security makes it difficult to grant external test access simply via email. I implemented a workaround so judges can test the integration live. 
 

 What I AM Most Proud Of: 

 The entire end-to-end system is 100% functional and working live.

title: GraphWeave
pitch: GraphWeave: The agentic architecture canvas for W3C WebMCP. AI co-pilots autonomously design, stress-test with chaos engineering, and self-heal cloud topologies in real time.
about_excerpt: GraphWeave: The agentic architecture canvas for W3C WebMCP. AI co-pilots autonomously design, stress-test with chaos engineering, and self-heal cloud topologies in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Vision Agent assisted architecture design Automated threat analysis and simulation GraphWeave Inspiration Anyone who has spent time designing backend architectures knows the routine: you open Draw.io or Miro, spend an hour aligning boxes and arrows, and by the end of the sprint, the diagram is already outdated. When LLMs came along, I hoped they would make this easier. Instead, I got walls of text, ASCII art, or raw Mermaid snippets pasted into chat windows. You couldn't drag the boxes, you couldn't click an edge to inspect TLS settings, and you couldn't test how the system handled failures. When OpenAI announced the WebMCP challenge, I realized I should try to bridge that gap. Instead of having an AI talk about architecture in a side panel, WebMCP lets the model directly interact with the app's DOM. I wanted to build a canvas where an agent works alongside me as a real collaborator: provisioning components, running audits, injecting chaos failures, and fixing vulnerabilities live on screen. How I Built It I kept the stack lightweight, fast, and entirely client-side: Next.js & React Flow: Powers the interactive visual graph, handling pan, zoom, custom node components, and animated connection lines. WebMCP: Inside a React hook ( useWebMCP ), I register tools like add_service_node , connect_services , simulate_chaos_outage , and run_architecture_audit . I also expose two live resources: canvas://topology (the raw graph state) and canvas://audit-report (the current linter results). Zustand: All state lives in a centralized store. Whether an action comes from a human dragging a box or an agent calling a WebMCP tool, it hits the same reducer. Dagre.js: Automatically calculates clean left-to-right hierarchical coordinates so nodes snap into place without overlapping. Architecture Rules Engine: A client-side linter that evaluates the topology against common production pitfalls (missing database replicas, plaintext channels, un-cached read bottlenecks). Challenges I Faced Tool Registration Lifecycles: During local development, Next.js Fast Refresh triggered re-renders that either caused duplicate tool registrations or dropped them completely. I had to implement proper AbortController signals to cleanly bind and unbind tool specifications as components mounted and unmounted. This might be something unnecessary or random. But it worked out. Bi-Directional State Authority: The human and the agent needed equal control over the canvas. If a user manually drags a database node and turns off TLS encryption on an edge, the agent’s next read of canvas://topology had to reflect that change immediately. Using Zustand's synchronous store getters avoided stale React closures and kept the agent in sync with the user's manual edits. What I Learned Tool-calling the DOM beats text output every time: Watching an agent create nodes, connect protocols, and fix security flaws in front of your eyes feels completely different from reading advice in a chatbot. It transforms the model from a search engine into an actual pair programmer. Client-side state is fast and simple: By keeping all topology logic deterministic in the browser, GraphWeave requires zero backend databases or server roundtrips. It deploys statically to Vercel and responds instantaneously. Visual feedback drives better security: Seeing a database node turn red under a simulated chaos outage makes single points of failure obvious in a way that static spreadsheets or compliance checklists never do.
