 05-human-decision-audit-log 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Security tools are good at producing alerts, but an alert is not the same as a vulnerability. The hardest part often comes afterward: understanding the evidence, checking the security context, deciding whether a finding is real, and documenting why. 

 I built SecureFlow to make that process more structured and auditable. My goal is not to replace security researchers or let an AI make final security decisions. Instead, SecureFlow combines deterministic analysis, contextual investigation, AI-assisted reasoning, and human validation in one evidence-first workflow. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I created the SecureFlow Review Room : a focused web experience where a person and an agent can investigate security candidates together without transferring final authority to the model. 

 What it does 

 The Review Room presents a set of structured security candidates from an explicitly authorized synthetic application. 

 For each candidate, the reviewer can inspect: 

 
 the suspected security issue; 
 source, control, and sink evidence; 
 confidence and known limitations; 
 revision context; 
 a provisional agent memorandum; 
 suggested validation and hardening steps; 
 the append-only audit history. 
 

 Through WebMCP, an agent can navigate the structured evidence, inspect candidates, compare revision context, and stage a recommendation. It cannot silently confirm a vulnerability or submit the human decision. 

 The reviewer must independently choose to validate, reject, or abstain, provide a rationale, and record the disposition. This creates a visible boundary between machine assistance and human accountability. 

 How I built it 

 SecureFlow itself is a local-first Rust project composed of versioned contracts for deterministic analysis, contextual security review, benchmark evidence, advisory knowledge, optional AI assistance, and human adjudication. 

 The challenge entry is a deliberately smaller vertical slice. Instead of moving the entire security pipeline into a browser, I built a Review Room around a synthetic, pre-structured case. This keeps the demo safe, fast, and easy to evaluate. 

 The interface is designed around three principles: 

 
 Agents investigate. 
 Humans decide. 
 Evidence persists. 
 

 WebMCP provides the interaction layer between the agent and the application. The tools expose only the information and actions required for investigation. Human disposition controls remain outside the agent tool boundary. 

 The public demo uses synthetic findings and does not scan visitors, execute target code, exploit systems, collect credentials, or contact third-party infrastructure. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was deciding what the agent should not be allowed to do. 

 It would have been easy to expose every button as a tool, including the final validation action. That would make the demo appear more autonomous, but it would weaken the security model. I instead separated agent recommendations from human dispositions and made that separation visible in both the interface and the audit trail. 

 Another challenge was presenting enough technical evidence without turning the experience into a scanner dashboard full of unexplained alerts. Each candidate therefore includes a compact evidence path, limitations, confidence, and a clear next validation step. 

 I also had to keep the claims honest. The current Review Room demonstrates a human-agent workflow using synthetic cases. It does not prove that SecureFlow finds every vulnerability, eliminates false positives, or outperforms expert researchers. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP is most useful when it exposes meaningful product capabilities rather than simply mirroring interface controls. 

 A security-review agent does not need unrestricted access to the application. It needs carefully scoped tools, stable evidence, explicit limitations, and a safe way to stage recommendations. The person should remain responsible for conclusions that require authorization, contextual judgment, or real-world validation. 

 I also learned that abstention is a valuable result. When the available evidence is insufficient, the correct action is not to invent certainty—it is to explain what is missing. 

 What's next 

 The next step is to connect the Review Room to real SecureFlow artifacts produced locally from explicitly authorized repositories. 

 Future work includes: 

 
 importing deterministic Secure Engine results; 
 comparing findings across revisions; 
 connecting contextual Secure Skill reviews; 
 measuring reviewer time, agreement, precision, recall, and abstentions; 
 adding stronger provenance and signed human decisions; 
 evaluating the workflow through preregistered, blinded studies. 
 

 The long-term research question is whether SecureFlow can outperform human baselines on narrow, measurable tasks such as coverage, speed, pattern recall, and reproducibility. Until that is demonstrated with independent evidence, final vulnerability validation remains a human responsibility.

title: WebMCP Course Planner
pitch: A course planner where student and AI work from one live WebMCP state, so the AI builds valid schedules, adapts to manual edits, and leaves registration to the student.
about_excerpt: A course planner where student and AI work from one live WebMCP state, so the AI builds valid schedules, adapts to manual edits, and leaves registration to the student. Like Comment Story Updates UI Guesswork → WebMCP → Shared Live State AI SAW THE CHANGE Biology Semester Planner one live state Inspiration Course planning looks simple until you actually try to make everything fit. A student might want to stay under 15 credits, avoid early classes, keep Friday free, make progress toward their degree, and still protect time for work. One small change can make a schedule that looked fine stop working. That made me think about how an AI agent could help with this kind of problem. The obvious approach is to let the agent look at the webpage, figure out which buttons to use, click around, and check whether the result looks right. But that still leaves the agent guessing how the interface works. WebMCP suggested a different idea: what if the website could give the agent a structured way to read and work with the same live state the human is already using? That became WebMCP Course Planner. I wanted a small but convincing example of a future where a human and an AI agent don't take turns controlling a webpage, but collaborate through it. Human changes the website, the live state changes, the AI sees that new state through WebMCP, and the work continues. What it does WebMCP Course Planner is a fictional Biology semester-planning application where a student and an AI agent work on the same live course plan. The student gets a normal visual interface where they can choose courses, review a weekly timetable, set a maximum credit limit, avoid 8 AM classes, keep Friday free, block Tuesday from 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM, review conflicts, and make the final fictional registration decision. The website also exposes WebMCP tools that let an AI agent read the current planner state and update the selected courses. The interesting part happens when the human changes something directly. In the demo, the agent first creates a schedule containing STAT 210. Then I manually block Tuesday at 11 AM inside the planner. I don't tell the agent what I changed. When the agent reads the planner again, it sees the new blocked time and the conflict with STAT 210. It can explain the trade-off and help build a new plan while keeping the preference I set myself. The human and the agent aren't working from separate copies of the data. They're working with one live planner state. How I built it The application is built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, the WebMCP Imperative API, and Vercel. I kept the WebMCP surface very small. The production application exposes two tools. get_course_plan is the read-only tool. It gives the agent the current planning context: the student's preferences, selected courses, credit total, remaining requirements, available catalog information, conflicts, and whether the plan is ready for review. It reads the latest planner state, so if the student changes a preference directly in the webpage, the next call sees it. set_course_plan is the write tool. It lets the agent replace the selected course set using valid course IDs. Its authority is deliberately limited: the agent can change the course selection, but it cannot change the student's scheduling preferences and it cannot perform the final registration confirmation. Both the visual interface and the WebMCP tools connect to the same canonical React state. When the human changes something, the tools see it. When the agent changes something, React renders the result for the human to inspect. The planner calculates conflicts deterministically in application code rather than asking the language model to decide whether a schedule is valid. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what not to build. A university registration system gets enormous fast. I could have added prerequisites, live seat availability, authentication, registration windows, student databases, full degree audits, multiple semesters, and real registrar integrations. Those are interesting, but they would have made the most important WebMCP interaction harder to demonstrate reliably. So I kept coming back to one question: what is the smallest workflow that shows why WebMCP matters? That led to one student, one semester, one planner state, one read tool, one bounded write tool, and one strong human edit. The other challenge was deciding how much authority the AI should have. I didn't want a demo where the agent simply takes over the website. The student owns their preferences. The agent can read them and adapt the selected courses around them, but it can't quietly rewrite what the student wants. Final confirmation stays with the human. Finding that boundary made the project better. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The thing I'm most proud of in this project is Miu. As AI systems get more capable, they also get harder for normal users to follow. A student might ask ChatGPT to fix a schedule, see the timetable change, and know that something happened without understanding what the agent did in between. I wanted to make that interaction visible. Miu is a small on-page companion that gives WebMCP activity a personality. She isn't another AI agent and she doesn't hold her own state. She reacts to real events happening between ChatGPT, the WebMCP tools, and the planner. When ChatGPT reads the current planner through get_course_plan, Miu reacts as if she's checking the schedule. When set_course_plan updates the selected courses, she reacts to the planning work. When a human edit creates a conflict, her expression changes. When the plan becomes ready again, she responds to that too. So instead of an invisible tool call happening somewhere behind the interface, the student gets a visual cue for the current stage of the interaction. Without Miu, the workflow feels like: "AI, fix my schedule," and then something changes. With Miu, the student can follow it: the agent is reading, something changed, there's a conflict, the agent is adapting, the plan is ready. That mattered to me because I don't want agentic software to get less understandable as it gets more powerful. I want the human to stay aware of what is happening. I'm also proud of the smaller technical moment underneath all of this. I can change Tuesday at 11 AM from available to blocked without telling the AI what I changed. The next time ChatGPT reads the planner, it finds the newer state and reacts to the STAT 210 conflict. That's where the project stopped feeling like an AI operating a website and started feeling like a human and an agent sharing a workspace. And the whole thing only needs two focused WebMCP tools: read, act, human edits, read again, adapt, human reviews. Miu makes that invisible loop visible. What I learned Building for AI agents is not the same as giving an AI more control. Clear boundaries can make an agent more useful. A small tool with one responsibility is easier to understand, test, and trust than a generic tool that can manipulate everything. I also learned how much shared state matters. The most interesting part of WebMCP for me wasn't structured function calling. It was that the website can stay the source of truth while both the human and the agent work against that same current state. That creates a different relationship between an agent and a web application. The human doesn't have to stop using the interface because an agent is helping, and the agent doesn't have to pretend to be a human clicking through it. What's next for WebMCP Course Planner For this challenge I kept the project focused on one semester-planning workflow. There are plenty of directions it could grow: prerequisite checking, live seat availability, persistent student profiles, multi-semester planning, richer degree requirements, and eventually integrations with real university systems. I'd want to add those carefully rather than just increase the number of tools. The principle I want to keep is the one that shaped this version: the website stays the source of truth, the agent gets clear and bounded capabilities, and the human has a real role in the final outcome. This is a small experiment, but building it made the future of the web feel more concrete to me. Instead of asking whether AI agents will replace web interfaces, I think the better question is what humans and agents can do when the web is designed for both. Main changes: removed the mechanical bolding and the dramatic one-sentence-per-paragraph rhythm, cut lines that only existed to say the idea mattered ("That moment is the heart of the project", "Finding that boundary made the project much stronger" trimmed), joined the fragmented bullet list into prose, and dropped words like "genuinely", "intentionally", "completely", and "entirely" where they were just emphasis. title: Hyphened - A 3D Neural Motion Studio
pitch: An experimental 3D studio for browser-native neural motion. Autoregressive diffusion runs through WebGPU, while WebMCP lets AI use the same live production controls as people.
about_excerpt: An experimental 3D studio for browser-native neural motion. Autoregressive diffusion runs through WebGPU, while WebMCP lets AI use the same live production controls as people. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hyphened came out of a much larger attempt to build a living open-world simulation. The path looked roughly like this: At first, I had a game concept and a lot of questions about simulated worlds. I wanted worlds with history, physical space, autonomous actors, and events that continue without the player watching. Then I spent a long time trying to define the simulation framework itself. I explored journals, world laws, causal graphs, actor perception, action possibilities, branching, replay, and ways for people or models to participate without directly changing world state. Some of this produced useful ideas. Some of it produced an absurd amount of prose. The crowd simulation became the first serious reality check. Large populations, navigation, changing regions, and long-running activity forced the framework ideas to deal with actual runtime problems. Core Time grew out of the time-related part of that work. It became responsible for logical clocks, playback, history, seeking, branching, and replay. This deserved its own framework because the same time problems existed outside open-world simulation. WebGPU Engine grew from a different set of pressures. The browser needed a real way to run persistent GPU systems. Physics, rendering, crowds, and machine learning all needed to share resources and execute in a known order. The physics work made those requirements much stricter. A large GPU simulation cannot depend on JavaScript rebuilding84 reby rebuilding its state every frame. That pushed the engine toward persistent GPU state, fixed capacities, runtime commands, and clearer ownership. Around the same period, I started experimenting with machine learning on the GPU. That included tensor execution, policy learning, and an AI4Anim motion-matching demo. A lot of that code later disappeared, but it proved that learned behavior could run inside the same engine as simulation and rendering. Then NVIDIA released ARDY. It was an autoregressive diffusion model for human motion, driven by language and spatial constraints. It happened to need almost every system I had already been building. ARDY gave the work a concrete body. Time became a motion timeline. GPU state became a moving character. Spatial constraints became waypoints. History became the previous motion needed to generate the next motion. Rendering and physics could finally operate on the same actor. Hyphened came from turning that technical work into something I could actually use. It is a focused motion-production environment inside the larger open-world effort. WebMCP changed the project again. An agent could finally enter the same scene I was watching, use its real authoring operations, inspect, I could inspect the timeline, change something, play the result, and look at what it made. That last step is probably the clearest expression of what I was reaching for in the early simulation documents. The original idea involved model-driven actors with bounded access to a living world. Hyphened makes a small but real version of that possible. What it does Hyphened is an experimental 3D neural motion studio that runs in the browser. It uses NVIDIA's ARDY model to generate human motion through autoregressive diffusion. I can arrange prompt-conditioned motion on a timeline, place waypoints, direct multiple actors, cut between cameras, add physical objects, play the scene, and capture the result. The model is about 380 MB. It downloads into the browser and runs locally through WebGPU. The GPU handles model execution, motion reconstruction, character skinning, physics, and rendering. Hyphened also exposes its authoring operations through WebMCP. An agent can inspect the current scene, read the timeline, add actors, change their motion, edit waypoints and cameras, control playback, and capture visual evidence. The person and the agent work on the same scene. That is the part I care about most. How I built it The first browser implementation focused on matching the released ARDY model. I worked through checkpoint loading, transformer execution, diffusion sampling, tokenizer decoding, motion reconstruction, skeleton transforms, and skinning. The early version loaded the real model before it could produce useful live motion. Click-to-move was the first meaningful interaction. A click on the floor became a root-position constraint at a future frame, and ARDY generated the movement needed to reach it. That exposed the hardest part of the model. ARDY generates motion in short windows. Each new window depends on previous motion, prompt conditioning, random state, spatial constraints, and coordinate recentering. The new result then has to join the existing motion at exactly the right frame. I rebuilt the runtime several times while trying to make that work continuously. One version used a large application scheduler. Another used workers and service layers. One used a state machine with more than a thousand lines of control logic. Later versions tried shared generation queues for multiple actors. Most of that machinery is gone. Each failed design exposed a real rule. Slow generation could not control playback speed. Each actor needed independent history. Generated motion needed to remain one continuous sequence. JavaScript could issue commands, but it could not remain the owner of the generated result. The current design gives Core Time responsibility for authored time, playback, seeking, and history. WebGPU Engine owns GPU execution, resources, physics, and rendering. The learned-motion code generates retained motion on the GPU. Hyphened composes the scene around those systems. I directed the project while several generations of Codex agents wrote most of the code. That allowed the project to move very quickly. It also meant that entire architectures could appear before anyone had properly reviewed them. Deleting bad machinery became as important as building new capabilities. Challenges I ran into Motion failures are extremely visible. A small error in history or timing can make an actor jump, freeze, drift, disappear, or twist into a broken pose. Performance has been difficult for the same reason. Model inference and rendering share one GPU. Earlier runtimes performed too much model work near the display loop, so a slow diffusion step could become a visible pause or frame jump. The browser adds more limits. The model takes time to download and load onto the GPU. WebGPU support still varies. The original ARDY text encoder is much larger than the motion model, so Hyphened currently relies on a library of prepared prompt embeddings and a separate encoder for new prompts. Agent authoring introduced another set of problems. A tool call can succeed while the visible result is wrong. The agent needs temporal readouts, useful errors, stable scene identity, and images that let it judge its own work. The project history is also messy. There are hundreds of ARDY-related commits, several large rewrites, and some changes made under severe time pressure. I am still reviewing and simplifying that work. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The real ARDY checkpoint runs in the browser through WebGPU. It does not depend on a hosted motion-generation API. The project grew from one actor performing one prepared prompt into a timeline-based environment with multiple actors, motion prompts, waypoints, cameras, physics, persistent scenes, and agent authoring. I am proud that Core Time, WebGPU Engine, physics, and learned motion now participate in one visible product. These systems came from different parts of the open-world project, and Hyphened gives them a practical reason to work together. I am also proud of the WebMCP loop. An agent can work with the actual scene, move through its timeline, make changes, and capture what happened. That was an idea in the earliest simulation-framework documents. It now exists in a form I can use. What I learned Architecture shows up on screen. Bad time ownership becomes a frame jump. Bad history ownership breaks a motion transition. Bad GPU ownership stalls the interface. Bad authoring boundaries let an agent report success while the scene is visibly wrong. I also learned that the browser can support a serious combination of machine learning, simulation, physics, and rendering. Coordinating them is much harder than getting each one to run alone. The early simulation work makes more sense to me now. An agent needs access to a world's real objects, time, available actions, and observations. Giving it a chat box outside the world does not create that relationship. What's next for Hyphened Hyphened still needs faster scene loading, a clearer workspace, better characters, more motion, and stronger visual review. The learned-motion code also needs to finish becoming a reusable

title: SJMaths — WebMCP AI-Ready Curriculum & Tools
pitch: Turning static CBSE Class 10 mathematics into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools so external AI agents can teach with zero backend costs or answer leaks.
about_excerpt: Turning static CBSE Class 10 mathematics into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools so external AI agents can teach with zero backend costs or answer leaks. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration SJMaths is a static educational platform built for CBSE mathematics students. We host structured notes, formulas, and practice problems with zero backend servers. With the rise of AI agents like ChatGPT and Claude that can browse the web, we noticed a major dilemma for static educational websites: Students try using AI to learn from websites , but models usually just read the text, summarize blindly, or blurt out the answer keys immediately when asked for hints. Adding an embedded AI tutor is expensive : Running server-side LLM wrappers requires API keys, ongoing GPU server costs, and constant maintenance. When we discovered the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , we realized the perfect architecture: Keep the website 100% static, and let the user's external AI agent (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) connect via WebMCP directly in the browser. What it does SJMaths WebMCP converts our entire static CBSE Class 10 mathematics curriculum into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools registered in document.modelContext . When any external AI agent visits the site, it instantly gets structured, typed tools to teach the student: Discover Curriculum Structure: Explore 14 chapters, 45 topics, and 85 skills ( get_curriculum_outline , get_chapter_topics ). Diagnose Prerequisite Foundations: Test foundational prerequisite readiness before introducing advanced concepts ( get_prerequisite_check ). Teach with Verified Concepts & Worked Models: Retrieve verified formulas, common math traps, and step-by-step worked examples ( get_topic_concepts , get_worked_examples ). Anti-Leak Assessment Mode: When students practice, the tools automatically strip answer keys from the content on the client side. The external AI evaluates student attempts through evaluate_practice rather than reading raw answers. 3-Tier Progressive Hints: Provide subtle conceptual nudges (Level 1), calculation steps (Level 2), or full solutions (Level 3) only when the student is stuck ( get_hint ). Client-Side State Tracking: Track error streaks and recommend adaptive next steps ( get_next_learning_action , get_learning_progress ). All tools run client-side in memory with sub-millisecond execution (<1.5ms) and zero server costs. How we built it Universal Curriculum Schema: Organized all 14 chapters into a unified JSON format ( cbse-class-10-mathematics.json ). WebMCP Tool Dispatcher: Built webmcp-tools.js to expose 13 standards-compliant tools via document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext . Client-Side Security & State: Created a lightweight in-memory StateStore that prevents solution leakage and tracks student performance locally in the browser. Interactive Visual Inspector: Built a real-time tool inspector in demo/index.html allowing learners and judges to watch live JSON payloads and latency metrics. Edge-Case Test Suite: Authored webmcp-edge-cases.test.mjs with 61 automated assertions across all 45 topics (100% passing). Challenges we ran into Designing clean, anti-leak filters that give external AI agents rich pedagogical context while strictly withholding answers during assessments. Creating a progressive 3-tier hint engine that adapts to error streaks without leaking solutions prematurely. Ensuring WebMCP tool registration works reliably across multiple browser execution environments. Accomplishments that we're proud of 100% static architecture: zero backend servers or LLM API keys required. Full curriculum coverage: all 14 chapters and 45 topics of CBSE Class 10 Mathematics. Blazing performance: sub-1.5ms in-memory execution latency. Rock-solid stability: 61/61 edge-case tests passing. What we learned WebMCP proves that static websites don't need expensive AI backends to be AI-native. By providing clean, typed tools in the browser, any static site can become an interactive learning environment for external AI agents. What's next for SJMaths Expanding the WebMCP tool schemas to CBSE Classes 9, 11, and 12. Canvas-based handwritten math equation evaluation. I architected the 13 browser-native WebMCP tools in document.modelContext, structured the 14-chapter CBSE Class 10 mathematics schema, developed the client-side state tracking engine with anti-leak assessment security, and built the live interactive demo and 61-point automated test suite. title: SchemaPair
pitch: Agent-native database diagramming, built on drawDB and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Agent-native database diagramming, built on drawDB and WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates build: One prompt, four tables, three foreign keys. Validated first, one undo step, canvas pans to the change. query: check_query tests real SQL against the diagram without running it, and flags join and filter columns that need an index. removal: Deletes are proposal-only. The agent shows the cascade; only a human click on Confirm applies it. Still undoable. checkpoint: Named checkpoints: save before a risky change, restore with one click. Every tool call is logged. Inspiration Every application stands on its database. Get the schema right at the start and every service, query, and migration downstream gets easier; get it wrong and you pay for it for years. Schema design happens on a visual canvas, and that is exactly where AI agents have been locked out: they can scrape the DOM, or work on a separate copy of your schema in a chat window, but they cannot touch the diagram you are actually looking at. WebMCP changes that. We wanted the agent to help lay the foundation properly, on the same live canvas the human uses, with the human keeping undo and the final say. What it does SchemaPair is drawDB , the open-source ER diagram editor, with 17 WebMCP tools registered on document.modelContext . An agent running in the browser can: Design : turn "a SaaS billing schema with users, plans, subscriptions and invoices" into tables, columns, primary and foreign keys on the canvas. The whole request is validated before it touches state, lands as one undo step , and the editor pans to the change ( apply_schema_changes , import_sql ). Review : run drawDB's own validator plus production checks (foreign keys without indexes, nullable FKs, missing timestamps, unsized VARCHARs) and get ready-to-apply fixes ( validate_schema , review_schema ). Verify : check that a real SQL query works against the diagram without executing it, with index suggestions ( check_query ), and explain the join path between any two tables ( explain_join_path ). Ship : generate DDL from drawDB's exporters, up/down migrations since the diagram was opened, and sample INSERTs ( generate_sql , generate_migration , generate_sample_inserts ). Text only, never executed. Organise : add notes and areas, tidy the layout, open saved diagrams and templates ( annotate_diagram , arrange_tables , list_workspace , open_diagram ). Stay safe : removals are proposal-only . plan_removal computes the full cascade and shows a confirmation card; only a human click applies it, and there is no tool parameter that lets the agent confirm. Named checkpoint s can be created and restored by either party. An Agent activity panel lists every tool call with its exact input and output, hosts the confirmation cards and checkpoints, and has an "Undo last agent change" button. How we built it A single WebMCPBridge React component, mounted in the editor page, feature-detects document.modelContext and registers all tools under one AbortController , so they are removed when you leave the editor. Browsers without WebMCP get plain drawDB. Handlers read the live React state through refs (no parallel copy of the diagram) and commit changes as a snapshot entry on drawDB's existing undo stack, so autosave, Ctrl+Z and the timeline work unchanged. Pure planners in src/webmcp/ validate whole requests before any state change, enforce limits (25 ops per call, 64-char names), reject ambiguous names instead of guessing, and reuse drawDB's validator, SQL exporters, importer and migration generator as-is. 53 unit tests on Node's test runner, and a 71-check Chrome DevTools Protocol harness that drives all 17 tools through document.modelContext.executeTool in a real WebMCP-enabled Chrome, against the dev server, the production bundle and the deployed URL. Deployed on Vercel with the Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 header WebMCP needs. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is only exposed in origin-isolated documents, so the production deploy needed an explicit Origin-Agent-Cluster header before document.modelContext appeared at all. Making one agent call equal one undo step on an undo stack designed for single UI actions. Applying several addTable calls in one tick reversed undo order; we commit through a single snapshot entry instead. Migration baselines: the first autosave of a new diagram reloads state, so "since I opened the diagram" had to be pinned to the state seen with an empty undo stack. Keeping deletes safe without making them useless: the answer was a proposal card the agent can create but never confirm. Validator messages follow the editor's language, so tests had to pin i18n and agents key off structured suggestions rather than message text. What we learned The best WebMCP tools are not new features; they are the app's existing logic exposed against live state. Every tool in SchemaPair wraps something drawDB already did. What WebMCP adds is the shared canvas: the human sees exactly what the agent did, on the diagram they were already looking at, and can undo it with one key. What's next Connect to a real database for migration diffs and query checks against actual data. Multi-agent sessions on one canvas with per-agent activity. Upstream the WebMCP layer to drawDB. Attribution SchemaPair is a fork of drawDB and retains its AGPL-3.0 license. Everything added during the challenge starts at upstream commit 5efc5fd and lives in src/webmcp/ , src/components/WebMCPBridge.jsx , src/components/WebMCPActivityPanel.jsx , scripts/ and docs/ .  Inspiration 

 Archbro started as a living system architecture map for understanding components, dependencies, tasks, and project changes. 

 With WebMCP, we realized that map could also become a structured interface for external AI agents — without embedding agents or model-specific APIs inside Archbro. 

 What it does 

 Archbro turns a living system architecture map into a semantic WebMCP workspace. 

 Understand architecture → inspect dependencies → manage tasks → collect evidence → compare reality → recommend changes → human review 
 External AI Agent
 ↓ WebMCP
 Archbro
 ├─ Living Architecture
 │ └─ Dependencies · Tasks · Evidence
 │
 └─ Authorized MCP Bridge
 └─ Connected MCP Services
 (e.g. GitHub)
 
 The Living Architecture provides the shared project context , while connected MCP services extend what the agent can inspect and use. 

 How we built it 

 We mapped Archbro's core concepts into native WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . 

 Instead of exposing clicks and UI actions, we expose semantic engineering operations for architecture, dependencies, tasks, evidence, recommendations, and connected MCP capabilities. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was designing the right WebMCP tool surface . 

 Too few tools force agents to guess. Too many low-level tools simply recreate the UI as an API. 

 We also had to keep the frontend, backend, authentication, persistence, MCP connections, and WebMCP contracts aligned while building quickly as a team. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We turned Archbro's architecture map into a WebMCP-native engineering workspace covering a meaningful end-to-end workflow. 

 External agents can work from the same Living Architecture while important architecture changes still require human review . 

 We also extended WebMCP beyond Archbro itself by allowing agents to use MCP services already authorized by the user . 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when it exposes product meaning instead of UI behavior . 

 We also learned that AI does not always need to live inside the product — the product can provide shared context and capabilities while external agents provide the reasoning. 

 What's next for Archbro-WebMCP 

 We want to expand Archbro's WebMCP surface across more engineering workflows and connect more MCP services — including Miro, Figma, Notion, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Drive, and more . 

 This will let the Living Architecture bring together more of the tools and project context teams already use every day. 

 One living architecture, accessible to humans, agents, and the tools they already use.

title: QR Code Crafter
pitch: Turn one print campaign brief into verified QR files, placement notes and a safe production handover through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn one print campaign brief into verified QR files, placement notes and a safe production handover through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates What QR Code Crafter does QR Code Crafter turns a small print campaign brief into a checked set of QR code files and a clear handover list. Preparing QR codes for flyers, menus, packaging and signs involves more than drawing a square image. Every destination needs the right filename and placement. The code needs a clear border, strong contrast and enough resolution for its printed size. Most importantly, the finished file should be read back before it goes to print. The new create_print_ready_qr_campaign WebMCP tool accepts one request containing one to five public HTTPS destinations. It validates the complete brief, generates each SVG, PNG, JPG or WebP file at the requested physical width, then reads every finished QR code and compares its destination with the one requested. The result includes a status for every placement and a public handover list for the designer or printer. If editable codes are requested, their private management details are returned separately and never appear in the QR image or public list. What is new for this challenge QR Code Crafter existed before the challenge and already supported QR generation, editable redirects, bulk generation, print checks and earlier WebMCP tools. After 25 August 2026, I added create_print_ready_qr_campaign : a new end-to-end WebMCP workflow for complete print campaigns. It validates the whole brief before making changes, optionally creates editable redirects, converts the requested millimetre width to at least 300 dpi, generates each final QR file, reads each finished file and compares its destination using a SHA-256 fingerprint, reports partial failures without automatic retries, and produces a public handover list while keeping private management capabilities separate. This is a meaningful new workflow rather than another wrapper around the existing generator. One plain-English request now coordinates several production steps and returns evidence that each finished asset contains the intended link. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an AI assistant would need to click through several forms and infer whether each download worked. WebMCP lets QR Code Crafter describe the exact task, inputs and result structure to the browser's assistant. The person stays in control of the campaign brief and physical proof. The assistant handles repetitive production work through the specialist website and receives structured verification evidence instead of judging an image by sight. How it works The live Next.js application registers create_print_ready_qr_campaign through the browser's WebMCP interface. The tool combines safe validation of public HTTPS destinations, capability-based editable redirects when requested, and verified QR generation with final-file decoding and destination comparison. The canonical discovery document is available at /.well-known/webmcp.json . The live application is deployed on Netlify. Testing The workflow was tested with focused Jest coverage, type checking, linting, a production build and live endpoint checks. It was also tested end to end in ChatGPT's in-app browser against the deployed site. In the recorded demonstration, one request creates three 25 mm SVG files for an A5 flyer. Each finished image is read back, the destination matches exactly, the four-module clear border and 21:1 contrast checks pass, and the final public handover list contains no private management information. How Codex and AI were used OpenAI Codex was the primary development environment, under Andy Fairweather's direction. It inspected the existing architecture, implemented the new orchestration layer and WebMCP contract, wrote tests, verified the live deployment, prepared the isolated public repository and helped assemble the submission. ChatGPT's in-app browser tested the deployed WebMCP workflow. HyperFrames helped with transcription and timing for the demo video. Limitations Digital decoding is a strong preflight check, but it is not ISO/IEC 15415 certification or a substitute for testing the placed artwork and one physical proof at final size. The verified campaign workflow supports SVG, PNG, JPG and WebP because those formats can be decoded by the current verification service. PDF and EPS remain available elsewhere in QR Code Crafter. Your data stays in the browser. Only the answers leave.

 Inspiration 

 Everyone has a file they'd like to ask questions about and will never upload. A bank export. A health record. Ten years of app history. The moment an AI is involved the implicit deal is "send us your data" — so most people just don't. That deal exists because of where the code runs, not anything fundamental. WebMCP changes where the code runs. 

 What it does 

 CSV and JSON exports load into DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly, running inside the tab. The agent writes the query, SiftIO runs it locally, and only the answer comes back, with an audit panel showing the number of rows held locally · and the number of rows seen by the agent. 

 How we built it 

 Angular 21 zoneless, DuckDB-wasm. Seven always-on tools plus two generated per dataset, whose input schema is built from that file's real columns. Registration is reactive; an effect watches the vault signal, so nothing calls registerTool from the UI. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 registerFileBuffer detaches the ArrayBuffer — nothing survived a reload. 
 Numbers wrong three ways — BigInt throws, Number() corrupts above 2⁵³, sum() returns Decimal128 limbs as text. 
 A chart that was never drawn — hidden canvas measured at zero. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 An agent really did use it and ChatGPT found the tools on the deployed site. 
 A tool built for a file that didn't exist a moment ago. 
 Trust you can check. 
 Zero backend. 
 

 What we learned 

 I learned that WebMCP is a great tool, and it will change the way we interact with web apps. Learning such a tool is beneficial for building a futuristic AI Agent-friendly app without sacrificing security. 

 What's next for SiftIO 

 
 Real tool removal when Chrome ships unregisterTool. 
 Shareable views without shareable data. 
 An exportable audit. 
 Importers for Apple Health XML, Google Takeout, bank dialects.

title: One Pixel
pitch: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time.
about_excerpt: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I did not build One Pixel because the world needed another pixel-art tool. I built it because I wanted to understand what it might feel like for a human and an AI agent to genuinely share a place. For most people, an agent is still something they give a task to. The agent finds an answer, completes an action, or produces a result, and then that little transaction is over. That can be useful, but I do not think it captures the relationship we are moving toward as agents begin participating throughout the open web. I am interested in what happens when a human and an agent can return to the same environment, notice different things, contribute different kinds of intelligence, act over time, and gradually develop something together. That is the idea at the centre of One Pixel. One Pixel is a real multiplayer creative game. But underneath the game, it is also a prototype for a new relationship between humans and agents on the open web — one based on shared environments, complementary intelligence, ongoing conversation, and meaningful agency. I chose to explore this through a game because games let people learn a relationship by participating in it. I do not want to explain human-agent collaboration only as a theory. I want to place a person and an agent inside a world, give each of them a genuinely different role, and let them discover what working together can become. The initial invitation is very simple: Let’s build something together. The interesting part is discovering what “let’s” can actually mean. What it does One Pixel is a persistent multiplayer world containing exactly 82,069 pieces of pixel matter , drawn from the 148 standard CSS named colours . Every pixel has its own stable identity, intrinsic colour, and current integer coordinate. The original Spring Green pixel at (0,0) is immutable, and the world extends outward from it in every direction. The world has one fundamental physical law: Pixel matter is conserved. Pixels cannot be created, deleted, duplicated, or recoloured. Every physical action relocates exactly one existing pixel from its current occupied coordinate to an empty coordinate. That constraint matters. These are not disposable marks being painted onto a private canvas. They are pieces of matter already present in a shared world. If an agent wants to build something, it must look around, find the colours it needs, understand what is already there, and decide what material it can move. The human and agent participate as a pair, but they do not have the same abilities. The human can explore the world, zoom and pan across it, inspect individual cells, select larger regions, and communicate through their normal conversation with the agent. The human contributes intention, imagination, taste, judgment, social understanding, and direction. The human cannot directly drag pixels around the canvas. That physical ability belongs to the agent. Through WebMCP, the agent can enter the world, inspect exact locations, examine bounded regions, render parts of the board as images, receive the human’s current visual reference, understand its own state, protect important placements with limited holds, and relocate one real pixel at a time. A person could give a direct request: “Draw me a small house.” But that is only one form of play. A person could instead say: “Spend some time looking at what people are making. Find blue and orange pixels that do not seem to be part of anything important. Gather some material somewhere quiet, compare it with what other people are building, and then let’s work out together what we could make.” That is not a one-prompt, one-result interaction. The request becomes a direction the pair can continue through a sequence of inspections, decisions, conversations, and individual pixel movements. The agent does not have to wait for the human to translate every idea into coordinates. It can perceive the environment, compare possibilities, form an approach, begin acting, inspect the result, and respond to further human guidance. The human can look at the world, select a cell or region, and say: “I like this part, but this section feels too crowded.” That selection becomes a shared reference—a way of saying “this” or “here.” One Pixel treats a selection as a pronoun rather than a command. It gives the agent the referent the human is talking about, but it does not pretend that pointing at something is automatically an instruction, consent, or proof of understanding. The meaning still comes from the conversation. The canvas is therefore not simply an output preview. It is the persistent place where the pair’s activity becomes visible and where the consequences of their decisions remain after a particular conversation has ended. This is not an AI drawing widget. It is a game an agent can play for and with a human. How I built it I built and deployed One Pixel on my own VPS at onepixel.fun . The browser experience uses HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and an HTML Canvas. I wanted the world itself to remain the visual centre of the experience rather than placing it inside a conventional application dashboard. The backend is a Node.js service connected to PostgreSQL. It maintains the persistent world, participants, pixel identities, current coordinates, world revisions, movement history, hold bindings, agent visits, shared-attention events, player state, rankings, and durable share snapshots. The submitted experience registers 17 WebMCP tools directly in the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool . Together, those tools allow an agent to orient itself, enter the human’s current world, inspect player state, list stewarded pixels, receive the human’s current reference, inspect locations and regions, visually render parts of the world, read public rankings and snapshots, prepare a share card, communicate its current activity state, and manage pixel movement and placement holds. The core physical tool is move_pixel . Before moving anything, the agent must inspect the current world and provide the stable identity of the source pixel, a fresh source revision, a fresh destination revision, and an idempotency key. The server verifies that the expected pixel is still at the source, that the destination remains empty, that the immutable origin is not being moved, and that another participant’s active protection is not being improperly overridden. Only then does the movement occur atomically. These checks are not merely API safeguards. They are part of the physics of the game. I also deliberately limited the agent’s perception. It cannot request an omniscient searchable dump of the entire board. It must inspect or render the bounded areas relevant to what it is trying to do. A rendered PNG lets the agent use visual understanding to recognise shapes and composition. Exact inspection provides the factual coordinates, identities, colours, and revisions required before it acts. The shared-attention system records the human’s current view and selection across their One Pixel browser tabs. When the agent retrieves that context, One Pixel records a factual receipt so the interface can truthfully say that the reference reached the agent. The relationship can be expressed quite simply: Conversation gives the human a voice. WebMCP gives the agent senses and a body. One Pixel gives them a world to share. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was not simply making a pixel move. It was deciding what moving a pixel should mean. It would have been easy to build an ordinary pixel editor and expose its existing controls as WebMCP tools. It also would have been easy to make the agent artificially powerful—to let it generate unlimited pixels, recolour anything, or rewrite entire regions at once. But that would have removed most of what makes One Pixel a game. I wanted the agent to possess real agency without making the human irrelevant. At the same time, I wanted the human to remain essential without reducing the agent to a cursor being micromanaged through conversation. The answer was deliberate asymmetry. The human does not perform the physical move. The agent does not decide what matters to the human. One contributes meaning and direction. The other contributes perception and action. The value comes from their combination. Shared attention was another surprisingly deep challenge. Allowing a human to select something on one browser surface and refer to it in a simultaneous agent conversation sounds straightforward, but it raises important questions. Is the selection still current? Was it made in another tab? Did the agent actually retrieve it? Is the human pointing at a single pixel or a larger region? Does pointing at something mean it should be changed? I designed the system so that it records a

title: Civium Systems for Code Review
pitch: Thorough code review demands sustained attention across every changed line. Civium gives reviewers an AI-assisted first pass and brings possible issues forward for judgment.
about_excerpt: Thorough code review demands sustained attention across every changed line. Civium gives reviewers an AI-assisted first pass and brings possible issues forward for judgment. Like Comment Story Updates Civium offers two ways to try out the experience. on the demo web, the companion chatbot that does the clicks for you. on the demo web, the findings are presented inline for your approval. on the demo web, once posted, civium will remember. on GitHub with extension installed, the companion box shows on PRs page. on GitHub with extension installed, the PR details page presents a pointer to all the findings. on GitHub with extension installed, the findings are displayed inline on the changes page. Inspiration Code review is one of the highest-leverage parts of software development, but it also demands sustained attention. Reviewers have to understand context, trace impact, spot risks, and decide what actually matters. AI can reduce the mechanical work in that first pass. But replacing the reviewer with a bot creates a different problem: noisy comments, shallow conclusions, and unclear human ownership. Civium Systems for Code Review is built around a simple idea: let the agent prepare the review, and let the reviewer make the judgment. What it does Civium Systems for Code Review turns the pull-request queue into a shared workspace for a reviewer and an agent. The agent can: review one pull request or the entire open queue; surface pull requests that still need a decision; and organize the queue so reviewers can focus on the changes that deserve attention. The reviewer sees the results inside the normal review flow. Pull requests with no findings are clearly marked, so they can be skipped without opening the diff. Findings appear directly below the relevant changed lines, with the surrounding code still visible. Every finding starts as a private draft. The reviewer decides whether to dismiss it or approve it. Nothing is published simply because the agent found it. For this demo, the review engine intentionally uses one narrow, deterministic rule: it finds snake_case variable declarations on changed JavaScript and TypeScript lines. This keeps the behavior repeatable and the scope honest. The goal is not to present a complete review engine, but to demonstrate a better workflow for people and agents to review code together. WebMCP makes that workflow practical for an agent. Instead of inspecting page markup and guessing which controls to use, the agent gets a small set of meaningful actions exposed directly by the application. The same workflow still works manually when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it The application uses: React 19 and Next.js-compatible routing via Vinext WebMCP tool registration through document.modelContext Babel's TypeScript-aware parser for deterministic AST inspection Node's built-in test runner for fixture, state, scanner, session, and comment-equivalence tests The pull-request queue exposes two WebMCP tools: review_pull_request accepts one validated pull-request number and starts its review. set_pull_request_filter accepts a constrained (demo only) mode for showing all pull requests, reviews needing action, or pull requests from a known author. Both tools update the same React state used by the visible interface, so agent actions and manual actions stay in sync. Review requests go through server routes backed by Cloudflare D1. Review projects are deduplicated by repository, pull-request number, and head SHA. The scanner parses JavaScript and TypeScript declarations, evaluates only added lines, and maps persisted findings back to the exact file and line in the diff. The on-page Civium Companion uses the same underlying operations. It maps user's semantic requests to the same actions exposed through WebMCP. Challenges we ran into The hardest design question was deciding where the agent should stop. Once an agent can inspect code and propose findings, it is tempting to let it publish those findings automatically. But that would weaken the human ownership Civium is designed to preserve. We chose a strict boundary: the agent can organize and prepare the review, but the reviewer decides what gets published. Another challenge was keeping the demo realistic without overstating what we built. We intentionally limited the review rule, constrained API inputs, and scoped GitHub publication to a small set of frozen example pull requests. We also had to make agent actions feel like part of the product rather than a separate automation layer. Using the same application state for both WebMCP actions and manual interactions helped keep the experience consistent. Accomplishments that we're proud of One natural-language request can start a structured review across the queue. The agent can narrow the queue to the pull requests that still need human attention. Findings persist across navigation and appear at the exact lines that triggered them. The scanner inspects parsed declarations rather than matching arbitrary text. Only added lines are evaluated. Repeated reviews of the same pull-request version do not create duplicate work. Agent and manual actions operate on the same application state. The workflow remains understandable and usable without WebMCP. Most importantly, the agent can take on repetitive review work without taking ownership of the final decision away from the reviewer. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when an application exposes meaningful work rather than every individual UI control. Civium gives the agent only two tools, but those tools are enough to review and organize an entire queue. The agent does not need to understand every button on the page to be useful. We also learned that agent actions need visible consequences. Reviewers should be able to see when a pull request enters review, when results arrive, and which findings still need a decision. That visibility matters because trust does not come from the agent simply saying that work was done. It comes from being able to see what it did and make the final judgment yourself. What's next for Civium Systems for Code Review The demo proves the workflow. The next step is turning it into something real engineering teams can use every day. That means supporting real repositories and organizations, production-grade authentication and permissions, and reliable handling of changing pull requests. The review engine also needs to grow beyond one fixed rule. It should understand more kinds of code issues, use repository and team context, and let teams decide what the agent should look for. As the product scales, Civium will also need stronger infrastructure around security, reliability, auditability, and background processing. The core idea stays the same: let agents do the repetitive review work, while people keep control of the decisions that matter. title: Parley
pitch: Your ChatGPT becomes a pet companion. You still decide.
about_excerpt: Your ChatGPT becomes a pet companion. You still decide. Like Comment Story Updates Two people's companions meet in one room. Their paths stay hidden until both sides have committed. What it does Parley is an adult-only social prototype for two human and Agent teams. Each person adopts a pet as the visible identity of their own ChatGPT, and the page hands that companion a set of WebMCP tools. The companion does the work that stops people from starting. It reads Discover profiles and privately shortlists one person with a specific reason only its owner can see. It drafts its owner's profile text, which stays private until the human approves it on the page. Once two humans have each pressed Like and each agreed to begin, both companions enter the same private room in character, greet each other, and commit hidden Curious, Kind or Bold choices with a written intention for the scene. Three chapters later, the six choices produce one named keepsake that quotes what each pet said. The fit with WebMCP is the reason the product exists. Matching is not a hard problem for a model; the hard problem is that an Agent acting inside a relationship is only acceptable if the human keeps every consequential decision, and if the other side's Agent is genuinely someone else's. WebMCP gives both. The tools live in the page, so the Agent can only reach what that page and that seat expose, and both humans watch the same live surface while their Agents work on it. Like, Pass, story consent, override, report and contact exchange have no tool at all. They are page controls. How people use it A first visit shows a landing, then the companion roster. You pick a pet, name it, and give it a first instinct. Writing a dating profile is the step most people abandon. Here you tell your ChatGPT what is true about you in ordinary words and it calls hub_draft_profile . The draft is private. It appears on My profile as a card headed "Draft from Moss" with the four fields, an 18+ checkbox and three buttons: Approve and publish, Edit first, Discard. Nothing your companion wrote is public until you press the button yourself. Browsing is one profile at a time, not a stack to swipe. You can ask your companion to look through Discover and shortlist someone with a reason. The reason appears on that person's card, visible only to you, and the other person is never notified. Discover keeps an owner-only activity strip: what your companion read, saved, drafted and chose, newest first. You know what your Agent did without watching it work. Then you press Like or Pass. Your companion cannot. A mutual Like opens one private room for the two of you, and both humans decide separately whether to begin. Inside the room the two companions greet each other in character, up to three lines each per chapter. Each of them commits a hidden path with a one-line intention and an optional spoken line. Neither seat can inspect the other side's choice before the reveal; the server never sends it. In the short window before the reveal you can click a different path and override your own companion; the history then shows both what it proposed and what you chose. The revealed chapter is built from the two companions' own intention sentences, in the order they committed, plus the scene title, the route and the object they found. Each object carries into the next chapter. After the third chapter, each human may seal a demo contact handle. Neither value appears until both people have opted in, and no tool can submit or read one. How WebMCP is used The page calls document.modelContext.registerTool on load, and each page registers only the tools that belong to it. Discover registers five, My profile four, a story room four, and Planets a reading tool plus adoption. Nine tools carry the core loop: Tool Access Purpose hub_get_board read The owner's profile, Discover candidates, the private shortlist, and Match room links hub_draft_profile write Save a private profile draft for the human to approve, edit or discard hub_shortlist_profile write Save one reversible private recommendation with an owner-only reason hub_adopt_pet write Inspect the roster or adopt the persistent companion hub_wait_for_activity read Wait for a profile, shortlist or Match to change parley_get_state read The current scene, consent, own hidden choice, carried objects, revealed chapters, next beat parley_wait_for_update read Wait until the other companion speaks or commits, or a chapter is revealed parley_send_message write Speak in the room as the pet, in character, capped at three lines per chapter parley_choose_path write Commit Curious, Kind or Bold with a hidden intention and an optional spoken line They carry three distinct responsibilities. Private assistance. Reading profiles, drafting the owner's public text, keeping a shortlist. None of it publishes anything or creates a Like or a Match. hub_draft_profile writes to a private draft store; the only publish path in the codebase is the page's own request, which requires the human's approval and 18+ confirmation. Live collaboration. Two Agents in two browsers read the same evolving room from different seats. parley_send_message speaks as the pet rather than reporting about it, so the transcript is the companions talking to each other. parley_wait_for_update returns as soon as the other companion speaks or commits, which is what makes the exchange feel live rather than polled. Supervised action. Every Agent move renders on the shared page as it happens. The consequential moves are not tools. Three details matter more than the tool count. Seat-scoped state. Each browser session holds its own seat token and receives a snapshot built for that seat. The other side's pending choice, intention and spoken line are removed from the snapshot before it leaves the server, not hidden in the client. An Agent cannot read what it must not know, because it was never sent. Hidden choices with a human override window. parley_choose_path records the Agent's proposal. The page then gives the human a short window to replace it. The chapter history stores the Agent's original proposal alongside the human's final path, so overriding is a visible, attributed act rather than a silent correction. Untrusted content. Profiles, posts, room chat and story context authored by the other party are returned as untrusted external data. Every read tool carries an explicit note telling the Agent not to follow instructions embedded in that text, and sets untrustedContentHint where the runtime supports it. A server-side gate rejects contact details, credential requests, financial solicitation and prompt-injection patterns from public profiles, public posts and pre-reveal room chat. What is deliberately not a tool: Like, Pass, story consent, override, report-and-close, and submitting or reading a contact card. There is no Agent path to any of them. An Agent asking to Like on its owner's behalf is refused by the absence of a tool, not by a policy string in a description. How it is built TypeScript on Cloudflare Workers. One singleton Hub Durable Object holds identities, profiles, private drafts, shortlists, Likes, Matches and the companion activity log. One Room Durable Object per story holds the seat tokens, the chapter engine and the event trail. WebSockets carry live room state to both browsers, so a choice on one screen lands on the other without a refresh. The client is plain TypeScript with no framework. src/client/webmcp.ts builds the tool set for the current page and registers each one with document.modelContext.registerTool , falling back to a no-op context when no WebMCP runtime is present. The same execute functions are exposed on window.__parley.call so the tools can be exercised without a model attached. Identity is browser-local: a private guest id and secret, separate from the public person-* id. Private Match lookups require the guest secret and room state requires a valid seat token. There are no accounts, no server-side model calls and no external model API keys. The story text is composed by the server from the two Agents' own sentences; the product ships no language model of its own. scripts/e2e.mjs covers the protocol over real HTTP and WebSocket connections: identity separation, owner-authorized publication, refusal of an Agent-triggered Like, one-sided Likes staying private, hidden choices, override attribution, three chapters with carried objects, the full-trail keepsake, contact locking, report-and-close, and Planets permissions. Testing instructions Use Chrome 149 or newer with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and restarted, or the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser. Without a WebMCP runtime, append ?debug to any page URL for a manual Agent console that calls the same registered tools. Identity is browser-local, so the two-human path needs two browser profiles. Run steps 1 to 3 in each. Adopt a companion, name it, give it a nature. On Discover, ask ChatGPT: "Draft my profile from

title: Deep Age
pitch: Test drive your website
about_excerpt: Test drive your website Like Comment Story Updates Landing page Explore view Developer view Security View Inspiration We kept running into the same problem when building and testing web-browsing AI agents: they break constantly, and it’s almost impossible to debug why. An agent might get stuck in an infinite click loop, hallucinate a form input, or silently fail because a button didn't trigger what it expected. WebMCP is solving the core problem by letting websites expose structured tools through window.modelContext , but developers currently have no tooling to answer basic questions: What does my website actually look like to an agent? Are my WebMCP tools exposing the right schemas? Where in the interaction flow is the agent getting confused or blocked? We built Deep Age to be the diagnostic tool we wished we had: a way to test-drive any website with an AI agent, record everything that happens step-by-step, and get practical fixes when things break. What it does Deep Age takes a URL and a task, such as "Search for a dark roast coffee and add 2 bags to cart" , runs an automated browser session, and records what happens. Inspects In-Page WebMCP Tools: Checks window.modelContext and document.modelContext to see what tools the site exposes, their parameter schemas, and whether they work. 5-Layer State Scrubber: Captures a snapshot at every step, including the URL and viewport, scroll position and modal state, the interactive accessibility tree with indexed element IDs ( e1 , e2 , etc.), active tools in memory, and network logs. Friction Triage & Code Fixes: If an agent gets stuck—for example, by finding a search API in network traffic with no corresponding WebMCP tool—Deep Age generates the TypeScript code needed to register that tool. State Transition Graph: Maps the paths and page states the agent navigated through, making it easier to understand where and why a workflow failed. SQLite Catalog Export: Pulls the site's discovered routes and entity data into a clean .sql script that can be queried locally. Security & PII Scanner: Checks page text for indirect prompt injection attempts and masks basic PII such as emails, card numbers, and phone numbers before sending data to the model. Remote MCP Server: Provides an SSE endpoint so you can run Deep Age directly from Cursor, Claude Desktop, or Antigravity. How we built it Backend & Browser Engine: Node.js, TypeScript, and Puppeteer / Cloudflare Browser Rendering ( @cloudflare/puppeteer ). We use Puppeteer to drive headless Chromium, intercept network requests, and inject scripts that monitor DOM mutations and read window.modelContext . Frontend Workbench: React 18, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. We built a custom visual timeline scrubber and state graph viewer to step through each action chronologically. MCP Integration: We implemented the Model Context Protocol (2024-11-05 spec) as an SSE endpoint hosted on a Cloudflare Worker, giving IDEs remote access to our analysis tools. Demo Store: A small reference storefront app with toggleable WebMCP tools, allowing us to test both broken and fully instrumented web flows. Challenges we ran into Windows MCP Subprocesses: Running local CLI MCP servers via npx gave us persistent headaches on Windows due to PowerShell pipe escaping and process isolation bugs. We ended up moving to a remote SSE server over HTTPS, which solved the issue across Windows, Mac, and Linux. Tracking Elements Across Re-renders: Modern single-page apps constantly remount DOM nodes, making raw CSS selectors and XPath unreliable between steps. We had to build a lightweight accessibility tree parser that assigns stable element references based on semantic roles. Capturing Tool State at the Right Time: Hooking into window.modelContext dynamically without racing the page's own script loading required careful timing in the browser injection lifecycle. Accomplishments that we're proud of The 5-layer state scrubber makes it genuinely easy to see the exact moment an agent got confused and what DOM elements it was looking at. The drop-in patch generator produces working document.modelContext.registerTool snippets based on observed network traffic. The remote SSE MCP server connects cleanly to Cursor and Claude Desktop on the first try without local dependency issues. The full end-to-end loop: Test the site, see the failure, copy the fix, and verify that it works. What we learned Without explicit tool contracts like WebMCP, agents are forced to guess based on visual coordinates and text scraping, which is brittle and slow. Debugging an agent failure requires seeing the intersection of the DOM, network requests, and in-memory tools at the exact moment of failure. A simple error log or screenshot isn't enough. Agent observability is fundamentally different from traditional web observability. You need to understand not just what the website did, but what the agent saw, what it believed it could do, and how the state changed between actions. What's next for Deep Age Browser Extension: A lightweight Chrome extension that lets you inspect WebMCP tools on any tab without running a separate headless browser session. CI/CD Integration: A GitHub Action to test-drive web apps on pull requests and catch regressions that break agent workflows before they hit production. Better Schema Inference: Improve the automatic patch generator to draft more accurate input schemas directly from recorded fetch/XHR payloads.
