title: LaunchPad
pitch: An evidence factory where browser agents research, challenge, and trace one defensible solution while humans retain control of sensitive decisions.
about_excerpt: An evidence factory where browser agents research, challenge, and trace one defensible solution while humans retain control of sensitive decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Short summary LaunchPad turns one messy problem into one evidence-backed solution. A WebMCP-capable browser agent works inside the same live workspace as the human: it reads the current state, researches evidence, closes explicit gaps, tests counterfactual evidence policies, preserves counter-signals, and traces every recommendation component back to its source. Human consent remains mandatory for evidence acceptance, finalization, and private-data export. What it does Most research agents end with a persuasive answer. LaunchPad ends with an auditable decision. A person enters a real product or business problem. LaunchPad plans the research, collects and validates sources, extracts atomic findings, preserves counter-evidence, synthesizes mechanisms, generates candidate solutions, stress-tests them, and returns one recommendation with a concrete validation plan. The result includes the full lineage from each proposed feature to the insight, finding, and source that supports it. The interface is a live production line rather than a chat transcript. The human can see the current stage, the evidence ledger, the selected candidate, the gaps that remain, and every workspace version transition. The agent operates that exact workspace through WebMCP instead of copying context into a separate assistant conversation. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This workflow depends on state that only the current page truly knows: the active problem brief, research stage, current evidence, privacy scope, policy, selected candidate, stale-version boundary, and consent status. A conventional chatbot must ask the user to paste that context, risks acting on an old snapshot, and cannot prove that its answer matches what the page displays. WebMCP makes the browser page an agent-operable evidence environment: The agent discovers only the tools valid for the current workflow stage. Pure read tools expose live state, gaps, candidate structure, proof traces, and previews without mutating anything. Mutation tools return compact receipts with before/after workspace versions, modified IDs, recovery guidance, and useful next operations. Browser-found evidence enters atomically with provenance, retrieval time, evidence lane, caveat, and public/private scope. Policy comparison answers questions such as “What changes if we exclude community sources or require two independent sources?” without modifying the ledger. Apply and rollback make policy effects visible and reversible. Evidence review, finalization, and private export pause at visible human-consent dialogs bound to exact finding IDs and the current workspace version. A stale agent call fails safely instead of silently overwriting newer human work. The result is not “an AI button.” It is a long-running human-agent collaboration with live shared state, explicit authority boundaries, recoverable operations, and proof that survives the final answer. What people and agents can do together now Before LaunchPad, a researcher could ask an agent to browse, then manually move citations into a document, reconcile contradictions, rerun the analysis under a stricter policy, and hope the final recommendation still matched the evidence. That process loses provenance and makes it hard to tell which decision changed and why. With LaunchPad, the human sets the mission and retains responsibility while the agent performs the high-volume work: Read the exact live state and identify the next evidence gap. Search different evidence lanes and ingest a provenance-rich batch. Preserve negative or contradictory evidence instead of optimizing it away. Compare a stricter policy as a pure preview. Apply or roll back that policy and see the candidate ranking change on the same page. Ask for human approval before committing sensitive judgments. Trace any final feature through component → insight → finding → source. Export a public-safe blueprint that automatically excludes private evidence. Humans supply intent, judgment, and consent. Agents supply breadth, repetition, gap closure, and exact stateful operations. The product makes that division of responsibility visible. How WebMCP is implemented LaunchPad registers a stage-aware catalog through document.modelContext.registerTool . The catalog grows and contracts as the workspace moves through planning, research, evidence review, synthesis, ideation, stress testing, and finalization. The full implementation exposes 22 tools, including: get_foundry_state , get_evidence_gaps , inspect_candidate , and trace_evidence for pure inspection; plan_research , search_sources , ingest_evidence_batch , extract_findings , synthesize_insights , and generate_idea_candidates for the evidence workflow; compare_evidence_policy , apply_evidence_policy , and rollback behavior for reversible counterfactual analysis; review_evidence_with_consent , finalize_blueprint_with_consent , and export_blueprint_with_consent for human-authorized commits; preview_finalization and preview_export so an agent can inspect the consequence before requesting consent. Schemas reject undeclared fields. Pure reads carry read-only hints. Evidence-returning tools mark untrusted content. Registration is asynchronous and abortable, and the UI reports readiness only after every stage-valid tool has registered. Receipts are capped so the agent gets the information needed for its next move without flooding context. The same TypeScript domain service owns page interactions and WebMCP calls, so the browser agent cannot drift into a hidden parallel workflow. State changes use optimistic workspace versions. Connected evidence retains its origin and privacy scope. Public export is generated from the same graph but omits private evidence by construction. Demonstrated WebMCP journey The final public build was exercised inside ChatGPT’s in-app browser against the exact judging URL. The browser discovered the 22-tool stage-aware catalog and completed 26 calls from workspace version 1 to version 19: six evidence lanes searched; nine findings extracted, including a retained caution; human evidence review completed; five insights and three candidates generated; a stricter evidence policy compared, applied, and rolled back; the selected candidate inspected and stress-tested; a four-hop proof path traced; finalization previewed and approved; a public-safe Markdown blueprint exported. The winning candidate in this reproducible mission was Admin Guild , supported by eight findings and one caution, with 100% component coverage. The final reload preserved the finalized workspace, showed the completed run state, and produced zero browser console errors. The exact receipts are recorded in artifacts/demo/webmcp-journey.json . What was added during the submission period LaunchPad is an existing project that was materially rebuilt for the WebMCP Challenge after August 25, 2026. The hackathon work transformed an early agent surface into a WebMCP-native evidence system: expanded the catalog from 17 general tools to 22 stage-aware tools; removed mutation from legacy read behavior and added explicit pure previews; added batch provenance and privacy-aware ingestion; added evidence-gap actions and counter-evidence requirements; added pure policy comparison, non-destructive apply, and rollback; added version-bound consent for review, finalization, and private export; added compact versioned receipts, stale-version recovery, and agent-visible next operations; added an in-page judge mission and WebMCP activity rail; added provider-backed tool-selection evals covering ambiguity, denied consent, stale state, and mid-chain recovery; ran and recorded a 26-call production journey on the final public deployment; added regression coverage for the shared human/WebMCP workflow and finalized UI state. Challenges The hardest problem was not registering many tools; it was designing a trustworthy protocol for a long-running agent workflow. Reads had to be truly pure. Mutations needed version boundaries. Evidence from a browser had to remain untrusted until reviewed. Private evidence could not leak into public export. And the interface had to make all of this understandable to a judge without exposing implementation noise. A second challenge was eval honesty. The configured provider-backed selection harness completed a rich live run in which four cases passed before the provider account began returning HTTP 429. The committed report records the rate limit rather than fabricating a green result. Independent deterministic tests and the complete production browser journey remain green. Accomplishments A complete, coherent product experience rather than a tool-registration demo. 22 stage-aware WebMCP tools sharing one state machine with the visible UI. Human consent and stale-version safety for consequential actions.
video_title: LaunchPad — The Trust Layer for AI Business Decisions | WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: Hi, I'm Casey and I built Launchpad because teams are making expensive decisions with a process that is far more fragile than it looks. Imagine your product lead deciding what to build next. You have customer conversations in one place, market research in another, a handful of promising links, conflicting feedback, and an AI summary that sounds convincing. But you can't tell exactly why it made the recommendation. So the real work begins after the answer. Someone has to check the sources, find what's missing, reconcile contradictions, and defend the decision in the next morning. That is the business problem Launchpad solves. Launchpad is a decision intelligence workspace for product, research, and strategy teams. It turns a messy question into one evidence-backed recommendation that the whole team can actually inspect, challenge, and act on. What makes it different is that it doesn't treat AI as a black box that gives you a polished conclusion. The agents works inside the live workspace, finds the gaps in the evidence, gathers support and counter evidence, and shows exactly what changed. If the team decides to trust only recent public sources or raise the standard for corroboration, Launchpad can show how that policy changes the recommendation before anyone commits to it. And when someone asks, "Why are we building this feature?" Launchpad can trace that decision all the way back to the insight, finding, and original source. This is what companies would pay for, not another AI answer, but faster decisions that are still defensible. Less time stitching research together. Less rework when someone challenges the logic. More confidence when a team needs to put real money, engineering time, and reputation behind a choice. WebMCP is what makes that collaboration real. The agent is just the same live browser context the team sees, while people keep control of sensitive evidence, policy changes, and final approval. We start with product and strategy teams, where one wrong bet can cost months. But the bigger opportunity is becoming the trust layer between AI research and real business decisions. Launchpad doesn't just help teams move faster. It helps them know what they can stand behind. Thank you.

title: TagTitan Listing Studio
pitch: A listing studio for print-on-demand sellers where the agent presses the same buttons you do, in the same grid, with every action visible and overridable.
about_excerpt: A listing studio for print-on-demand sellers where the agent presses the same buttons you do, in the same grid, with every action visible and overridable. Like Comment Story Updates The grid, and the activity log that stamps every action as agent or human. Inspiration A print-on-demand seller with forty designs does the same chore forty times, multiplied by every marketplace they sell on. Etsy allows a 140 character title and 13 tags. Amazon Merch allows 60 characters, no price claims, and two bullets. Redbubble wants 15 tags of up to 30 characters each. The work is not creative. It is compliance, and it eats a day. Handing it to an AI has always meant choosing between two bad options. Either the agent described what to write and the seller pasted forty listings by hand, or the seller handed an opaque tool their credentials and hoped. One is dictation. The other is abdication. Neither is collaboration. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP changes the shape of the problem, because the tools live on the page the seller is already looking at. The studio is a grid. Designs down the side, marketplaces across the top, one listing per square. It publishes twelve tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Ask the agent to fill the grid and the squares fill in front of you. Every field stays editable. Every action, yours or the agent's, lands in the same activity log stamped with who did it. The design rule the whole project follows is that a tool is never a private back door . Each one is a thin wrapper over an action that a button in the interface also calls. One store, one set of mutations, one log. buttons (app.js) ---+ +---> studio.js ---> live TagTitan API tools (webmcp.js) --+ | +---> one grid, one activity log That symmetry is what makes the collaboration legible. The agent cannot do anything the seller cannot see, undo, or do themselves. How it creates a better user experience The seller never leaves the page, never pastes anything, and never loses sight of what was done on their behalf. They can interrupt at any square. A batch that would have been forty context switches becomes one instruction and a grid they supervise. It also degrades honestly. With no agent connected the studio is a complete tool you can drive by hand, and the header states plainly which mode you are in. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Supervised bulk work. "Take all four designs, do Etsy and Redbubble, premium voice." The agent calls the same actions the buttons call, and the seller watches each square resolve, fixing anything wrong in place. A critique loop against a real scorer. The agent calls grade_listing , reads back a 0 to 100 score broken into title, tags, description and readability with concrete fixes, then calls update_listing to apply one. It checks its own work against the same grader the seller sees. Marketplace rules as shared context. list_marketplaces returns live character and tag limits for 18 marketplaces, so the agent reasons about real constraints instead of guessing. Correction without restarting. "The Etsy title is too generic, make it about cottagecore." One field changes. Nothing else regenerates and no context is lost. Knowing when to stop and ask. account_status reports remaining quota, so before a large batch the agent can tell the seller to sign in rather than burning what is left. How we built it The front end is deliberately plain: no build step, no framework, no dependencies. studio.js holds all state and every mutation. app.js renders it and wires the buttons. webmcp.js registers the tools. The last two are peers, and neither can reach past the store. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "generate_listings", description: "Write full listings for products across the selected marketplaces...", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { /* ... */ } }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); Every execute is wrapped so a thrown error becomes a readable tool error rather than a crash, and each call writes to the shared activity log before returning. The listing engine behind it is the live TagTitan API, a shipped commercial product, so the output is what real sellers actually publish rather than demo filler. The twelve tools Tool What it does read_studio Full state: products, marketplaces, listing status, scores account_status Whether the seller is signed in and how much quota remains list_marketplaces 18 marketplaces with live title, tag and content limits add_product Add a design as a new row remove_product Drop a row and its listings set_marketplaces Choose which marketplaces are columns set_tone Set the brand voice for everything generated after suggest_keywords Real buyer search phrases for a seed term generate_listings Write listings across the grid grade_listing Score a listing 0 to 100 and return fixes update_listing Rewrite one field of one listing export_csv Every finished listing as bulk-upload CSV Challenges we ran into The API restricts CORS to an allowlist. Calling it from a new origin returned 400 with no allow header. Rather than widen the allowlist we proxy /api server-side, so the browser only ever makes same-origin requests and the backend needed no change at all. That also let the session cookie ride along without any SameSite juggling. The free tier allows one listing per browser, in total. Cookie tracked, and it silently truncates a multi-marketplace request to a single marketplace. Anyone opening the site cold got one square filled and then a wall, which made the whole studio look broken. Adding sign-in fixed it, and signed in the API writes every marketplace in a single call. The backend sleeps. It runs on a free instance that takes about 23 seconds to wake. A judge whose first click hangs that long assumes the project is broken, so a scheduled function now pings it every ten minutes. What we learned The interesting constraint in WebMCP is not what the agent can do. It is what the human can still see. It would have been easier to give the agent a fast private path to the API and let the UI catch up afterwards. Everything good about this project came from refusing that and making both paths identical. What's next Unifying the studio session with the main TagTitan app, image-driven listings so a design can be dropped straight in, and pushing finished rows to marketplace APIs directly instead of exporting CSV. title: Infinite Canvas — Agent Design Lab
pitch: One WebMCP brief becomes three safe, editable design experiments a person can compare, cancel, promote, and undo.
about_excerpt: One WebMCP brief becomes three safe, editable design experiments a person can compare, cancel, promote, and undo. Like Comment Story Updates Infinite Canvas is a browser-based visual design canvas where people and AI agents inspect, create, and edit the same live document through native WebMCP tools. Problem Visual design applications are built for pointer-and-keyboard interaction. An AI agent approaching the same application usually has to infer state from pixels, guess which controls to click, and repeat brittle UI actions. That makes substantial design work slow, unreliable, and difficult for a person to supervise. Solution For this WebMCP Challenge proof of concept, one agent brief starts three named hypotheses in isolated editable branches. A person can keep working on the original while the lanes run, inspect status and layout checks, cancel a lane, promote one branch only if the source revision is still current, and undo that promotion in one history step. Why WebMCP Visual design is state-heavy and precision-dependent: selections, trees, styles, tokens, pages, and history. The app registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, so an agent operates on the live document model instead of guessing from rendered pixels. The same MobX stores and handlers power both the visible editor and agent calls. What people and agents can do together The person keeps working visually while delegating a bounded exploration task. The agent reads the real selection and tree, starts three hypotheses, and reports progress. The person can compare structured editable branches, cancel work, promote a result, or undo it. A fingerprint-based stale-revision check rejects a completed branch when the person changed the original instead of silently overwriting that work. Implementation The hosted build exposes 54 tools: 34 core canvas tools, 14 design-lab tools, and six experiment tools: start_design_experiment, get_experiment_status, compare_experiment, cancel_experiment_lane, promote_variant, and undo_experiment_commit. Experiment jobs are orchestrated together, while writes to the single editor document are serialized. Operation IDs make retries idempotent; cancellation is cooperative; promotion is atomic and undo-compatible. Live demo Open the public URL and use the judge prompt in the repository README. No login is required. title: VisaFlow: The Adaptive WebMCP Agent
pitch: VisaFlow turns a 55-field visa form into a guided voice conversation. It uses WebMCP to select the right path, derive answers, fill the live application, and flag only what needs review.
about_excerpt: VisaFlow turns a 55-field visa form into a guided voice conversation. It uses WebMCP to select the right path, derive answers, fill the live application, and flag only what needs review. Like Comment Story Updates Application completed Meet VisaFlow WebMCP in action One answer, many fields Inspiration Long forms force people to translate their life story into an unfamiliar sequence of fields. Conditional applications make this worse: users answer questions that may not apply, repeat information across sections, and often discover missing evidence only near the end. We wanted to explore a different future for the web—one where a person explains their situation naturally, an agent connects the details, and the website remains responsible for its own rules and safety constraints. What it does VisaFlow turns a deliberately long 55-field visitor-visa application into a guided voice or text conversation. A user can describe their trip naturally, speak their answers, type them, or attach supporting documents. The agent then: identifies whether the application is for tourism, business, or a family visit; selects the correct funding and prior-travel branches; removes questions that do not apply; extracts multiple supported facts from each answer; calculates transparent derived values such as trip duration; fills reasonable interpretations while clearly flagging them for review; asks one story-shaped follow-up covering several related gaps; shows every WebMCP action and live application progress; and consolidates uncertain and sensitive values into one editable final-review queue. After every applicable field and review item is resolved, the user can finish the fictional application and see a completion receipt. Why WebMCP An LLM alone could generate a possible JSON object, but it would need a hardcoded copy of the form schema, routing rules, and validation logic. Alternatively, it would have to manipulate fragile DOM selectors and click through every conditional page. WebMCP gives the agent a live semantic contract owned by the website. VisaFlow publishes 22 typed tools that let an agent inspect possible routes, select the applicable flow, discover missing requirements, apply structured answers, attach evidence references, calculate derived insights, resolve conflicts, and request human review. WebMCP is not decorative in this project: application changes go through website-owned tool handlers. Every write is validated for route applicability, field type, allowed choices, date ranges, confidence, provenance, and review requirements before it reaches shared application state. This enables something that was previously difficult: a person can tell one coherent story, an agent can connect that story across many conditional fields, and the website can safely accept only the values allowed by its current rules—without page-by-page navigation. Human-agent collaboration The human provides meaning and judgment. The agent extracts, connects, derives, and decides what to ask next. The website validates every action and keeps uncertainty visible. Explicit user statements, document facts, deterministic derivations, and AI proposals remain visibly separate. Sensitive or uncertain values are never silently treated as verified. The user reviews and corrects them once before completing the application. How we built it The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite with a government-service-inspired interface. On page load, VisaFlow registers 22 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . A WebMCP-capable agent can discover these tools at runtime and execute them without knowing the DOM structure. A same-origin Worker endpoint uses the OpenAI Responses API with GPT-5.6 Terra and a strict structured-output schema. Each turn includes the current route, resolved answers, remaining applicable questions, recent conversation history, remembered partial facts, and pending review fields. The LLM returns a plan containing explicit facts, document facts, safe derivations, reviewable proposals, route decisions, and the next question. It never writes application state directly. The client converts the plan into WebMCP calls, and the website validates and applies them. Voice recognition, spoken questions, multilingual interfaces, document extraction, visible WebMCP activity, browser-local drafts, and the completion flow are integrated into one coherent experience. Challenges The hardest problems were preventing the conversation from forgetting previously stated facts, resolving phrases such as “this year,” extracting many useful facts from one answer, and avoiding repeated address questions. We also had to ensure route changes happened before field validation, preserve incomplete facts between turns, batch WebMCP writes safely, distinguish derived values from invented values, and keep document extraction useful without allowing documents to act as instructions. Accomplishments A working 55-field adaptive application rather than a single autofill demo 22 non-trivial WebMCP tools with typed schemas and validation Dynamic application routing with irrelevant-question removal Voice, text, document, and multilingual interaction Visible provenance, derived values, progress, and semantic actions A consolidated final-review experience A gated fictional completion receipt 32 automated tests across domain, WebMCP, and integrated UI behavior What we learned The most important lesson was that an agent should not own a website’s rules. The website should publish capabilities and remain authoritative, while the model focuses on understanding natural language and planning. WebMCP makes that separation possible. It allows an agent to be flexible without making application writes opaque or unsafe. We also learned that conversational form completion works best when the agent asks for coherent parts of a person’s story, rather than disguising several traditional form labels as a chatbot question. What's next Next, we would test VisaFlow with more external WebMCP agents, expand accessibility testing, support additional document formats and application domains, and add encrypted cross-device draft storage. The same architecture could support healthcare enrollment, insurance claims, benefits applications, university admissions, and other conditional workflows. Turn messy launch feedback into evidence-backed product actions with a WebMCP-powered triage workspace.

 After triage, Signal Desk drafts evidence-linked claims and proposes a product-owned follow-up action for review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Behind the Scenes panel showing the 8 WebMCP tools exposed by the page for browser agents. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most WebMCP demos answer "can an agent operate this page?" We wanted to answer the harder question that follows: once an agent can operate your app, what stops it from quietly doing the wrong thing? 

 Product and support teams get launch feedback from everywhere — support tickets, community posts, sales calls, release comments. The hard part is never reading one message. It is finding the repeated pain, proving it with evidence, deciding what product should do next, and being able to show later who decided what. 

 That workflow is a good stress test for agent governance, because every step produces a claim someone will eventually be held to. 

 What it does 

 Signal Desk is a customer-request triage workspace where a human and an agent share one visible surface. 

 The agent can search requests, group them into pain patterns, explain the evidence behind a pattern, draft a customer-impact brief, and propose product-owned actions. What it cannot do is decide. 

 Three properties hold no matter who is driving: 

 
 Every claim is traceable. Each brief claim links back to the specific customer requests supporting it. There are no unsourced assertions. 
 Writes are approval-gated. The agent proposes product actions into a review queue. A human approves before anything is treated as decided. 
 One shared decision log. Human and agent changes land in the same audit trail — what changed, who changed it, when. 
 

 The demo case is an admin import launch: customers import their workspaces successfully, then stall because nobody knows the next required admin step, the owner, or the validation path. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 Signal Desk registers 8 tools on the page, split deliberately between reads and gated writes: 

 
 
 Tool 
 Type 
 
 
 
 search_signals 
 read 
 
 
 explain_evidence 
 read 
 
 
 get_audit_trail 
 read 
 
 
 cluster_signals 
 write 
 
 
 draft_brief 
 write 
 
 
 propose_actions 
 write — lands in an approval queue, never auto-applied 
 
 
 set_review_state 
 write — records an audit event 
 
 
 reset_demo 
 write 
 
 

 The design decisions that matter: 

 
 Tool calls mutate the same state the UI renders. There is no shadow model. A human watching the screen sees exactly what the agent did, as it happens. 
 Calls are idempotent. Re-running propose_actions or set_review_state does not duplicate proposals or double-apply approvals — important when an agent retries. 
 Writes are separated from decisions. The agent's most consequential tool, propose_actions , deliberately cannot finalize anything. 
 Every state change emits an audit event , tagged by actor, so agent activity is reconstructable after the fact. 
 

 Tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool with a navigator.modelContext fallback. 

 What this enables that was hard before: an agent can run a real multi-step operational workflow inside a business app — not by scraping the DOM or driving synthetic clicks, but through typed tools with schemas — while a human keeps veto power over every consequential write. 

 What makes it useful 

 The interesting claim is not that an agent can triage faster. It is that you can let an agent into a workflow with real consequences and still answer, afterwards, three questions auditors and managers actually ask: 

 
 What did the agent change? 
 What evidence was that based on? 
 Who approved it? 
 

 Most agent integrations cannot answer any of the three. Signal Desk is built so all three are answerable by construction rather than by logging bolted on afterwards. 

 How we built it 

 A lightweight static web app — HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript — with a small Worker wrapper for hosting. Synthetic, public-safe customer-request data; no private accounts, no external services, no local background process. State lives in browser localStorage and is resettable via reset_demo . 

 Deployed as a public HTTPS app on ChatGPT Sites. Full source is on GitHub under the MIT license. 

 It also works without WebMCP. In a browser with no WebMCP host, the app degrades to a normal operator UI, and a Run Triage button exercises the identical workflow locally. The agent path is an enhancement to a product that stands on its own — not a demo that collapses without a special browser. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was resisting the pull toward a technical proof of concept. 

 A WebMCP demo is easy to build as a page with buttons wired to tool handlers. Making it behave like a product meant adding the things that are unglamorous but load-bearing: review states, evidence links, idempotent tool calls so agent retries do not duplicate work, a fallback path for non-WebMCP browsers, and an audit trail that treats human and agent actions as equal citizens. 

 The second challenge was drawing the write boundary in the right place. The first version let the agent apply actions directly, which demoed well and was exactly wrong. Splitting propose_actions from set_review_state — proposal from decision — is what turned it from an automation demo into something you could imagine shipping. 

 What's next 

 
 Real connectors (support inbox, community forum, CRM notes) behind the same evidence contract 
 Per-tool permission scopes, so an operator can grant an agent read and draft access without proposal rights 
 Exportable decision records for teams that need the audit trail outside the app

pitch: Using edge compute resources and WebMCP interface to enable ai agents to manipulate infrastructures on "frontend" monitor.

Like Comment Story Updates 1. explanation of using webmcp in this project(6 tools) 2.1 agent itself build the datacenter 2.2 agent itself build the datacenter 2.3 agent checking building standards and regulation rules 3. agent generate datacenter schema manifest 4. using cli to get 3. agent-generating datacenter schema manifest 5. simulation process 6 in chatgpt desktop, using web mcp to let agent itself(5.6 SOL) build the datacenter 7. in chatgpt desktop final building results/explanation/and certification. Inspiration Durning the process of preparing CCSP, we've learned that data center's real PUE, cooling architecture and physical layout are commercial secrets — yet every certification scheme on earth asks the operator to hand exactly those numbers to an auditor to earn a badge. Also, we happened to be micraft and lego fans. We wanted to remove that trade-off: design a facility in a 3D voxel builder, score it deterministically against 13 real international standards, and publish only the verdict — never the design — via a zero-knowledge proof. Then WebMCP arrived and raised a second, sharper question: if an AI agent can operate your builder, how much is it allowed to know? An agent is a third party in every sense that matters — it is a language model, it keeps transcripts, and it is not the person who drew the layout. That made our privacy problem and the agent problem the same problem, and this hackathon the natural place to solve it. What it does Build — a 32×8×32 voxel grid, 47 block types across structure, site, power, cooling, IT, safety and network. Simulate — SimCity for facilities: NPCs walk the floor, live power/thermal gauges, deterministic staffing / OPEX / carbon / water projections. Score — 37 rules, every one citing a real standard (Uptime Tier I–IV, TIA-942-C, EN 50600, ASHRAE TC 9.9, NFPA 75/76/855, ISO/IEC 27001, EU EED, and more). Six axes roll into one score: $$S = 0.20 \cdot \text{redundancy} + 0.20 \cdot \text{power} + 0.15 \cdot \text{cooling} + 0.15 \cdot \text{safety} + 0.15 \cdot \text{efficiency} + 0.15 \cdot \text{security}$$ Prove — a real Noir + Barretenberg (UltraHonk) proof generated in the browser in ~1.4 s, asserting one sentence and nothing more: "I know a design whose digest is D, which rule pack V scored ≥ threshold T." Mint — the certificate becomes a Soulbound ERC-721 on Polygon / Ethereum / BSC / Base / Arbitrum / Optimism. WebMCP — the builder page registers 6 tools on document.modelContext , so an agent sitting next to the page operates the live 3D builder : the same Zustand actions a mouse click calls, the same placement validation, the same undo stack.
